title: Advantage Distillation in Paired-State Quantum Key Distribution
abstract: We investigate advantage distillation for paired-state Loop-Back quantum key distribution, with a fixed optical station serving a lightweight portable terminal. Alice prepares two polarization-encoded pulses, Bob selects and applies a polarization filter to each pulse, and Alice infers his selections from the returned detection pattern. The proposed advantage-distillation step selects consistent blocks of three two-bit records using two independent public parity checks on a minimal connected graph. The closing edge of a parity polygon is shown to be redundant: any spanning tree of the same vertices has the same acceptance set. We derive exact acceptance probabilities, residual-error laws, and retention rates. Under independent bit errors, the three-record filter reduces the leading error term from e to e^2, while its cost in discarded records and public information is accounted for explicitly. A modular security theorem bounds the additional guessing advantage available to an adversary after syndrome disclosure and block acceptance, including arbitrary quantum side information. We also evaluate a specified single-photon passive-tap optical channel, obtaining a positive conditional entropy bound and exact accepted-block security quantities. This parity-based advantage-distillation step detects discrepancies by postselection; it does not correct individual errors and is intended to precede conventional reconciliation. The architecture suggests two further directions: hybrid filtering and reconciliation, and key establishment between portable users accessing a shared quantum station.
one_liner: A three-record parity filter suppresses first-order bit errors in paired-state loop-back QKD while explicitly accounting for leakage and retention.
why_it_matters: The protocol strengthens a lightweight portable-terminal QKD architecture and provides security bounds that include syndrome disclosure, postselection, and quantum side information.
detailed_summary: The scheme filters blocks of three two-bit records using two independent public parity checks, with any spanning tree giving the same acceptance set as the corresponding parity polygon. For independent bit errors, acceptance changes the leading residual-error contribution from order e to order e² while explicitly tracking discarded data and public leakage. A modular theorem bounds Eve's added guessing advantage with arbitrary quantum side information, and a passive-tap single-photon channel is evaluated as a concrete optical case.
main_result: The proposed advantage-distillation filter quadratically suppresses the leading independent bit-error term and yields exact retention, residual-error, and security quantities.
application_angle: It could improve key establishment for portable users connected to a shared fixed quantum station before conventional error reconciliation begins.

title: Long-distance quantum secure direct communication with Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill qubits
abstract: The Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code possesses a lattice periodic structure that enables the effective correction of small displacement errors induced by noise in phase space, which is indispensable for quantum computation. The GKP code was also used to construct a long-distance entanglement channel in quantum repeaters and distribute random keys in quantum key distribution (QKD). Using GKP encoding, we propose a quantum secure direct communication (QSDC) protocol that not only transmits the secret message directly, but also helps protect the safety of communication personnel. The exponential attenuation loss of photons can be overcome by the third-generation quantum repeater. Numerical simulation results demonstrate that secure transmission distance exceeding 1000 km is achievable with a 23 dB squeezing level. Furthermore, we establish a cost-based optimization framework to characterize the trade-off among secure communication distance, secrecy capacity, and repeater resources, enabling optimized repeater deployment and providing a systematic design strategy for scalable quantum repeater architectures. The results demonstrate the potential of combining GKP error correction for long-distance QSDC and quantum networks.
one_liner: GKP-encoded QSDC with third-generation repeaters is numerically projected to exceed 1000 km at 23 dB squeezing.
why_it_matters: It connects bosonic error correction with direct secure messaging and introduces resource optimization for designing scalable long-distance repeater networks.
detailed_summary: The proposed protocol encodes quantum secure direct communication in Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill states, using their lattice structure to correct small phase-space displacement errors. Third-generation repeaters are invoked to overcome exponential photon attenuation, with simulations predicting secure distances beyond 1000 km at 23 dB squeezing. A cost-based framework jointly optimizes distance, secrecy capacity, and repeater resources.
platform_or_system: GKP bosonic qubits in quantum repeater links
main_result: Numerical modeling predicts secure direct communication beyond 1000 km with 23 dB GKP squeezing and optimized repeater placement.
application_angle: The framework offers a design route for long-haul quantum networks that deliver confidential messages directly rather than only distributing keys.

title: Rapid high-purity loading of barium ion via relayed selectivity from naturally abundant source
abstract: Trapped ions is one of the promising platforms for realizing quantum information processing and quantum simulation. Selective and rapid loading of a specific isotope lays the critical foundation for such purpose particularly when scaling up the system size. Here we demonstrate a new method for rapid isotope-selective loading of $^{137}\mathrm{Ba}^{+}$ or $^{135}\mathrm{Ba}^{+}$, two types of promising ion qubits, from naturally abundant source using a three-step, ultraviolet-free photoionization scheme. Neutral atoms are selected on the narrow 791 nm $6s^2\,{}^1S_0\rightarrow6s6p\,{}^3P_1^o$ transition, resonantly transferred at 554 nm to $6s6d\,{}^3D_1$, and ionized using an existing 532 nm Raman beam. A spectral-overlap analysis based on isotope and hyperfine shifts shows relayed selectivity that the second step can further suppress undesired-isotope excitation and no contaminant ion is detected during our entire experiment. Besides, the resonant drive of the second step excitation yields a prominent loading rate of the selected species. This strategy using multi-step excitations to establish relayed selectivity can be extended to high-purity loading of other species of ions.
one_liner: A UV-free three-step photoionization sequence rapidly loads high-purity 137Ba+ or 135Ba+ qubits from a natural-abundance source.
why_it_matters: Fast, isotope-selective loading without enriched sources or ultraviolet lasers can simplify scaling and maintenance of barium-ion quantum processors.
detailed_summary: Neutral barium is first selected on the narrow 791 nm transition, transferred resonantly at 554 nm, and ionized with an existing 532 nm Raman beam. Isotope and hyperfine shifts provide relayed selectivity, allowing the second excitation step to further reject unwanted isotopes. The experiment reports a prominent selected-isotope loading rate and no detected contaminant ions over its duration.
main_result: The three-color scheme rapidly and selectively loads 137Ba+ or 135Ba+ from natural barium with no contaminant ion detected during the experiment.
application_angle: The method can reduce loading overhead in scaled trapped-ion systems and may generalize to high-purity preparation of other ion species.

title: A Universal Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Architecture with Globally Driven Atom Arrays
abstract: Scalable quantum computation requires reconciling programmability with simple, high-fidelity control. Here, we propose a universal fault-tolerant architecture using globally driven dual-species atom arrays. In a hybrid neutral-atom system, interspecies Rydberg interactions enable qubit addressability without locally addressed quantum gates. We construct a universal native instruction set, Global Rydberg Atom Instruction Language (GRAIL), and show that crosstalk errors can be suppressed to the $10^{-4}$ level. We compile surface-code error correction and magic state cultivation into GRAIL, and parallelize the compilation to suppress crosstalk. Under a hardware-inferred circuit-level noise model, we obtain an error-correction threshold of $1.43\%$ for the resulting quantum memory and a logical error rate below $10^{-9}$ for magic states cultivated at an experimentally accessible Rydberg Rabi frequency. By replacing local gate addressing with atom-mediated selectivity, this architecture removes the associated calibration requirements, offering a route to simpler control for large-scale fault-tolerant neutral-atom computation.
one_liner: Dual-species neutral-atom arrays use global Rydberg drives and atom-mediated selectivity to support universal fault-tolerant computation.
why_it_matters: Eliminating locally addressed gates could sharply reduce calibration complexity while retaining surface-code operation and high-quality magic states.
detailed_summary: The architecture combines two atomic species so that interspecies Rydberg interactions provide effective qubit selectivity under global driving. Its GRAIL instruction set is compiled for surface-code error correction and magic-state cultivation, with parallel scheduling used to limit crosstalk. Simulations under a hardware-inferred circuit noise model give a 1.43% memory threshold, crosstalk near 10^-4, and cultivated magic-state logical error below 10^-9 at an accessible Rydberg Rabi frequency.
main_result: The compiled architecture achieves a simulated 1.43% error-correction threshold and below-10^-9 cultivated magic-state error without locally addressed gates.
application_angle: It offers a potentially simpler control stack for scaling neutral-atom processors toward universal fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Modular and Looping Quantum Photonic Processing Unit for Quantum Computing
abstract: Photonic processors are emerging as promising platforms in the race towards the realization of practical universal quantum computers. Several architectures with universal capabilities have been proposed for their implementation via a photonic platform, each with their own set of benefits and drawbacks. In this work we propose an architecture for a universal photonic quantum computer. The proposed architecture is modular, allowing for a high degree of flexibility and scalability, and relies on a loop-based structure, significantly reducing the number of physical components required to implement it experimentally. We prove that our architecture is universal, deterministic, and compatible with the quantum circuital model, as well as reprogrammable and capable of adaptive measurements. Furthermore, we showcase its functioning via numerical simulation on specific examples, by using machine learning techniques on a set of fundamental linear and nonlinear optical components to obtain some of the building blocks used in the architecture. The obtained results can be used to highlight the benefits and the drawbacks of the proposed architecture, as well as the route for future developments towards its physical implementation.
one_liner: A modular loop-based photonic processor architecture is shown theoretically to be deterministic, universal, reprogrammable, and adaptive.
why_it_matters: Loop reuse can reduce optical component count, offering a more compact route to flexible circuit-model photonic quantum processors.
detailed_summary: The proposed photonic processing unit reuses a loop-based optical structure within modular blocks to reduce the number of physical components. The authors prove compatibility with deterministic universal circuit-model computation, including reprogramming and adaptive measurements. Numerical examples use machine-learning-designed linear and nonlinear optical components to explore candidate building blocks, but physical implementation remains future work.
main_result: The study establishes theoretical universality and deterministic adaptive operation, supported by numerical simulations of representative optical building blocks.
application_angle: If experimentally realized, the design could enable scalable photonic quantum computers with fewer duplicated optical components and flexible module replacement.

title: Silicon and silicon nitride photonic ring resonator arrays for photonic trimming metrology
abstract: Proposed silicon on silicon oxide 4x4 matrix multiplier for use in refractive index measurements, based on the Advanced Micro Foundry deep ultraviolet process. Agreement between simulated spectra and analytic design spectra demonstrate the intended performance of the components given a 1550 nm wavelength spectrum analysis. Intended purpose of the design includes optical damage analysis of the cladding, and photonic chip refractive index analysis following sub-threshold laser ablation. Femtosecond multi-shot tuning of refractive index is not a recommended application, due to round trip-losses causing quality factor and transfer function degradation.
one_liner: A 4×4 silicon photonic ring-resonator matrix is designed for refractive-index and laser-damage metrology around 1550 nm.
why_it_matters: The design targets on-chip measurement of cladding damage and post-ablation refractive-index changes while identifying loss-driven limits on repeated trimming.
detailed_summary: The work proposes a silicon-on-oxide 4×4 matrix multiplier based on an Advanced Micro Foundry deep-ultraviolet process. Simulated 1550 nm spectra agree with analytic design spectra for the intended resonator components. The target measurements are cladding optical-damage assessment and refractive-index characterization after sub-threshold laser ablation; repeated femtosecond trimming is discouraged because round-trip loss degrades quality factor and transfer response.
main_result: Analytic and simulated spectra agree for a 4×4 resonator matrix designed to measure photonic-chip refractive-index changes and cladding damage.
application_angle: The array could serve as an integrated metrology structure for monitoring fabrication, trimming, and laser-processing effects on photonic chips.

title: High Rate Quantum Block Turbo Codes
authors: Jean-Louis de Bougrenet de la Tocnaye
abstract: Quantum Block Turbo Code is an iterative decoding technique for concatenated quantum error correction codes in product form. In this paper, we study new high rate quantum block turbo codes with different constituent codes. We examine the impact of the change of codes parameters and the order of constituent codes on turbo performance.
one_liner: High-rate quantum block turbo codes are evaluated across constituent-code choices, parameter sets, and concatenation orders.
why_it_matters: The study identifies code-design variables that can improve iterative quantum error correction while retaining high coding rates.
detailed_summary: The paper studies high-rate quantum block turbo codes formed from product-style concatenations of quantum constituent codes. It examines how constituent parameters and their ordering affect iterative decoding performance. The work is a coding and performance study rather than a physical hardware demonstration.
main_result: Quantum block turbo-code performance is characterized for multiple constituent codes, parameter choices, and concatenation orders.
application_angle: The results can guide error-correction design for quantum processors and communication systems requiring low redundancy and iterative decoding.

title: X-ray parametric down-conversion probes radiation-induced dynamics in hybrid perovskite MAPbBr3
abstract: We report minute-timescale time-resolved measurements of X-ray parametric down-conversion (PDC) of X-rays into ultraviolet photons in a MAPbBr3 single crystal under continuous irradiation. Despite the known radiation sensitivity of hybrid perovskites and the high photon flux required to detect the intrinsically weak PDC signal, the nonlinear response remains measurable throughout the irradiation sequence. Both PDC and Bragg diffraction exhibit a slow decay consistent with diffusion-driven damage dynamics on timescales reported for bromide-vacancy and proton migration. However, despite their similar decay rates, the PDC and Bragg signals evolve toward markedly different steady states, while an additional fast decay component is observed in the Bragg response but absent in the PDC signal. Density functional theory calculations identify N 2s states of the methylammonium cation as the most likely contributors to the measured PDC response and show that their Fourier component is only weakly affected by bromide-vacancy formation. These results establish nonlinear X-ray diffraction as a channel-selective probe of radiation-induced dynamics and demonstrate that radiation damage can couple differently to nonlinear and linear X-ray responses.
one_liner: X-ray-to-UV parametric down-conversion tracks channel-specific radiation damage in MAPbBr3 over minute timescales.
why_it_matters: The experiment shows that nonlinear X-ray diffraction can isolate material dynamics that conventional Bragg measurements combine or obscure.
detailed_summary: The authors measure X-ray parametric down-conversion into ultraviolet photons from a MAPbBr3 single crystal during continuous irradiation and compare it with Bragg diffraction. Both signals show slow, diffusion-consistent decay, but reach different steady states; Bragg diffraction also contains a fast decay absent from PDC. Density-functional calculations associate the PDC response mainly with methylammonium N 2s states that are comparatively insensitive to bromide vacancies.
main_result: Nonlinear PDC and linear Bragg channels exhibit distinct radiation-damage responses despite similar slow decay rates.
application_angle: Channel-selective X-ray PDC could diagnose defect migration and radiation degradation in sensitive optoelectronic materials.

title: Off-focus detection for SNR enhancement in coherent single-pixel imaging
abstract: Coherent single-pixel imaging (CSPI) enables amplitude- and phase-resolved computational imaging with a single coherent detector, offering particular advantages in spectral regimes where high-performance detector arrays remain unavailable. In conventional Fourier-plane CSPI, the detector is typically placed at the focal point to maximize the collected power. However, this focal position does not necessarily maximize the reconstruction fidelity for image reconstruction in the presence of system nonidealities. Here, we introduce detector position as an additional degree of freedom for CSPI optimization. We show that appropriately selected off-focus Fourier-plane positions can improve reconstruction performance by suppressing fluctuation-sensitive coherent backgrounds while preserving spatially encoded signals. Experimentally, using a programmable liquid-crystal terahertz spatial light modulator and coherent heterodyne detection, we demonstrate improved amplitude and phase reconstruction from selected off-focus channels compared with focal detection. A symmetric off-focus pair with complementary transverse-wave-vector weighting further enhances image fidelity, contrast, and compressive-sampling robustness through coherent channel fusion. These results establish detector-position engineering as a new strategy for enhancing the robustness and information efficiency of CSPI.
one_liner: Off-focus coherent detection and paired-channel fusion improve terahertz single-pixel amplitude and phase imaging.
why_it_matters: Detector-position engineering raises image fidelity and compressive-sampling robustness without requiring a detector array.
detailed_summary: The work treats Fourier-plane detector position as an optimization variable in coherent single-pixel imaging. Experiments combine a programmable liquid-crystal terahertz spatial light modulator with coherent heterodyne detection, showing improved amplitude and phase reconstructions at selected off-focus positions. Fusion of a symmetric off-focus pair provides complementary transverse-wave-vector weighting and further improves contrast, fidelity, and undersampled reconstruction.
main_result: Selected off-focus channels, especially a symmetric fused pair, outperform focal detection in image quality and compressive-sampling robustness.
application_angle: The method can improve coherent imaging in terahertz and other spectral bands where capable focal-plane arrays are scarce.

title: Deploying QKD on the fiber links of the National Quantum Communication Infrastructure in Sweden
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is being deployed across Europe to evaluate its performance and practicality in real-world scenarios. When preparing this deployment, it is important to survey the properties of the fiber links that will be used for the quantum channel, cross-checking them with those of QKD devices, to ensure compatibility and optimal performance. We report here our studies from the Swedish chapter of this endeavor, the National Quantum Communication Infrastructure in Sweden. We focus on procedures to characterize the links and evaluate their suitability for QKD. We relate measurable properties to the key factors that affect the secret key rate using a simplified model that aims at the essence of QKD performance. Finally, we confirm the feasibility of QKD on one of our links by reporting a one-month long successful test.
one_liner: Sweden's quantum-network team develops fiber qualification procedures and validates one link with a month-long QKD trial.
why_it_matters: It connects measurable field-fiber properties to secret-key performance and supplies operational evidence for national QKD deployment.
detailed_summary: The study describes procedures for surveying deployed fiber links and checking their compatibility with QKD equipment in Sweden's national quantum communication infrastructure. A simplified model relates measurable link properties to the main factors governing secret-key rate. Feasibility is then demonstrated through one month of successful QKD operation on a selected link.
main_result: A characterized field link supported successful continuous QKD testing for one month.
application_angle: The workflow helps network operators qualify existing telecom fibers and match them to QKD systems before deployment.

title: Calibration-free quantum thermometry with strain-swept two-level defects
abstract: Superconducting qubits operate within a well-defined temperature range, making local temperature monitoring important. Here we show that intrinsic two-level defects in Josephson-junction barriers can act as local thermometers by exploiting the shape of their population response, without requiring calibration of the readout offset or contrast. Marginalizing over these unknown parameters imposes an identifiability requirement absent from single-parameter thermometric bounds: for narrow sweeps, usable information scales as the fourth power of the sweep width. Hence, a narrow sweep becomes locally indistinguishable from a change in offset or contrast. We illustrate this principle with a strain-swept two-level defect in a Josephson junction. For a reported defect with tunneling energy $Δ_{0}/h=\SI{1.3}{\giga\hertz}$, swept along one branch of its hyperbola to \SI{2.69}{\giga\hertz} (an asymmetry excursion of \SI{2.36}{\giga\hertz}, or \SI{8}{\volt} of piezo voltage), the analysis projects a single-defect fit precision of \SI{0.58}{\percent} at \SI{20}{\milli\kelvin}. The resulting response enables temperature estimation without prior calibration of the readout offset and contrast, while the same sweep overdetermines the Boltzmann form and identifies significant deviations from thermality. These results establish intrinsic junction defects as a resource for calibration-free local thermometry and highlight identifiability as a key design criterion for primary temperature sensing.
one_liner: Strain-swept junction defects enable local, calibration-free thermometry for superconducting circuits and tests of thermal equilibrium.
why_it_matters: The approach turns intrinsic two-level defects into in situ thermometers without prior calibration of readout offset or contrast.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes using the population curve of a strain-swept two-level defect in a Josephson-junction barrier as a local thermometer while marginalizing over unknown readout offset and contrast. It derives an identifiability constraint under which information from narrow sweeps scales with the fourth power of sweep width. For a reported defect swept from a 1.3 GHz tunneling scale to 2.69 GHz, the analysis projects 0.58% single-defect precision at 20 mK and permits consistency tests of the Boltzmann response.
main_result: The modeled defect sweep supports calibration-free temperature estimation with a projected 0.58% precision at 20 mK.
application_angle: Embedded defect thermometers could monitor local qubit-chip temperature and reveal nonthermal populations inside dilution refrigerators.

title: Optical frequency combs on thin-film lithium niobate: from principles to applications
abstract: Optical frequency combs, consisting of mutually coherent and equally spaced spectral lines, provide a powerful means of synthesizing, distributing, and processing optical frequencies on chip. Among integrated photonic platforms, thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) is particularly attractive for comb generation because it combines strong electro-optic (EO) functionality, accessible $χ^{(2)}$ and $χ^{(3)}$ nonlinearities, low-loss nanophotonic confinement, and versatile dispersion engineering. This review summarizes the physical foundations and representative realizations of TFLN combs, and discusses their applications in optical communication, microwave photonics, optical computing, and precision metrology. The integration of nonlinear functionality, EO control, and passive photonic components is expected to advance compact, energy-efficient comb sources and broaden the utility of TFLN in integrated photonics and quantum optics.
one_liner: This review surveys thin-film lithium-niobate frequency comb physics, implementations, and emerging applications.
why_it_matters: TFLN unifies electro-optic control, nonlinear conversion, low-loss confinement, and dispersion engineering on one photonic platform.
detailed_summary: This review covers the foundations and representative implementations of optical frequency combs on thin-film lithium niobate. It discusses electro-optic generation, accessible second- and third-order nonlinearities, nanophotonic confinement, and dispersion engineering. Application areas include optical communications, microwave photonics, optical computing, precision metrology, and quantum optics.
main_result: The review organizes established TFLN comb mechanisms and devices into a unified platform-to-application perspective.
application_angle: Integrated TFLN combs could provide compact, controllable, and energy-efficient sources for communications, metrology, computing, and quantum photonics.

title: Universal two-qubit control across dilution refrigerators via a 10-km coherent optical link
abstract: Distributed quantum networks are important for scalable quantum processors and for potential applications in communication, distributed computation, and sensing, in which direct classical links for adaptive control are essential to harness the shared entanglement. However, controlling superconducting quantum processors from a separate refrigerator over long distances remains elusive. Here, we introduce a coherent optical link (COL) that delivers microwave waveforms and their phase references between dilution refrigerators. Combining a laser, a microwave-to-optical transducer and an optical-to-microwave photodiode, the COL transmits microwave control signals over 10~km of fiber, while optical references derived from the same laser compensate for the frequency mismatch between devices. Through the COL, we deliver a universal gate set to a transmon qubit and a cavity qubit in another refrigerator and entangle them, and achieve a Bell-state fidelity of 80.6\%. Quantum control delivered through the COL thus provides a classical backbone for modular quantum processors.
one_liner: A coherent optical link delivers universal microwave control across 10 km of fiber between separate dilution refrigerators.
why_it_matters: Remote control and entanglement across cryostats provide a practical classical-control backbone for modular superconducting quantum processors.
detailed_summary: The coherent optical link converts microwave control waveforms to the optical domain, transports them over 10 km of fiber, and recovers them by photodetection at a remote dilution refrigerator. Laser-derived optical references compensate device-frequency mismatch and preserve the phase reference needed for coherent gates. The system implements a universal gate set on a transmon and a cavity qubit in separate refrigerators, entangling them with 80.6% Bell-state fidelity.
platform_or_system: Remote superconducting qubits linked by microwave photonics
main_result: Universal remote control and an 80.6%-fidelity Bell state were demonstrated between qubits in separate refrigerators over 10 km of fiber.
application_angle: The link could coordinate modular cryogenic processors without requiring direct long-distance microwave cabling between refrigerators.

title: All-to-all connectivity via adiabatic ZZ interactions in a superconducting flux qubit processor
abstract: Scalable superconducting quantum processors would benefit from high qubit connectivity, yet existing architectures connect neighbouring qubits via tunable couplers, which introduce substantial wiring and control overhead. Here, we propose a baseband-driven adiabatic ZZ gate that entangles any selected pair in a register of flux qubits coupled via a common cavity. The qubits stay dc-biased at their flux sweet spot. Strong drives applied selectively through local flux lines, at frequencies far below the qubit transitions, adiabatically tilt the quantization axes and generate an effective longitudinal ZZ interaction. The strength of the coupling is tunable and controlled by the amplitudes and relative phase of the drives rather than by any resonance condition. Numerical simulations give coherent gate errors below $10^{-4}$ over broad ranges of drive frequency, with comparable fidelities for two simultaneous gates in a four-qubit register. The protocol is robust against frequency fluctuations and remains effective even when many qubits are coupled to the cavity.
one_liner: Baseband-driven adiabatic ZZ interactions offer selectable all-to-all entangling gates for cavity-coupled superconducting flux qubits.
why_it_matters: The scheme increases processor connectivity while avoiding tunable couplers, resonance matching, and much of their associated wiring overhead.
detailed_summary: Flux qubits remain at their dc sweet spots while strong, low-frequency local flux drives adiabatically tilt selected quantization axes. A shared cavity then mediates an effective longitudinal ZZ interaction controlled by drive amplitudes and relative phase rather than resonance conditions. Simulations predict coherent errors below 10^-4 across broad drive ranges and comparable fidelity for two simultaneous gates in a four-qubit register.
main_result: Numerical simulations show selectable all-to-all ZZ gates with coherent errors below 10^-4 and support for simultaneous gate pairs.
application_angle: This approach could simplify highly connected superconducting processors by reducing coupler hardware, wiring, and calibration complexity.

title: Frequency-selective membrane-based metamaterial filters for low-insertion-loss harmonic crosstalk suppression in sub-harmonic THz receivers
abstract: Parasitic reflections and standing waves fundamentally limit amplitude stability and phase fidelity in coherent continuous-wave (CW) terahertz (THz) systems. We report a complementary metamaterial filter pair designed for frequency-selective isolation at 300 GHz and 600 GHz in sub-harmonic heterodyne architectures. Fabricated on ultra-thin polyimide membranes, the filters provide more than 30 dB stopband isolation while maintaining insertion losses below 1 dB in the passband. System-level coherent-imaging experiments demonstrate effective suppression of spurious-reflection-induced interference effects and improved spectral baseline stability. The filters mitigate wavefront distortions resulting from such interferences and enhance reconstruction robustness. These results establish membrane-based metamaterial filters as compact frequency-selective isolation elements for sub-harmonic heterodyne THz detection and highlight their potential for phase-engineered imaging and sensing applications.
one_liner: Ultra-thin membrane metamaterial filters suppress harmonic crosstalk in coherent 300/600-GHz sub-harmonic receivers.
why_it_matters: More than 30 dB isolation with under 1 dB passband loss directly improves amplitude stability, phase fidelity, and THz image reconstruction.
detailed_summary: Complementary metamaterial filters fabricated on ultra-thin polyimide membranes selectively isolate 300 GHz and 600 GHz channels in a sub-harmonic heterodyne architecture. They provide more than 30 dB stopband suppression while keeping passband insertion loss below 1 dB. Coherent-imaging experiments show reduced reflection-induced interference, flatter spectral baselines, lower wavefront distortion, and more robust reconstruction.
main_result: The membrane filters achieved over 30 dB stopband isolation and below 1 dB passband loss while improving coherent-imaging stability.
application_angle: Compact low-loss isolation elements can improve phase-sensitive THz imaging, spectroscopy, and sensing instruments.

title: Spin Shuttling Through Quantum-Dot Based Chiral Molecular Bridges: Gauge Constraints, Holonomy, and Quantum Gates
abstract: Chiral molecular bridges between silicon quantum dots can provide novel two-qubit entangling resources via the chirality-induced spin-selectivity (CISS) effect. We evaluate this using Makhlin invariants. Modeling a phase-coherent bridge as an $\mathrm{SU}(2)$-valued hopping between two spins, a Schrieffer-Wolff reduction yields a twisted exchange interaction $J \mathbf{S}_1 \cdot \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S}_2$, whose Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya and symmetric anisotropic parts are fixed by a single bridge angle $α$. Using the Kaplan-Shekhtman-Entin-Wohlman-Aharony (KSEA) gauge argument, we prove this interaction is locally equivalent to isotropic exchange; thus, a single chiral bond does not constitute a new entangling class. Breaking this gauge symmetry reveals genuine chiral utility: chiral exchange converts a uniform transverse field into a synthetic gradient, bringing the two-qubit propagator within $7\times10^{-4}$ of the CNOT class in invariant space 4.7 times faster than an equivalent orthogonal gradient. Shuttling a spin through bridges with non-collinear axes implements a non-Abelian $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ holonomy, yielding rotationally non-reciprocal transport and closed-loop geometric gates that suppress dynamical-phase noise to second order. To address the unsettled microscopic origin of CISS, we introduce a unified transport channel combining coherent rotation, a direction-reversing spin filter, and pointer-basis dephasing. This model obeys an exact $\tanh$ composition law for pumped polarization and a closed-form transverse decay law, yielding four observables that experimentally over-determine the bridge's coherent fraction $F_c$. Finally, we quantify silicon-specific hardware constraints, establishing the Landau-Zener valley-adiabaticity window ($E_v \geq 2.1\sqrt{\hbar v}$) and charge-noise limit ($σ_J/J \leq 3\%$) required for $99\%$ gate fidelity.
one_liner: Chiral molecular bridges enable synthetic spin gradients and non-Abelian geometric control between silicon quantum dots.
why_it_matters: The analysis separates gauge-removable effects from useful chiral resources and defines measurable and hardware-level requirements for high-fidelity gates.
detailed_summary: A Schrieffer-Wolff reduction maps coherent bridge hopping to twisted exchange, but a single chiral bond is proved locally equivalent to isotropic exchange and therefore adds no new entangling class. With broken gauge symmetry, chiral exchange creates a synthetic field gradient and approaches the CNOT class within 7×10^-4 in invariant space, 4.7 times faster than an orthogonal-gradient reference. Non-collinear bridges generate non-Abelian SU(2) holonomy, while the proposed transport model and silicon constraints provide experimental tests and conditions for 99% gate fidelity.
platform_or_system: Silicon quantum dots connected by chiral molecular bridges
main_result: The theory identifies gauge-symmetry-breaking protocols for fast CNOT-class and geometric gates, with explicit 99%-fidelity hardware constraints.
application_angle: The results provide experimentally testable design rules for using molecular chirality in silicon spin-qubit control and transport.

title: Sequential vs parallel Strategies for Sharing Quantum Advantage in Communication Tasks
abstract: Information can be extracted from a quantum system in a sustainable manner, allowing the system to be reused for further information extraction through subsequent interactions. We investigate the possibility of consensus between two experimentally feasible methods, namely, parallel and sequential sharing, that enable multiple observers to extract information encoded in a quantum system. We show that any statistics generated by a parallel sharing strategy can be reproduced by a sequential strategy when only two observers are involved. However, when more than two observers participate in sharing quantum correlations, certain statistics achievable through parallel strategies cannot be reproduced by sequential strategies. Moreover, we demonstrate that sharing quantum advantage through a parallel strategy is impossible for a class of communication tasks involving two decoding measurements, thereby establishing an arbitrarily large gap between the sustainability of quantum advantage under sequential and parallel strategies. This naturally raises the question of whether this impossibility extends to communication tasks involving more than two decoding measurements. We show that, while parallel sharing of quantum advantage is impossible in a 3-bit random access code (RAC), it becomes possible in a 3-bit parity-oblivious RAC, where at most two observers can simultaneously obtain a quantum advantage by performing measurements on two imperfect clones of the initially prepared quantum system. Our findings have potential applications in the development of quantum communication networks and distributed quantum information processing.
one_liner: Sequential and parallel quantum-information sharing diverge beyond two observers, with task-dependent limits on shared advantage.
why_it_matters: The work identifies when reusable measurements or imperfect cloning can distribute quantum advantage among multiple network observers.
detailed_summary: For two observers, every statistic attainable through parallel sharing can also be reproduced sequentially, but this equivalence fails with more observers. Parallel quantum advantage is impossible for a class of tasks with two decoding measurements and for the 3-bit random access code, producing an arbitrarily large sustainability gap relative to sequential strategies. In a 3-bit parity-oblivious random access code, however, two observers can simultaneously retain quantum advantage using imperfect clones.
main_result: The study establishes separations between sequential and parallel sharing and finds a two-observer parallel advantage in parity-oblivious random access coding.
application_angle: These limits can guide protocol selection for reusable quantum messages, distributed decoding, and multi-user quantum networks.

title: Unified architecture for arbitrary two-qubit gates with neutral atoms
abstract: We propose a unified architecture for two-qubit gates in neutral-atom quantum processors which allows the implementation of the complete set of two-qubit gates. Our approach rests on a single resource that unlocks the entire gate set: an XXZ interaction with tunable anisotropy, combined only with single-qubit operations. We introduce a Rydberg-atom realization of the tunable XXZ interaction and combine it with optimally controlled global microwave pulses to implement the B, QFT, iSWAP, and $\sqrt{\mathrm{iSWAP}}$ gates, as well as a continuous gate family interpolating from CZ to iSWAP via the B gate. This work allows the implementation of any two-qubit gate natively in neutral-atom platforms, enabling flexible switching between instruction sets to reduce circuit depth and compilation overhead in quantum algorithm implementation.
one_liner: A tunable XXZ interaction provides a unified native route to arbitrary two-qubit gates in neutral-atom processors.
why_it_matters: Native access to diverse entanglers can reduce circuit depth and compilation overhead while allowing processors to switch instruction sets.
detailed_summary: The architecture combines a Rydberg-mediated XXZ interaction with tunable anisotropy and single-qubit operations to span the complete two-qubit gate set. Optimally controlled global microwave pulses realize B, QFT, iSWAP, and square-root-iSWAP gates, together with a continuous family connecting CZ and iSWAP through the B gate. The proposal uses one configurable interaction resource instead of separate mechanisms for different entanglers.
main_result: The proposed tunable-XXZ architecture natively implements arbitrary two-qubit gates and a continuous CZ-to-iSWAP family.
application_angle: Flexible native entanglers could shorten compiled neutral-atom circuits and support workload-specific quantum instruction sets.

title: GARI++: A General-Purpose Decoder for Quantum Error Correction
abstract: We present GARI++, a two-stage decoding pipeline achieving accuracy competitive with the state of the art across surface, bivariate bicycle and color codes without relying on ensembles. The first stage uses GARI, a normalized min-sum decoder with random serial scheduling on the GARI transformed matrix. The second stage decoder is used only for the cases that the first stage does not converge, and the decoder is configurable based on the choice of the QEC code. The first stage pipelines towards the second stage both the residual syndrome and the soft information. GARI++ pipelining is predictive, meaning that GARI++ chooses the first stage iteration outputs which are expected to deliver the best accuracy in the second stage. GARI++ motivates a hybrid FPGA-CPU architecture for real-time decoding. For example, under uniform circuit-level depolarising noise with a physical error rate of 0.001, the FPGA implementation of GARI achieves average latencies per round ranging from $201 ns$ to $11.8μs$ for surface code distances between 7 and 25. At the same time, due to the very low weight residuals output by the first stage, the average residual decoding time per round remains near constant and below one microsecond on a single Apple M2 core for surface code distances even up to 51 when using Union-Find and accuracy on par with correlated MWPM.
one_liner: GARI++ combines predictive min-sum and residual decoding for accurate, low-latency error correction across several quantum-code families.
why_it_matters: Its FPGA–CPU design offers a practical route to real-time decoding as logical qubits and code distances scale.
detailed_summary: GARI++ first applies normalized min-sum decoding with random serial scheduling, then sends selected residual syndromes and soft information to a code-specific second-stage decoder. Under circuit-level depolarizing noise at physical error rate 0.001, an FPGA implementation of the first stage reaches average per-round latencies from 201 ns to 11.8 μs for surface-code distances 7–25. Union-Find residual decoding on one Apple M2 core remains below 1 μs on average through distance 51, with accuracy comparable to correlated MWPM.
main_result: The pipeline achieves competitive decoding accuracy across surface, bivariate bicycle, and color codes while supporting microsecond-scale real-time operation.
application_angle: The architecture could serve as a scalable classical-control backend for fault-tolerant quantum processors requiring rapid syndrome processing and feedback.

title: Enhancing valley splitting in Si/SiGe Wiggle Well quantum dots through integrated stressor-gate architectures
abstract: Engineering large and reproducible valley splittings is essential for the scalable operation of silicon spin qubits. In Si/SiGe quantum dot devices, valley splitting arises predominantly from atomic-scale disorder and is therefore inherently random, motivating approaches that introduce a large deterministic contribution. Strain-assisted Wiggle Wells provide a route to deterministic valley splitting by combining an oscillatory Ge concentration in the Si well with shear strain; however, generating the required strain in a manner compatible with large-scale architectures remains a challenge. Here, we propose patterned stressed thin films as a scalable approach for generating shear strain in the quantum well of Si/SiGe quantum dot devices. Finite-element simulations show that compressively stressed TiN films can generate shear strains exceeding 0.1% at the quantum well, sufficient for deterministic valley splittings of hundreds of $μ\text{eV}$ in strain-assisted Wiggle Wells. We show that this strain can extend across multiple quantum dots and is maintained in realistic gate geometries, providing a fabrication-compatible approach for scaling deterministic valley splitting to quantum dot arrays.
one_liner: Patterned stressed TiN gates are proposed to create scalable shear strain and deterministic valley splitting in Si/SiGe Wiggle Well quantum dots.
why_it_matters: More uniform valley splittings would suppress a major source of device variability in large silicon spin-qubit arrays.
detailed_summary: Finite-element simulations show that compressively stressed TiN films can generate shear strain above 0.1% at a Si/SiGe quantum well. In strain-assisted Wiggle Wells, this level is predicted to produce deterministic valley splittings of hundreds of μeV. The calculated strain persists across multiple dots and within realistic gate layouts, although the result is presently simulation-based rather than an experimental device demonstration.
main_result: Simulated integrated TiN stressor gates generate sufficient, spatially extended shear strain for deterministic valley splittings of hundreds of μeV.
application_angle: The fabrication-compatible scheme targets reproducible silicon spin-qubit operation and reduced calibration overhead in scaled quantum-dot processors.

title: The simulability frontiers of photonic quantum computing
abstract: Estimates of when photonic devices outgrow classical simulation are hard to compare: even for single-photon boson sampling, quoted thresholds range from 50 to 98 photons, as they rest on different tasks and assumptions. We propose as a common unit the time a classical computer needs to draw one sample from the device's exact output distribution, up to floating-point rounding. Only exactness applies equally to every kind of light, since the cost of approximate sampling depends on the accuracy required. The simulability frontier is the device size at which our fastest exact sampler produces one sample per second on a fixed machine; this device size increases with better hardware and algorithms. As the time per sample grows exponentially with the number of detected photons, doubling the machine speed moves the frontier by about one photon, whereas a better algorithm changes the growth rate. We measure the frontier with photonic-engines, an open-source GPU library of exact samplers for single photons, entangled photons from quantum emitters, vacuum-single-photon superpositions and squeezed light. Each sampler is validated against a simulator sharing no code with it. On one NVIDIA H100 GPU, with Haar-random interferometers, twice as many modes as photonic inputs and photon-number-resolving detectors, the frontier lies at 38.3 single photons and at 31.0 entangled photons from one emitter. For squeezed light, a timing model fitted to measurements places it at 41.5 squeezed photonic inputs of mean photon number 0.5. For our samplers, coherence alone makes simulation harder: sources that emit a photon with probability one half reach 64.2 when vacuum and photon are mixed incoherently, as for lossy single photons, but only 50.0 when they are in coherent superposition. Feed-forward from mid-circuit measurement of up to three modes lowers the single-photon frontier only from 38.3 to 38.1.
one_liner: An open-source GPU benchmark establishes exact classical-simulation frontiers for several photonic quantum-computing source types.
why_it_matters: A common exact-sampling metric enables defensible comparisons between photonic experiments and their best classical simulators.
detailed_summary: The authors define the simulability frontier as the device size where the fastest exact sampler produces one output sample per second on fixed hardware. Using validated photonic-engines samplers on one NVIDIA H100 GPU, they find frontiers of 38.3 single photons, 31.0 emitter-entangled photons, and an estimated 41.5 squeezed inputs at mean photon number 0.5. They also quantify how source coherence and limited mid-circuit feed-forward alter exact-sampling cost.
main_result: The study supplies source-specific exact-sampling thresholds and a reproducible benchmark for locating photonic devices relative to classical capability.
application_angle: Experimental teams can use the framework to design and substantiate photonic quantum-advantage tests under explicit hardware and source assumptions.

title: Chiral waveguide model for error-correctable quantum computation
abstract: We develop a first-principles framework connecting microscopic waveguide scattering to quantum error correction and algorithmic performance. For polarization-encoded single photons interacting with an ensemble of two-level atoms in a chiral waveguide, we derive an effective polarization quantum channel by tracing out the frequency degree of freedom. Using this channel as the physical noise model for a rotated planar code, we observe threshold behavior as the number of atoms $N$ and the atom-waveguide coupling strength $Γ$ are varied. An asymptotic analysis of the microscopic scattering model explains the threshold scaling with $NΓ/σ$, where $σ$ is the photon spectral bandwidth. For identical, lossless atoms with symmetric real coupling and a photon spectrum centered at resonance, the effective noise is strongly biased toward $X$ errors. We then incorporate the resulting logical errors into quantum phase estimation and demonstrate that the noise bias can guide circuit design. In particular, a Hadamard-basis implementation reduces sensitivity to the dominant error, improving algorithmic performance.
one_liner: A microscopic chiral-waveguide scattering model is mapped through quantum error correction to logical and algorithm-level performance.
why_it_matters: It connects experimentally tunable photonic hardware parameters directly to code thresholds and noise-aware circuit choices.
detailed_summary: Polarization-encoded photons scatter from two-level atoms in a chiral waveguide, after which frequency is traced out to obtain an effective polarization channel. Applying this channel to a rotated planar code reveals threshold behavior governed asymptotically by NΓ/σ, relating atom number and coupling to photon bandwidth. For the symmetric lossless resonant case, noise is strongly X-biased, and a Hadamard-basis phase-estimation circuit improves algorithmic performance.
main_result: The framework derives QEC threshold scaling from microscopic scattering and shows that the resulting X-biased noise can be mitigated through basis-aware circuit design.
application_angle: It provides a co-design method for optimizing waveguide hardware, error-correcting codes, and algorithms using experimentally meaningful parameters.

title: Quantum simulation of real-time bosonic dynamics with binary and unary position encodings on superconducting and trapped-ion processors
abstract: Simulating a bosonic degree of freedom on qubit hardware requires discretizing its position space, and the qubit encoding of the resulting lattice determines the circuits that realize its real-time dynamics. We compare binary and unary encodings of a position lattice on superconducting (IBM) and trapped-ion (IonQ) processors. Binary encoding applies the kinetic term through the quantum Fourier transform; unary encoding uses one qubit per site, single-qubit rotations for the potential and excitation-conserving exchange gates for the kinetic term. For a single degree of freedom the unary dynamics is a free-fermion problem, and its product formula compresses exactly into a nearest-neighbor circuit of fixed size. With about two hundred two-qubit gates, these circuits resolve tunneling in a symmetric double well on both processors, with the right-well probability falling from 0.97 to 0.06 on IBM and from 0.96 to 0.12 on IonQ, whereas binary product-formula circuits with several thousand two-qubit gates do not reproduce the transfer. Noiseless emulation indicates that this contrast reflects the compilation as well as the encoding: without the fixed-size optimization, a unary product formula that captures the transfer also requires several thousand two-qubit gates. Post-selection on the single-excitation subspace removes leakage, and because every energy eigenstate of the symmetric grid populates both wells equally, the measured population reversal bounds the coherence between energy eigenstates from below. Coupled-oscillator benchmarks, where inter-register interactions prevent this exact compression, show that the preferred encoding depends on the grid size and the evolution time.
one_liner: Compressed unary circuits reproduce bosonic tunneling on IBM and IonQ processors where much deeper binary circuits fail.
why_it_matters: The cross-platform results show that encoding and compilation choices can determine whether useful bosonic dynamics survive hardware noise.
detailed_summary: The work compares binary and unary position encodings for real-time bosonic dynamics on IBM superconducting and IonQ trapped-ion processors. For one degree of freedom, free-fermion structure permits exact compression of the unary product formula into a fixed-size nearest-neighbor circuit with roughly 200 two-qubit gates. These circuits resolve double-well tunneling on both platforms, while binary circuits containing several thousand two-qubit gates fail to reproduce the transfer; coupled oscillators expose regimes where neither encoding is universally best.
platform_or_system: IBM superconducting and IonQ trapped-ion processors
main_result: Optimized unary circuits experimentally capture double-well population reversal on two hardware platforms with far fewer gates than binary implementations.
application_angle: The findings guide encoding and compilation choices for near-term simulations of vibrational, field, and other discretized bosonic dynamics.

title: Field-induced phase-matching in Josephson traveling wave parametric amplifiers
abstract: Superconducting Josephson traveling wave parametric amplifiers (JTWPAs) enable broadband, quantum-limited amplification of weak microwave signals. JTWPAs are essential for the single-shot readout of superconducting qubits, broadband vacuum squeezing, or the generation of microwave cluster states. Phase-matching between signal and pump modes in such JTWPAs represents a major engineering challenge, which is typically solved by integrating resonators in a nonlinear medium in order to tailor electromagnetic dispersion relations and achieve a broadband, high-gain amplification. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a phase-matching approach using a homogeneous nonlinear medium based on Josephson elements by exploiting a magnetic field inhomogeneity. We show how the latter may lead to the sign reversal of the 3-wave mixing nonlinearity and stabilization of the parametric amplification. We envision this technique as a viable alternative to conventional phase-matching approaches.
one_liner: A magnetic-field gradient enables phase matching and stable three-wave-mixing gain in a homogeneous Josephson traveling-wave amplifier.
why_it_matters: The method may simplify broadband quantum-limited microwave amplifiers by avoiding conventional resonator-based dispersion engineering.
detailed_summary: The experiment uses an inhomogeneous magnetic field to control a homogeneous Josephson nonlinear medium. The field profile can reverse the sign of the three-wave-mixing nonlinearity, enabling phase matching and stabilizing parametric amplification without integrated phase-matching resonators. This offers an alternative electromagnetic-design strategy for broadband Josephson traveling-wave parametric amplifiers.
main_result: Field-induced nonlinearity reversal is experimentally shown to provide phase matching and stabilize parametric microwave amplification.
application_angle: The technique could support simpler broadband amplifiers for superconducting-qubit readout, microwave squeezing, and cluster-state generation.

title: Surface codes with coherent errors: optimal decoding and finite-size crossovers
abstract: We study the surface code under uniform coherent $Z$ rotations $\exp{(iθZ)}$ followed by perfect syndrome measurements, a setting known to exhibit strong finite-size effects that complicate the extraction of the asymptotic decoding threshold. We identify finite-size behavior of both Pauli decoding measures and the coherent information with two characteristic lengths: an algebraic ballistic-crossover scale $d_{\mathrm{ba}}\sim 1/β_R^α$ ($α=1$ for odd $d$ and $α=2$ for even $d$) and a much larger renormalization-group scale $d_\mathrm{RG}\sim \exp{(C/β^{4}_R)}$, where $β_R=-\tfrac{1}{2}\ln\tanθ$ and $d$ is the system size. As $θ$ approaches the ballistic SWAP point $π/4$, the two length scales diverge at very different rates, leaving a broad intermediate regime $d_{\mathrm{ba}}\ll d\ll d_\mathrm{RG}$ in which these quantities show substantial finite-size drift and approximate plateaus. To establish the microscopic basis of this crossover picture, we derive a leading inter-flavor quartic interaction of order $β_R^2$ in the replicated Majorana theory, which provides a route to the class-D nonlinear sigma model. The resulting marginal RG flow motivates the scaling variable $X_4=β_R^4\ln d$, in which free-fermion simulations show approximate collapse of decoding measures. These results are consistent with a Pauli-decoding threshold at $θ_c=π/4$ in the thermodynamic limit. For any even $d$, we prove that maximum-likelihood Pauli decoding maximizes entanglement fidelity over all deterministic syndrome-conditioned quantum recoveries, and that its decoding threshold attains the quantum-optimal limit, coinciding with the one defined by coherent information.
one_liner: Surface-code decoding under coherent Z rotations exhibits two widely separated finite-size crossover scales near the ballistic SWAP point.
why_it_matters: The analysis clarifies misleading finite-size threshold behavior and proves quantum-optimal maximum-likelihood Pauli recovery for every even code distance.
detailed_summary: The authors analyze perfect-syndrome surface codes subject to uniform coherent Z rotations and identify ballistic and renormalization-group crossover lengths with parametrically different divergences near θ=π/4. A replicated Majorana description produces an inter-flavor quartic interaction and motivates the scaling variable β_R^4 ln d, which approximately collapses free-fermion simulation results. For even code distance, maximum-likelihood Pauli decoding is proven optimal among deterministic syndrome-conditioned quantum recoveries.
main_result: The work supports an asymptotic threshold at θc=π/4 and proves that even-distance maximum-likelihood Pauli decoding reaches the quantum-optimal limit.
application_angle: It provides practical guidance for interpreting finite-device QEC benchmarks and selecting recovery strategies for hardware with coherent control errors.

title: Finite Measured Entropy Production Does Not Imply Finite Microscopic Irreversibility
abstract: Coarse-grained measurements provide a lower bound on entropy production, but how much microscopic irreversibility can they conceal? We construct a driven quantum system in which an imperfect counter registers a finite, strictly positive arrow of time while the microscopic entropy production is infinite. The system is a degenerate parametric oscillator below threshold, coupled to a thermal reservoir through repeated interactions with bosonic ancillas. The oscillator sustains a finite, positive heat current into the vacuum bath, where absorption is forbidden and forward and reverse trajectory laws have different supports. A photon counter with finite collection efficiency, gated time bins, and independent dark counts defines a common coarse-graining of the aligned trajectory laws. For fixed observation duration $\mathcal T$ and detector parameters, we prove that the observed relative entropy remains uniformly bounded as the bath temperature $T_b$ vanishes and is strictly positive at vacuum. The hidden contribution obeys $Σ_{\mathrm{hid}}(\mathcal T,T_b)=\mathcal T\dot Q_0/(k_BT_b)+O(1)$, where $\dot Q_0>0$ is the stationary vacuum heat current. False positives conceal the support mismatch while preserving measurable time asymmetry. Thus, finite and informative measurements of entropy production can coexist with infinite microscopic irreversibility.
one_liner: An imperfect photon counter can report finite entropy production even when the underlying driven quantum dynamics is infinitely irreversible.
why_it_matters: It shows that detector inefficiency, time binning, and dark counts can conceal divergent microscopic dissipation while retaining a measurable arrow of time.
detailed_summary: A below-threshold degenerate parametric oscillator exchanges energy with bosonic ancillas and sustains a positive heat current into a vacuum bath, producing incompatible forward and reverse trajectory supports. Finite collection efficiency, gated bins, and independent dark counts restore common support in the measured records, keeping their relative entropy bounded and positive as bath temperature vanishes. Meanwhile, the hidden entropy production diverges as T·Q̇0/(kBTb) plus a bounded correction.
main_result: The authors prove that finite, informative measured entropy production can coexist with infinite microscopic irreversibility at zero bath temperature.
application_angle: The result sets limits on inferring thermodynamic irreversibility from realistic photon-counting experiments with loss, finite timing resolution, and false detections.

title: FusionQ: A Generic and Optimal Decoding Framework for Ultra-Low-Latency Quantum Error Correction
abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) decoding has traditionally been organized around fixed decoding instances: a monolithic space-time detector error model (DEM), or a predetermined temporal window, is handed to a backend decoder after enough syndrome data has arrived. This paper presents FusionQ, a fusion decoding framework that changes this paradigm by deriving local decoding tasks from the observed syndrome and then fusing their results into a single global correction. Instead of forcing every shot through the same global or windowed problem, FusionQ builds open-boundary local DEMs around fired detector clusters and expands the corresponding footprints only when a local optimum uses virtual boundary errors. FusionQ is generic in the decoder backend: the scheduler requires only a local solution and a boundary-use flag, so exact solvers, matching-style decoders on graphlike DEMs, and heuristic decoders can share the same runtime. We prove a compositional optimality theorem: with an exact minimum-weight local backend and boundary-free publication, fusing the published local decoding results yields a global most-likely error (MLE) solution of the original DEM. Our evaluation shows that, with an exact backend, FusionQ matches the monolithic MLE result on every shot. Across decoder backends, FusionQ substantially reduces decoding latency by overlapping local decoding with hardware syndrome acquisition.
one_liner: FusionQ decodes fired syndrome clusters locally and fuses their corrections to reduce QEC latency without sacrificing exact-backend optimality.
why_it_matters: Its local, streaming architecture overlaps decoding with syndrome acquisition and can support multiple decoder backends in real-time fault-tolerant processors.
detailed_summary: FusionQ constructs open-boundary local detector-error models around observed detector clusters and expands a footprint only when the local optimum uses virtual boundary errors. The scheduler needs only a local solution and a boundary-use flag, allowing exact, matching-based, or heuristic backends. With an exact minimum-weight backend and boundary-free publication, the authors prove that fused local results form a global most-likely-error solution and report agreement with monolithic MLE on every evaluated shot.
main_result: FusionQ preserves monolithic MLE outcomes with an exact backend while substantially reducing latency by decoding concurrently with syndrome acquisition.
application_angle: The framework targets ultra-low-latency feedback pipelines needed to keep large fault-tolerant quantum processors operating within hardware timing budgets.

title: How wide must an eavesdropper be? Leakage of a toric-code logical bit to a strip and the Nishimori point
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computers hand pieces of each logical qubit to separate decoder modules and shared readout lines. How much does a piece reveal? We prove that for any region and any Pauli noise, including correlated noise, an observer's optimal advantage in learning a logical bit is exactly 1 - 2 P_fail, where P_fail is the failure probability of maximum-likelihood decoding confined to that region. Two lessons follow. Geometry, not noise, provides the protection: a region that misses a single column of the code learns exactly nothing at any noise level, while a region that spans the code is protected by noise only at impractical distances (d > 350 for one row at a 10^-3 flip rate). And width is a poor guide to risk: under i.i.d. noise a two-row strip learns exactly as little as one row, yet below threshold an eavesdropper needs a width growing only as ln d. Through the identity, the strip's operational threshold is the Nishimori point of the random-bond Ising model, and a Walsh-Hadamard transfer matrix up to width 16 locates it to within a few thousandths. On two IBM Heron processors (d = 3, 5), an emulated strip adversary shows the predicted jump at width three, and non-uniform qubit errors let a trained attacker profit from the second row that uniform noise makes useless. We turn these results into design rules for partitioned decoding and multiplexed readout. Code and data are included.
one_liner: Toric-code logical leakage to a strip is exactly tied to region-confined decoding failure and is governed more by geometry than nominal width.
why_it_matters: IBM Heron experiments and theory yield concrete security rules for partitioned decoders and shared readout paths in fault-tolerant hardware.
detailed_summary: For any region and Pauli noise, including correlated noise, the observer's optimal logical-bit advantage is proven to equal 1−2P_fail for maximum-likelihood decoding restricted to that region. A region missing one complete code column reveals no logical information, whereas a spanning strip can leak information at unexpectedly small widths; under independent noise the required width below threshold grows only logarithmically with distance. Emulated strip adversaries on two IBM Heron processors at distances three and five reproduce the predicted geometric transition and expose sensitivity to nonuniform errors.
platform_or_system: toric code on IBM Heron processors
main_result: The work derives an exact leakage-decoding identity, connects strip leakage to the Nishimori point, and experimentally observes the predicted width-dependent jump.
application_angle: The findings inform secure partitioning of decoder modules and multiplexed readout so that hardware subsystems cannot reconstruct protected logical data.

title: Quantized memory of measurement records near the light cone of quantum circuits
abstract: Quantum processors now measure qubits in the middle of a circuit, and the stream of outcomes is the raw output of error correction, measurement-based state preparation and monitored dynamics. For a scrambling circuit, predicting the statistics of this stream is as hard as simulating the processor, so there is no exact reference to check it against once the device outgrows classical simulation. We show that near the light cone the problem becomes exactly solvable, for any two-qubit gate. In a brickwork circuit with one polarized qubit in a maximally mixed background, measurements along the edge of the light cone form a two-state Markov chain, and measurements $d$ sites inside the edge are generated by $\lfloor d/2\rfloor+1$ qubits that move with it, while the rest of the chain, however large, acts on them as a memoryless bath. The memory of the record is therefore quantized, one bit on the edge and at most one more for every site of displacement, a bound that generic gates attain. The same causal structure determines which hardware noise the record can see, removes that sensitivity at no gate cost, and yields a tomography-free witness of dual-unitarity. On a 156-qubit superconducting processor, a demonstration with its analysis specified in advance finds the predicted memory one and two sites inside the light cone, and none where the theory forbids it. This gives dynamic circuits an exact reference at any system size, and shows that the collision models of open-system theory arise exactly inside chaotic dynamics.
one_liner: Measurement records near a scrambling circuit's light cone have exactly bounded, quantized memory that remains tractable at arbitrary system size.
why_it_matters: A 156-qubit experiment turns dynamic-circuit records into a scalable exact reference for validation, noise diagnosis, and dual-unitarity tests.
detailed_summary: In a brickwork circuit with one polarized qubit in a maximally mixed background, edge measurements form a two-state Markov chain for any two-qubit gate. At depth d inside the light-cone edge, the record is generated by only floor(d/2)+1 co-moving qubits, giving one bit of edge memory and at most one additional bit per site of displacement. A preregistered demonstration on a 156-qubit superconducting processor observes the predicted memory one and two sites inside the light cone and its absence where causality forbids it.
main_result: The authors establish an exact finite-memory model for near-light-cone records and verify its spatial memory pattern on a large superconducting processor.
application_angle: The solvable record statistics offer system-size-independent benchmarks for dynamic circuits, hardware-noise sensitivity, and tomography-free device characterization.

title: Exceptional points in non-Markovian quantum-state diffusion: From coefficient dynamics to state signatures
abstract: An exceptional point of a memory-coefficient equation need not have the same signature in every quantum-state observable. We examine this relation within exact non-Markovian quantum-state diffusion (NMQSD), following the same operator closure from its coefficient dynamics to the non-Markovian master equation obtained by noise averaging. A finite homogeneous lift identifies the Jordan chains reached by the causal initialization, while state reconstruction determines which contributions survive in a specified readout. Two models expose the distinction. For common-bath qubits restricted to zero and one excitation, a noise-independent lowering-form $O$ operator gives a closed master equation. Every defective decaying mode transfers its full pole order to a suitable unconditional excitation--reference coherence. A known third-order configuration illustrates both a quadratic--exponential coherence and cancellation of its highest-order term in another quadrature. For a position-coupled oscillator in a fixed-photon-number optomechanical sector, the exact closure contains a scalar noise-history term. On the regular normalizable branch studied for bath decay rates below the oscillator frequency, two second-order coefficient blocks lead to a double pole in the conditional displacement response to the NMQSD noise history, at long preparation age and fixed lag. The purely algebraic coefficient tail cancels from the conditional Gaussian width. Complete noise averaging changes the master-equation coefficients and combines conditional width with the weighted spread of state centers. Together, the models show how causal preparation, state reconstruction, and averaging give coefficient exceptional points a precise, readout-dependent meaning.
one_liner: Exceptional points in non-Markovian coefficient dynamics produce readout-dependent state signatures shaped by preparation, reconstruction, and averaging.
why_it_matters: The framework identifies which exceptional-point pole orders survive in measurable coherences or optomechanical responses, avoiding ambiguous state-level claims.
detailed_summary: Using exact non-Markovian quantum-state diffusion, the authors trace defective coefficient modes through operator closure, master-equation construction, and observable reconstruction. In common-bath qubits, suitable excitation-reference coherences retain the full pole order, although particular quadratures can cancel the highest-order term. In a photon-number-resolved optomechanical sector, second-order coefficient blocks yield a double pole in conditional displacement, while Gaussian widths and noise-averaged states exhibit different cancellations and combinations.
platform_or_system: common-bath qubits and cavity optomechanical oscillator
main_result: The study shows that coefficient exceptional points map to state observables only through readout-specific pole survival, cancellation, and noise averaging.
application_angle: It supplies design rules for selecting optical or coherence measurements that reliably expose non-Markovian exceptional-point dynamics.

title: Molecular Gas Optics Using Vibrational Population Density Refraction
abstract: Gas optics holds promise for development of advanced optical elements with 2-3 orders of magnitude higher damage threshold than any solid-state optics. Here, we demonstrate a new concept for refracting the laser beam using vibrationally excited molecules as gas optics instead of traditional control of thermodynamic gas temperature. The transient, vibrational population density grating is formed in a CO2 gas by interfering two mid-IR lasers to imprint spatial modulation in the linear refractive index (Delta n0 >=2x10-5) of the neutral gas via enhancement of the molecular polarizability. It is increased by pumping the asymmetric stretching mode of CO2 at optimal wavelengths to resonantly produce a highly nonequilibrium state that increases the effective vibrational mode temperature to greater than 2000 K in a room temperature gas. The measured beam steering efficiency of such a volume gas grating exceeds 90% that makes this approach a candidate for producing other large-aperture, high-throughput molecular optics elements, with expected damage thresholds 0.5-1 kJ/cm2, much-needed for future ultrahigh-power lasers.
one_liner: A transient CO2 vibrational-population grating steers laser beams with over 90% efficiency using molecular-polarizability modulation.
why_it_matters: Gas-based refractive optics could enable large-aperture beam control at damage thresholds far beyond those of conventional solid optics.
detailed_summary: Two interfering mid-infrared pumps create a transient vibrational-population grating in room-temperature CO2. Resonant excitation of the asymmetric-stretch mode produces an effective vibrational temperature above 2000 K and a linear-index modulation of at least 2×10^-5. The resulting volume gas grating achieves greater than 90% beam-steering efficiency.
main_result: The molecular gas grating produced a refractive-index modulation of at least 2×10^-5 and steered a laser beam with over 90% efficiency.
application_angle: The approach could support large-aperture optical elements for ultrahigh-power lasers, with projected damage thresholds of 0.5–1 kJ/cm².

title: A Compiler for Fault Tolerant Quantum Computing
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) needs compiler intermediate representations (IRs) that preserve error-correcting-code choices, syndrome information, and non-Clifford resource requirements through analysis, simulation, and hardware lowering. We report practical experience building FTQC, an open-source Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect that makes logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames typed static single assignment (SSA) values. Its error-correction-aware type system, two-level lowering design, and IR-resident resource analysis provide one inspectable pipeline to Open Quantum Assembly Language~3 (OpenQASM~3), the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR), Stim, and IQM hardware. Case studies across three code families show that typed metadata makes code-specific decisions verifiable and retargetable: on the 20-qubit Pathfinder at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3 times. They also expose hidden architectural costs: for a three-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT-3), a magic-state factory requires five times the peak qubits of the encoded circuit. These experiences demonstrate a practical foundation for developing and evaluating fault-tolerant compiler transformations across software and hardware targets.
one_liner: An open-source MLIR compiler represents logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames as typed values for FTQC workflows.
why_it_matters: A unified, inspectable compiler pipeline makes error-correction choices and hardware resource costs easier to verify, compare, and retarget.
detailed_summary: The FTQC MLIR dialect encodes logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames as typed static single-assignment values. Its two-level lowering pipeline targets OpenQASM 3, QIR, Stim, and IQM hardware while retaining code-specific metadata and resource analysis. On ORNL's 20-qubit Pathfinder, decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3×; analysis also found that a QFT-3 magic-state factory required five times the encoded circuit's peak qubits.
main_result: The compiler enabled retargetable error-correction-aware lowering and achieved a 3.3× logical-readout-error reduction on the 20-qubit Pathfinder.
