application_angle: It provides a practical toolchain for evaluating fault-tolerant transformations and exposing hardware costs before deployment.

title: Multicomponent Isotope Engineering of Phonon Polaritons in Hexagonal Boron Nitride
abstract: Isotopic enrichment provides a non-invasive means of tuning the vibrational and optical properties of van der Waals crystals (vdW) without altering their lattice structure. We investigate two doubly enriched hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) compositions, h10B15N and h11B15N, to determine how isotope substitution on both sublattices modifies mid-infrared hyperbolic phonon polaritons (HPhPs). Polarization-resolved room temperature and cryogenic far-field reflectance measurements reveal optical-phonon blue shifts of approximately 35 cm-1 in h10B15N relative h11B15N, translating both Reststrahlen bands (RBs) and their polariton dispersions. For the upper RB, the combined accessible range expands from 1360-1614 cm-1 in natural hBN to 1356-1640 cm-1 across the B- enriched 14N crystals and 1339-1640 cm-1 when the 15N enriched crystals are included. Near-field imaging confirms deeply sub-diffractional propagation and shows that both crystals exhibit lower polariton damping and longer lifetimes than natural hBN, with performance comparable to monoisotopically enriched crystals. Further, we compare the conventional reduced-mass description with a phenomenological two-component inverse-mass model that captures the isotope dependence of the phonon frequencies and LO-TO coupling while resolving the contributions of the individual sublattices. These results establish multicomponent isotope engineering as a materials design strategy for positioning the HPhPs spectral range while preserving low-loss propagation in polar vdW crystals.
one_liner: Dual-isotope engineering shifts hBN phonon-polariton bands while retaining deeply sub-diffractional, low-loss mid-infrared propagation.
why_it_matters: Independent isotope control offers a non-invasive route to broaden and position nanophotonic operating bands without changing the crystal lattice.
detailed_summary: The study compares doubly enriched h10B15N and h11B15N crystals using polarization-resolved reflectance at room and cryogenic temperatures. Substitution produces an approximately 35 cm^-1 optical-phonon shift and expands the combined upper-Reststrahlen coverage to 1339–1640 cm^-1 when 15N materials are included. Near-field imaging confirms deeply sub-diffractional propagation with lower damping and longer lifetimes than natural hBN.
platform_or_system: Isotopically enriched hBN van der Waals crystals
main_result: Multicomponent isotope substitution shifted the hyperbolic phonon-polariton spectrum while preserving propagation losses comparable to monoisotopically enriched hBN.
application_angle: The method enables spectral design of low-loss mid-infrared nanophotonic components for confinement, routing, and spectroscopy.

title: Syndrome extraction for quantum LDPC codes in silicon: Distributed entanglement and mobile ancillas
abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes can reduce the number of data qubits required per logical qubit, but their checks require long-range interactions on a planar device. We develop a singlet fabric for bivariate-bicycle codes on a silicon node network. Spin singlets are generated on shuttling lanes and distributed between nodes, where local operations consume them to measure non-local stabilizers. We construct two syndrome-extraction circuits, based on distributed GHZ states and ancilla teleportation, and evaluate them using hardware-constrained schedules and circuit-level memory simulations. We compare these circuits with CAbLECAR, which transports a mobile ancilla between the data qubits of each check. Teleportation can outperform CAbLECAR on its original layout when transport includes spin flips as well as dephasing. Placing the mobile ancilla on our node lattice, however, shortens the mean scheduled route for the [[144,12,12]] Gross code from 350 to 153 $μ$m and lowers its logical error rate up to 50-fold in the sampled bit-flip regime. Direct transport then achieves a lower logical error rate than either singlet circuit at every sampled Gross-code point. With frequent transport bit flips, the GHZ circuit overtakes direct transport once two-qubit gate and readout errors fall below about $4$-$5\times10^{-4}$, roughly half the value assumed here. Fixing the ancilla's data-visit order reveals a trade-off between shorter routes and the correlated errors produced by ancilla faults. Source heralding improves both singlet circuits, whereas phase purification helps the GHZ circuit only above a noise-dependent crossover and worsens teleportation throughout. These results show that the physical layout and interaction order can be as consequential as the choice of extraction circuit, and that cleaner entangled resources do not necessarily produce a more reliable logical memory.
one_liner: Hardware-constrained simulations compare distributed-entanglement and mobile-ancilla syndrome extraction for silicon qLDPC memories.
why_it_matters: The results show that chip layout and ancilla interaction order can dominate logical performance, guiding realistic silicon fault-tolerant designs.
detailed_summary: The authors design a silicon-node singlet fabric and syndrome-extraction circuits based on distributed GHZ states and ancilla teleportation, then compare them with direct mobile-ancilla transport. On the proposed node lattice, the mean scheduled route for the [[144,12,12]] Gross code falls from 350 to 153 μm, reducing logical error by up to 50× in the sampled bit-flip regime. Direct transport performs best at the sampled parameters, while GHZ extraction wins under frequent transport flips once gate and readout errors fall below roughly 4–5×10^-4.
main_result: Layout-aware mobile-ancilla routing shortened transport by 56% and lowered logical error by up to 50×, with distributed GHZ extraction favored only in cleaner regimes.
application_angle: The comparison provides concrete layout, routing, and error targets for implementing qLDPC syndrome extraction in planar silicon processors.

title: Sample complexity of learning fermionic and bosonic Gaussian states with single-copy and entangled measurements
abstract: With single-copy measurements, every mixed fermionic Gaussian state on $m$ modes, pure modes included, is learned to trace distance $ε$ from $Θ(m^3/ε^2)$ copies, with no logarithmic factor, against the known $Θ(m^2/ε^2)$ for collective measurements. We prove the upper bound, resolving Conjecture 10.1 of arXiv:2609.23189 (lower bound for $ε\le1/3600$), and fill most open entries of the sample-complexity table of fermionic and bosonic Gaussian states, for single-copy, $k$-copy and collective measurements. The single-copy measurement's noise is matched to the metric at every occupation scale. With blocks of $k$ copies, the covariant highest-weight measurement of arXiv:2611.07271, read out through the Weyl-shift estimator, is exactly unbiased for every state; it gives $Θ(\max\{m^3/k,m^2\}/ε^2)$ in Frobenius norm on all states and in trace distance on every class at a fixed distance from the pure boundary. The gain $1/k$ ($k\le m$) away from the pure boundary, against $1/\sqrt k$ on cold number-conserving states, is therefore attained. For bosonic Gaussian states with bounded covariance, any displacement and squeezing, and occupations $n_1\le\dots\le n_m$, $O((m^2+r^3+\sum_{i,j>r}1/(n_i+n_j))/ε^2)$ single-copy measurements suffice, $r$ the largest index with $r\,n_r\le2$; this is the minimax rate on dyadic-interval classes, with no spectral gap or cold-mode count assumed, and holds with no covariance bound for displaced passive states. With no bound on energy or squeezing, non-Gaussian measurements learn centred one-mode states, mixed included, from $O(ε^{-2})$ and centred pure $m$-mode states from $O(m^2/ε^2)$ single copies, free of the $\log\log E$ term of Gaussian measurements, and $m$-mode states from $O(m^3/ε^2)$ copies, entangled only in a first round on blocks of $4m+6$.
one_liner: The work establishes near-complete sample-complexity bounds for learning fermionic and bosonic Gaussian quantum states.
why_it_matters: Tight copy requirements clarify when single-copy or entangled measurements offer practical advantages in characterizing many-mode quantum systems.
detailed_summary: The paper proves that arbitrary mixed fermionic Gaussian states on m modes can be learned with single-copy measurements using Θ(m^3/ε^2) copies, versus Θ(m^2/ε^2) collectively. Block-entangled measurements achieve Θ(max{m^3/k,m^2}/ε^2) under stated metrics and state classes. It also derives occupation-dependent bounds for bounded-covariance bosonic Gaussian states and energy-independent results using non-Gaussian measurements in selected settings.
platform_or_system: Multimode fermionic and bosonic Gaussian states
main_result: The authors derive tight or minimax copy-complexity rates across single-copy, block-entangled, and collective measurement models.
application_angle: These bounds help experimentalists choose measurement architectures and estimate tomography resources for photonic and fermionic Gaussian platforms.

title: Double-quantum enhanced coherent control and magnetic sensing of spin defects in hexagonal boron nitride
abstract: The negatively charged boron vacancy ($V_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}$) in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is a promising spin defect for quantum sensing in two-dimensional material systems. Previous hBN experiments have mainly exploited the two spin-triplet ground-state single-quantum transitions separately. Here we implement a double-quantum driving scheme based on simultaneous resonant microwave excitation of both ground-state single-quantum transitions, establishing coherent control of the $Δm_s=2$ manifold in a $V_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}$ ensemble. We compare the resulting double-quantum response with the corresponding single-quantum protocol under identical experimental conditions. The double-quantum protocol enhances the optical readout contrast and yields a 2.6-fold signal-to-noise improvement in AC magnetometry. We further use the double-quantum relaxation channel as a differential probe of electric-field and strain noise, showing that the present data are compatible with correlated-surface or volume-distributed fluctuations, while short-range uncorrelated surface-noise models are disfavored within the assumptions of our analysis. These results establish double-quantum coherent control and frequency-resolved AC magnetometry in hBN spin ensembles, and identify the sample-dependent measurements needed to determine the microscopic origin of the dominant relaxation channels.
one_liner: Double-quantum control of boron-vacancy ensembles in hBN improves AC-magnetometry signal-to-noise by 2.6× over single-quantum driving.
why_it_matters: The protocol advances two-dimensional spin-defect sensing while adding a differential probe of electric-field and strain noise.
detailed_summary: Simultaneous resonant microwave excitation of both ground-state single-quantum transitions establishes coherent control of the Δm_s=2 manifold in V_B^- ensembles. Under matched conditions, double-quantum operation increases optical contrast and produces a 2.6-fold signal-to-noise improvement in AC magnetometry. Double-quantum relaxation measurements also disfavor short-range uncorrelated surface-noise models under the analysis assumptions.
platform_or_system: Negatively charged boron-vacancy ensembles in hBN
main_result: Double-quantum driving delivered coherent Δm_s=2 control and a 2.6× AC-magnetometry signal-to-noise enhancement.
application_angle: The technique supports more sensitive nanoscale magnetic sensing and helps diagnose electric-field and strain noise in two-dimensional devices.

title: Real-time spectral combs from delayed quantum feedback in multimode cavity QED
abstract: We study the time-dependent physical spectrum of light for a two-level atom coupled to a large, but discrete, number of modes of an electromagnetic cavity. Radiation emitted by the atom, placed at the center of the cavity, returns after the round-trip time $t_r$, re-excites it, and is re-emitted, producing a sequence of atomic population revivals. For a coupling approximately flat over the atomic linewidth, the emission dynamics reduces to a delay-differential equation of Bixon--Jortner type. Using its analytical solution in terms of Laguerre polynomials, we investigate how successive emission and reabsorption cycles shape the time-dependent spectrum. The physical spectrum exhibits revivals during which a transient frequency comb of spacing $2π/t_r$ develops. The comb results from the quantum interference between successive emission stages; its teeth sit not at the cavity modes but at the resonances of the effective two half-cavities created by the resonantly reflecting atom. The visibility scales as $e^{-Γt_r}$ with the filter bandwidth $Γ$, and at long times the comb converges to the dressed-mode spectrum, which we also obtain analytically in quantitative agreement with exact diagonalization. We show that the physical spectrum resolves the feedback phase, to which the atomic population is insensitive in the regime of well-separated emission stages, and provides additional frequency-resolved signatures of the atomic position. We discuss two feasible experimental implementations of our results with transmons (artificial atoms) coupled to microwave and surface-acoustic-wave resonators.
one_liner: Delayed quantum feedback produces transient spectral combs through repeated emission, reabsorption, and re-emission in multimode cavity QED.
why_it_matters: The spectrum reveals feedback phase and atomic-position information hidden from population dynamics, offering new diagnostics for engineered quantum resonators.
detailed_summary: A two-level emitter in a discrete multimode cavity reabsorbs its radiation after each round trip, creating population revivals and a transient frequency comb with spacing 2π/t_r. The comb arises from interference between successive emission stages, with teeth aligned to effective half-cavity resonances rather than bare cavity modes. Analytical delay-equation solutions agree with exact diagonalization and motivate microwave and surface-acoustic-wave implementations using transmons.
platform_or_system: Transmon coupled to microwave or SAW resonators
main_result: The study predicts analytically tractable real-time spectral combs whose structure encodes feedback phase, emitter position, and dressed cavity modes.
application_angle: The effect could enable frequency-resolved calibration and sensing of feedback paths and emitter placement in superconducting and acoustic quantum hardware.

title: Development of a versatile modular system to study the ablation and plume expansion in a thin film
abstract: Time-resolved investigation of laser ablation of thin films requires stable, repeatable, and efficient experimental environment. Conventional approaches often rely on multiple laser-ablation shots acquired at different delay times to reconstruct the temporal evolution of the process, thereby assuming shot-to-shot reproducibility. This work presents a novel modular experimental setup that addresses these challenges and enables a systematic pump--probe study of laser--matter interaction. The setup provides reliable single-pulse measurements with controlled sample positioning inside the high vacuum chamber, as well as integrated data recording, which improves redundancy and ease with which experiments can be performed. Further, the setup serves as an advanced diagnostic tool for investigating the time evolution of laser--matter interactions, ablation dynamics and laser-produced plasmas in a single laser shot, in various configurations with a temporal resolution better than 15 ns. Using this capability, we show that for a fixed ablation geometry, the transient reflectivity and transmission response depends strongly on the probing side, indicating that probing direction is an independent diagnostic variable whose omission can lead to incomplete or misleading picture of the ablation dynamics. This experimental technique can advance the understanding of surface modification and plume expansion, which are relevant to fundamental studies and also for range of applications, including laser cleaning of tokamak viewports and mirrors, pulsed laser deposition (PLD), surface structuring and laser-induced forward transfer (LIFT), among others. The present setup is versatile enough to perform these studies under different ablation configurations without implementing major changes in the experimental configuration.
one_liner: A modular high-vacuum pump–probe platform captures thin-film ablation and plume evolution in single shots with sub-15-ns resolution.
why_it_matters: Single-shot acquisition avoids assumptions about shot reproducibility and exposes probe-direction effects that can bias ablation diagnostics.
detailed_summary: The system integrates controlled sample positioning, synchronized acquisition, and flexible optical access for single-pulse studies of thin-film ablation in vacuum. It resolves transient reflectivity and transmission with better than 15 ns temporal resolution across multiple geometries. Measurements show that probing from opposite sides can produce strongly different responses, making probe direction an essential diagnostic variable.
main_result: The apparatus enables repeatable single-shot mapping of ablation and plume dynamics while revealing a strong dependence of transient optical signals on probe direction.
application_angle: The platform supports diagnostics for pulsed-laser deposition, laser cleaning, surface structuring, and laser-induced forward transfer.

title: Circuit-aware protection against burst errors in lattice surgery
abstract: Large-scale quantum computing will require logical operations protected against high-energy impacts that disturb many superconducting qubits at once. Gap engineering suppresses relaxation induced by these impacts, but protecting only a subset of qubits requires choosing where that protection is placed. During lattice surgery, measurements change as patches merge and split, exposing different ancillas and temporal boundaries to burst errors. Here we compare three static protection layouts for a simulated lattice-surgery CNOT, matching the numbers of protected ancillas and the X:Z check-type splits. At distance 9, protecting the check type measured during each merge reduces burst-induced excess risk by $38^{+6}_{-5}\%$ relative to a deep geometric band under correlated background matching, without giving the decoder the impact parameters. We attribute this difference to report errors at temporal boundaries and ancilla faults propagating to data, which interact to increase the excess risk of a shallow band. We also find that the typed layout reaches the shallow-band reference risk with an estimated $49^{+2}_{-14}$ fewer protected ancillas. At distance 13, the advantage is not resolved under oracle decoding, and a five-round burst cap reverses the shallow-band ordering. These results indicate how the measurements of a logical circuit can guide protection placement within the simulated decoder and burst-duration regimes tested here.
one_liner: Circuit-aware placement of burst-error protection improves simulated lattice-surgery CNOT reliability while reducing protected-qubit overhead.
why_it_matters: It shows that logical-circuit measurements—not geometry alone—can guide economical protection against correlated radiation-induced faults.
detailed_summary: The work simulates three static gap-engineering layouts for a lattice-surgery CNOT under correlated burst errors. At code distance 9, protecting the check type active during each merge lowers burst-induced excess risk by 38% relative to a deep geometric band under matched background conditions. The typed layout also reaches the shallow-band reference risk with an estimated 49 fewer protected ancillas, although the ordering depends on distance, decoder assumptions, and burst duration.
main_result: Measurement-aware protection placement reduced excess burst risk by 38% at distance 9 and achieved a reference risk with substantially fewer protected ancillas.
application_angle: The approach can guide selective gap engineering when full-chip radiation protection is impractical or too costly.

title: Packet-wise multi-hop quantum routing of hybrid quantum-classical packets
abstract: The ability to dynamically route quantum information across multiple nodes is a key requirement for realizing versatile and scalable quantum networks. Quantum routers are devices to achieve packet-level routing beyond static point-to-point connections by handling hybrid packets combining classical headers and quantum payloads. Previously proposed methods have selectively accessed the classical and quantum components of the packets utilizing wavelength splitters and optical switches, and repacked the hybrid packets before transmission through the outgoing link with regenerating classical headers. This work reports a novel optical-fiber-based quantum router that minimizes the disturbance and latency on the hybrid packets through more transparent operation. We experimentally demonstrate double-hop routing via two cascaded routers to three distinct receivers without regeneration of the headers. As a practical application, quantum key distribution packets based on time-bin qubits and a BB84 protocol with a two-decoy-state method are successfully delivered to the three receivers achieving nonzero secret key rates. These results demonstrate the feasibility of extensive quantum networks interconnected by multiple-step router nodes.
one_liner: Two cascaded fiber routers dynamically deliver hybrid classical–quantum packets and time-bin QKD traffic across multiple hops.
why_it_matters: The experiment advances packet-level quantum networking without regenerating classical headers at intermediate routers.
detailed_summary: The fiber-based router transparently handles packets containing classical headers and quantum payloads while minimizing added disturbance and latency. Two cascaded routers route packets over two hops to three distinct receivers without header regeneration. Time-bin BB84 packets using a two-decoy-state protocol yield nonzero secret-key rates at all three destinations.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates double-hop packet-wise quantum routing to three receivers with successful decoy-state BB84 key delivery.
application_angle: Transparent multi-hop routing is a practical building block for scalable, dynamically reconfigurable metropolitan quantum networks.

title: Machine-learning decoders for fusion-based quantum computing in real time
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires decoders that combine accuracy, throughput, low latency, and scalability to large numbers of physical qubits. In photonic fusion-based architectures, erasures from photon loss and probabilistic fusion measurements are a dominant error mechanism, motivating decoders that remain accurate at high erasure rates. We introduce PRISM, a transformer-based machine-learning decoder designed to exploit the known locations of erasures in protocols subject to both Pauli and erasure errors. We benchmark PRISM across a wide range of fault-tolerant protocols based on surface codes, color codes, and quantum low-density parity-check codes, with distances up to 24. Across these benchmarks, PRISM matches the logical error rates of integer-programming-based decoders while being significantly faster, including at error rates up to 50% of threshold. We further optimize the decoder and its real-time hardware implementation to reduce latency while maintaining accuracy. Our optimized implementation on an AMD VP1902 FPGA can decode logical blocks of distance 8 in both space and time, demonstrating a latency of 6.59 microseconds and an amortized decoding time of 1.56 microseconds per logical block is possible. These results show that machine-learning decoding can provide accurate, low-latency inference for erasure-dominated fault-tolerant quantum architectures.
one_liner: PRISM uses a transformer decoder and FPGA acceleration to provide accurate, microsecond-scale decoding for erasure-heavy quantum architectures.
why_it_matters: Real-time decoding of known erasure locations addresses a central control bottleneck in photonic fusion-based fault-tolerant computing.
detailed_summary: PRISM is a transformer-based decoder that explicitly exploits known erasure locations alongside Pauli-error information. Across surface, color, and quantum LDPC codes up to distance 24, it matches integer-programming logical error rates while decoding substantially faster, including near half-threshold error rates. An AMD VP1902 FPGA implementation decodes distance-8 space-time blocks with 6.59 μs latency and 1.56 μs amortized time per block.
main_result: PRISM combines competitive decoding accuracy with a demonstrated 6.59 μs FPGA latency for distance-8 logical space-time blocks.
application_angle: The decoder offers a hardware-ready path to low-latency feed-forward and error correction in photon-loss-dominated quantum processors.

title: Observation of strong electric dipole-dipole interactions between two atoms
abstract: We have prepared pairs of atoms at densities exceeding $ 10^{16}/\rm{cm}^3$ corresponding to $n\lambdabar^3>10$ and studied how they interact with light. In this regime, the coherent part of the electric dipole-dipole interaction is larger than the dissipative part, and a single photon emission can transfer large momenta (larger than ten times the single photon recoil) to the atoms. For off-resonant laser light, the atoms are dressed with an electric dipole moment of $\approx$ 1 Debye and interact coherently. This light-induced dipole-dipole interaction has been previously observed only in the far-field mean-field regime. For two atoms, the resonance is shifted by the two-body Lamb shift which is dominated by the near-field part of the dipolar interaction. Dipolar resonance shifts have been observed before only for many atoms interacting with the far-field part of the dipolar interaction. Our work sheds new light on photoassociation processes and paves the way for studying driven quantum systems with strong electric dipole-dipole interactions.
one_liner: Dense atom pairs exhibit near-field electric dipole–dipole interactions strong enough to dominate dissipation and produce large recoil.
why_it_matters: Direct access to coherent two-atom near-field coupling opens a controlled regime for studying collective light–matter physics and photoassociation.
detailed_summary: Atom pairs are prepared above 10^16 cm−3, corresponding to nλ̄^3 greater than 10, where coherent dipolar coupling exceeds its dissipative component. Photon emission can impart more than ten single-photon recoils, while off-resonant dressing induces dipole moments of about 1 Debye. The measured two-body resonance shift is dominated by the near-field dipolar contribution to the Lamb shift.
main_result: The experiment observes strong coherent near-field electric dipole–dipole interactions and associated two-body Lamb shifts between two atoms.
application_angle: The platform enables controlled studies of driven interacting atoms, momentum exchange, and light-assisted molecular formation.

title: Quantum-Assisted Generative Anomaly Detection: A Dimension-Controlled Study of Latent Refinement
abstract: Anomaly-based malware detectors learn what benign files look like and flag deviations. Generative approaches to this problem can make use of a "latent" or "prior" data representation, which is often chosen to be a Gaussian distribution. We ask whether the choice of prior distribution matters, and whether one produced by quantum hardware behaves differently from a classical one. Building on SAGEGAN, a style-based detector trained only on benign data, we compare three latent distributions: the original 512-dimensional Gaussian, a 48-dimensional Gaussian, and a 48-dimensional distribution sampled from an ORCA Computing PT-2 photonic quantum processor. We then refine each trained model's frozen representation using greedy and reinforcement-learning methods. Across ten random seeds, the quantum-derived model shows richer internal structure with better effective rank and latent similarity. It also benefits most from refinement. Though final detection accuracy is similar to that of the refined Gaussian latent, these findings show differences in latent geometry and refinement behavior between the trained configurations.
one_liner: A 48-dimensional latent prior sampled from an ORCA PT-2 photonic processor yields richer geometry for generative malware anomaly detection.
why_it_matters: It isolates hardware-derived latent-space effects at fixed dimension, showing improved effective rank and refinement response despite similar final accuracy.
detailed_summary: The study compares 512- and 48-dimensional Gaussian priors with a 48-dimensional prior sampled from an ORCA Computing PT-2 photonic quantum processor in a SAGEGAN malware detector. Across ten seeds, the quantum-derived configuration develops higher effective rank and stronger latent similarity structure. Greedy and reinforcement-learning refinement benefit it most, although refined detection accuracy remains comparable to the Gaussian baseline.
main_result: The photonic-hardware prior produced richer learned latent structure and larger refinement gains than dimension-matched Gaussian sampling.
application_angle: The work tests whether quantum-generated samples can improve trainable representations in practical anomaly-detection pipelines beyond headline accuracy alone.

title: Controlled preparation and unconditional transport on a fluctuating quantum graph
abstract: Lieb--Robinson bounds limit the spread of quantum information, but do not establish that a prescribed input can be prepared and transmitted with appreciable probability. For quantum graphs with fluctuating edges, connecting spectral propagation to unconditional readout also requires control of graph coherence, finite boundaries, and preparation errors. We address this problem in a one-probe model on a prescribed square candidate lattice, combining a generalized Rokhsar--Kivelson parent, spectral reduction, adiabatic preparation, and local dynamical estimates. Assuming a supplied coherent graph ground state, we construct a finite-source wave packet and a hopping ramp that populate an isolated branch with strictly positive group velocity. We prove an unconditional arrival probability of at least $5/8$ in a specified receiver region of a sufficiently large finite open square. Explicit bounds on local joint-state and Hamiltonian errors retain a lower probability of $9/16$, without requiring global many-body state closeness or postselection on graph measurements. Exact arithmetic certificates and a separate small-system numerical diagnostic support the quantitative analysis. The construction provides a model-specific benchmark for transport and readout in fluctuating quantum networks, linking a propagation mechanism to an observable lower bound and identifying the local error budgets required to preserve it. It distinguishes suppression of unwanted influence from guaranteed signal delivery, a useful separation for quantum-network and emergent-geometry models. The resource estimates are conservative, graph-state supply is assumed, and the result does not establish background-free geometry or gravitational dynamics.
one_liner: A controlled wave packet achieves provably unconditional transport across a finite quantum graph with fluctuating edges.
why_it_matters: The result converts spectral propagation into a guaranteed receiver probability with explicit local error budgets and no graph postselection.
detailed_summary: For a one-probe model on a fluctuating square candidate lattice, the authors combine a Rokhsar–Kivelson parent Hamiltonian, spectral reduction, adiabatic preparation, and local dynamical bounds. Assuming a supplied coherent graph ground state, a finite-source packet is loaded into an isolated positive-group-velocity branch. The receiver-region arrival probability is at least 5/8 ideally and remains at least 9/16 under bounded local state and Hamiltonian errors, without global-state closeness or graph-measurement postselection.
main_result: The construction guarantees unconditional receiver arrival with probability at least 5/8, or 9/16 under specified local errors.
application_angle: It provides a quantitative benchmark for reliable preparation, transport, and readout in fluctuating quantum-network architectures.

title: Stress-controlled avoided-crossing evolution of an optical microresonator induced by inter-fibre side coupling
abstract: Analogies between quantum mechanics and photonics provide a powerful means of transferring concepts and phenomena between the two fields. Photonic analogues offer a distinctive advantage by allowing us to engineer and continuously vary parameters fixed by the microscopic structure of quantum systems, revealing richer behaviour. Building on these analogies, the recent demonstration of widely tunable microresonators formed by side coupling between optical fibres marked a significant advance in the development of reconfigurable resonant photonic systems. However, those methods offered no direct way to reach the centre of the avoided crossing, where the uncoupled fibre cutoff frequencies coincide and the modes hybridise most strongly. Here, we introduce an additional tuning degree of freedom by axially stretching a straight fibre coupled to a bent fibre. At essentially fixed coupling geometry, this lets us sweep the detuning between their uncoupled cutoff frequencies through zero. As the avoided crossing is approached, the induced microresonator's resonance band widens. Beyond the crossing, the band narrows and, strikingly, appears to "hang" below the stretched fibre's rising cutoff frequency. Our experimental results agree with coupled-mode theory and indicate the feasibility of 100 MHz-scale control of the straight-fibre cutoff frequency and the resonator spectral height over a tuning range of about 100 GHz, using a relative elongation of order $10^{-3}$.
one_liner: Axial strain sweeps an inter-fibre microresonator through its avoided crossing while retaining nearly fixed coupling geometry.
why_it_matters: The method enables continuous, mechanically controlled access to maximum mode hybridization and roughly 100 GHz of spectral tuning.
detailed_summary: A straight optical fibre is axially stretched while side-coupled to a bent fibre, independently tuning cutoff-frequency detuning through zero. The resonance band broadens toward the avoided crossing, then narrows and appears pinned below the rising straight-fibre cutoff beyond it. Measurements agree with coupled-mode theory and indicate 100 MHz-scale cutoff and spectral-height control across about 100 GHz using relative elongation near 10^-3.
platform_or_system: side-coupled straight and bent optical fibres
main_result: Stress tuning drives the coupled-fibre resonator through zero detuning and controls its spectrum over an approximately 100 GHz range.
application_angle: The reconfigurable resonance control could support tunable fibre photonics, precision spectral filtering, and strain-sensitive optical devices.

title: Hierarchical interfacial anchoring for durable perovskite solar cells
abstract: Although inverted perovskite solar cells now deliver certified efficiencies approaching their single-junction limits, their practical deployment remains constrained by the thermo-mechanical fragility of buried interfaces under realistic temperature fluctuations. Here, we identify thermo-mechanically driven, stress-accumulation-dominated adhesion failure at self-assembled monolayer-based buried interfaces as a critical failure mode in inverted perovskite solar cells. To address this issue, we propose an interfacial robustness design strategy based on a homometallic halide pretreatment, which constructs a chemically compatible and highly anchorable interfacial environment on transparent conductive oxides to guide the ordered assembly of SAMs. This interfacial treatment increases the density of surface hydroxyl species and enables hierarchical multipoint interfacial anchoring dominated by metal-oxygen coordination, with Cl- induced hydrogen-bonding interactions acting cooperatively, thereby enhancing anchoring robustness and improving tolerance to thermo-mechanical stress accumulation. With this interfacial strategy, the devices achieve a power conversion efficiency of 27.3% (26.9% certified) and retain 94% of their initial efficiency after 400 temperature cycles between -40 and 85 degrees C (ISOS-T-3). These results demonstrate that rational regulation of buried interfacial anchoring architectures can simultaneously enhance device efficiency and long-term operational reliability, offering a viable pathway toward high-efficiency and durable perovskite photovoltaics.
one_liner: Hierarchical chemical anchoring strengthens buried interfaces in inverted perovskite cells, combining 26.9% certified efficiency with thermal durability.
why_it_matters: It targets thermo-mechanical interface failure directly and preserves 94% efficiency after 400 cycles from -40 to 85 °C.
detailed_summary: The authors identify stress-accumulation-driven adhesion failure at self-assembled-monolayer buried interfaces as a key weakness of inverted perovskite cells. A homometallic halide pretreatment increases surface hydroxyl density and promotes multipoint metal–oxygen coordination with cooperative chloride-mediated hydrogen bonding. Devices reach 27.3% power-conversion efficiency, 26.9% certified, and retain 94% after 400 ISOS-T-3 cycles between -40 and 85 °C.
main_result: The treated cells deliver 26.9% certified efficiency and retain 94% of initial performance after 400 severe temperature cycles.
application_angle: The interface design addresses a deployment-critical reliability bottleneck while maintaining near-record photovoltaic efficiency.

title: A Hardware-Trained Generative Quantum Eigensolver for Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization of Organotin Hydroxides up to 70 Qubits
abstract: Quantum hardware can provide feedback for training circuit generators beyond the reach of exact classical simulation. We train generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) policies, transformers conditioned on molecular descriptors, to generate the state-preparation circuits for sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD). Training runs first on a noiseless simulator and then with the IBM Heron processor ibm_kobe inside the loop, at 46 and 70 qubits ($1.2 \times 10^8$ shots for the four main training runs). A classical CCSD(T) reference energy of the training molecules enters only an admission gate and two auxiliary reward terms. During hardware training, a reward penalty prevents collapse to circuits that sample only the Hartree-Fock determinant. Policies trained on transition-metal complexes are applied without retraining to Sn(OH)$_3$-Me and its hydrates, minimal models of organotin photoresists for extreme-ultraviolet lithography, from 32 to 70 qubits. After one round of hardware sampling, followed by classical ranking and recovery of the cached counts with the molecular Hamiltonian and no further QPU calls, 27 of 28 runs at 46-70 qubits are within 15 mHa of the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) reference (median 4.5 mHa), and in all eight runs with an untrained control the trained policy is more accurate. At 56-70 qubits the selected circuits use 34-72 times fewer two-qubit gates than the local unitary cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) circuit transpiled for the same device. These results demonstrate that circuit generators can be trained with quantum hardware at 70 qubits.
one_liner: A hardware-trained circuit generator enables sample-based quantum diagonalization of organotin hydroxides on IBM Heron processors up to 70 qubits.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates 70-qubit hardware-in-the-loop training, accurate transferred chemistry predictions, and sharply reduced two-qubit gate counts.
detailed_summary: Transformer policies are trained to generate state-preparation circuits for sample-based quantum diagonalization, first in simulation and then with the 46- and 70-qubit IBM Heron processor ibm_kobe in the loop. Applied without retraining to organotin hydroxides and hydrates, 27 of 28 hardware runs lie within 15 mHa of DMRG, with a 4.5 mHa median error. At 56–70 qubits, selected circuits use 34–72 times fewer two-qubit gates than device-transpiled LUCJ circuits.
main_result: Hardware-trained policies achieved near-DMRG energies on 27 of 28 runs up to 70 qubits while using far fewer entangling gates.
application_angle: The method supports hardware-efficient electronic-structure modeling for chemically relevant materials such as organotin EUV photoresists.

title: Eigenmode and field imaging of a compact superconducting resonator array
abstract: Superconducting resonator arrays can tailor the photonic environment for quantum information processing, but conventional port-based microwave spectroscopy alone does not resolve the rich spatial structure of their modes. Here, we apply laser scanning microscopy (LSM) and nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center magnetometry to a two-dimensional superconducting resonator array consisting of 33 lumped-element resonators arranged in a honeycomb lattice hosting topological edge states. We demonstrate the complementarity of the two techniques: LSM images the eigenmodes, while NV magnetometry maps the local microwave magnetic field amplitude. Using this spatial information, we experimentally validate that the realized lattice matches the design, we image the topological edge state and measure its sublattice polarization, and place an upper bound of $\approx0.3\%$ on the relative on-site frequency disorder in the lattice. Our work establishes a combined spatial characterization approach for compact superconducting resonator arrays with applications in hybrid spin--superconducting quantum systems.
one_liner: Laser scanning microscopy and NV magnetometry spatially resolve eigenmodes and microwave fields in a 33-resonator superconducting lattice.
why_it_matters: The combined imaging validates lattice realization, reveals a topological edge state, and bounds on-site frequency disorder below about 0.3%.
detailed_summary: The experiment studies 33 lumped-element superconducting resonators arranged as a honeycomb lattice supporting topological edge states. Laser scanning microscopy images eigenmode structure, while NV-center magnetometry maps local microwave magnetic-field amplitude. Spatial measurements verify the fabricated lattice, resolve the edge state and its sublattice polarization, and constrain relative on-site frequency disorder to approximately 0.3%.
main_result: Complementary spatial probes directly imaged the topological mode and microwave field while quantifying sub-percent lattice disorder.
application_angle: The approach enables device-level diagnostics and field mapping for superconducting photonic lattices and hybrid spin–superconductor hardware.

title: Analog quantum approximate optimization algorithm for solving the weighted MaxCut problem on three-dimensional single-atom Rydberg array
abstract: We theoretically investigate an analog implementation of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) for the weighted maximum cut problem (MaxCut) problem. The protocol uses a three-dimensional array of individually trapped Rydberg atoms driven by globally addressed laser pulses, with site-dependent detunings applied near the Rydberg resonance. As benchmarks, we consider twenty randomly weighted 3-regular graphs with 12 vertices each. Problem weights are encoded directly in the interatomic interaction energies by choosing appropriate three-dimensional atom positions. We compare two parameter-optimization strategies: discretized quantum annealing and warm-start initialization using a graph neural network (GNN). The combined optimization strategy creates a portfolio that outperforms the Goemans-Williamson (GW) rounding almost in all instances in the noiseless case. We analyze the sampling statistics and the total pulse-time cost of both approaches. Finally, we emulate the performance of the optimized schedules on quantum trajectories using a realistic error model of the Aquila neutral-atom quantum processor.
one_liner: Analog QAOA maps weighted MaxCut instances directly onto the geometry and interactions of a 3D Rydberg-atom array.
why_it_matters: The study connects graph embedding, learned schedule initialization, realistic neutral-atom noise, and pulse-time costs in a hardware-oriented optimization workflow.
detailed_summary: The proposal encodes graph weights in Rydberg interaction energies by positioning 12 individually trapped atoms in three dimensions and applies globally addressed pulses with site-dependent detunings. Across twenty weighted 3-regular graphs, a portfolio combining discretized quantum annealing and GNN warm starts surpasses Goemans-Williamson rounding on almost every noiseless instance. Quantum-trajectory emulation with an Aquila-inspired error model evaluates how the optimized schedules may perform on realistic hardware.
main_result: A combined annealing and GNN-initialized analog-QAOA portfolio outperforms Goemans-Williamson rounding on nearly all tested noiseless instances.
application_angle: Direct geometric encoding could support hardware-native combinatorial optimization on programmable neutral-atom processors.

title: Coherent Optical Readout of Neutral-Atom Qubits via Homodyne Detection of Resonant Fluorescence
abstract: Fast, non-destructive qubit readout is essential for repeated sampling, mid-circuit measurement, and fault-tolerant neutral-atom quantum processing, but camera-based fluorescence detection introduces electronic latency beyond fluorescence-collection time. We propose coherent readout of the state-dependent resonant fluorescence using balanced homodyne detection with photodiodes. An analytic model quantifies the effect of atomic motion on the time-integrated quadrature signal and noise, showing that harmonic motion causes phase averaging while photon recoils produce trajectory-dependent signal fluctuations; the competition between signal accumulation and motion-induced decoherence sets an optimal detection time. Three-dimensional Monte Carlo simulations validate the model and predict state-detection fidelities exceeding 99% within 100 $μ\mathrm{s}$ for experimentally realistic parameters. These results establish the readout conditions and physical constraints for rapid coherent fluorescence readout of neutral-atom qubits.
one_liner: Balanced homodyne detection could read neutral-atom qubits from coherent resonant fluorescence with over 99% fidelity in under 100 μs.
why_it_matters: Replacing camera readout with fast photodiodes could reduce electronic latency for repeated sampling, mid-circuit measurement, and fault-tolerant operation.
detailed_summary: The authors model balanced-homodyne measurement of state-dependent resonant fluorescence, including harmonic-motion phase averaging and recoil-induced trajectory fluctuations. The competition between coherent signal accumulation and motional decoherence produces an optimal detection interval. Three-dimensional Monte Carlo simulations predict experimentally realistic state-detection fidelities above 99% within 100 μs.
platform_or_system: Neutral-atom qubits with balanced homodyne readout
main_result: Simulations predict greater than 99% state-detection fidelity within 100 μs using coherent fluorescence homodyne detection.
application_angle: Low-latency photodiode readout could enable faster feedback and mid-circuit measurements in neutral-atom quantum processors.

title: Additively manufactured ceramic platforms for miniaturized optical frequency references and robust atomic sensor systems
abstract: Transferring atomic quantum sensors from laboratory-scale physics packages to compact, alignment-free sensor heads suitable for field and space deployment requires a structural platform that combines mechanical, thermal, and optical functionality within a single, manufacturable component. We present such a platform based on additively manufactured technical ceramics: lithography-based ceramic manufacturing is used to fabricate monolithic micro-optical benches with application-specific mounting geometries, while high-precision active alignment and adhesive bonding realize long-term stable optical assemblies through micro-integration. As a first system-level demonstrator, we present a micro-integrated optical frequency reference based on Doppler-free spectroscopy of the rubidium D2 line, integrated within a 6 mL Al2O3 module. A laser stabilized to the reference reaches a fractional frequency instability of $3\times10^{-12}$ at 1 s. We extend the platform to a compact optically pumped magnetometer, exploiting the magnetic cleanliness and tailored thermal properties of high-purity ceramics for a 7 mL sensor head with picotesla sensitivity aimed at space-borne biomagnetometry, and to a micro-integrated optical dipole trap with active MEMS-mirror beam steering for cold-atom manipulation. Together, these demonstrators show that ceramic additive manufacturing and optical micro-integration form a versatile, robust platform for compact atomic sensor systems in field and space applications.
one_liner: 3D-printed ceramic microbenches integrate compact rubidium references, picotesla magnetometers, and steerable cold-atom traps.
why_it_matters: A common monolithic platform addresses alignment, thermal management, magnetic cleanliness, and manufacturability for deployable atomic sensors.
detailed_summary: Lithography-based ceramic manufacturing creates monolithic micro-optical benches with application-specific mounts, followed by active alignment and adhesive micro-integration. A 6 mL Al2O3 rubidium-D2 reference achieves fractional frequency instability of 3×10^-12 at 1 s. The platform also supports a 7 mL optically pumped magnetometer with picotesla sensitivity and a MEMS-steered optical dipole trap.
main_result: The platform delivers a 6 mL optical frequency reference at 3×10^-12 instability at 1 s and extends to compact magnetometry and cold-atom trapping.
application_angle: The robust, alignment-free modules target fieldable and space-compatible clocks, biomagnetometers, and cold-atom instruments.

title: Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM): A Unified Learning-Based Framework for Noise Resilience in Quantum Machine Learning
abstract: Error mitigation stands between variational quantum algorithms and useful results on today's noisy hardware, yet in practice a mitigation method is usually chosen once, by hand, and applied unchanged for the life of an experiment. This is a poor fit for quantum machine learning (QML), where the circuit and the noise drift as training proceeds, so the best strategy in one regime is often wrong in another. We present a generalized form of Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM), which treats the choice of mitigation technique as an online decision made from an algorithm's own feedback. A single contextual-bandit controller observes signals any variational algorithm already produces, such as fidelity, entropy, reward or loss, and gradient behavior, and selects among Zero-Noise Extrapolation, Probabilistic Error Cancellation, Measurement Error Mitigation, Dynamical Decoupling, and circuit optimization per step. Because it depends only on this shared feedback interface, the framework applies unchanged across supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and hybrid quantum-classical learning. Evaluated on five paradigms across 80 algorithm-and-noise conditions, adaptive selection reaches 95.5% of an oracle that always picks the best technique and significantly outperforms all six fixed strategies (Friedman $χ^{2}=92.18$, $p\approx1.1\times10^{-17}$; pairwise Wilcoxon $p<4\times10^{-6}$). The learned policy is noise-aware: its favored technique shifts as depolarizing and readout error rise. On noise models from eight real IBM devices, APGEM tracks the oracle almost exactly (99.9% of oracle utility) at a flat cost of roughly $1.3\times10^{4}$ shots from three to eight qubits.
one_liner: APGEM uses a contextual bandit to select error-mitigation methods online as quantum-learning circuits and noise conditions evolve.
why_it_matters: Adaptive mitigation can avoid committing an entire noisy-hardware experiment to one technique when training dynamics and device errors change.
detailed_summary: APGEM observes algorithm-native signals such as fidelity, entropy, loss, reward, and gradient behavior, then chooses among five mitigation families and circuit optimization at each step. Across 80 algorithm-and-noise conditions, it reaches 95.5% of oracle utility and significantly outperforms six fixed strategies. On noise models derived from eight IBM devices, it attains 99.9% of oracle utility with roughly 1.3×10^4 shots for three-to-eight-qubit cases.
main_result: Adaptive policy selection achieves 95.5% of oracle utility overall and 99.9% on eight IBM-device noise models.
application_angle: The method offers an automated mitigation layer for QML workloads operating under drifting, hardware-specific noise.

title: Correlations carried and controlled by coupled non-Markovian environments
abstract: An environment can retain quantum information and carry it between spatially separated systems. Describing the combined influence of these processes requires a treatment of both environmental memory and spatial correlations. Here, we formulate a local hierarchy of pure states for quantum systems coupled to spatially correlated, non-Markovian environments whose modes themselves exchange excitations. We use this method to describe the reduced spin dynamics of a chain of locally coupled Rabi spin--cavity pairs motivated by cavity-QED implementations, where photon hopping in the eliminated cavity environment generates correlations and entanglement between otherwise isolated spins. Monitoring intermediate cavities and feeding their measurement records back onto the corresponding spins further enhances correlations between endpoint spins that receive no direct feedback. The delayed response when feedback starts, and continued entanglement growth after it stops, support a mechanism in which coherent environmental dynamics carry the effects of earlier feedback to the endpoint spins. Finally, tensor-network simulations of XXZ and Heisenberg chains show how environmental transport changes many-body correlation patterns. These results show how coupled environments and local feedback can control correlations between distant spins. We provide a numerically exact stochastic pure-state framework for simulating these processes, opening up avenues to explore the coherent and dissipative control of interacting non-Markovian many-body systems.
one_liner: Coupled cavity environments and local feedback can transport quantum information and enhance entanglement between distant spins.
why_it_matters: The framework turns environmental memory and transport from unwanted effects into possible resources for nonlocal correlation control.
detailed_summary: A local hierarchy of pure states models spatially correlated non-Markovian environments whose modes exchange excitations. In chains of Rabi spin-cavity pairs, photon hopping through eliminated cavities generates spin correlations, while monitoring and feedback at intermediate cavities further enhance endpoint entanglement. Tensor-network calculations for XXZ and Heisenberg chains show how environmental transport reshapes many-body correlations.
main_result: Numerically exact simulations show that coupled environments and local feedback can generate and strengthen correlations between otherwise isolated distant spins.
application_angle: Engineered reservoirs could provide coherent and dissipative routes to distributing correlations in cavity-QED and many-body quantum devices.

title: Quantum propagation of vibrational excitation in harmonically confined trapped-ion crystal
abstract: Vibrational excitations, or phonons, in trapped ions serve as useful resources for quantum information processing, including quantum simulation and computing. Localized excitations of ions' vibrational motion (local phonons) can be used for simulating quantum particles that propagate over a system. Here, we experimentally investigate the propagation of a localized vibrational excitation in a one-dimensional trapped-ion crystal. A 10-ion crystal confined in a harmonic potential is used. It is found that inhomogeneity in the spacing between the ions leads to characteristic behaviors such as adjacent hopping and global movement. A comparison of the experimental results with numerical simulations shows agreement up to fine details. The system explored here may be extended to many-body systems of bosonic particles as well as more complex quasiparticles.
one_liner: A localized phonon was launched and tracked across a 10-ion crystal, revealing transport shaped by nonuniform ion spacing.
why_it_matters: Directly controlled phonon propagation provides a hardware testbed for bosonic transport, quasiparticle dynamics, and trapped-ion quantum simulation.
detailed_summary: The experiment initializes a localized vibrational excitation in a harmonically confined one-dimensional crystal of ten ions and observes its subsequent propagation. Spatially varying ion separations produce characteristic adjacent hopping and global motion. Numerical simulations reproduce the experimental dynamics in fine detail, supporting extension toward interacting bosons and more complex quasiparticles.
main_result: The experiment resolves localized phonon propagation and quantitatively reproduces spacing-induced adjacent hopping and global motion.
application_angle: The platform can emulate quantum-particle transport and may scale toward many-body bosonic and quasiparticle simulations.

title: Maximal Violation of Mermin Inequality for Commuting von Neumann Algebras and Multipartite Vacuum Entanglement in QFT
abstract: Summers and Werner proved that Bell inequalities are violated maximally and generically in the vacuum of a relativistic quantum field theory in [S. J. Summers and R. Werner, Commun. Math. Phys. 110 (1987), 247-259]. Their criterion concerns two-party case, that is, there are two algebras of quantum observables: one algebra and its commutant. In this case, the maximal CHSH value is converged to in every normal state exactly when the algebra is strongly stable. In the paper, we study the corresponding question for three and more mutually commuting von Neumann algebras. We focus on the multipartite Mermin inequalities instead of CHSH ones. For the tripartite Mermin functional we show that maximal violation in every normal state is equivalent to the existence of a common sequence of asymptotic GHZ stabilizers. Strong stability of each local factor is an necessary condition for maximal violation, and a joint embedding of an infinite GHZ tensor product is sufficient. Counterexamples show that strong stability and type III_1 of the individual algebras, even together with tripartite duality, do not suffice to arrive at the maximal violation. The results are also extended to n>=3 parties.
one_liner: Characterizes maximal multipartite Mermin violations for mutually commuting von Neumann algebras using asymptotic GHZ stabilizers.
why_it_matters: The results clarify the operator-algebraic conditions required for robust multipartite vacuum entanglement in relativistic quantum field theory.
detailed_summary: The work generalizes the Summers–Werner bipartite Bell-violation criterion to three or more mutually commuting von Neumann algebras using Mermin inequalities. For three parties, maximal violation in every normal state is equivalent to a common sequence of asymptotic GHZ stabilizers. Strong stability of each local factor is necessary, while embedding an infinite GHZ tensor product is sufficient; individual type III_1 structure and tripartite duality alone are not sufficient.
platform_or_system: Commuting local algebras in relativistic QFT
main_result: It establishes necessary and sufficient operator-algebraic structures for state-independent maximal multipartite Mermin violation.
application_angle: The framework informs rigorous analyses of multipartite entanglement resources in quantum fields and relativistic quantum-information protocols.

title: CV-TF-QKD
abstract: We introduce a continuous-variable version of twin-field quantum key distribution, using independent Gaussian-modulated coherent states and an untrusted single-photon relay. Full-record reconciliation and a binary phase-disclosure protocol achieve nearly equal asymptotic key rates against collective attacks. At fixed weak input-referred excess noise per arm, both rates per relay use scale as $\sqrtη$, where $η$ is the end-to-end transmissivity. For phase disclosure, we establish composable security against general coherent attacks using a bounded test of preparation intensities and sign-parity complementarity. For specified apparatus parameters, finite-key calculations incorporating detector inefficiency, dark counts, phase fluctuations, and reference overhead predict rates exceeding the pure-loss and matched thermal-loss repeaterless bounds. These results extend the twin-field advantage to Gaussian-modulated continuous-variable quantum cryptography.
one_liner: A continuous-variable twin-field QKD protocol achieves square-root transmissivity scaling using Gaussian coherent states and an untrusted relay.
why_it_matters: Finite-key modeling predicts rates beyond repeaterless pure- and thermal-loss bounds under specified realistic detector, noise, and phase parameters.
detailed_summary: The protocol sends independently Gaussian-modulated coherent states to an untrusted single-photon relay and supports full-record reconciliation or binary phase disclosure. Both variants attain asymptotic key-rate scaling proportional to the square root of end-to-end transmissivity under fixed weak input-referred excess noise. The phase-disclosure construction receives composable security against coherent attacks, and finite-key calculations include detector inefficiency, dark counts, phase fluctuations, and reference overhead.
main_result: The proposed CV-TF-QKD schemes achieve square-root-loss scaling and can surpass matched repeaterless bounds with modeled practical apparatus parameters.
application_angle: It offers a route to longer-distance continuous-variable secure links using coherent-state transmitters and an untrusted central relay.

title: Dynamical GKP codes
abstract: Dynamical codes protect quantum information with sequences of measurements, generalizing the stabilizer formalism of static codes. However, the dynamical formalism has been developed exclusively for qubit systems. While Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes are promising candidates for quantum computing that encode qubits in the continuous phase space of oscillators, no dynamical formalism has been developed for them. In this work, we bridge this gap and introduce dynamical GKP codes, combining continuous-variable lattice encodings with time-dependent translation measurement dynamics. To obtain the update rules and the distance of a given measurement sequence, we first generalize GKP codes to subsystem GKP codes using scaled symplectic lattices. Building on this structure, we adapt the ancestry, detector, and benign-error machinery originally developed for dynamical qubit codes. From this construction, we obtain a general and efficient method to compute the syndrome and distance of a dynamical GKP code from a persistent stabilizer lattice and a bounded inference window. We illustrate the framework with the example of the two-mode square-hexagonal Floquet GKP code. This code has reduced measurement weight compared to both the square and hexagonal GKP codes, while combining their set of logical gates, resulting in easier implementation of the full single-qubit Clifford group. Finally, we show that measurements with irrational symplectic overlap, which have no analog in discrete qubit codes, reduce to destructive homodyne detection in the single-mode case. These results extend an important qubit-code tool to continuous-variable systems and identify a new bridge between discrete stabilizer measurements and continuous homodyne detection.
one_liner: Introduces dynamical GKP codes that combine oscillator lattice encodings with time-dependent translation measurements and efficient distance tracking.
why_it_matters: The framework lowers measurement weight while retaining useful logical gates, potentially simplifying continuous-variable fault-tolerant hardware.
detailed_summary: The authors extend dynamical-code machinery from qubits to GKP-encoded oscillators by defining subsystem GKP codes on scaled symplectic lattices. Persistent stabilizer lattices and bounded inference windows provide efficient syndrome and code-distance calculations. A two-mode square-hexagonal Floquet GKP example reduces measurement weight while combining the logical gates of square and hexagonal codes, and irrational symplectic overlaps connect to destructive homodyne detection.
main_result: A general dynamical GKP formalism is derived, including efficient syndrome and distance rules and a lower-weight two-mode Floquet construction.
application_angle: The construction may reduce measurement complexity for bosonic quantum processors while supporting the full single-qubit Clifford group.

title: Cross-Platform Benchmarking of GHZ-State Generation in Quantum Processors via Cloud Services
abstract: Quantum computing has rapidly evolved into a diverse ecosystem of hardware platforms that differ in their underlying technologies and operational characteristics. Consequently, benchmarking has become essential for identifying the strengths of quantum processors, comparing their performance, and enabling informed decisions when selecting the most appropriate quantum computing platform for specific applications. In this work, we benchmark nine commercially accessible quantum processors from five vendors, spanning superconducting and trapped-ion technologies, using the multipartite entanglement benchmark from the QuSquare suite. All experiments were performed through remote cloud-access services, with the default compilation of each provider and without error mitigation, reflecting the performance experienced by end users. The benchmark estimates the fidelity of Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger (GHZ) states by direct fidelity estimation and searches for the largest GHZ state whose fidelity is compatible, within the statistical error, with the genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) threshold $F=1/2$. Our results reveal a substantial gap between the total number of physical qubits available on a processor and the size of the largest GHZ state passing the benchmark: the best superconducting processors reach $N^*=27$ and $N^*=24$ qubits, less than a quarter of their registers, whereas the 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes with its full register. We further show that median calibration data are poor predictors of the benchmark outcome, and that the reported sizes depend strongly on the statistical decision rule: requiring certified GME reduces the number of devices that succeed at any tested size from nine to four. These results provide a baseline for future cross-platform benchmarking of quantum processors.
one_liner: Cloud experiments benchmark GHZ-state generation across nine superconducting and trapped-ion processors from five vendors.
why_it_matters: The study exposes the gap between advertised qubit count and usable multipartite entanglement, while showing that calibration medians predict performance poorly.
detailed_summary: Nine commercial processors are tested through provider cloud services using default compilation and no error mitigation. Direct fidelity estimation identifies the largest GHZ state compatible with the genuine multipartite-entanglement threshold of one half. Leading superconducting devices reach 27 and 24 qubits, whereas a 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes across its full register; stricter certification reduces successful devices from nine to four.
main_result: The benchmark finds maximum passing GHZ sizes of 27 and 24 on leading superconducting systems and all 12 qubits on a trapped-ion system.
application_angle: The results provide end-user evidence for hardware selection and a reproducible baseline for tracking processor-level entanglement performance.

title: Secure Information Flow in Quantum Programs
abstract: Information-flow security aims to prevent the leakage of confidential information through program execution. This problem becomes fundamentally subtler for quantum programs, because their states may involve superposition and entanglement, and their executions may involve intricate interactions between classical and quantum variables. This paper develops semantic foundations and verification methods for secure information flow in quantum programs. We formulate two notions of information-flow security. The first is a noninterference-based definition that naturally generalizes its classical counterpart. The second is a simulation-based definition that explicitly models an attacker, providing a clear operational interpretation of security. We prove that these two notions are equivalent. To verify the information-flow security of quantum programs, we develop a proof framework based on quantum Hoare logic. A key challenge is that the standard self-composition technique, which expresses information-flow security in Hoare logic by composing a program with a renamed copy of itself, fails in the quantum setting due to an obstruction analogous to the no-cloning theorem. To overcome this challenge, we introduce self-conjugation, a novel technique that leverages the deferred measurement principle and properties of unitary operations. We demonstrate our framework on examples drawn from the quantum one-time pad, quantum error correction, and anonymous entanglement generation.
one_liner: Develops equivalent semantic definitions and a quantum Hoare-logic method for detecting confidential-information leakage in quantum programs.
why_it_matters: Its self-conjugation technique enables security verification despite the no-cloning obstruction that breaks classical self-composition methods.
detailed_summary: The paper defines noninterference-based and attacker-simulation notions of information-flow security for hybrid classical-quantum programs and proves their equivalence. It introduces self-conjugation, using deferred measurement and unitary structure to replace classical self-composition, which is invalid for unknown quantum states. The proof framework is demonstrated on quantum one-time pads, quantum error correction, and anonymous entanglement generation.
main_result: A quantum Hoare-logic framework verifies information-flow security using self-conjugation, with equivalent noninterference and simulation guarantees.
application_angle: The method can support security auditing of control software and protocols running on quantum processors and communication systems.

title: Quantum-Enhanced QSAR for DYRK1A: Evaluating Complementary and Utility QPU-Derived Molecular Representations
abstract: In drug discovery, hit identification selects a limited set of compounds for experimental evaluation from a larger collection of candidates. Because laboratory screening capacity is limited, that choice determines which chemical series continue into further investigation. A hit that is not assayed does not enter confirmation or the analog series, and that chemical series is not opened. For the DYRK1A kinase, the same test molecules were scored from a tabular representation of molecular descriptors and from a vector measured on a quantum processor, with the same RBF-SVM. The question is whether the two models propose the same set for experimental evaluation: they propose different compounds. The model on the vector measured on the quantum processor includes compounds that the tabular representation leaves out, and among them are already-labeled actives. The tabular representation includes actives that the vector measured on the quantum processor leaves out. What is reported is that set: who enters, with what label, and whether published chemistry already mentions it. No formal quantum advantage is claimed, nor a mechanism for why the two vectors separate differently. Those compounds fall within the neighborhood that both representations already cover; what changes is which model marks them active. From that follows the cost of predictive disagreement: each model would send a different chemical series to experimental evaluation.
one_liner: Compares classical molecular descriptors with QPU-measured vectors for DYRK1A screening and finds materially different predicted hit sets.
why_it_matters: The QPU-derived representation recovers labeled actives omitted by the descriptor model, showing how representation choice redirects scarce laboratory assays.
detailed_summary: The same DYRK1A compounds are classified by identical RBF-SVM models using either tabular molecular descriptors or vectors measured on a quantum processor. The resulting hit lists disagree: each representation includes labeled actives omitted by the other and would advance different chemical series. The study reports selection utility and published-chemistry context without claiming quantum advantage or a causal separation mechanism.
main_result: QPU-measured and classical descriptor representations produce complementary DYRK1A hit selections, including different known actives.
application_angle: The approach could diversify compound triage when experimental screening capacity is limited, although prospective validation remains necessary.

title: Electrical Stark Tuning and In Situ Field Sensing of $V_{2}$ Silicon Vacancies in a 4H-SiC a-Plane Lateral pin-Diode
abstract: Silicon carbide has emerged as a highly promising platform for scalable quantum technologies, with the silicon vacancy serving as a robust spin qubit and quantum sensor. However, conventional c-plane 4H-SiC restricts the experimental scheme and resonant optical excitation to the sample's geometry. The usage of a-plane substrates enables more versatile resonant optical access to the color center through the wafer surface. Here, we demonstrate the electrical control and optical addressability of $V_{2}$ (cubic lattice site) silicon vacancies within the intrinsic region of lateral pin-diodes fabricated on a-plane 4H-SiC wafers using a scalable complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) process. Despite extensive semiconductor processing, the integrated color centers exhibit good optical quality, evidenced by narrow optical transition linewidths below 80 MHz at zero bias. These embedded quantum sensors are utilized for in situ measurement of local electric fields at cryogenic temperatures via the Stark effect. Comparisons with macroscopic technology computer-aided design simulations reveal the value of these integrated quantum sensors to help understand cryogenic device behavior, for example in predicting highly localized field crowding. Furthermore, to address the spectral indistinguishability required for quantum networks, we precisely tune the zero-phonon line (ZPL) of individual emitters via the reverse-bias Stark effect. This successfully compensates for the spectral variations of distinct emitters. Following the relaxation of transient charge fluctuations, the Stark-tuned emitters exhibit spectral stability over measurement periods exceeding four hours. Our results establish a-plane 4H-SiC as a robust platform for future interference experiments and quantum photonic integrated circuits.
one_liner: CMOS-fabricated lateral diodes electrically tune and locally sense fields with optically narrow silicon vacancies in a-plane 4H-SiC.
why_it_matters: It combines stable emitter tuning, cryogenic field mapping, and surface-accessible optics in a scalable platform for indistinguishable photons and integrated quantum devices.
detailed_summary: Individual V2 silicon vacancies embedded in the intrinsic region of CMOS-processed a-plane 4H-SiC lateral pin diodes retain optical linewidths below 80 MHz at zero bias. Their Stark shifts map local cryogenic electric fields and expose field crowding beyond macroscopic device simulations. Reverse bias also compensates emitter-to-emitter ZPL variation, with spectral stability exceeding four hours after transient charge relaxation.
platform_or_system: V2 centers in a-plane 4H-SiC lateral pin diodes
main_result: The devices provide narrow-line optical access, in situ electric-field sensing, and stable electrical matching of distinct emitters' zero-phonon lines.
application_angle: The platform supports cryogenic semiconductor diagnostics, indistinguishable-photon generation, interference experiments, and scalable quantum photonic circuits.

title: Dynamical Casimir emission from Floquet-driven Landau polaritons: Gauge invariance forbids a superradiant phase transition
abstract: Ultrastrong light--matter coupling of linear systems, such as Landau polaritons formed by a two-dimensional electron gas in a terahertz cavity, is described by the bosonic Hopfield model, and gauge invariance forbids a superradiant phase transition (SRPT). Modulating the magnetic field alone has been predicted to enhance the cycle-averaged coupling and induce a Floquet SRPT. We develop an exact theory of periodically driven Landau polaritons. Including the electric field induced by the modulated flux (Faraday's law), the problem reduces exactly, by Kohn's theorem, to the electronic center-of-mass mode coupled to the cavity, whose Hamiltonian is a sum of squares at every instant. A theorem of Krein then guarantees stability to all orders above a computable drive frequency, the Krein frequency, for which we give a self-contained proof. Below it, the system is stable except within resonance tongues where the drive creates pairs from the vacuum, the dynamical Casimir effect. At high drive frequency the electrons experience the mean field plus a ponderomotive trap (the Fock--Darwin problem), not an enhanced coupling. A gauge theorem excludes a Floquet photon condensate for any band structure, including Kane nonparabolicity, for which we derive a generalized Thomas--Reiche--Kuhn (TRK) sum rule. The predicted transition arises from averaging the coupling in a fixed Landau-level basis, which yields an effective model that violates the TRK sum rule; under driving, gauge invariance also requires the induced Faraday field. The rule to modulate and average the minimal-coupling Hamiltonian, not the parameters of its projection, applies to any linear, minimally coupled system. Instead of an SRPT, magnetic modulation produces dynamical Casimir emission: Faraday-driven polariton--magnetoplasmon pairs at low threshold, and two-color photon pairs with up to 5--10~dB of two-mode squeezing.
one_liner: A gauge-invariant theory replaces the predicted Floquet superradiant transition in driven Landau polaritons with dynamical Casimir pair emission.
