why_it_matters: It corrects an unphysical instability while identifying experimentally useful regimes for correlated terahertz photons and up to 5–10 dB two-mode squeezing.
detailed_summary: The exact driven Hopfield treatment includes the Faraday electric field induced by magnetic-flux modulation and reduces the electronic response to its center-of-mass mode. Gauge invariance and a generalized TRK sum rule forbid a Floquet photon condensate, while Krein analysis gives a high-frequency stability boundary. Below that boundary, resonance tongues enable polariton–magnetoplasmon and two-color photon-pair creation from vacuum.
main_result: Magnetic modulation cannot induce the proposed superradiant phase transition but can generate dynamical Casimir pairs with predicted two-mode squeezing of 5–10 dB.
application_angle: The analysis provides a physically consistent design framework for driven ultrastrong-coupling devices and correlated terahertz photon sources.

title: High-Speed Control of a Fluxonium Qubit via Picosecond Pulses from Josephson Digital Circuits
abstract: We develop a control strategy for fluxonium qubits based on picosecond single-flux-quantum (SFQ) pulses generated by Josephson digital circuits. A major challenge is that SFQ protocols originally designed for transmon control become inefficient for low-frequency fluxonium. In this regime, the asymmetry of flux and charge couplings leads either to excessive leakage or excessively long gate times. We show that this limitation can be overcome by two complementary protocols. The first protocol employs high-frequency SFQ pulse packets applied through the flux channel, offering a simple, analytically transparent, and robust approach for high-fidelity single-qubit control. The second protocol combines phase-shifted flux and charge pulse sequences to enhance the resonant drive and reduce the gate duration. Multilevel simulations demonstrate single-qubit gate fidelities above $99.99\%$; the simpler protocol remains robust under moderate variations of qubit parameters and flux bias, while the combined protocol preserves high fidelity while substantially accelerating the gate. These results establish SFQ-based cryogenic control as a realistic route to fast, accurate, and scalable manipulation of fluxonium qubits.
one_liner: Picosecond SFQ pulse protocols deliver simulated fluxonium single-qubit gates above 99.99% fidelity while addressing leakage and speed limits.
why_it_matters: The work offers a credible route to compact cryogenic digital control that can reduce wiring and latency in scalable fluxonium processors.
detailed_summary: The study adapts single-flux-quantum control to low-frequency fluxonium, where conventional transmon-oriented sequences suffer from leakage or long gates. High-frequency SFQ packets through the flux channel provide a simple and robust protocol. A second protocol combines phase-shifted flux and charge sequences to strengthen resonant driving and shorten the gate, with multilevel simulations exceeding 99.99% fidelity.
platform_or_system: Fluxonium qubit with Josephson SFQ control circuits
main_result: Two SFQ protocols achieve simulated single-qubit fidelities above 99.99%, with one emphasizing robustness and the other substantially reducing gate duration.
application_angle: On-chip cryogenic pulse generation could enable faster, lower-overhead, and more scalable control of fluxonium quantum processors.

title: Implementing rapid reset of superconducting qubits with on-chip dissipation
abstract: Rapid and high-fidelity qubit reset is essential for quantum state initialization and quantum error correction. Conventional reset protocols for superconducting qubits often rely on dissipative elements connected to external circuitry, exposing qubits to thermal noise from higher-temperature environments. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a scalable approach to qubit reset and leakage removal over multiple transmon qubits using dedicated dissipation units comprising resonators coupled to on-chip resistive loads. This architecture provides Purcell protection while isolating the qubits from warmer external circuitry. We achieve a median reset time constant of approximately 48 ns for the $|g\rangle-|e\rangle$ transition, with an effective bath temperature of 30 mK. A 400-ns reset pulse yields residual excited-state populations of $0.29\%$ and $0.67\%$ for qubits initialized in $|g\rangle$ and $|e\rangle$, respectively. We further demonstrate efficient leakage removal from the $|f\rangle$ state, reducing its residual population to $0.51\%$. These results establish a simple, reproducible, and easy-to-integrate approach to dissipation engineering in superconducting quantum processors.
one_liner: On-chip resistive dissipation resets multiple transmons in hundreds of nanoseconds while suppressing leakage and isolating them from warmer circuitry.
why_it_matters: Fast, low-residual reset with integrated cold loads directly supports repeated error-correction cycles and scalable processor initialization.
detailed_summary: Dedicated dissipation units combine resonators with on-chip resistive loads to reset several transmon qubits without coupling them directly to warmer external circuitry. The measured median reset time constant is about 48 ns with a 30 mK effective bath temperature. A 400 ns pulse leaves 0.29% or 0.67% excitation after ground- or excited-state initialization and reduces residual |f⟩ population to 0.51%.
platform_or_system: Multi-transmon chip with resistively loaded reset resonators
main_result: The integrated reset units achieve a 48 ns median decay constant, sub-0.7% residual excitation, and 0.51% residual leakage after active reset.
application_angle: The reproducible architecture can be integrated into superconducting processors for rapid initialization, leakage cleanup, and quantum error correction.

title: Multidimensional Quantum Block Turbo Codes
authors: Jean-Louis de Bougrenet de la Tocnaye
abstract: The theory of turbo iterative decoding was brought into the quantum coding framework through the development of quantum serial turbo codes and quantum block turbo codes. In this paper, we present a theory for multidimensional quantum block turbo codes, a turbo decoding technique for multi layer product codes. We describe its algorithm and simulate the performance for the 3D case on a depolarizing channel.
one_liner: A multidimensional quantum block turbo decoder extends iterative decoding to multilayer product codes and is simulated for a 3D construction.
why_it_matters: The framework broadens quantum product-code decoding options, although its current evidence is limited to depolarizing-channel simulations rather than hardware tests.
detailed_summary: The paper develops a multidimensional extension of quantum block turbo coding for multilayer product codes. It specifies the iterative decoding algorithm and evaluates a three-dimensional instance over a depolarizing channel. The abstract reports simulated performance but does not state numerical thresholds, resource costs, or an experimental implementation.
main_result: A general multidimensional block-turbo decoding method is formulated and demonstrated numerically for a 3D code under depolarizing noise.
application_angle: The method may inform decoders for structured quantum memories and fault-tolerant hardware, pending quantitative comparisons and implementation studies.

title: Finite-Key Readiness and Authentication-Key Replenishment in QKD-Assisted UAV Edge Computing
abstract: A service that needs fresh quantum keys must wait for key release, and may be denied it, before protected computation starts. We quantify this cost for a trusted stationary UAV serving two ground gateways, each obtaining its keys from one finite-key decoy-state BB84 attempt with parameters fixed in advance. A count-level Monte Carlo model, reproduced by a semi-analytic model, links key acceptance to protected upload, computation, and download, including failed attempts and hover energy. At 26~dB effective optical loss, with authentication hashing at its proxy-benchmarked, near-zero cost, fresh keys raise the 95th-percentile completion time of both tasks from 10.37 to 28.65~s; hover energy grows in proportion. The scalar rate models evaluated here miss the deadline limit on the block size. The pulse budget lies in a window bounded below by authentication-key replenishment and above by the deadline; for a fixed source, channel, and acceptance model, the authentication debit shifts the floor, whereas hashing cost does not. At a 35-s deadline the largest tested loss with a non-empty window is 27~dB at 1\% misalignment and 22~dB at 2\%; at 3\% no tested setting has one. Conditional on the assumed acquisition probability, the selected configurations meet this deadline with simultaneous lower confidence bounds of 96.9--97.3\% on held-out trials, at 26~dB and at 18--20~dB with 2\% misalignment. A high-cost stress reference that charges hashing in full narrows the window and lowers these loss limits to 26 and 20~dB at the reference processing capacity. A small rise in error rate or loss pushes the deadline probability well below its target and drains authentication keys, while the protocol's security parameter is unchanged.
one_liner: Finite-key modeling exposes a narrow pulse-budget window for deadline-constrained, QKD-assisted UAV edge computing.
why_it_matters: It shows that key acceptance and authentication replenishment—not hashing time alone—can dominate latency, hover energy, and service feasibility.
detailed_summary: A count-level Monte Carlo model, checked against a semi-analytic model, couples finite-key decoy-state BB84 attempts to protected upload, computation, download, and UAV hover energy. At 26 dB loss, fresh-key provisioning raises the 95th-percentile completion time from 10.37 to 28.65 s. Under a 35 s deadline, feasible pulse-budget windows disappear as loss or misalignment rises, with no tested configuration surviving at 3% misalignment.
platform_or_system: Trusted UAV with finite-key decoy-state BB84 links
main_result: The study quantifies deadline-feasible operating windows and finds that authentication-key replenishment and finite-block acceptance sharply constrain QKD-assisted UAV service.
application_angle: The model helps size sources, link budgets, authentication reserves, and mission deadlines for practical airborne secure edge-computing deployments.

title: Thin-film lithium niobate integrated photonics at 493 nm
abstract: Visible and near-ultraviolet light underpins applications from biophotonics to quantum computing, which demand fast control of optical amplitude and phase. Integrated photonics offers scalable control, yet most visible-wavelength platforms lack gigahertz-scale modulation. We demonstrate a thin-film lithium niobate platform at 493 nm integrating grating couplers, beamsplitters, ring resonators, and modulators. Segmented traveling-wave modulators achieve a half-wave voltage--length product of 450 mV$\cdot$cm, $>$20 dB extinction, and bandwidth beyond 50 GHz. Ring resonators show $2.9 \pm 0.2$ dB/cm propagation loss and quantify the platform's photorefractive response. This enables agile visible beam delivery for trapped-ion systems, although photorefraction and substrate uniformity remain key challenges to scaling.
one_liner: A thin-film lithium-niobate platform delivers ultrafast visible-light modulation at 493 nm for integrated trapped-ion photonics.
why_it_matters: The platform combines visible-wavelength routing and >50 GHz modulation, addressing a key control bottleneck for scalable trapped-ion quantum systems.
detailed_summary: The work integrates grating couplers, beamsplitters, ring resonators, and segmented traveling-wave modulators on thin-film lithium niobate at 493 nm. The modulators achieve a 450 mV·cm half-wave voltage–length product, over 20 dB extinction, and bandwidth beyond 50 GHz. Ring measurements indicate 2.9 ± 0.2 dB/cm propagation loss while exposing photorefraction and substrate uniformity as remaining scaling constraints.
main_result: The integrated modulators exceed 50 GHz bandwidth with >20 dB extinction and a 450 mV·cm voltage–length product.
application_angle: It could provide fast, scalable amplitude and phase control for visible beam delivery in trapped-ion quantum processors and related instruments.

title: Optical trapping of neutral atoms via magnetic-dipole transitions
abstract: Optical trapping of neutral atoms is almost universally described as an electric-dipole (E1) effect. We show that the magnetic field of light, acting on a magnetic-dipole (M1) transition, can induce an ac Zeeman shift significantly larger than the ac Stark shift, thereby enabling magnetic trapping. We construct the M1 polarizability tensor and identify a critical detuning $δ_c$, independent of optical power, below which the magnetic interaction dominates. We analyze suitable trapping parameters and possible loss mechanisms, particularly for the intraconfigurational transitions $^3H_6\rightarrow{}^3H_5$ of erbium at $1437.13$~nm and $^5I_8\rightarrow{}^5I_7$ of dysprosium at $2418.84$~nm. We propose two trapping configurations: a hybrid magnetic/electric optical tweezer and an optical lattice with separated magnetic and electric antinodes, producing state-dependent purely magnetic and purely electric trapping wells. Our results present optical magnetic fields as a suitable resource to expand the toolbox for atomic manipulation.
one_liner: Magnetic-dipole optical transitions are proposed as a route to neutral-atom traps dominated by the light field's magnetic component.
why_it_matters: State-dependent magnetic and electric trapping could add a qualitatively new control mechanism for neutral-atom quantum simulation and processing.
detailed_summary: The authors derive the magnetic-dipole polarizability tensor and identify a power-independent critical detuning below which the ac Zeeman shift exceeds the ac Stark shift. Candidate implementations use erbium's 1437.13 nm and dysprosium's 2418.84 nm intraconfigurational transitions. Proposed geometries include a hybrid magnetic/electric tweezer and a lattice with spatially separated magnetic and electric antinodes.
main_result: The analysis identifies realistic regimes in which optical magnetic fields dominate trapping and enable distinct magnetic and electric potential wells.
application_angle: The scheme could enable new state-selective trapping, manipulation, and lattice architectures for neutral-atom quantum hardware.

title: Nonperturbative string dynamics in a (2+1)D lattice gauge theory on a superconducting quantum processor
abstract: Electric flux strings underpin confinement in gauge theories. In two spatial dimensions, their evolution involves competing processes of charge motion, pair creation, and transverse deformation. Accessing these dynamics beyond perturbative limits challenges classical approaches, as entanglement growth restricts the times accessible to tensor-network simulations. Here we use quantum simulation to investigate a (2+1)D Z2 lattice gauge theory with dynamical matter and an explicit magnetic plaquette interaction, spanning strongly confined and nonperturbative deconfined regimes. Using 63 superconducting qubits, including 12 ancillas, we evolve initially localized strings with static or dynamical endpoint charges. Spatially resolved measurements reveal rapid charge and flux spreading in the deconfined regime, enhanced matter occupation in the string interior near the pair-creation resonance, and suppressed spreading at strong electric fields. String-path occupations further probe transverse rearrangements between configurations connected by plaquette operations. Retaining separate matter and gauge degrees of freedom makes local Gauss-law constraints directly accessible for error detection. Combining these constraints with ancilla checks and noise rescaling, we measure dynamics in circuits containing up to 15 second-order Trotter steps. Our results establish quantum simulation as a practical approach to exploring nonperturbative string dynamics in two spatial dimensions, with gauge redundancy serving as an experimental resource.
one_liner: A 63-qubit superconducting processor simulates nonperturbative string dynamics in a two-dimensional lattice gauge theory.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates experimentally accessible gauge-theory dynamics beyond classically tractable time scales while using gauge constraints for error detection.
detailed_summary: The experiment implements a (2+1)D Z2 lattice gauge theory with separate matter and gauge degrees of freedom on 63 superconducting qubits, including 12 ancillas. Measurements resolve charge and flux spreading, resonant matter creation inside strings, and transverse string rearrangements driven by plaquette interactions. Gauss-law constraints, ancilla checks, and noise rescaling support circuits with up to 15 second-order Trotter steps.
main_result: The processor resolves confined and deconfined string evolution, pair-creation signatures, and transverse flux rearrangements in a nonperturbative 2D gauge model.
application_angle: The approach advances quantum processors as practical simulators of high-energy gauge dynamics and shows how physical redundancy can aid error detection.

title: Probing Krylov Dynamics in Driven Many-Body Systems
abstract: Krylov complexity has become a central probe of operator growth, scrambling, and quantum chaos. Yet, a basic fact hinders its experimental study: laboratory quantum systems are routinely driven in time, whereas the Krylov construction assumes a fixed generator and breaks down once the Hamiltonian varies. Here, we solve the time-dependent many-body Krylov problem exactly and in closed form for scale- and rotation-invariant systems realized in current quantum-simulation and control platforms. We find exact relations that map the driven dynamics onto mutually orthogonal Krylov subspaces and yield a closed-form spread complexity, determined solely by the spectral properties of the initial Hamiltonian and the driving schedule. The construction extends to Liouville space and solves the time-dependent density-matrix Krylov problem, which makes the Krylov dynamics of initial thermal states experimentally accessible. In scale-invariant quantum gases, such as the driven Lieb-Liniger model, the Tonks-Girardeau gas, and the Calogero-Sutherland model, the complexity is set by the width of the atomic cloud and its rate of change, directly accessible via in situ and time-of-flight imaging. In rotation-invariant spin systems such as the Haldane-Shastry and central-spin models, it is governed by collective spin precession that can be probed and read out in trapped-ion, cavity-QED, and circuit-QED platforms.
one_liner: Closed-form Krylov dynamics for driven many-body systems links abstract complexity measures to directly measurable observables.
why_it_matters: The theory makes time-dependent Krylov complexity experimentally accessible in quantum gases, trapped ions, and cavity- or circuit-QED systems.
detailed_summary: The work exactly maps scale- and rotation-invariant driven dynamics onto mutually orthogonal Krylov subspaces and derives closed-form spread complexity. Its Liouville-space extension also covers density matrices and initial thermal states. In quantum gases the complexity follows cloud width and expansion rate, while in spin systems it is determined by measurable collective precession.
platform_or_system: Driven quantum gases and collective-spin simulators
main_result: The authors derive exact driven-system Krylov solutions whose complexity can be extracted from cloud imaging or collective-spin readout.
application_angle: It supplies experimentally usable diagnostics of scrambling and operator growth for trapped-ion, cold-atom, cavity-QED, and circuit-QED platforms.

title: Squeezed Light Generation by Cooper Pair Recombination in a Superconductor-Semiconductor Structure
abstract: We theoretically demonstrate squeezed light generation in a compact, electrically driven device utilizing the nonlinear light-matter interaction of Cooper-pair recombination in a hybrid superconductorsemiconductor structure. On the basis of second-order perturbation theory, we developed an effective Hamiltonian which incorporates the electronic component of the interaction as a photon coupling strength coefficient, enabling a model to describe the quadrature squeezing effect of Cooper-pair recombination on the photonic state. We find the squeezing strength to be proportional to the superconducting energy gap squared and device length, as well as increasing with applied voltage. For practical device length, materials and voltage bias, we calculated squeezing values comparable to those of existing squeezed light generation methods when operating below the critical temperature. This theoretically developed concept shows viability for electrically pumped squeezed light generation and can pave the way towards realization of squeezing in compact integrated structures.
one_liner: Cooper-pair recombination is proposed as an electrically pumped source of squeezed light in a compact hybrid device.
why_it_matters: An integrated electrical source could reduce the size and optical-pump complexity of squeezed-light systems used in sensing and quantum photonics.
detailed_summary: The theoretical model uses second-order perturbation theory to derive an effective photon-coupling Hamiltonian for Cooper-pair recombination in a superconductor-semiconductor structure. Predicted squeezing grows with the square of the superconducting gap, device length, and applied voltage. For practical parameters below the critical temperature, the calculated squeezing is comparable to established generation methods.
main_result: The model predicts practically competitive optical quadrature squeezing from electrically driven Cooper-pair recombination.
application_angle: The concept could support compact integrated squeezed-light sources for precision sensing, continuous-variable photonics, and quantum communication.

title: Towards Distributed Quantum Computing: Quantum Gate Teleportation via Satellite-Distributed Entanglement under Atmospheric Depolarization
abstract: We investigate quantum gate teleportation as a primitive for satellite-enabled distributed quantum computing. In the considered architecture, a satellite distributes entangled photon pairs to two optical ground stations, which transfer the shared quantum resource to remote quantum processing units. This entanglement is then used to implement a nonlocal controlled-NOT gate between two circuit qubits located in different processors. We formulate the minimal four-qubit protocol, consisting of two network qubits that provide the entangled resource and two circuit qubits on which the distributed gate is performed. Atmospheric propagation effects in the gravitational field are modeled through an effective two-qubit depolarizing channel whose parameters depend on atmospheric and optical quantities, including the Fried parameter and receiver aperture. The performance of the protocol is quantified by the fidelity between the ideal CNOT output state and the state produced by noisy quantum gate teleportation. Our results show that the fidelity is governed by the quality of the distributed entanglement and depends jointly on atmospheric coherence, aperture size, and effective depolarization strength. These findings connect physical-layer modeling of satellite optical channels with gate-level performance in distributed quantum computing.
one_liner: A satellite-entanglement model connects atmospheric depolarization directly to the fidelity of a teleported nonlocal CNOT gate.
why_it_matters: It translates optical-channel conditions into a gate-level metric for designing satellite-linked distributed quantum computers.
detailed_summary: The study models a four-qubit protocol in which a satellite distributes an entangled photon pair to ground stations, enabling a remote CNOT between two processor qubits. Atmospheric propagation is represented by an effective two-qubit depolarizing channel parameterized by quantities such as Fried coherence length and receiver aperture. Simulated output fidelity is governed by distributed-entanglement quality and the combined atmospheric and optical parameters.
main_result: The analysis quantifies how atmospheric coherence, receiver aperture, and depolarization determine teleported-CNOT fidelity.
application_angle: The model can guide link budgets and receiver design for satellite-enabled distributed quantum processing, though experimental validation remains necessary.

title: Quantum Computing Enhanced Search for Wavelike Dark Matter
abstract: Identifying a weak, stochastic signal hidden within a broad frequency band is a central challenge in the search for wavelike dark matter. We explore quantum computing enhanced sensing based on the Grover search algorithm to address this problem and find that a long integration time stabilizes the accumulated sensing phase, reducing quantum signal processing (QSP) errors induced by dark matter fluctuations. We further propose alternating the signs of the QSP angles between oracle calls to suppress the coherent accumulation of the intrinsic QSP approximation errors during the search. Combining these strategies in a transmon-based benchmark, we obtain a projected sensitivity to axion dark matter beyond existing astrophysical limits. This opens access to substantial unexplored parameter space across the $10$-$100\,μ\mathrm{eV}$ mass range and offers an accelerated discovery channel for wavelike dark matter. With $10^6$ entangled sensing qubits, the projected sensitivity reaches the QCD axion band. Although illustrated with transmons, the protocol can be adapted to other experimental platforms for wavelike dark matter detection.
one_liner: Grover search and error-suppressed quantum signal processing could accelerate broadband searches for wavelike axion dark matter.
why_it_matters: A transmon benchmark projects sensitivity beyond astrophysical limits at 10–100 μeV, with a million-qubit system potentially reaching the QCD axion band.
detailed_summary: The proposal treats broadband wavelike-dark-matter detection as a Grover search over frequency bins. Long integration stabilizes the accumulated sensing phase, while alternating QSP-angle signs suppresses coherent approximation-error buildup between oracle calls. A transmon-based benchmark projects sensitivity beyond current astrophysical limits across the 10–100 μeV mass range, although the million-entangled-qubit QCD-axion target remains prospective.
main_result: The combined integration and QSP-error-suppression strategy yields projected axion sensitivity beyond existing astrophysical limits.
application_angle: The protocol offers a potentially faster route to scanning wide frequency ranges for weak wavelike-dark-matter signals on quantum hardware.

title: A Grover-Accelerated Search for Dark Matter
abstract: We show that Grover's algorithm can be used to parametrically accelerate wave-like dark matter searches. Despite having a finite coherence time $τ$, wavelike dark matter can imprint a coherent $O(1)$ phase onto a sensor through a dispersive coupling over an integration time which significantly exceeds $τ$. As such, we show that dark matter can be used as a repeatable quantum phase gate in a quantum device. If the sensor is prepared in a superposition of frequencies, we show that this phase can be transferred to a qubit register and digitized. The qubits are thus available for quantum computational processing in which dark matter can take part as a coherent gate. We show that Grover's algorithm can be used to speed up a search for dark matter in $N_{\rm bins}$ frequency bins by a factor of $\sqrt{N_{\rm bins}}$. Although the technological challenges to implementing such a search remain substantial, this demonstrates that there is no fundamental obstruction to accelerating wave-like dark matter searches with quantum computational techniques over many coherence times.
one_liner: Wavelike dark matter can act as a repeatable phase gate, enabling a Grover search with a square-root speedup over frequency bins.
why_it_matters: The work identifies no fundamental coherence-time barrier to quantum-accelerated dark-matter scans, though implementation still demands substantial hardware advances.
detailed_summary: A dispersively coupled sensor can accumulate an order-one phase from wavelike dark matter over an integration time much longer than the field coherence time. Preparing the sensor across frequencies allows that phase to be digitized into a qubit register and used as a repeatable oracle-like gate. Grover search then reduces the frequency-bin search complexity by a factor scaling as the square root of the number of bins.
platform_or_system: Frequency-superposition quantum sensor and qubit register
main_result: The proposed protocol provides a parametric √N-bin acceleration for broadband wavelike-dark-matter searches.
application_angle: It supplies a quantum-computing architecture for accelerating wideband dark-matter experiments despite finite signal coherence.

title: Quantum synchronization in XX chains under relaxation
abstract: We study stable synchronization in qubit XX chains with site-dependent frequencies and exchange couplings under multi-local amplitude damping noise, extending the uniform-chain results of B. Çakmak et al., [Phys. Rev. A 114, L030202 2026] in several directions. We establish that the dark-mode energies are precisely the eigenvalues shared by all undamped segments separated by the damped sites. Generic stable synchronization of the edge qubits occurs if and only if these segments share exactly one eigenvalue and this eigenvalue is nonzero, in which case every qubit on the support of the corresponding dark mode is synchronized with locking constants independent of the initial preparation. This spectral matching condition identifies the Hamiltonian parameters that support synchronization, while the couplings to the damped sites control the relative oscillation amplitudes. We present analytical examples which show how inhomogeneity can create synchronization absent in uniform chains and turn preparation-dependent locking into generic synchronization. We also calculate the asymptotic pairwise concurrence and prove that, in the single-dark-mode regime, every pair participating in synchronized oscillations remains entangled with a nonzero, constant concurrence.
one_liner: Spectral matching rules identify when dissipative, inhomogeneous XX qubit chains exhibit stable synchronization and persistent entanglement.
why_it_matters: The results turn disorder and engineered damping into design parameters for synchronized quantum networks with preparation-independent locking.
detailed_summary: The authors show that dark-mode energies equal the eigenvalues shared by undamped chain segments separated by damped sites. Generic edge synchronization occurs exactly when those segments share one nonzero eigenvalue, with locking constants independent of the initial state. In the single-dark-mode regime, every synchronized pair retains a nonzero constant concurrence.
main_result: A necessary-and-sufficient spectral condition is derived for stable generic synchronization, together with persistent pairwise entanglement.
application_angle: The design rules could guide dissipative synchronization and coherent signal distribution in engineered qubit arrays.

title: Bounding Freedom of Choice via Causal Network Embeddings
abstract: Standard Bell inequalities rely on measurement independence, the assumption that measurement settings are perfectly decoupled from the source of correlations. We demonstrate that embedding Bell scenarios into larger causal networks naturally overcomes this limitation. This embedding yields experimentally accessible lower and upper bounds on measurement dependence, the incompatibility of which certifies nonclassicality directly from data, without assuming a priori freedom of choice. We formulate a general linear-programming framework to systematically derive these measurement-dependence consistency (MDC) Bell inequalities. By bypassing standard non-convexity hurdles, this approach significantly outperforms existing techniques in computational simplicity and noise robustness. Finally, we reveal that genuine quantum nonlocality can be certified even for correlations exceeding the Tsirelson bound, and demonstrate our method's broad applicability to multi-outcome and multipartite Bell tests.
one_liner: Causal-network embeddings enable Bell nonclassicality tests without assuming perfect independence between sources and measurement settings.
why_it_matters: The linear-programming method makes freedom-of-choice loopholes experimentally quantifiable while improving computational tractability and noise robustness.
detailed_summary: The framework embeds a Bell experiment in a larger causal network and derives experimentally accessible upper and lower bounds on measurement dependence. Incompatible bounds certify nonclassicality directly from observed data without presupposing measurement independence. Linear programming generates the resulting MDC Bell inequalities for multi-outcome and multipartite settings, including correlations beyond the Tsirelson bound.
main_result: The method certifies quantum nonlocality from data while explicitly bounding imperfect freedom of measurement choice.
application_angle: It can strengthen photonic Bell tests, device-independent protocols, and quantum-network validation against setting-source correlations.

title: Zeroth persistent homology of ground-state correlations at clean and disordered quantum transitions
abstract: The antiferromagnetic Ising chain in transverse and longitudinal fields exhibits a continuous critical point, a mixed-order transition line and, with quenched disorder, an infinite-disorder fixed point and reentrant order. Using exact free-fermion solutions and the density-matrix renormalization group, we examine what the zeroth persistent homology of staggered ground-state correlations adds to conventional responses. Its barcode records the merge scales of the single-linkage hierarchy, and the maximum of its persistence-landscape velocity defines a threshold-free pseudocritical point. This point locates the clean critical point and the mixed-order line with an accuracy comparable to conventional responses. In the reentrant regime, the global velocity misplaces the entry, which is recovered only by restricting the filtration to the ordering scale, and none of the tested estimators locates the exit. A domain wall forced by the boundary conditions suppresses the disorder-averaged reentrant lobe. For individual disordered realizations, the labelled merge tree recovers most strong-disorder renormalization-group clusters, including noncontiguous ones missed by lattice-restricted hierarchies, with increasing agreement at stronger disorder. This information resides in the full correlation matrix, while zeroth homology provides a stable, threshold-free hierarchy.
one_liner: Persistent homology extracts threshold-free transition markers and strong-disorder cluster structure from quantum ground-state correlations.
why_it_matters: The approach offers a stable analysis tool for diagnosing quantum transitions and disordered correlations, while clearly exposing its limits in reentrant phases.
detailed_summary: Zeroth persistent homology is applied to the full staggered-correlation matrix of clean and disordered antiferromagnetic Ising chains. Persistence-landscape velocity locates the clean critical point and mixed-order line comparably to conventional response functions, but requires a restricted filtration for reentrant entry and fails to locate the exit. Labelled merge trees recover most strong-disorder renormalization-group clusters, including noncontiguous clusters.
platform_or_system: Clean and disordered quantum Ising chains
main_result: A threshold-free topological hierarchy locates several quantum transitions and reconstructs disorder-induced correlation clusters.
application_angle: The method could support robust correlation-based diagnostics of quantum simulators and many-body hardware without manually chosen thresholds.

title: Higher-Order Exceptional Point Sensing with Rydberg Micro-Ensemble Arrays
abstract: Higher-order exceptional points arise from the coalescence of multiple eigenvalues and eigenstates, leading to enhanced spectral responses to weak perturbations. However, realizing and controlling such higher-order degeneracies in interacting many-body systems remains challenging due to the complex coupling among multiple interacting eigenstates. Here, we construct spatially structured microensemble arrays in cold Rydberg gas, where long-range interaction and spatial connectivity enlarge the effective non-Hermitian dimensionality, enabling higher-order exceptional points. By varying the spatial arrangement of these sites, we realize different orders of non-Hermitian exceptional points. We further show that interactions between Rydberg excitation sites can enhance the quantum Fisher information, thereby improving sensing sensitivity. The resulting higher-order exceptional points exhibit increasingly nonlinear phase-boundary responses, which can be further tuned by varying the measurement time and atom number. By tracking shifts of these phase boundaries, we achieve a sensitivity of 0.47(10) nV cm-1 Hz-1/2, surpassing the standard quantum limit. Our results establish Rydberg microensemble arrays as a platform connecting higher-order non-Hermitian criticality, many-body dynamics, and microwave sensing.
one_liner: Spatially structured Rydberg microensembles realize tunable higher-order exceptional points for interaction-enhanced microwave sensing.
why_it_matters: The reported 0.47(10) nV cm⁻¹ Hz⁻¹/² sensitivity surpasses the standard quantum limit and links many-body criticality to practical electrometry.
detailed_summary: Cold-Rydberg microensemble arrays use long-range interactions and spatial connectivity to enlarge the effective non-Hermitian dimension. Changing the site geometry produces exceptional points of different orders, while intersite interactions enhance quantum Fisher information. Tracking nonlinear phase-boundary shifts yields a reported sensitivity of 0.47(10) nV cm⁻¹ Hz⁻¹/², tunable through measurement time and atom number.
main_result: The platform realizes geometry-tunable higher-order exceptional points and achieves sub-standard-quantum-limit microwave-field sensitivity.
application_angle: The array provides a configurable route to ultrasensitive microwave electrometry using interacting atomic ensembles.

title: Quantum CSS codes: Decoder-aware multiobjective design and bound-certified selection
abstract: Quantum error-correcting codes trade decoding reliability against the resources needed to measure their checks. We formulate Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) code design at fixed encoding resources as a decoder-aware multiobjective problem. The objectives are failure probability under sector-wise degenerate maximum-likelihood decoding and check weight, the minimum total weight of an independent pure-type generator basis. For independent bit- and phase-flip noise with perfect syndrome extraction, deterministic truncation bounds support selection under a failure-rate constraint. At a per-sector error probability of 0.01, the bounds certify that a code encoding two logical qubits into 40 physical qubits meets a failure-rate target of 0.001 at check weight 139. The lower bound of every cheaper candidate in the corresponding (40,2) main menu exceeds this target. In paired searches sharing one annealing kernel and equal query budgets, decoder-aware guidance gives significantly higher mean final hypervolume than distance guidance in all eight tested configurations under the reported Holm correction. Against distance-multiplicity guidance, five configurations show significant gains and three do not, including one with a negative mean difference. All arms are scored in common truncated-reliability and normalized-check-weight coordinates. The framework connects reliability-check-weight trade-offs to bound-certified selection within evaluated CSS pools.
one_liner: Decoder-aware multiobjective search identifies CSS codes that balance logical failure probability against stabilizer-check weight.
why_it_matters: Certified code selection can reduce syndrome-measurement overhead while meeting explicit reliability targets in fault-tolerant hardware.
detailed_summary: The work optimizes CSS codes using degenerate maximum-likelihood decoding failure probability and the total weight of an independent pure-type generator basis. Deterministic truncation bounds certify that a [[40,2]] code with check weight 139 achieves failure probability below 0.001 at per-sector error probability 0.01, while every cheaper evaluated candidate fails the target. Decoder-aware guidance also outperforms distance-based guidance across all eight tested search configurations under the reported correction.
main_result: A [[40,2]] CSS code is bound-certified to meet a 0.001 failure target with check weight 139 under the specified noise model.
application_angle: The method supports hardware-conscious selection of error-correcting codes with fewer or lighter stabilizer measurements.

title: Effect of Gas Pressure and Molecular Structure in the Spatial-Mode Conversion of Terahertz Radiation from a Plasma Filament
abstract: In this work, the generation of terahertz (THz) radiation under single color filamentation of a femtosecond laser pulse in an optical cell with compressed gases (argon, nitrogen, CO2) in broad pressure range from 0.001 to 25 atm is experimentally studied for the first time. A nonmonotonic dependence of the integral energy of the THz signal on the gas pressure is revealed, which can be attributed to the competition between an increase in the plasma density and the development of plasma selfabsorption processes, multiple filamentation of the femtosecond pump, and collision induced absorption in the neutral medium. We show that the molecular structure of the gas critically determines the pressure optimum of generation, shifting the maximum of the THz energy yield to the region of elevated pressures (from 10 to 15 atm) for monatomic argon and to the region of subatmospheric pressures (approx. 0.1 atm) for molecular carbon dioxide due to strong vibrational rotational dissipation. On the basis of numerical 3D modeling, it is shown that the cylindrical metal waveguide insert used for signal collection operates in a strongly multimode regime and substantially transforms the angular spectrum of the THz source. We demonstrate that the conical structure of the THz radiation recorded in the experiment is a consequence of intermode interference and diffraction at the output end face of the waveguide, which transforms the true parameters of THz generation in the plasma channel.
one_liner: Gas pressure and molecular structure strongly reshape the yield and measured spatial modes of filament-generated terahertz radiation.
why_it_matters: The results expose collection-induced mode artifacts and provide pressure-selection guidance for efficient plasma-based THz sources and sensing systems.
detailed_summary: Single-color femtosecond filamentation was measured in argon, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide from 0.001 to 25 atm, revealing nonmonotonic THz energy versus pressure. The optimum occurs near 10–15 atm for argon but around 0.1 atm for CO2, reflecting molecular vibrational-rotational dissipation and competing plasma effects. Three-dimensional modeling shows that the collection waveguide is strongly multimode and produces the observed conical pattern through intermode interference and output diffraction.
main_result: The study maps gas-dependent pressure optima and shows that the collection waveguide substantially transforms the source angular spectrum.
application_angle: Accounting for gas chemistry and multimode collection is essential when optimizing THz emitters or interpreting spatially resolved THz measurements.

title: CSS Circuits: useful quantum circuits that can be simulated with $O(1)$ cost per gate
abstract: "CSS circuits" are quantum circuits generated by $X$, $Z$, $M_X$, $M_Z$, and CNOT gates. Although CSS circuits are extremely restrictive, they can implement important quantum protocols like teleportation, error correction, and entanglement purification. We present a simple CSS circuit simulator that uses $O(1)$ work per gate. The simulator corresponds to a local hidden variable model, so we use Bell inequalities to prove the simulator can't also support Hadamard gates, CZ gates, or S gates. We note that CSS circuits appear ideal for benchmarking quantum error correction in the presence of atom loss errors.
one_liner: A local-hidden-variable simulator executes each gate of useful CSS circuits with constant computational cost.
why_it_matters: Fast simulation can accelerate benchmarking of teleportation, error correction, purification, and atom-loss protocols without full stabilizer overhead.
detailed_summary: The simulator covers circuits generated by X, Z, X- and Z-basis measurements, and CNOT gates, requiring O(1) work per gate. Despite this restricted gate set, it captures protocols including teleportation, quantum error correction, and entanglement purification. Bell-inequality arguments establish that Hadamard, CZ, and S gates cannot be added while retaining the same local-hidden-variable construction.
main_result: Useful CSS protocols can be simulated with O(1) work per gate, with rigorous limits on extending the supported gate set.
application_angle: The simulator offers an efficient testbed for quantum-error-correction experiments, particularly benchmarks involving neutral-atom loss.

title: Time- and Photon-Optimal Paths for the Preparation and Logical Flip of Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill States
abstract: Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states are highly non-Gaussian, making their control challenging, particularly in the presence of photon loss. Here, we use the brachistochrone, the fastest path at bounded speed, to construct ideal nonlinear Hamiltonians for state preparation and logical gates, and compare it with the photon-optimal path. We find that the two paths nearly coincide for state preparation but differ markedly for logical operations, namely the brachistochrone preserves the encoded qubit during a bit flip, whereas the photon-optimal path flips a known state through the vacuum. We then introduce the tangential capacity to quantify how effectively gate sets track these paths. Using this analysis, we find that conditional squeezing achieves the highest capacity, preparing GKP states in 824 ns with a fidelity of 0.99 and a minimum closeness to the path of 0.90, compared with 0.98 and 0.51 for conditional displacements and 0.83 and 0.19 for SNAP gates.
one_liner: Brachistochrone and photon-optimal paths reveal how control sets prepare and logically flip bosonic GKP states under loss constraints.
why_it_matters: The framework connects ideal control geometry to experimentally available gates and identifies conditional squeezing as the strongest tested option.
detailed_summary: The authors derive time-optimal and photon-optimal trajectories for GKP-state preparation and logical bit flips using ideal nonlinear Hamiltonians. The paths nearly coincide during preparation but differ for logical flips: the fastest path preserves the encoded qubit, whereas the photon-optimal path routes a known state through vacuum. Tangential-capacity analysis finds conditional squeezing superior to conditional displacement and SNAP control, reaching 0.99 preparation fidelity in 824 ns with minimum path closeness 0.90.
main_result: Conditional squeezing most closely tracks the ideal preparation path, achieving simulated 0.99 fidelity in 824 ns.
application_angle: The results guide gate-set and pulse-design choices for faster, loss-aware preparation and control of bosonic logical qubits.

title: Reducing TLS Losses in Superconducting Circuits Using Solid Neon
abstract: Two level systems (TLSs) are a major source of loss in superconducting devices, limiting the performance of qubits, detectors, and resonators. These defects arise from a range of sources, including surface oxides, crystal defects, as well as fabrication residues which are often difficult to remove. Using NbTiN coplanar waveguide resonators, we show that depositing and subsequently removing a solid neon film can significantly improve device performance. Analysis of the temperature and power dependence indicates that this enhancement arises from reduced TLS dissipation, which we attribute to the redistribution and removal of surface contaminants during neon deposition and evaporation. Atomic force microscopy images of contaminated hexagonal boron nitride flakes before and after neon exposure show that neon treatment can redistribute and remove surface residues. These results demonstrate a simple, non-destructive approach for mitigating TLS losses in superconducting devices and other sensitive materials that cannot withstand aggressive cleaning processes.
one_liner: Depositing and evaporating solid neon reduces two-level-system loss in NbTiN microwave resonators by cleaning surface contamination.
why_it_matters: This gentle treatment could improve superconducting qubits, resonators, and detectors made from materials incompatible with aggressive cleaning.
detailed_summary: Solid neon was deposited onto NbTiN coplanar-waveguide resonators and subsequently removed, producing a significant performance improvement. Temperature- and power-dependent measurements attribute the gain to reduced two-level-system dissipation. Atomic-force microscopy of contaminated hexagonal boron nitride further shows redistribution and removal of surface residues after neon exposure.
main_result: A removable solid-neon film reduces TLS-associated dissipation through redistribution and removal of surface contaminants.
application_angle: The non-destructive process offers a practical route to lower dielectric loss in fragile superconducting circuits and sensitive material stacks.

title: High-precision measurement of level leakage via intelligent coherent control
abstract: Level leakage constitutes a dominant error source in quantum state control and necessitates accurate characterization for large-scale quantum computing. Quantum sensing provides a viable route for high-precision estimation of level leakage, but its sensitivity can be limited by non-unitary leakage dynamics and interference between the free Hamiltonian and signal generator. This work proposes a reinforcement learning-based quantum sensing algorithm for Hermitian three-level and effective dissipative two-level systems. The algorithm adopts an experimentally feasible pulse-parameter modulation strategy, enabling high-precision and reliable measurement under the specified control and measurement protocol. In both models, DQN-discovered pulse sequences enhance the measurement-model-specific sensing precision, while joint phase--detuning modulation further improves the performance and yields a CFI close to the corresponding QFI.
one_liner: Reinforcement-learned coherent-control pulses improve precision when estimating leakage in three-level and dissipative two-level quantum systems.
why_it_matters: Accurate leakage metrology is vital for calibrating multilevel quantum hardware and controlling errors that evade standard qubit measurements.
detailed_summary: A deep-Q-network algorithm optimizes experimentally feasible pulse parameters for leakage sensing in a Hermitian three-level model and an effective dissipative two-level model. The learned sequences improve classical Fisher information under the specified measurement protocol despite non-unitary dynamics and Hamiltonian interference. Joint phase and detuning modulation further raises the classical Fisher information close to the corresponding quantum Fisher information.
platform_or_system: Controlled three-level and dissipative two-level quantum systems
main_result: DQN-designed pulses enhance leakage-estimation precision, with combined phase-detuning control approaching the quantum Fisher-information limit.
application_angle: The approach could strengthen calibration and diagnostics for leakage-prone qubits and other multilevel quantum devices.

title: Sensing frequencies at the discrete Grover-Heisenberg limit using a single qubit
abstract: We consider a fundamental quantum sensing task: detecting weak oscillating fields with unknown strength and frequency. Recent work by Allen et al. established a fundamental lower bound on the required sensing time, which they named the "Grover-Heisenberg limit", and gave a protocol attaining this limit. The protocol relies on auxiliary qubits, which are used to run Grover's algorithm as a subroutine, leaving open the question of whether a single sensing qubit can achieve the same scaling. We show that a single qubit suffices for a discrete version of this problem, in which the signal strength is known and the frequency belongs to an arbitrary, but known, finite set of candidate frequencies. Our protocol's sensing time grows only as the square root of the number of candidate frequencies. We prove that this square-root dependence, which we refer to as the "discrete Grover-Heisenberg limit", is optimal in the worst case.
one_liner: A single sensing qubit identifies a known-strength signal among discrete candidate frequencies with optimal square-root sensing-time scaling.
why_it_matters: It removes the auxiliary-qubit requirement from a Grover-like sensing advantage, reducing hardware demands for discrete-frequency detection.
detailed_summary: The work considers detection of a weak oscillating field whose strength is known and whose frequency belongs to an arbitrary finite candidate set. It constructs a protocol requiring only one sensing qubit, with sensing time scaling as the square root of the number of candidates. A worst-case lower bound proves this discrete Grover-Heisenberg scaling is optimal.
main_result: A single-qubit protocol attains the optimal square-root dependence of sensing time on the number of candidate frequencies.
application_angle: The reduced qubit overhead could simplify quantum spectrum analyzers and narrowband detectors searching over predefined frequency grids.

title: Entanglement, correlations, and resource costs for symmetry-adapted quantum simulations of light through medium-mass nuclei
abstract: Entanglement governs both the classical cost of simulating correlated many-body systems and the quantum resources needed to treat them. In this work, we use nuclear symmetries to investigate the entanglement and correlations in nuclei using \textit{ab initio} symmetry-adapted no-core shell-model nuclear wavefunctions, illustrated here for $^{4,6,8}$He, $^8$Be, $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, $^{20}\mathrm{Ne}$, and $^{48}$Ca. In this many-body approach, deformation and collectivity naturally emerge from the underlying chiral potential, and we show that the Sp(3,$\mathbb{R}$) basis concentrates the ground state in far fewer basis states than the SU(3) basis. We compute single-mode entropies and two-mode mutual information, and examine the organization of like-particle two-nucleon correlations into symmetry channels. Single-mode entropies are largest in the valence shells, while two-mode mutual information reveals substantial correlations both within and between shells. In all cases considered, the dominant pair correlations are captured by fewer SU(3) channels than angular-momentum channels, which reduces the number of variational parameters. Since the number of operator components within the channels is comparable in the two schemes for the heavier nuclei, this gives the SU(3)-coupling scheme a clear advantage. Fiedler ordering of the correlation graph with local refinement reduces the register ordering cost by a factor of 2 to 3 relative to the original shell ordering, and by 10 when two more shells are included in the register. Together, these measures link nuclear correlations to the selection of active modes and candidate excitation operators and to the design of quantum register layouts, offering guidance for the development of hybrid quantum-classical calculations of nuclei.
one_liner: Nuclear symmetries compress correlated wavefunctions, excitation spaces, and quantum-register layouts for simulations of medium-mass nuclei.
why_it_matters: The analysis translates physical symmetries and entanglement structure into concrete reductions in variational parameters and register-connectivity cost.
detailed_summary: Using ab initio symmetry-adapted no-core shell-model states for nuclei through 48Ca, the study evaluates single-mode entropy, mutual information, and two-nucleon correlations. The Sp(3,R) basis concentrates ground states into fewer basis states, while SU(3) channels capture dominant pair correlations with fewer variational parameters than angular-momentum channels. Correlation-aware Fiedler ordering lowers register-ordering cost by factors of 2–3, or 10 when two additional shells are included.
main_result: Symmetry-adapted bases and correlation-guided ordering substantially reduce state, ansatz, and register-layout costs for nuclear simulations.
application_angle: The results guide active-space selection, ansatz construction, and qubit placement for hybrid quantum-classical nuclear calculations.

title: An Architecture for Real-Time Quantum Error Correction with Neutral Atoms
abstract: The latency of quantum measurement and classical decoding constrains the execution of adaptive fault-tolerant circuits. In neutral-atom processors, this requirement couples spatially resolved fluorescence detection to classical inference. Here we implement cascaded readout and decoding in a heterogeneous architecture that overlaps acquisition and processing at two spatial scales. Field-programmable gate arrays process camera rows as they arrive, while graphics processors decode an acquired logical block during acquisition of the next. This heterogeneous architecture offers flexibility in the choice of error-correcting codes and decoding algorithms. Direct communication preserves microsecond-scale transfer times for kilobyte payloads and supports interchangeable decoding algorithms. Hardware characterization and decoding benchmarks using circuit-level simulated syndromes yield a submillisecond post-exposure processing latency for selected small-code workloads ($d = 3, 5, 7$). By enabling logical blocks to be decoded before full-frame readout is complete, the architecture implements low-latency syndrome decoding, realizing real-time quantum information processing as required for fault-tolerant computation in atom arrays.
one_liner: A heterogeneous FPGA–GPU architecture overlaps neutral-atom fluorescence readout with decoding to enable real-time quantum error correction.
why_it_matters: Submillisecond post-exposure decoding addresses a critical feedback-latency bottleneck for adaptive fault-tolerant operation in atom arrays.
detailed_summary: Camera rows are processed by FPGAs as they arrive, while GPUs decode one logical block during acquisition of the next. Direct data transfer maintains microsecond-scale communication for kilobyte payloads and permits interchangeable codes and decoders. Hardware tests and circuit-level simulated syndromes produce submillisecond post-exposure latency for selected distance-3, 5, and 7 workloads.
main_result: Logical blocks can be decoded before full-frame readout completes, with submillisecond post-exposure processing for selected small codes.
application_angle: The architecture supplies the low-latency measurement-and-feedback path needed for adaptive circuits and fault-tolerant neutral-atom computing.

title: Trading Memory for Depth: Tight Bounds for LCU Block-Encodings
abstract: An LCU block-encoding of $A=\sum_jα_j U_j$ runs the $U_j$ in series on one register, so its select depth is the total work $\sum_j d_j$. Depth was the one block-encoding constraint with no knob: grouping the $T$ terms into $g$ registers that run in parallel gives it one, and the binning is the knob. For a $g$-branched realisation (up to $g$ oracles in parallel) the select depth is tight at $Θ(C+\log(g\,\max\{n,m\}))$ for $g\ge2$, with $C$ the binning makespan and $m$ the largest bin, in the $k$-local atomic-oracle model. The work floor is a two-way reduction to classical multiprocessor scheduling: every realisation \emph{induces} a $g$-machine schedule, and the construction realises any binning, so an optimal binning attains it. The additive logarithmic routing term is a light-cone cost, independent of the selector encoding and robust to register reuse, measurement, reset, and teleportation; width is at least $gn$. The standard $1/α$ subnormalisation and success probability are unchanged; the endpoints are sequential LCU ($g{=}1$) and the fully parallel realisation ($g{=}T$). Allowing the oracles to be split (McNaughton's rule) reaches the work floor $\sum_j d_j/g$. Two selector realisations trade space for depth: a dense (Möttönen) one is memory-tight at the standard LCU footprint but its multiplexed controls cost a $\log\log(m{+}1)$ factor on the makespan; a one-hot one is depth-tight at $T$ selector qubits. Neither reaches both at once.
one_liner: Parallel LCU block-encodings gain a tunable memory–depth tradeoff governed by oracle scheduling and unavoidable logarithmic routing overhead.
why_it_matters: Tight resource bounds clarify when extra registers can shorten a core quantum-algorithm primitive and which selector designs limit that gain.
detailed_summary: The paper distributes LCU terms across up to g parallel oracle registers and reduces optimal binning to classical multiprocessor scheduling. In the k-local atomic-oracle model, it derives tight select depth Θ(C+log(g max{n,m})) for g at least two, along with a width lower bound of gn. Dense and one-hot selectors expose an irreducible tradeoff between memory efficiency and depth optimality.
main_result: The authors establish tight depth and width bounds for g-branched LCU block-encodings and constructions attaining the scheduling work floor.
application_angle: The bounds support hardware-aware compilation of Hamiltonian simulation and other block-encoding algorithms under limited qubit and parallelism budgets.

title: Device-independent witnesses of genuine multipartite entanglement and nonlocality for GHZ states and Bell-pair tree
abstract: We derive and compare device-independent witnesses of genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) and genuine multipartite nonlocality (GMNL) for GHZ states and trees of Bell pairs. A binary-outcome family using four global measurement contexts has the tight biseparable bound independent of the number of parties. We distinguish these GME bounds from Svetlichny-hybrid bounds, which permit arbitrary communication within either side of a bipartition. For GHZ states, we also give a $2N$-context GMNL witness and compare it with MABK and Svetlichny tests. For Bell-pair trees, sums of CHSH and chained inequalities certify GME and GMNL, respectively, with explicitly specified input protocols and multi-bit local outputs. Separately, we prove the sharp four-context network bound $I_λ\leq2$ for every $N\geq3$ and $λ\geq2$, and bound the MABK scores of quantum networks assembled from bipartite sources. We successfully benchmark MABK, four-context, and Svetlichny witnesses on IBM Quantum GHZ preparations up to $10$ parties, under the local-measurement and sampling assumptions.
one_liner: Device-independent witnesses certify multipartite entanglement and nonlocality in GHZ states and Bell-pair trees with explicit measurement protocols.
why_it_matters: Low-context witnesses and network bounds make scalable certification more practical for multipartite quantum processors and communication networks.
detailed_summary: The authors derive a four-context binary-outcome GME witness with a tight biseparable bound independent of party count, plus a 2N-context GMNL witness for GHZ states. For Bell-pair trees, sums of CHSH and chained inequalities certify GME and GMNL using specified inputs and multi-bit outputs. MABK, four-context, and Svetlichny witnesses are benchmarked on IBM Quantum GHZ preparations containing up to 10 parties.
platform_or_system: GHZ states and Bell-pair tree networks
main_result: The work provides scalable device-independent GME and GMNL witnesses, sharp network bounds, and hardware benchmarks up to 10 parties.
application_angle: These tests can validate entanglement resources in quantum networks and distributed processors without requiring detailed device models.

title: Hybrid Classical-Quantum Optimization for CVRPTW: A Systems Framework with Provable Feasibility and Empirical Hardware Limits
abstract: Solving large-scale Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problems with Time Windows (CVRPTW) remains challenging because strict operational constraints and scale limit both exact and heuristic methods. We present a hybrid classical-quantum architecture combining Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) with vehicle-level Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO), solved using Toshiba SQBM+ and QAOA on Rigetti Ankaa-3 and IQM Emerald quantum processors. The decomposition avoids the variable growth and constraint-enforcement difficulties of monolithic CVRPTW QUBO formulations. We evaluate the framework on five realistic benchmarks derived from London traffic and location data, spanning 10--70 customers, using a validation pipeline enforcing feasibility and monotone improvement over classical baselines. SQBM+ achieves verified fleet-distance reductions of 2.80% (7,927 m) for the 25-customer instance and 0.22% (1,186 m) for the 55-customer instance. QAOA experiments establish a current hardware boundary for reliable constraint satisfaction at subproblems of up to 4 customers (16 qubits). Diagnostic results identify assignment-level time-window tightness, rather than local route optimization, as the dominant scalability bottleneck. The results demonstrate a practical near-term role for hybrid classical-quantum optimization while establishing empirical limits for current quantum hardware.
one_liner: A MILP–QUBO routing framework demonstrates feasible hybrid optimization while locating a 16-qubit reliability boundary on current processors.
why_it_matters: It separates verified operational gains from present hardware limits and identifies time-window assignment as the main scaling bottleneck.
detailed_summary: The framework decomposes capacitated vehicle routing with time windows into a classical MILP layer and vehicle-level QUBO subproblems. On London-derived benchmarks, SQBM+ yields validated distance reductions of 2.80% for 25 customers and 0.22% for 55 customers. QAOA runs on Rigetti Ankaa-3 and IQM Emerald reliably satisfy constraints only through four-customer, 16-qubit subproblems, with time-window assignment dominating scalability.
platform_or_system: Rigetti Ankaa-3 and IQM Emerald processors
main_result: The system achieves verified hybrid routing improvements and measures reliable QAOA constraint satisfaction up to four-customer, 16-qubit subproblems.
application_angle: The decomposition offers a near-term path for testing quantum optimization in logistics while providing realistic feasibility and scaling diagnostics.

title: Full Mesh Dynamic Four-User Entanglement-based Switched QKD Network Integrated with SD-KMS
abstract: We demonstrate a reconfigurable, four-user, full-mesh quantum key distribution network using polarization entanglement, integrated with a software-defined key management system to orchestrate dynamic optical switching and real-time key provisioning for quantum-safe applications.
one_liner: A four-user entanglement-based QKD network dynamically switches full-mesh links under software-defined key management.
why_it_matters: It combines reconfigurable entanglement distribution with automated, real-time key provisioning for deployable multi-user quantum-safe networks.
detailed_summary: The work demonstrates a four-user QKD network based on polarization entanglement and dynamically reconfigurable optical links. A software-defined key management system controls switching and provisions generated keys in real time. The full-mesh architecture allows quantum-key connectivity between arbitrary user pairs.
main_result: The system demonstrates dynamically switched, full-mesh entanglement-based QKD with software-orchestrated real-time key provisioning.
application_angle: The architecture supports flexible quantum-safe key delivery across multi-user metropolitan or enterprise networks.

title: Going beyond the standard quasiparticle picture: Entanglement spreading after quenching from highly entangled states
abstract: The quasiparticle picture provides a quantitative description of entanglement spreading after quantum quenches in integrable systems. In interacting models, however, it relies on the assumption that the quench creates entangled pairs of quasiparticles, which is justified only for the so-called integrable initial states. Here we go beyond this setting by studying quenches in the XXZ spin chain from the $n$-rainbow states, a family of macroscopically homogeneous states formed by increasingly long-range Bell pairs, which are not integrable for $n>1$. The local stationary state after the quench approaches the infinite-temperature state as $n\to\infty$, with corrections of order $1/n$, as we show analytically. Nevertheless, in the noninteracting XX chain the quench produces entangled multiplets of $2n$ species of quasiparticles. Although interspecies correlations vanish as $1/n$, they strongly suppress the growth of the entanglement entropy, whose rate vanishes as $n\to\infty$. We capture this behaviour within a generalized quasiparticle picture. In the interacting XXZ chain, instead, time-dependent density matrix renormalization group (tDMRG) simulations show that the entanglement entropy grows at the rate at which thermodynamic entropy is exchanged across the cut. Within the time scales accessible to tDMRG, the data show no trace of the multiplet suppression. This holds both after homogeneous quenches and after joining the $n$-rainbow state with an infinite-temperature state, for which we conjecture a formula for the von Neumann entropy.
one_liner: Long-range Bell-pair initial states reveal quasiparticle-multiplet suppression of entanglement growth in the XX chain.
why_it_matters: The results clarify when standard pair-based pictures fail and how interactions qualitatively reshape nonequilibrium entanglement transport.
detailed_summary: The study quenches n-rainbow states, built from increasingly long-range Bell pairs, in XX and XXZ spin chains. In the noninteracting XX model, the quench creates entangled multiplets of 2n quasiparticle species, suppressing the entropy-growth rate as n increases. In interacting XXZ simulations, tDMRG instead finds growth consistent with thermodynamic entropy transport, without visible multiplet suppression over accessible times.
platform_or_system: XX and XXZ quantum spin chains
main_result: A generalized quasiparticle description captures vanishing entanglement-growth rates in the XX limit, while interacting XXZ dynamics shows no such suppression.
application_angle: The findings inform the design and interpretation of quantum simulators probing entanglement transport from highly correlated initial states.

title: Extractable Work from Collective Dark-State Charging of Quantum Batteries
abstract: We consider two ensembles of superconducting qubits coupled to a common lossy resonator, one serving as the charger and the other the battery. Destructive interference between their collective decay amplitudes selects a tunable family of many-body dark states, allowing controlled excitation transfer from the charger to the battery. The collective charging dynamics preserves the symmetric Dicke subspace of the battery, so its reduced state has at most $N+1$ nonzero eigenvalues. Together with the $N$-fold degeneracy of the battery's first excited energy level, this restriction keeps the passive energy of the entire battery below the single-qubit excitation energy $ω_0$, independently of the battery size. When the average stored energy per battery qubit is fixed and nonzero, the total stored energy grows linearly with $N$, while the ratio of global ergotropy to stored energy approaches unity as $N$ increases.
one_liner: Collective dark states transfer excitation between superconducting-qubit ensembles while making stored battery energy nearly fully extractable.
why_it_matters: The scheme predicts scalable charging in a lossy circuit-QED setting, with global ergotropy approaching the total stored energy as battery size grows.
detailed_summary: Two superconducting-qubit ensembles act as charger and battery while coupling to a shared lossy resonator. Destructive interference in collective decay selects tunable many-body dark states that mediate controlled excitation transfer. Symmetric-Dicke-subspace dynamics bounds the passive energy below one qubit excitation, so at fixed nonzero energy density the global ergotropy fraction approaches unity with increasing ensemble size.
platform_or_system: Superconducting-qubit ensembles in a lossy resonator
main_result: The analysis shows linear growth of stored energy with qubit number while the globally extractable fraction asymptotically approaches one.
application_angle: Collective dark-state charging could enable loss-tolerant energy storage and transfer primitives in circuit-QED processors.

title: Restoring Heisenberg Scaling in Hamiltonian Estimation despite Noise Uncertainty
abstract: Noise degrades quantum coherence and limits the precision of quantum sensors. Quantum control can counteract these effects, but existing strategies typically assume that the noise is known. In practice, noise is often only partially characterized, so its parameters must be estimated jointly with the Hamiltonian parameters of interest. Here we show that uncertainty in the noise parameters can destroy otherwise attainable Heisenberg scaling, even when coherence is preserved. For general Markovian dynamics under arbitrary quantum control, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for each Hamiltonian parameter to retain this scaling and determine its optimal asymptotic precision when the condition holds. When the condition fails, we propose a protocol that uses a suitable noisy reference system to restore this scaling, and prove that a reference insensitive to the Hamiltonian parameters but subject to an independent copy of the sensor's noise recovers the optimal precision attainable with known noise. Our results reveal how incomplete knowledge of the noise affects the fundamental limits of quantum metrology, with broad implications for achieving quantum-enhanced precision in realistic environments.
one_liner: A noisy reference system can recover Heisenberg scaling for Hamiltonian estimation when sensor-noise parameters are initially uncertain.
why_it_matters: It provides exact criteria and a constructive route to quantum-enhanced precision without assuming that realistic Markovian noise is fully characterized.
detailed_summary: The authors derive a necessary and sufficient condition for each Hamiltonian parameter to retain Heisenberg scaling under general Markovian dynamics and arbitrary control when noise parameters are jointly unknown. They also determine the optimal asymptotic precision whenever that condition is satisfied. If it fails, an auxiliary reference insensitive to the target Hamiltonian but exposed to an independent copy of the noise restores the known-noise optimum.
platform_or_system: Controlled Markovian quantum sensor with noisy reference
main_result: The proposed reference-assisted protocol restores the optimal Heisenberg-scaling precision otherwise lost through uncertainty in noise parameters.
application_angle: The framework guides robust quantum-sensor architectures operating under drifting or incompletely calibrated environmental noise.

title: Quantum-logic detection of rotationally inelastic collisions of single molecules
abstract: Collisions between molecules govern chemical reactions and energy transfer across a range of different environments from interstellar space to the Earth's atmosphere. Despite their fundamental importance, molecular collisions have traditionally been studied through ensemble-averaged experiments which obscure the dynamics of individual scattering events on the quantum level. Probing single molecular collisions with quantum-state resolution has thus far remained a major experimental challenge. Here, we demonstrate a method for detecting individual rotationally inelastic collisions of single molecular ions with neutral atoms using quantum-logic techniques. We prepare individual trapped N$_2^+$ ions in their rotational ground state, subject them to a beam of helium atoms and detect isolated collision events through their effects on the motion of the trapped ions. Quantum-logic-spectroscopic measurements reveal changes of the molecular state upon collision enabling the determination of the probability of rotationally inelastic scattering. The experiments are analysed by comparison with quantum and classical scattering calculations yielding detailed insights into the underlying collision dynamics. By combining single-collision detection with non-destructive readout of the molecular quantum state, our approach establishes a new experimental framework for investigating molecular scattering beyond conventional ensemble measurements. It opens a route towards investigating state-to-state scattering in individual molecules and exploring molecular interactions at the level of single quantum-state resolved events.
one_liner: Quantum-logic readout resolves individual rotationally inelastic collisions between a trapped N2+ ion and helium atoms.
why_it_matters: It moves molecular-scattering studies beyond ensemble averages to nondestructive, quantum-state-resolved observation of single collision events.
detailed_summary: Individual N2+ ions are prepared in their rotational ground state, trapped, and exposed to a helium atomic beam. Collision-induced changes in ion motion flag isolated events, while quantum-logic spectroscopy identifies changes in the molecular rotational state. Comparison with quantum and classical scattering calculations yields the probability and dynamics of rotationally inelastic scattering.
platform_or_system: Trapped N2+ molecular ion with quantum-logic readout
main_result: The experiment detects single rotationally inelastic atom-molecule collisions and nondestructively resolves the resulting molecular-state changes.
application_angle: The method enables state-to-state collision measurements relevant to precision chemistry, atmospheric processes, and controlled molecular dynamics.

title: Critical excited states in quantum metrology
abstract: We investigate criticality-enhanced sensing near ground- and excited-state quantum phase transitions in a strongly coupled qubit-boson system. Accounting for finite-size effects, we design driving protocols that exploit diverging susceptibilities to enhance signal-to-noise ratios in parameter estimation using experimentally relevant generators.
