We show that the excited-state criticality provides a metrological advantage through single-mode bosonic squeezing in regimes that circumvent the 'death of adiabaticity', limiting conventional critical quantum metrology with ground-state criticality.
one_liner: Excited-state quantum criticality enhances parameter sensing through bosonic squeezing without the adiabatic bottleneck of ground-state protocols.
why_it_matters: It identifies an experimentally relevant route to criticality-enhanced sensing that remains effective where finite-size effects and failed adiabatic preparation limit alternatives.
detailed_summary: The work analyzes parameter estimation near ground- and excited-state quantum phase transitions in a strongly coupled qubit-boson model. Finite-size-aware driving protocols exploit divergent susceptibilities using experimentally relevant generators. Excited-state criticality produces single-mode bosonic squeezing and a metrological advantage in regimes that avoid the breakdown of adiabatic preparation affecting ground-state critical sensing.
main_result: Excited-state critical protocols enhance signal-to-noise through bosonic squeezing while circumventing the death of adiabaticity.
application_angle: The approach could improve sensing with cavity, circuit-QED, or trapped-ion platforms that realize strongly coupled spin-boson dynamics.

title: Buffer-Gas-Assisted Fluorescence Spectroscopy of Molecular Ions
abstract: Sustained fluorescence detection of generic molecules has been challenging due to the lack of cycling transitions and limited photon budgets. We demonstrate a nondestructive method for continuous fluorescence of strongly rovibronically open molecular ions, $^{232}$ThF$^+$. Effective quasi-cycling transitions are established by room-temperature buffer-gas collisions, which replenish the population back to the laser-addressed states. In situ images and rotationally resolved spectra are obtained without optical repumping or auxiliary atomic readout ions. Combined with low-background spectroscopic detection, this approach achieves a signal-to-noise ratio of approximately 6 in a 1 s exposure on the P(1) line of $^{232}$ThF$^+$, despite a thermal population of only approximately 0.17% in the addressed state at room temperature. The ability to repeatedly interrogate trapped ions is particularly promising for scarce molecular samples, broadband spectroscopic searches, and in situ monitoring of molecular reactions.
one_liner: Buffer-gas collisions enable sustained, nondestructive fluorescence spectroscopy of trapped ThF+ without optical repumping or atomic readout ions.
why_it_matters: Repeated interrogation of weakly populated molecular-ion states could improve measurements on scarce samples, broadband searches, and reaction monitoring.
detailed_summary: Room-temperature buffer-gas collisions continually return ThF+ population to laser-addressed rotational states, creating effective quasi-cycling transitions despite strongly open rovibronic structure. The experiment obtains in situ images and rotationally resolved spectra without repump lasers or co-trapped atomic readout ions. On the P(1) line, it reaches approximately 6 signal-to-noise in a 1 s exposure while only about 0.17% of the thermal population occupies the addressed state.
main_result: The study demonstrates continuous, nondestructive molecular-ion fluorescence with rotational resolution and approximately 6 signal-to-noise in one second.
application_angle: The technique supports repeated spectroscopy of scarce molecular ions, broad frequency searches, and real-time observation of trapped-ion chemistry.

title: Intense and stable second-harmonic generation in robust MePEA-based quasi-2D halide perovskite crystals
abstract: Quasi-2D halide perovskites offer a unique platform for nonlinear optics applications, where structural and optical properties are tuned by the variation of organic spacer cations. Notably, quasi-2D perovskite single crystals can demonstrate intense and stable second-harmonic generation signals when a proper composition is selected. Here, the influence of phenethylammonium and 4-methyl-2-phenylethylammonium spacers on the crystal symmetry and second-harmonic signal response of quasi-2D perovskite phases with a varying number of single-octahedron [PbX$_6$]$^{4-}$ layers ($n$) is investigated. High-quality perovskite crystals with lateral dimensions of several hundred micrometers are fabricated using a cavity-confined crystallization synthesis method. Optical characterization of the crystals shows strong and temporally stable second-harmonic generation. Power-dependent and polarization-resolved measurements confirm the second-order nonlinear origin of the observed response and reveal anisotropic emission patterns. Our results demonstrate a direct correlation between spacer-induced center-symmetry breaking and nonlinear optical activity. These results establish quasi-2D halide perovskites as a promising class of symmetry-engineered materials for efficient frequency conversion and integrated nonlinear photonics.
one_liner: Symmetry-engineered MePEA quasi-2D halide-perovskite crystals deliver strong, stable, and polarization-anisotropic second-harmonic generation.
why_it_matters: The material combines controllable inversion-symmetry breaking with robust nonlinear response, supporting compact frequency converters and integrated photonics.
detailed_summary: The authors grow high-quality quasi-2D perovskite crystals, several hundred micrometers across, using cavity-confined crystallization and compare phenethylammonium with MePEA spacer chemistries. Power-dependent measurements verify a second-order nonlinear response, while polarization scans reveal anisotropic emission. The results directly associate spacer-induced inversion-symmetry breaking with intense and temporally stable second-harmonic generation.
main_result: The crystals exhibit intense, temporally stable second-harmonic generation governed by spacer-controlled crystal symmetry.
application_angle: These symmetry-tunable crystals are promising active materials for compact frequency conversion and integrated nonlinear-photonic devices.

title: On Multi-Constrained Path Finding utilizing Grover Search and Decoded Quantum Interferometry
abstract: Finding a path whose totals under several additive metrics all fall inside prescribed ranges is weakly NP-complete. We ask what two quantum algorithms can do for it, against strong classical baselines. For directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) we give a Grover search whose state preparation builds the uniform superposition over all source-to-destination paths with one qubit per arc and no ancilla. We prove it correct, give its exact gate count, and show that measured strings form an error- detecting code whose distance is a girth-like graph parameter. We complete the oracle and count its gates: one search on our largest instance, 136 arc qubits and 262,144 paths, needs about 4.4 x 10^5 Toffoli gates, while classical dynamic programming decides the same instance with 18,754 labels. Grover search needs O(sqrt(N/M)) oracle calls for M good paths among N . Classical meet-in-the-middle matches this exponent in the worst case, and known quantum algorithms with quantum memory beat it. For a staged fabric with node-independent linear weights, maximizing the number of satisfied metrics is max-LINSAT, and with power- of-index weights it is Optimal Polynomial Intersection, where no known polynomial-time classical algorithm matches decoded quantum interferometry (DQI). We verify this translation in simulation and run two small binary instances on IBM Heron processors, which keep 67 % and 15 % of the ideal gain over uniform sampling.
one_liner: Grover and decoded-interferometry approaches are benchmarked against strong classical methods for routing under multiple additive constraints.
why_it_matters: The work quantifies when quantum routing methods may help and exposes severe resource costs that matter for future communication-network optimization.
detailed_summary: For directed acyclic graphs, the authors construct an ancilla-free, one-qubit-per-arc uniform path state and provide correctness proofs and exact gate counts for the Grover oracle. A 136-qubit instance with 262,144 paths requires about 440,000 Toffoli gates per search, whereas classical dynamic programming uses 18,754 labels. Small decoded quantum interferometry instances run on IBM Heron processors retain 67% and 15% of the ideal advantage over uniform sampling.
main_result: The study supplies resource-complete quantum routing constructions and demonstrates partial decoded-interferometry gains on two small hardware instances.
application_angle: It provides practical resource benchmarks for evaluating quantum optimization in constrained communication and transport networks.

title: Enhanced Entanglement Gate Fidelity via Correlated and Synchronized Atom Motion
abstract: Engineered collective dissipation can correlate and even synchronize the motion of quantum systems. We show that such motional correlations can suppress motion-induced errors in two-qubit controlled-phase gates based on the Rydberg blockade in neutral-atom tweezer arrays. To leading order in the Lamb-Dicke parameter, the motional contribution to the gate infidelity is determined solely by the two-atom motional occupations and correlations, and is independent of the gate protocol. We illustrate this result for correlated thermal states and synchronized quantum van der Pol oscillators. In each case, motional correlations reduce the gate infidelity relative to independent thermal atoms at finite temperature. Our results establish atomic-motion correlations as a resource for high-fidelity neutral-atom gates and may also find applications in analog quantum simulators.
one_liner: Correlating and synchronizing neutral-atom motion suppresses finite-temperature errors in Rydberg-blockade controlled-phase gates.
why_it_matters: It identifies engineered motional correlation as a hardware-level resource for improving neutral-atom gate fidelity without changing the gate protocol.
detailed_summary: The analysis shows that, to leading order in the Lamb-Dicke parameter, motion-induced controlled-phase-gate infidelity depends only on two-atom occupations and motional correlations, not on the chosen gate protocol. Calculations for correlated thermal states and synchronized quantum van der Pol oscillators yield lower errors than independent thermal motion at the same finite temperature. Engineered collective dissipation is proposed as the mechanism for preparing the beneficial correlations.
main_result: Correlated or synchronized atomic motion is shown to reduce Rydberg-gate infidelity relative to independent thermal atoms.
application_angle: Dissipative motional engineering could raise two-qubit fidelities in neutral-atom processors and improve analog quantum simulators.

title: k-partite quantum homomorphisms
abstract: $k$-partite XOR games and linear binary constraint system (BCS) games arise from systems of linear equations over $\mathbb{Z}_2$, providing distinct quantum relaxations of the same classical constraint satisfaction problem (CSP). Linear BCS games have been generalised to synchronous homomorphism games on arbitrary relational structures, with compositional semantics provided by the quantum monad. We introduce $k$-partite homomorphism games, extending $k$-XOR games from linear systems to arbitrary relational structures. This yields a framework for studying multipartite quantum CSPs and quantum homomorphisms. We characterise perfect strategies in both the tensor-product and commuting-operator models as Kleisli morphisms of suitable state-dependent graded quantum monads on a category of $k$-partite relational structures. We then study quantum advantage in the pseudotelepathic sense: the existence of a perfect quantum strategy without a perfect classical strategy. We show that synchronous and $k$-partite quantum advantage are incomparable at the level of CSP instances. The GHZ instance admits three-player quantum advantage but no synchronous commuting-operator advantage, whereas the magic-square instance admits synchronous quantum advantage but no $k$-partite commuting-operator advantage for any number of players or proper colouring. We also exhibit an explicit six-element template whose CSP is NP-complete and admits two-player quantum advantage. Finally, we prove that no bounded-width CSP template admits $k$-partite quantum advantage, even in the commuting-operator model.
one_liner: A generalized framework classifies perfect strategies and quantum advantage in multipartite constraint-satisfaction and homomorphism games.
why_it_matters: The results clarify which CSP structures can exhibit multipartite quantum advantage and identify a broad bounded-width class where it is impossible.
detailed_summary: The paper extends k-partite XOR games to homomorphism games over arbitrary relational structures and characterizes perfect tensor-product and commuting-operator strategies using graded quantum monads. It proves that synchronous and k-partite quantum advantages are incomparable, using GHZ and magic-square instances as separating examples. An explicit six-element NP-complete template has two-player quantum advantage, while no bounded-width CSP template supports such advantage in the commuting-operator model.
main_result: The authors characterize perfect multipartite strategies and prove structural separations and no-go results for quantum advantage across CSP families.
application_angle: The framework can guide the design of nonlocal games, verification tests, and quantum protocols built around distributed constraint solving.

title: Revealing Bell Nonlocality Does Not Require the Same Physical Measurement to be Performed Twice
abstract: Bell inequality violations, or Bell nonlocality for short, is not only central to testing the foundations of quantum physics but have also become an essential ingredient of numerous quantum information protocols, from quantum key distribution to the device-independent certification of randomness and secure communication. Existing analyses of Bell nonlocality assume that a small set of predefined measurement directions can be reproduced exactly. But what if these directions cannot be reproduced at all? This may happen for fundamental or technical reasons, such as variations in the measurement apparatus. Here we show that the violation of a Bell inequality remains possible and that it also retains its operational significance, even when the measurement directions never repeat. We experimentally confirm these results using polarization-entangled photons, detecting only one particle pair per randomly chosen analyzer direction. Our results establish the robustness of Bell inequality violations against imperfect measurement repeatability and further connect Bell tests with the broader framework of randomized measurements. Moreover, they extend quantum information protocols to settings with limited measurement control, including quantum device certification, communication complexity, and quantum cryptography.
one_liner: Polarization-entangled photons violate a Bell inequality even when every randomly chosen analyzer direction is used only once.
why_it_matters: Bell-based certification and cryptography can remain operational when measurement settings drift or cannot be reproduced exactly.
detailed_summary: The work removes the standard assumption that a small collection of measurement directions must be reproduced across repeated Bell trials. An experiment with polarization-entangled photons samples a fresh random analyzer direction for each detected pair and still reveals Bell nonlocality. The accompanying theory preserves operational interpretations relevant to certification and information-processing tasks despite nonrepeatable measurements.
main_result: Bell nonlocality is theoretically and experimentally demonstrated using nonrepeating, randomly selected analyzer directions.
application_angle: The result broadens device certification, secure communication, randomness certification, and cryptography to systems with limited measurement control.

title: Dual-species atom interferometry for axion dark matter
abstract: Atom interferometers are sensitive to oscillations of the masses and transition frequencies of atoms, which can be induced by axion dark matter. The main limitation is the sensitivity to gravity gradient noise (GGN). We propose a dual-species atom interferometry sequence that provides a suppression of GGN by up to three orders of magnitude and a sensitivity enhancement via the mass difference of the two atoms. We show that, under realistic experimental assumptions, a 10m-baseline dual-species atom interferometer is more sensitive to the axion gluon coupling than a 100m single-species gradiometer. Including a comprehensive noise analysis, we demonstrate that the Very Long Baseline Atom Interferometer (VLBAI) in Hannover with a baseline of 10m can probe the axion decay constant at levels almost competitive with leading laboratory constraints. The proposed 100m-baseline Atom Interferometer CERN Experiment (AICE) can extend this sensitivity by up to two orders of magnitude, surpassing laboratory constraints for axion masses of $10^{-19}\;\text{eV}/c^2 \lesssim m_a \lesssim 3\times10^{-15}\;\text{eV}/c^2$.
one_liner: A dual-species atom-interferometer sequence suppresses gravity-gradient noise while enhancing sensitivity to axion-induced atomic oscillations.
why_it_matters: The design could let a 10 m instrument outperform a 100 m single-species gradiometer and enable competitive laboratory searches for ultralight axion dark matter.
detailed_summary: The proposed sequence compares two atomic species to reject gravity-gradient noise by as much as three orders of magnitude while exploiting their mass difference to strengthen the axion signal. Under realistic noise assumptions, the 10 m Hannover VLBAI could approach leading laboratory bounds on the axion-gluon coupling. A 100 m AICE implementation is projected to improve sensitivity by up to two orders of magnitude over part of the 10^-19 to 3×10^-15 eV/c² axion-mass range.
main_result: The analysis predicts that a 10 m dual-species interferometer can exceed the axion sensitivity of a 100 m single-species gradiometer.
application_angle: The sequence provides a practical route to ultralight-dark-matter searches using planned long-baseline atom-interferometry facilities.

title: U(1)-Symmetric Spin SYK Models: Ordering, Chaos, and Transport
abstract: The Sachdev--Ye--Kitaev (SYK) model provides an analytically controlled setting for strongly interacting quantum dynamics and holography, but its fermionic formulation leads to nonlocal encoding overheads on qubit-based quantum processors. We study a U(1)-symmetric spin analogue of the complex SYK model, constructed from random charge-conserving $q$-spin interactions that are native to a qubit Hilbert space. In the large-$N$, large-$q$ limit, the model reproduces the leading saddle-point structure of complex fermionic SYK under the identification of chemical potential with magnetic field and charge density with magnetization. We investigate the finite-$N$, finite-$q$ regime using exact diagonalization. A U(1)-invariant ordering susceptibility increases with system size for $q = 2, 4$ but decreases for $q = 6$, while bulk-spectrum level statistics are consistent with the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble at half filling and the Gaussian unitary ensemble in the adjacent magnetization sector. We further construct coupled-cluster chains and obtain domain-wall dynamics consistent with diffusive magnetization transport in a small-cluster regime accessible to matrix-product-state simulations. These results establish analytical benchmarks and finite-size signatures of ordering, quantum chaos, and magnetization transport in U(1)-symmetric spin-SYK models, and they motivate quantum simulation of the low-temperature, large-system regime, which remains difficult for classical methods.
one_liner: A qubit-native, charge-conserving spin-SYK model reproduces key SYK structure and exhibits ordering, chaos, and diffusive transport signatures.
why_it_matters: The model removes fermion-to-qubit encoding overhead and supplies benchmarks for quantum simulation of strongly interacting dynamics beyond classical reach.
detailed_summary: The authors construct random charge-conserving q-spin interactions that act directly in a qubit Hilbert space and recover the leading complex-SYK saddle-point structure at large N and q. Exact diagonalization reveals q-dependent ordering susceptibility and symmetry-sector-dependent GOE or GUE level statistics. Coupled-cluster chains show domain-wall dynamics consistent with diffusive magnetization transport in the matrix-product-state-accessible regime.
main_result: The spin model reproduces analytical SYK behavior and finite-size signatures of ordering, quantum chaos, and diffusive magnetization transport.
application_angle: Its native spin formulation makes low-temperature SYK physics more accessible to future qubit-based quantum simulators.

title: Efficient refractive-index sweeps in the discrete dipole approximation using shifted Krylov methods
abstract: The discrete dipole approximation (DDA) is a flexible numerical method for simulating electromagnetic scattering by particles of arbitrary shape and internal structure. In many applications, such as optical-database generation, the same particle geometry must be simulated for many values of the complex refractive index, which are currently handled independently with proportional increase of computational time. For homogeneous particles, however, variations of the refractive index affect only the diagonal polarizability term of the interaction matrix. The corresponding linear systems therefore differ only by scalar shifts of the identity matrix, making them suitable for shifted Krylov-subspace methods. In this work, we use a shifted Krylov solver adapted to the complex-symmetric formulation of the matrix and implement it in the ADDA code. The method is evaluated for a homogeneous spherical particle over a two-dimensional domain of complex refractive indices. The shifted solver reproduces the extinction cross sections obtained from independent simulations with relative differences below the iterative-method tolerance, while reducing the number of matrix-vector products by a factor of 130 for the tested configuration. We further analyze how the achievable speedup depends on the number of refractive-index values, the computational backend, and the variation of the convergence rate across the parameter space. The final wall-time acceleration for large refractive-index sweeps was demonstrated to be up to 40 times, which can be further improved by optimizing the scattered-fields calculations that became a new bottleneck.
one_liner: A shifted Krylov solver accelerates discrete-dipole refractive-index sweeps by reusing one subspace across many complex-index values.
why_it_matters: The ADDA implementation cuts expensive matrix-vector products by 130× and achieves up to 40× wall-time speedup without sacrificing solver-level accuracy.
detailed_summary: For homogeneous particles, changing the complex refractive index shifts only the diagonal polarizability term, allowing all resulting linear systems to share a Krylov subspace. The complex-symmetric shifted solver was implemented in ADDA and tested on a sphere over a two-dimensional refractive-index domain. Extinction cross sections agreed with independent runs within the iterative tolerance, with 130× fewer matrix-vector products and up to 40× lower wall time.
main_result: The solver reproduced independent extinction calculations while reducing matrix-vector products by 130× and sweep wall time by up to 40×.
application_angle: The method can greatly accelerate optical-database generation and parameter sweeps for particles with fixed geometry.

title: Comprehensive quantum electrodynamics of fast electrons interacting with dissipative nanostructures and quantum light
abstract: Theoretical descriptions of the quantum electrodynamical interaction between fast electrons and nanostructures conventionally rely on standard macroscopic quantum electrodynamics (MQED), which, when applied to bounded objects in vacuum, formally requires an asymptotic limiting procedure to account for free-space radiation modes. To explicitly incorporate these modes from the outset, we employ the modified Langevin noise formalism (MLNF), which independently quantizes both the asymptotic scattering modes and the electromagnetic field generated by dissipative material sources. Utilizing an exact second-order Magnus expansion, we derive a closed-form, nonperturbative master formula for the transverse-momentum-resolved energy exchange probability. In the unilluminated regime, we demonstrate that at finite nanostructure temperatures, the vacuum scattering and thermal material fluctuations do not mathematically recombine into the total imaginary part of the dyadic Green's function. This breakdown does not violate the Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem, because the explicit zero-temperature scattering field acts as an independent dynamical system that maintains the configuration out of global thermodynamic equilibrium. This fundamental separation reveals an intrinsic Stokes--Anti-Stokes asymmetry, yielding distinct transverse diffraction patterns for energy loss and thermal energy gain, and establishing a generalized detailed-balance relation that governs the radiative reduction of the apparent temperature in nanoscale electron thermometry. In the illuminated regime, our framework rigorously incorporates quantum-optical states into macroscopic dissipative electrodynamics, demonstrating that...
one_liner: A nonperturbative QED framework unifies fast-electron scattering, dissipative nanostructures, and quantum-light excitation with explicit radiation modes.
why_it_matters: It exposes loss–gain diffraction asymmetry and radiative temperature bias relevant to nanoscale electron spectroscopy, thermometry, and quantum-light interactions.
detailed_summary: Using modified Langevin noise quantization and an exact second-order Magnus expansion, the work derives a closed-form transverse-momentum-resolved energy-exchange probability. At finite nanostructure temperature, vacuum scattering modes and thermal material fluctuations remain dynamically distinct rather than recombining into the full imaginary Green tensor. This produces different diffraction patterns for electron energy loss and thermal gain, together with generalized detailed balance and a radiative reduction of apparent nanoscale temperature.
main_result: The theory predicts intrinsic Stokes–Anti-Stokes diffraction asymmetry and a generalized detailed-balance law for nanoscale electron thermometry.
application_angle: The framework supports quantitative design and interpretation of electron-energy spectroscopy, nanoscale thermometry, and quantum-light-driven nanophotonics.

title: The importance of shear strain in narrow Si/SiGe quantum wells
abstract: Several heterostructure profiles have been proposed for Si/SiGe quantum wells, to improve the operation of quantum-dot spin qubits. These structures share a common goal of generating either of the two wave vectors that govern the conduction-band valley coupling, dubbed $k_0$ and $k_1$. Here, we focus on the long-wavelength $k_1$ term that couples valleys when paired with shear strain, and which governs the Dresselhaus spin-orbit coupling. We show that shear strain induced by metal top gates may be enough to activate the $k_1$ valley-coupling mechanism, mitigating the need for "ultrasharp" interfaces, as commonly assumed for large valley energy splittings. We propose a scheme featuring narrow quantum wells that does not require ultrasharp interfaces, but should still provide large deterministic valley splittings (when paired with shear strain), and large spin-orbit couplings and $g$-factor corrections, which are of great interest for experimental implementations.
one_liner: Gate-induced shear strain may activate long-wavelength valley coupling in narrow Si/SiGe wells without requiring ultrasharp interfaces.
why_it_matters: The mechanism could deliver deterministic valley splitting, stronger spin-orbit coupling, and useful g-factor shifts in manufacturable silicon spin-qubit stacks.
detailed_summary: The study analyzes the long-wavelength k1 contribution to conduction-band valley coupling, which becomes active when paired with shear strain and also controls Dresselhaus spin-orbit coupling. It argues that metal top gates can induce sufficient shear strain to reduce dependence on ultrasharp heterointerfaces. A narrow-well design is proposed to obtain large deterministic valley splittings, spin-orbit couplings, and g-factor corrections.
main_result: The analysis shows that realistic gate-induced shear strain can activate k1 valley coupling and enable large valley and spin-orbit effects without ultrasharp interfaces.
application_angle: This offers a potentially more fabrication-tolerant heterostructure strategy for reliable silicon quantum-dot spin qubits.

title: Quantum Material Generation via Coherent Hamiltonian Search
abstract: Discovering new materials with targeted properties is a central goal of materials science, yet the space of candidates is vast. Data-driven generative models learn the distribution of known materials, but they extrapolate poorly, and a generated structure is not known to be stable. A material's properties follow from its Hamiltonian, and a quantum computer can calculate them from it. We introduce the quantum material generative algorithm (QMage), a coherent search, guided by the Hamiltonian, over crystalline configurations of atomic composition, unit cell structure, and atomic positions, for one whose calculated properties meet the targets to within a given error tolerance. The computation is a single coherent quantum circuit in which each configuration's Hamiltonian is block-encoded, its target eigenstate isolated and properties evaluated, and the satisfying configurations amplified by fixed-point search and measured. One framework covers many targets, from formation energy and band gaps to elasticity and conductivity. We design the algorithm for the mature fault-tolerant era and estimate its cost in logical qubits and Toffoli depth from a classically routine benchmark to targets where established methods are unreliable. The approach generates candidate materials from first principles, rather than generalizing from those known, and could enable materials discovery when the target properties are difficult to predict classically.
one_liner: QMage coherently searches crystalline configurations using block-encoded Hamiltonians and fixed-point amplification to find materials meeting target properties.
why_it_matters: The proposal shifts quantum materials generation from learned extrapolation to first-principles property evaluation, targeting regimes where classical prediction is unreliable.
detailed_summary: QMage encodes composition, unit-cell structure, and atomic positions in a coherent search over candidate crystals. For each configuration, the circuit block-encodes its Hamiltonian, isolates a target eigenstate, evaluates requested properties, and amplifies candidates satisfying a chosen tolerance. The fault-tolerant resource analysis spans classically routine benchmarks through property targets for which established computational methods become unreliable.
main_result: The algorithm provides a unified coherent workflow for generating crystals that satisfy targets including formation energy, band gap, elasticity, and conductivity.
application_angle: In the mature fault-tolerant era, it could identify first-principles material candidates in design spaces that defeat classical prediction or data-driven extrapolation.

title: Mapping the High-Field Response of Superconducting Nanowire Single-Photon Detectors
abstract: Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) are increasingly being integrated into cryogenic quantum-sensing platforms that operate in large magnetic fields. Here, the high-field limits of these measurements were probed by characterizing the dark count response of a NbTiN SNSPD at up to 14~T using in situ control of the detector orientation and benchmarking that performance against normal detector operation in smaller magnetic fields. The detector performance is strongly anisotropic: perpendicular magnetic fields rapidly reduce the usable bias-current range, whereas near-parallel alignment enables operation at substantially larger total fields, with a finite operating margin retained to 12~T and measurable dark-count response at the 14~T field limit. The angular dependence is governed predominantly by the perpendicular component of the magnetic field, consistent with vortex-mediated suppression of the superconducting current scale. The same field-dependent current scale also determines the electrical pulse amplitude, linking high-field detector operation directly to readout performance. These results establish a practical route for deploying SNSPDs in multi-tesla quantum-sensing and high-field cryogenic experiments.
one_liner: A NbTiN SNSPD remains operational in near-parallel magnetic fields to 12 T, with measurable dark counts at 14 T.
why_it_matters: The orientation-dependent limits provide practical guidance for integrating single-photon detection into high-field cryogenic sensing experiments.
detailed_summary: The authors characterize a NbTiN superconducting nanowire single-photon detector up to 14 T while controlling its in situ orientation. Perpendicular fields rapidly shrink the usable bias-current range, whereas near-parallel alignment preserves finite operating margin through 12 T and measurable response at 14 T. Both dark-count behavior and electrical pulse amplitude track a field-dependent current scale governed mainly by the perpendicular field component, consistent with vortex-mediated suppression.
main_result: Near-parallel alignment enables SNSPD operation with finite bias margin at 12 T and measurable dark-count response at 14 T.
application_angle: The measured angular constraints enable reliable detector placement and readout design in multi-tesla quantum-sensing and cryogenic platforms.

title: Optical symmetry breaking for single-image field reconstruction
abstract: Light carries information in both amplitude and phase, although cameras record only intensity. Reconstructing the optical field is at the heart of wavefront sensing, microscopy and coherent communications. Existing methods often rely on multiple measurements or iterative phase retrieval. In fields described by known spatial modes, intensity is determined by pairwise products of their complex coefficients. Yet optical symmetries can make these products indistinguishable, leaving different fields with nearly identical images. Here, we show that engineering the optical measurement to break these symmetries enables direct reconstruction of the complex field from a single intensity image. We optimise a phase mask followed by propagation to separate pairwise modal signatures while retaining light on the detector. A calibrated linear inverse and rank-one projection then recover modal amplitudes and relative phases without iterative phase retrieval. In simulations, optimised masks satisfy conditioning and light-capture requirements unmet by random masks. Experiments reconstruct 42-mode fibre fields using either a spatial light modulator or a passive diffuser, with median complex-field errors of 9.1% and 4.6%, respectively, against holographic references. This extends an earlier five-mode experimental demonstration of fast intensity-only modal decomposition. Per-frame computation takes 2.1 ms, and batched throughput exceeds 4,000 frames per second. These results establish measurement-space symmetry breaking as a route to rapid single-image optical field reconstruction.
one_liner: An optimized symmetry-breaking optical mask reconstructs 42-mode complex fibre fields from one camera image at millisecond latency.
why_it_matters: Single-shot, non-iterative recovery of amplitude and phase could accelerate wavefront sensing, coherent links, and multimode-fibre control.
detailed_summary: The method optimizes a phase mask and propagation stage so that otherwise degenerate pairwise modal signatures become distinguishable in a single intensity measurement. A calibrated linear inverse followed by rank-one projection retrieves modal amplitudes and relative phases without iterative phase retrieval. Experiments on 42-mode fibre fields achieve median complex-field errors of 9.1% with an SLM and 4.6% with a passive diffuser, with 2.1 ms per-frame processing and batched rates above 4,000 frames per second.
platform_or_system: 42-mode fibre with SLM or passive diffuser
main_result: The system reconstructs a 42-mode complex optical field from one intensity image with median errors as low as 4.6%.
application_angle: Fast intensity-only field recovery supports real-time fibre characterization, adaptive optics, microscopy, and coherent communication receivers.

title: Infinite or indefinite: the query cost of simulating the quantum switch
abstract: The quantum switch applies two operations in a coherent superposition of their causal orders and is a simple example of indefinite causal order. No quantum circuit that uses each operation once in a definite order can even describe it, yet photonic experiments have demonstrated its physical realization. We ask how many calls to the black-box operations a quantum computer in the circuit model needs to reproduce the switch. If one of the black boxes is known to be unitary, three calls suffice. For general channels on a $d$-dimensional system, we prove three results. In all three, circuits may use classical feed-forward and unlimited ancillary quantum memory. First, no finite number of calls suffices for exact simulation in the worst case. Second, approximation to any fixed error below $1/2$, measured in half the diamond norm, requires $Ω(d^{1/4})$ calls, exponential in the number of qubits. Third, an ordinary circuit can require exponentially many calls to obtain a single bit that the switch extracts with a few uses. We consider a device whose actual noise is dephasing in a fixed unknown basis and test it against a theoretical depolarizing model. The two channels have the same entanglement and average gate fidelities, so these figures alone do not distinguish them. At fixed noise strength, the quantum switch tells them apart with a number of device uses independent of $d$, whereas the circuit model requires $Ω(d^{1/16})$ calls. Noise characterization is needed for quantum error correction, and this gives a provable query advantage of the switch in a task relevant to practical quantum computing. We invite future work that extends such advantages to more practical computing tasks.
one_liner: The quantum switch yields provable query advantages for simulating channel order and distinguishing realistic noise models.
why_it_matters: It identifies a noise-characterization task where indefinite causal order can outperform every definite-order circuit by a dimension-dependent margin.
detailed_summary: The work studies the number of black-box channel calls required for definite-order circuits to reproduce or approximate the quantum switch. Exact worst-case simulation of general channels requires infinitely many calls, while approximation below half-diamond-norm error 1/2 needs Ω(d^1/4) calls; three calls suffice if one box is known to be unitary. For distinguishing unknown-basis dephasing from depolarizing noise with matched standard fidelities, the switch uses a dimension-independent number of queries while ordinary circuits require Ω(d^1/16).
platform_or_system: Quantum switch with black-box quantum channels
main_result: Indefinite causal order provides dimension-independent noise discrimination where definite-order circuits require polynomially growing channel queries.
application_angle: The advantage could improve characterization of device noise that conventional entanglement and average gate fidelities fail to distinguish.

title: Bright and Uniform Silicon Carbide Nanophotonic Arrays for Scalable Nanoscale Quantum Sensing
abstract: Silicon carbide (SiC) spin defects are emerging as powerful platforms for nanoscale quantum sensing due to their near-surface stability, near-infrared emission, and CMOS compatibility. However, poor photon collection efficiency and the reliance on randomly distributed defects hinder the realization of practical, large-scale devices. Here, we demonstrate scalable, ultra-bright, and highly uniform SiC quantum nanophotonic arrays. By combining a self-aligned fabrication process with localized oxygen ion implantation, we deterministically position PL5 and PL6 centers at the exact center of 4H-SiC nanopillars. This architecture yields record-high photon count rates of $\sim$1 Mcps (PL5) and $\sim$2 Mcps (PL6), establishing a new benchmark for SiC color centers while maintaining near-identical brightness across the array. Furthermore, we apply these devices to nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), successfully demonstrating external nanoscale nuclear-spin detection. These results establish our SiC nanopillars as robust building blocks for scanning quantum probes and scalable sensor networks.
one_liner: Deterministic SiC nanopillar arrays deliver uniform PL5 and PL6 emitters at up to 2 Mcps and detect external nuclear spins.
why_it_matters: The combination of brightness, deterministic placement, and demonstrated nanoscale NMR addresses key barriers to scalable quantum sensors.
detailed_summary: A self-aligned process and localized oxygen implantation place PL5 and PL6 defects at the centers of 4H-SiC nanopillars. The arrays achieve near-uniform brightness with photon rates around 1 Mcps for PL5 and 2 Mcps for PL6. The devices are further used to detect external nuclear spins through nanoscale NMR, demonstrating sensing functionality beyond optical characterization.
main_result: The arrays combine deterministic defect placement, photon rates up to about 2 Mcps, and external nanoscale nuclear-spin detection.
application_angle: CMOS-compatible, uniform nanopillar arrays could serve as scanning probes or as scalable networks for nanoscale magnetic and NMR sensing.

title: Hierarchical Decoding for Quantum Error Correction
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires classical decoders that can keep up with syndrome data streams and supply correction information and logical measurement outcomes to the quantum control system. Meeting these requirements at scale requires high throughput while controlling the end-to-end latency from readout to usable correction. In this paper, we organize decoding algorithms, execution strategies, and code constructions using common classifications and examine their performance and trade-offs under the reported evaluation conditions. We distinguish decoder-level hierarchy, where multiple decoding stages or resources cooperate to decode a single code, from code-level hierarchy, where the code construction itself introduces multiple decoding levels. We first review single-code hierarchical decoders and their cascaded predecoding and windowed, streaming, and distributed implementations. We then study hierarchical and concatenated codes, focusing on how decoding is coordinated across code levels through hard decisions, soft reliability information, or syndrome information. We also examine how qubit modalities shape decoding workloads and timing requirements, and review how different decoding platforms meet these requirements, including central processing units (CPUs), graphics processing units (GPUs), field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), and cryogenic platforms. By assessing design trade-offs, this paper clarifies connections across the literature and provides a shared foundation for QEC design exploration. It also identifies gaps in performance reporting and system integration to guide future research toward practical quantum error correction.
one_liner: A systems-level review maps hierarchical QEC decoders, code hierarchies, execution strategies, and hardware implementation trade-offs.
why_it_matters: Its unified framework exposes latency, throughput, reporting, and integration gaps that must be resolved for real-time fault-tolerant control.
detailed_summary: This review separates decoder-level hierarchy, where stages or resources cooperate on one code, from code-level hierarchy involving concatenated or multilevel constructions. It compares cascaded predecoding, windowed and streaming execution, distributed implementations, and the exchange of hard decisions, reliabilities, or syndromes between levels. The analysis spans CPU, GPU, FPGA, ASIC, and cryogenic platforms while emphasizing inconsistent performance reporting and incomplete control-system integration.
main_result: The paper provides a common taxonomy and system-oriented comparison of hierarchical decoders, hierarchical codes, and their implementation platforms.
application_angle: The framework helps architects select decoder and hardware combinations that can meet syndrome throughput and feedback-latency requirements at scale.

title: Optically-detected room-temperature spin-coherence from the GaV$^-$ in diamond
abstract: Solid-state quantum defects (point crystal imperfections with optically addressable spins) are among the most promising platforms for quantum information science due to their long-lived electron and nuclear spin lifetimes. The negatively-charged nitrogen-vacancy (NV$^-$) and negatively-charged group IV vacancies (G4V's) in diamond are some the most promising quantum defects but, the NV$^-$ is highly susceptible to charge noise and has low emission from its zero-phonon line while the G4V's require low operating temperatures. Here we report the physical properties of the newly discovered negatively-charged gallium-vacancy in diamond, GaV$^-$. We find that the GaV$^-$, created through FIB implantation and high-pressure high-temperature annealing, exhibits a combination of the best properties of both the NV$^-$ and G4V's: optically-detectable spin coherence at room temperature ($T_2(293K) = 1.06 μ$s), a large Debye-Waller factor $\sim$0.4, a short radiative lifetime ($\sim$3.83 ns), strong temperature dependence of the zero-field splitting (16x that of the NV$^-$), and charge-noise-protected D$_{3d}$ symmetry. These features (along with improved performance at low temperature) position the newly discovered GaV$^-$ as a key resource for quantum sensing, networking, and computation.
one_liner: GaV− centers in diamond show optically detected room-temperature spin coherence alongside bright, fast, zero-phonon-line-rich emission.
why_it_matters: GaV− may combine room-temperature operation with inversion symmetry and efficient optical emission for robust sensing and networking nodes.
detailed_summary: GaV− defects are produced by focused-ion-beam implantation followed by high-pressure, high-temperature annealing. At 293 K they exhibit optically detected spin coherence with T2 = 1.06 μs, a Debye–Waller factor near 0.4, and a radiative lifetime of about 3.83 ns. Their zero-field splitting is reported to be 16 times more temperature-sensitive than that of NV−, while D3d symmetry offers protection against charge noise.
platform_or_system: Negatively charged gallium-vacancy centers in diamond
main_result: GaV− combines 1.06 μs room-temperature spin coherence, strong zero-phonon-line emission, fast radiative decay, and enhanced thermal sensitivity.
application_angle: These properties make GaV− promising for room-temperature thermometry and magnetometry, as well as optically interfaced quantum-network and computing devices.

title: An optical-frequency-comb-enabled unified infrastructure for quantum networks
abstract: Quantum networks require precision timing and classical communication to coordinate distributed quantum operations, yet these functions are typically supported by separate infrastructures, increasing system complexity and limiting scalability. Here we demonstrate an optical-frequency-comb-enabled infrastructure that unifies precision timing, classical communication and quantum communication over a shared fibre link. By encoding classical data onto the intensity of the comb while retaining its pulse timing, we simultaneously transmit data at 100 Mbit/s and achieve a timing stability of 0.85 fs at 1 s over 100 km. We develop a spectral-engineering strategy to suppress the coupling between data modulation and timing extraction. We further establish a power-dependent model of the excess noise induced in a co-propagating continuous-variable quantum key distribution channel, identifying optical power, wavelength allocation and propagation direction as the principal control parameters. After optimization, the system introduces only 0.0037 shot noise unit of additional excess noise and limits the secret-key-rate penalty to 6.7%. Furthermore, quantum-secured timestamp transmission additionally enables absolute time synchronization with a stability of 0.26 fs at 1 s. These results establish optical frequency combs as a common physical layer for integrated quantum-network services.
one_liner: A shared 100-km fiber carries 100-Mbit/s data, sub-femtosecond timing, and continuous-variable QKD using an optical frequency comb.
why_it_matters: It consolidates three essential quantum-network services onto one physical link while adding only 0.0037 shot-noise units of excess noise.
detailed_summary: The system intensity-modulates an optical frequency comb to transmit 100-Mbit/s classical data while preserving pulse timing over 100 km of fiber. Spectral engineering reduces modulation-to-timing coupling, yielding 0.85-fs timing stability at 1 s and only 0.0037 shot-noise units of added CV-QKD excess noise. Quantum-secured timestamps further provide 0.26-fs absolute synchronization stability at 1 s.
main_result: The experiment unifies classical data, precision timing, and CV-QKD over 100 km with a 6.7% secret-key-rate penalty.
application_angle: A common comb-based physical layer could reduce the infrastructure complexity of scalable metropolitan and long-haul quantum networks.

title: Training quantum neural networks one job at a time
abstract: When a quantum processor is reached through a cloud queue, a variational algorithm pays for every round trip, and a single round trip can carry many circuits. The classical optimizer therefore decides how much is learned per job, not only per shot. We study this for a quantum neural network classifier. We compare optimizers that are given the same number of jobs and the same shots per job, and that differ only in how they fill each job. This comparison treats hybrid quantum-classical training as an execution-efficiency problem: how to obtain useful optimization progress from each costly interaction with a quantum processor. The resulting perspective connects optimizer design to overhead amortization and efficient use of accelerator resources. A direct port of a batched pattern search that worked for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm stalls once the model has a few dozen parameters. What does transfer is the principle behind it: fill each job with a batch of parameter vectors that is fixed before the job is sent. For circuits built from Pauli rotations the natural batch is the parameter-shift stencil. We show that its gradient error falls as the inverse of the shots per job, while the error of simultaneous-perturbation methods (SPSA) has a floor that no number of shots removes. In simulation, batched parameter-shift training needs between a fifth and a half of the jobs SPSA needs, for 24 to 48 parameters, and the ordering holds at two noise levels. A new structure-aware stencil search reads the same kind of rows as sinusoids and also beats SPSA. On IBM's ibm_fez processor, in three interleaved runs at six and eight qubits, the batched optimizer reached SPSA's final training loss within 4 to 20 of its 50 jobs. Its test accuracy was clearly higher at eight qubits; at six qubits the difference was not significant. All hardware numbers can be re-derived from the raw shots.
one_liner: Job-batched parameter-shift optimization trains cloud quantum neural networks with substantially fewer processor submissions than SPSA.
why_it_matters: The method targets cloud-queue overhead directly and reaches comparable training loss in as few as 4–20 jobs on IBM hardware.
detailed_summary: The study treats each cloud submission, rather than each shot, as the costly resource in hybrid quantum-classical training. For Pauli-rotation circuits, fixed parameter-shift stencils fill each job efficiently and exhibit gradient error that decreases inversely with shots per job, unlike the reported SPSA error floor. On IBM's ibm_fez processor, the batched method reached SPSA's final loss within 4–20 of SPSA's 50 jobs across six- and eight-qubit runs.
main_result: Batched parameter-shift training used roughly one-fifth to one-half as many jobs as SPSA in simulation and converged faster in interleaved hardware runs.
application_angle: Fewer cloud submissions can lower queue latency and accelerator overhead for practical variational learning workloads.

title: No Convergence in Learned Eavesdropping-Detection Dynamics for BB84 Quantum Key Distribution
abstract: In prior work we showed that a reinforcement-learning eavesdropper can intercept BB84 quantum key distribution while holding the quantum bit error rate below the abort threshold and keeping a usable distillable key. In this paper we ask whether an equally adaptive learning detector can close this stealth window. We cast the interaction as an alternating best-response game between a tabular eavesdropper and a tabular threshold-adapting detector. We measure exploitability, which is the detection rate and distillable key fraction achieved by a fresh attacker best-responding to the final detector. Across three learning rules (Q-Learning, SARSA, Double Q-Learning), three channel-noise levels, and a uniform false-alarm discipline, the dynamics do not settle out to twenty rounds. The exploitability does not approach a fixed point, and its round-to-round swings do not decay. Two controls, one retraining the attacker against a frozen defender and one retraining the defender against a frozen attacker, show that the swings on each side match the variance of the best-response procedure itself. The dynamics fluctuate at the scale of best-response variance rather than converging, with neither player settling to a fixed response. The behavior is noise-dependent, and the stealth window stays open at the low noise where practical QKD operates. The defender contains the attacker on average at intermediate noise without the contest settling, and at high noise the channel rather than the learned policy suppresses the attack. As a candidate mechanism we examine a last-mover information asymmetry, supported by significant anti-persistence at intermediate noise and consistent with best-response noise at low noise. The results suggest that a learned detector cannot be certified from any single round, and that closing the window calls for breaking the information structure rather than out-adapting the attacker.
one_liner: Adaptive BB84 eavesdroppers and learned detectors fail to converge, leaving a stealth window open under low-noise operating conditions.
why_it_matters: The result warns that a detector selected from one training round cannot be treated as a certifiable defense against adaptive QKD attacks.
detailed_summary: The authors model a tabular reinforcement-learning eavesdropper and a threshold-adapting detector as an alternating best-response game. Across Q-learning, SARSA, Double Q-learning, and three noise levels, exploitability continues to fluctuate through 20 rounds without approaching a fixed point. Control experiments attribute the swings to best-response variance, while the attack remains viable at the low channel noise relevant to practical QKD.
main_result: Learned attack-and-detection dynamics show no convergence, and the low-noise stealth window persists across the tested learning rules.
application_angle: Robust QKD monitoring may require changing the information structure or security protocol rather than relying on iteratively retrained detectors.

title: Exact Quantum Algorithms for Composed Boolean Functions
abstract: We study exact quantum algorithms for block compositions of total Boolean functions. For an outer function $f$ of degree $D$ and an inner function $g$ on $m$ bits, we prove $$ Q_E(f\circ g)=O\!\left(mD+Q_E(f)Q_{1/(4D)}(g)\right). $$ The algorithm combines approximate inner evaluations with a finite exact correction. Its two costs are governed by different parameters of the outer function: exact query complexity determines the cost of simulation, whereas polynomial degree determines the number of inner blocks used in the correction. We first establish the construction with an arity-dependent error threshold and then obtain the degree-dependent threshold above. For recursive ternary not-all-equal, this gives an exact algorithm using $(3/\sqrt2)^{k(1+o(1))}$ queries asymptotically. More generally, for every fixed nonconstant total gadget $h$, we determine the exact recursive rate as $\max\{\textrm{deg}(h),\operatorname{Adv}^{\pm}(h)\}$ and prove $Q_E(h^{\circ k})=\widetilde O_h(R(h^{\circ k})^2)$. The composition limit also allows to transfer separations from $Q_{\varepsilon}$ and $°$ to exact quantum query complexity $Q_E$ (similar to fractional block sensitivity to block sensitivity transfer in Tal and Kulkarni 2016, Chicago Journal of Theoretical Computer Science). We construct a family with $s=\operatorname{bs}=\operatorname{fbs}\ge Q_E^{3/2-o(1)}$, improving the previous exponent $1.1527\ldots$. A second construction gives $R \ge Q_E^{2-o(1)}$, improving the previous exponent $3/2$. We also allow different inner functions and give analogous quantitative separations in quantum communication.
one_liner: New composition bounds yield faster exact quantum algorithms and stronger query and communication-complexity separations.
why_it_matters: The work sharpens the theoretical limits of exact quantum computation and transfers query-complexity separations into communication settings.
detailed_summary: The paper derives an upper bound for exact quantum evaluation of block-composed total Boolean functions by combining approximate inner evaluations with finite exact correction. For recursive ternary not-all-equal, it obtains an asymptotic query count of (3/√2)^{k(1+o(1))}. It also establishes recursive rates governed by polynomial degree and the adversary bound, improves several complexity separations, and extends analogous results to quantum communication.
main_result: The authors prove new exact-composition bounds and improve separations to s ≥ Q_E^{3/2-o(1)} and R ≥ Q_E^{2-o(1)}.
application_angle: Although theoretical, the bounds clarify which composed computational and communication tasks can obtain exact quantum advantages.

title: Circuit-Level Analysis of Quantum Error Correction in Second-Generation Quantum Repeaters
abstract: We present a circuit-level simulation of second-generation quantum repeaters with stabilizer-based quantum error correction. We model a two-segment repeater link including encoding, syndrome extraction, decoding, and entanglement swapping, and compare the performance of the single-error-correcting Steane and five-qubit stabilizer codes under different noise scenarios. To that extent, we consider noise sources with incoherent (depolarizing and dephasing) and coherent (systematic over-rotation) errors and incorporate them directly at the circuit level. While the Steane code outperforms the five-qubit code at coherent errors, the five-qubit code achieves higher end-to-end fidelities under incoherent noise in the low-noise regime when a large number of physical qubits is affected by it. At higher noise regimes, employing no code turns out to be the best option. In mixed noise scenarios, we observe moderate cross-effects between the noise classes regarding the error correction performance. We conclude that code selection in second-generation quantum repeaters must be adapted to the dominant physical noise mechanism and that circuit complexity and hardware-aware implementation options influence performance in coherent-error-dominated regimes, providing design insights for error correction in quantum repeaters.
one_liner: Circuit-level repeater simulations show that the best quantum error-correcting code depends strongly on the underlying physical noise.
why_it_matters: The findings replace code-agnostic repeater assumptions with hardware-aware guidance spanning coherent, incoherent, and mixed errors.
detailed_summary: A two-segment second-generation repeater is simulated at circuit level, including encoding, syndrome extraction, decoding, and entanglement swapping. The five-qubit code gives higher end-to-end fidelity for low incoherent noise affecting many qubits, whereas the Steane code performs better under coherent over-rotation errors. At sufficiently high noise, the additional correction circuitry makes an uncoded link preferable.
main_result: No single code dominates: Steane favors coherent-error regimes, the five-qubit code favors low incoherent noise, and no coding can win at high noise.
application_angle: Repeater designers can use the results to match error-correction codes and circuit complexity to measured hardware noise.

title: TARANG: an open-source, cost-controlled design workflow for silicon nitride microcomb chips
abstract: Designing a microresonator frequency comb chip means solving a chain of coupled problems: a waveguide with anomalous dispersion that survives fabrication errors, a ring with the right free spectral range and quality factor, a bus gap that sets the coupling regime, and grating couplers, all made in one lithography step. We present TARANG, an open-source Python package that takes a silicon nitride platform from tabulated refractive indices to a GDSII mask in fourteen stages, built on the Tidy3D mode, FDTD and eigenmode-expansion solvers. Every cloud simulation is priced before it runs and capped, every result is cached by a fingerprint of the full simulation, and every quoted number carries a numerical check. We show that snapping the grid onto the core's faces, a common way to steady dispersion calculations, leaves the field samples on the faces to floating-point rounding, and that averaging solves with the grid just inside and just outside the faces makes the group-velocity dispersion $D$ independent of the computer and steady to about 1 ps/(nm km) from mesh to mesh. Two complete air-clad designs are presented, at 1550 nm ($700\times1000$ nm core, $D = 372.9 \pm 0.6$ ps/(nm km)) and at 780 nm ($350\times500$ nm, $D = 196.4 \pm 0.9$ ps/(nm km)), each with a 200 GHz ring, critical and over-coupled gaps, grating couplers, and a fibre-to-fibre budget. The predicted dispersion agrees with two measured devices from the literature to within 1 and 4%, and an independent Lugiato-Lefever solver forms stable single solitons from the exported parameters of both designs, which are ready for fabrication.
one_liner: TARANG automates cost-capped silicon-nitride microcomb design from refractive-index data through fabrication-ready GDSII masks.
why_it_matters: The open workflow couples reproducible simulation, numerical checks, and cloud-cost controls with complete 1550- and 780-nm chip designs.
detailed_summary: TARANG is a 14-stage Python workflow using mode, FDTD, and eigenmode-expansion solvers to design waveguides, rings, coupling gaps, and grating couplers. Grid-offset averaging stabilizes calculated dispersion to about 1 ps/(nm km) across meshes and computers. Complete 200-GHz-ring designs at 1550 and 780 nm agree with measured literature devices within 1% and 4%, respectively, and exported parameters support stable single-soliton states in an independent solver.
main_result: The package produces fabrication-ready 1550- and 780-nm microcomb layouts with validated dispersion and simulated stable single-soliton operation.
application_angle: The workflow lowers simulation cost and reproducibility barriers for developing microcomb sources in communications, metrology, and sensing.

title: Effect of atomic interactions on quantum communication protocols
abstract: We develop a first-principles framework for analyzing photonic quantum communication in an atomic medium. Starting from a real-space quantization of the electromagnetic field coupled to an ensemble of two-level atoms, we derive an effective model for polarization-encoded single-photon states. We apply this framework to superdense coding to study communication efficiency and to the BB84 quantum key distribution protocol for communication security. For superdense coding, we evaluate the protocol capacity of the fixed Bell-state alphabet under erasure, dephasing, and depolarizing channels and show that it decreases monotonically with increasing atom-field coupling. For BB84, we formulate a modified protocol that discards erasure outcomes and uses the microscopic model to estimate the intrinsic loss rate. We derive the corresponding asymptotic key rate and show that it decreases monotonically with coupling strength and vanishes beyond a finite critical coupling.
one_liner: A microscopic atom–photon model quantifies how atomic media degrade superdense coding capacity and BB84 secret-key rates.
why_it_matters: It connects measurable atom–field coupling to communication loss, noise, protocol capacity, and a finite security cutoff.
detailed_summary: The authors quantize the electromagnetic field in real space and couple it to an ensemble of two-level atoms, deriving an effective channel for polarization-encoded single photons. For a fixed Bell-state alphabet, superdense-coding capacity falls monotonically under coupling-induced erasure, dephasing, and depolarization. A modified BB84 protocol discards erasures, but its asymptotic key rate still vanishes above a finite atom–field coupling.
platform_or_system: Single photons in a two-level atomic medium
main_result: Both superdense-coding capacity and BB84 key rate decrease with atom–field coupling, with BB84 losing secure key generation beyond a critical coupling.
application_angle: The framework can guide security and link-budget assessments for quantum networks whose photons propagate through resonant atomic media or memories.

title: PISim: A Unified Photonic Inference Simulator for Hardware-Aware Cross-Layer Design-Space Exploration
abstract: Photonic neural accelerators offer ultra-low latency linear algebra, yet their usable numerical precision, sustainable throughput, and application accuracy remain tightly bounded by surrounding electro-optical interfaces and physical non-idealities. Pre-fabrication design-space exploration (DSE) requires a cross-layer electronic design automation (EDA) framework capable of evaluating disparate optical topologies under identical neural workloads and physical assumptions. We present \textbf{PISim}, a unified Photonic Inference Simulator that couples pretrained deep neural network execution with physics-based models of six accelerator architecture families, six electro-optic modulator technologies, four optical source organizations, and direct or coherent readout schemes. PISim embeds stage-resolved impairment operators---covering control and analog-to-digital quantization, finite extinction ratio, shot noise, correlated relative-intensity noise (RIN), thermal drift, propagation loss, and channel crosstalk---alongside an analytical cycle-level interface timing model to expose electronic-optical bottlenecks. Using simulated MNIST multilayer perceptron (MLP) benchmarks, we demonstrate how PISim identifies optimal precision operating points under multi-impairment stress (peaking at 6 bits for Mach--Zehnder and microring modulators), quantifies a 52.5 percentage-point accuracy gap between VCSEL-array and parallel-fanout laser architectures arising, under the modeled conditions, from power partitioning and correlated source noise, and models interface-limited throughput scaling across emitter-array widths from 32 to 128 channels. This comprehensive framework establishes an extensible, reproducible foundation for accuracy-constrained Pareto optimization prior to photonic tape-out.
one_liner: PISim jointly models neural workloads, photonic accelerator architectures, device choices, impairments, and interface timing before tape-out.
why_it_matters: It exposes cross-layer accuracy and throughput bottlenecks that isolated optical-component or neural-network simulations can miss.
detailed_summary: PISim combines pretrained-network execution with physical models spanning six accelerator families, six modulator technologies, four source organizations, and direct or coherent detection. Its impairment stack includes quantization, extinction limits, shot noise, correlated RIN, thermal drift, propagation loss, and crosstalk, alongside cycle-level interface timing. Simulated MNIST studies identify 6-bit optima for Mach–Zehnder and microring modulators and a modeled 52.5-percentage-point accuracy gap between two laser-source organizations.
main_result: The simulator identifies accuracy-optimal precision points, source-dependent accuracy gaps, and interface-limited scaling from 32 to 128 optical channels.
application_angle: PISim supports reproducible, accuracy-constrained architecture selection and Pareto optimization before costly photonic fabrication.

title: Gatemon qubits based on in-situ ternary InAsSb/Al nanowire Josephson junctions
abstract: Ternary InAsSb/Al nanowires combine compositionally engineerable semiconductor properties with epitaxial proximity superconductivity, making them attractive for hybrid quantum circuits and mesoscopic superconductivity. Here, we realize gatemon qubits based on shadow-defined in-situ InAsSb/Al Josephson junctions in a single growth process. Gate-dependent microwave spectroscopy demonstrates electrostatic tuning of the qubit transition over several gigahertz. Rabi oscillations and Ramsey interference show coherent qubit control, with representative values T1 = 0.79 us and T2* = 0.91 us. Across five gatemons distributed over three chips, the measured relaxation times range from approximately 0.2 us to 1 us and decrease with increasing qubit frequency. Their magnitude is comparable to a circuit estimate of spontaneous emission into the electromagnetic environment. These results establish in-situ InAsSb/Al junctions as coherent, gate-tunable circuit elements and introduce cQED architecture as a microwave probe of the dynamics of the ternary weak link.
one_liner: In-situ InAsSb/Al nanowire Josephson junctions enable gate-tunable gatemon qubits with coherent microwave control.
why_it_matters: The work validates a compositionally tunable hybrid material system as a coherent circuit element and spectroscopy platform for ternary weak links.
detailed_summary: Shadow-defined InAsSb/Al Josephson junctions are grown in situ and embedded in circuit-QED gatemon devices. Microwave spectroscopy shows electrostatic tuning across several gigahertz, while Rabi and Ramsey measurements demonstrate coherent control. Representative values are T1 = 0.79 µs and T2* = 0.91 µs; across five devices, T1 spans roughly 0.2–1 µs and decreases with qubit frequency.
main_result: Five gatemons across three chips show multi-gigahertz gate tunability and coherent control with relaxation times reaching about 1 µs.
application_angle: The platform offers gate-controlled superconducting qubits and a circuit-QED probe for engineered semiconductor–superconductor weak links.

title: Beauty and charm jet identification with end-to-end training on a superconducting quantum processor
abstract: The identification of heavy-flavor jets, i.e. collimated streams of particles originating from the fragmentation of beauty and charm quarks produced in proton-proton collisions, represents one of the most challenging classification tasks in measurements at Large Hadron Collider experiments. In recent years, advanced machine learning techniques have been successfully employed to address this problem, while quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising alternative approach. However, the high dimensionality of the problem, typically involving hundreds of observables, raises an open question: whether the current generation of quantum computers, characterized by limited qubit count, can effectively tackle such complex tasks. In this work, a variational quantum circuit for the classification of b- and c-jets at the LHCb experiment is implemented on a 5-qubit superconducting quantum computer manufactured by IQM and installed at the Politecnico di Torino. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a quantum algorithm for jet identification using simulated data from an LHC experiment in which all stages of the machine-learning workflow, including training and testing, are performed on real quantum hardware. The results demonstrate that the impact of hardware-induced quantum noise does not significantly degrade the performance. A framework for the evaluation of the training time on the quantum hardware and for the circuit optimization is also proposed. These findings pave the way for future applications on larger quantum devices based on superconducting qubits, featuring a larger number of qubits enabling the encoding of information beyond the reach of classical simulation and providing a step toward investigating whether quantum advantage may eventually be achievable in high-energy physics classification tasks.
one_liner: A five-qubit superconducting processor performs end-to-end training and testing for beauty-versus-charm jet classification.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates a complete high-energy-physics machine-learning workflow on real quantum hardware rather than hardware-only inference.
detailed_summary: A variational quantum classifier for simulated LHCb beauty- and charm-jet data is implemented on a five-qubit IQM superconducting processor. Both training and testing run on the physical device, and the measured hardware noise does not significantly reduce classification performance. The authors also introduce methods for estimating hardware training time and optimizing the circuit.
main_result: The processor completes end-to-end variational training and testing for b- versus c-jet classification without significant noise-induced performance loss.
application_angle: The study provides an experimental workflow for assessing quantum classifiers on complex scientific data as superconducting processors scale.

title: Spectroscopy of ultracold molecules in the mid-infrared
abstract: Unlike the microwave and optical domains, frequency metrology in the mid-infrared has not yet benefited from the long coherence times and exquisite control provided by ultracold particles. We use a quantum cascade laser operating at 17.5 THz to drive ro-vibrational transitions in ultracold calcium monofluoride molecules. The laser linewidth is narrowed to 15 kHz by locking it to a custom mid-infrared ring cavity, which is in turn locked to an ultrastable laser. We study the spectrum for molecules confined in red-detuned and blue-detuned magneto-optical traps, and in an optical dipole trap. In the dipole trap, the spectroscopic linewidth is close to that of the laser. We consider the stability and accuracy that can be reached using these methods in the context of a broader programme for improving frequency metrology in the mid-infrared.
one_liner: A cavity-stabilized 17.5-THz quantum cascade laser resolves ro-vibrational transitions in trapped ultracold CaF molecules.
why_it_matters: It brings ultracold-particle coherence and control into mid-infrared spectroscopy, where precision metrology has remained comparatively limited.
detailed_summary: A quantum cascade laser at 17.5 THz is narrowed to 15 kHz using a custom mid-infrared ring cavity referenced to an ultrastable laser. The system drives ro-vibrational transitions in ultracold calcium monofluoride held in red-detuned and blue-detuned magneto-optical traps and an optical dipole trap. In the dipole trap, the molecular linewidth approaches the laser linewidth, establishing a route toward substantially improved mid-infrared metrology.
platform_or_system: Ultracold CaF molecules with a stabilized quantum cascade laser
main_result: The experiment achieves near-laser-limited mid-infrared spectroscopy of optically trapped ultracold CaF using a 15-kHz-linewidth source.
application_angle: The technique could underpin precision molecular clocks, fundamental-physics searches, and traceable mid-infrared frequency references.

title: Hilbert's 17th problem for symmetric functions: undecidability and a counterexample
abstract: We study inequalities between symmetric functions that hold in every number of variables. First, we prove that it is undecidable whether a symmetric function with rational coefficients is nonnegative in all dimensions, answering a question posed by Acevedo, Blekherman, Debus and Riener. As a consequence, the validity of dimension-free moment criteria for entanglement in quantum information is undecidable. Second, we present a homogeneous symmetric function of degree 8 which is positive definite in every dimension but admits no sum of squares multiplier that is uniform in the number of variables. Consequently, Artin's solution of Hilbert's 17th problem and the Krivine-Stengle Positivstellensatz have no any-dimensional analog and any-dimensional Positivstellensätze asked for by Levin and Chandrasekaran cannot hold in general.
one_liner: Dimension-independent positivity of rational symmetric functions—and associated moment-based entanglement criteria—is shown to be undecidable.
why_it_matters: It establishes a fundamental computational limit on universal entanglement tests based on dimension-free moment inequalities.
detailed_summary: The authors prove that deciding whether a rational symmetric function is nonnegative for every number of variables is undecidable. This directly makes the validity of dimension-free moment criteria for quantum entanglement undecidable. They also construct a degree-eight positive-definite symmetric function lacking any sum-of-squares multiplier uniform in dimension, ruling out broad any-dimensional Positivstellensatz extensions.
platform_or_system: Dimension-free quantum moment and entanglement tests
main_result: Universal positivity—and therefore universal validity of certain moment-based entanglement criteria—cannot be decided algorithmically in general.
application_angle: The result delineates which scalable entanglement-certification strategies cannot admit complete, dimension-independent automated tests.

title: Optical fiber shape sensing using picosecond spatiotemporal single-photon reflectometry
abstract: Inferring the three-dimensional configuration of a flexible optical fiber from a single accessible end remains a fundamental challenge in photonic sensing. Existing approaches typically require specialised multicore fibers, coherent interferometry, or distributed spectral encoding.
