Here, we demonstrate a fundamentally different sensing paradigm in which fiber geometry is reconstructed from the spatiotemporal dynamics of returning single photons. Using a laser-engineered multimode fiber interrogated by a time-resolved 32x32 single-photon avalanche diode array, we show that fiber deformation imprints unique signatures onto the distribution and arrival time of back-reflected photons. We map these high-dimensional photon-return states onto a low-dimensional geometric manifold, enabling continuous bend-angle estimation and reconstruction of previously unseen two- and three-dimensional shapes from measurements acquired entirely at the proximal fiber end. Measurements show a median pixel-wise signal-to-noise ratio of approximately 26 dB and below 1% repeatability variation. Our results establish multimode single-photon dynamics as an information-rich channel for distributed geometric sensing, introducing a new framework for single-ended fiber shape reconstruction and minimally invasive photonic navigation.
one_liner: Single-ended, time-resolved photon returns reconstruct bends and unseen 2D/3D shapes in a laser-engineered multimode fiber.
why_it_matters: The method avoids multicore fiber and coherent interferometry, offering a promising route to compact shape sensing and minimally invasive navigation.
detailed_summary: A picosecond source and time-resolved 32×32 SPAD array measure the spatial distribution and arrival times of photons reflected through a laser-engineered multimode fiber. A low-dimensional geometric manifold learned from these photon-return states supports continuous bend-angle estimation and reconstruction of previously unseen 2D and 3D shapes using only proximal-end access. The measurements achieve about 26 dB median pixel-wise SNR and below 1% repeatability variation.
platform_or_system: Laser-engineered multimode fiber with 32×32 SPAD array
main_result: The system reconstructs continuous bends and unseen 2D/3D fiber shapes from proximal-end spatiotemporal single-photon measurements.
application_angle: Single-ended operation could enable shape-aware catheters, endoscopes, robotic fibers, and other minimally invasive photonic probes.

title: Ground-State Spin Squeezing and Collective Excitations in $\mathbb{Z}_2$-Symmetric Systems
abstract: Ground-state spin squeezing is a resource for quantum-enhanced measurements, but is commonly associated with a closing excitation gap near a quantum critical point. A closing gap can complicate state preparation and reduce thermal robustness. Here we identify the physical mechanism linking squeezing to collective excitations and establish when stronger squeezing accompanies a larger many-body gap. Using the anisotropic Lipkin--Meshkov--Glick model, we show that, for a quadratic collective mode, the ratio of two transverse fluctuation costs determines squeezing, whereas their geometric mean sets the collective gap. The pair terms responsible for unequal costs are allowed, but not guaranteed, by $\mathbb Z_2$ parity. To extend this picture beyond a single mode, we derive an exact relation between squeezing, polarization, and excitation energies weighted by their collective-spin transition strengths. For XXZ chains, weak-coupling and spin-wave analyses explain how squeezing can develop while both the collective and many-body gaps increase. Exact finite-size calculations for power-law interactions, including the nearest-neighbor limit, confirm a negative-coupling branch on which the two gaps coincide and increase as squeezing improves. For nearest-neighbor interactions, this branch also retains squeezing at higher temperatures than a gap-closing branch with comparable ground-state squeezing. In the Ising chain, by contrast, a staggered excitation can lower the many-body gap without directly contributing to collective fluctuations. Our results explain why ground-state squeezing can accompany either a closing or an opening collective gap, and identify a gap-opening branch with enhanced thermal robustness and the potential for faster adiabatic preparation.
one_liner: A collective-mode framework identifies regimes where stronger ground-state spin squeezing coincides with larger excitation gaps.
why_it_matters: Gap-opening squeezing can improve thermal robustness and potentially shorten adiabatic preparation, strengthening the practicality of quantum-enhanced sensors.
detailed_summary: For the anisotropic Lipkin–Meshkov–Glick model, the ratio of transverse fluctuation costs determines squeezing while their geometric mean sets the collective gap. An exact multimode relation connects squeezing and polarization to excitation energies weighted by collective-spin transition strengths. Analyses and finite-size calculations for XXZ systems identify a negative-coupling branch where squeezing improves as both collective and many-body gaps grow, with better finite-temperature persistence than a comparable gap-closing branch.
platform_or_system: Collective-spin LMG and interacting XXZ spin systems
main_result: The work establishes conditions under which enhanced ground-state squeezing accompanies an increasing many-body gap and improved thermal robustness.
application_angle: The identified operating branch may support faster, more thermally tolerant preparation of squeezed states for quantum metrology.

title: Reduced filtering using classical control hierarchy with linear optimality for continuous quantum error correction
abstract: Continuous quantum error correction promises reduced thresholds and hardware overhead compared to the digital paradigm, but its complex model estimation has greatly reduced its practicality. We recast this problem as a classical control-theoretic state hierarchy made of an exact bilinear reduced model, an exact conditional filter, and standard estimation and feedback design. For any $[[n,k,d]]$ stabilizer code whose generators are all continuously monitored and which is driven by a single Pauli recovery channel, we prove that the exact filter closes at dimension $3\cdot2^{\,n-k-1}$. This dimension is set by the syndrome space instead of the Hilbert space and is minimal within invariant-subspace filtering. The reduced model exposes and corrects two failure mechanisms of the feedback loop. Strong monitoring damps the rotational partner through which the controller steers the stabilizer and injects back-action diffusion along the recovery path; lowering the measurement strength during correction raises the entanglement fidelity of partner-steering LQR control by $0.096$ in the three-qubit code with three monitored parities. Linearizing at the codespace leaves the syndrome uncontrollable, so the controller can stall; a gain designed at a shifted operating point removes this degeneracy. In the limit of zero measurement during correction, we prove that a syndrome-only filter is exact at every recovery boundary. The resulting committed-recovery controller needs only $2^{\,n-k}$ class probabilities and gives the highest entanglement fidelity compared among the methods tested in the literature, $0.947$ against $0.920$ for a measurement-based estimator protocol in the three-qubit bit-flip code, and $0.726$ vs at most $0.407$ for continuous controllers in the five-qubit perfect code.
one_liner: A syndrome-scaled classical-control hierarchy sharply reduces continuous quantum-error-correction filtering and improves recovery fidelity.
why_it_matters: The framework replaces Hilbert-space estimation with minimal syndrome-based filters, reducing a major implementation barrier for continuous QEC hardware.
detailed_summary: For continuously monitored stabilizer codes with one Pauli recovery channel, the exact conditional filter closes at dimension 3·2^(n−k−1), set by syndrome space rather than Hilbert-space size. The analysis identifies monitoring-induced damping and back-action diffusion, then improves control by lowering measurement strength during correction and designing gain around a shifted operating point. A committed-recovery controller uses only 2^(n−k) class probabilities and reaches entanglement fidelities of 0.947 for the three-qubit bit-flip code and 0.726 for the five-qubit perfect code.
main_result: Reduced filtering and committed recovery outperform compared estimators and continuous controllers while scaling with syndrome classes.
application_angle: The approach lowers real-time estimation and control demands for hardware-efficient continuous error correction.

title: Inter-city 18.9 km free-space QKD over a dense urban corridor
abstract: Terrestrial free-space quantum key distribution (QKD) provides a flexible complement to fiber-based networks, but its deployment over long horizontal paths in dense metropolitan environments remains challenging, as atmospheric turbulence, demanding pointing and tracking requirements, and operational constraints can substantially increase system complexity. We experimentally demonstrate the operation of a decoy-state BB84 system over an 18.9~km free-space link across a densely populated urban area in the metropolitan region of Barcelona using an aviation-compliant optical architecture. The system operates at 785~nm using room-temperature single-photon detectors and requires no adaptive optics at the receiver. The modular QKD transmitter, based on a deployment-oriented design, is interfaced with a versatile free-space optical terminal and an independent GPS-disciplined synchronization architecture, facilitating its integration into heterogeneous optical infrastructures. We present the transmitter performance and optical-link characteristics, together with a 40-minute field test characterized by an average channel attenuation of approximately 19~dB and a mean QBER of 1.31\%. From the measured channel parameters, we estimate an average finite-size secret key rate exceeding 11~kbit/s. These results demonstrate the feasibility of inter-city free-space QKD over dense urban areas using a comparatively simple architecture.
one_liner: Decoy-state BB84 delivered an estimated finite-size secret-key rate above 11 kbit/s across an 18.9 km urban free-space link.
why_it_matters: The field test shows practical metropolitan QKD with room-temperature detectors, no receiver adaptive optics, and aviation-compliant optics.
detailed_summary: A 785 nm decoy-state BB84 transmitter was integrated with a modular free-space optical terminal and independent GPS-disciplined synchronization. During a 40-minute test across metropolitan Barcelona, the 18.9 km channel showed about 19 dB average attenuation and 1.31% mean QBER. The measured parameters imply an average finite-size secret-key rate exceeding 11 kbit/s using room-temperature single-photon detectors and no adaptive optics at the receiver.
platform_or_system: 785 nm urban free-space decoy-state BB84 link
main_result: The 18.9 km field link sustained low QBER and an estimated finite-size secret-key rate above 11 kbit/s.
application_angle: Its comparatively simple, modular architecture supports deployment of QKD across metropolitan gaps where dedicated fiber is unavailable.

title: Key Relay and Secure Network Coding: One-Shot Equivalence and Separation on Undirected Networks
abstract: Motivated by quantum key distribution networks, we compare key relay protocols with secure network coding on the same undirected graph. In this comparison, we fix the finite field, terminal set, and wiretap family. Each edge supplies one independent uniform symbol to its endpoints for key relay, or carries one symbol once for network coding. The network code may choose its source terminal, edge orientations, and causal transmission order before execution. In this setting, the standard one-time-pad simulation readily converts every secure network code to key relay. We investigate the reverse conversion to linear network coding. For two terminals and a one-symbol key, arbitrary key relay is equivalent to scalar linear acyclic network coding over the prescribed field. The proof uses connectivity and flow conservation, related to the binary $st$-flow protocol. However, this equivalence fails in general when several terminals seek one common key. A doubled triangle separates key relay from acyclic coding but admits causal coding on a cyclic orientation. On the four-terminal complete graph, a linear key relay protocol over the ternary field withstands the three perfect-matching wiretap sets, whereas no linear causal network code distributes a source symbol of the same size, even with private randomness at every vertex and its use in decoding. We also establish a linear key relay normal form that removes interaction and private randomness and bounds public communication. All results concern one-shot feasibility with exact agreement and perfect secrecy.
one_liner: One-shot key relay equals scalar linear acyclic coding for two terminals but can strictly outperform causal linear coding for multiple terminals.
why_it_matters: The separations clarify which classical networking abstractions can faithfully model trusted-node key distribution in QKD networks.
detailed_summary: The paper compares exact, perfectly secret one-shot key relay with secure network coding on the same undirected graph, field, terminal set, and wiretap family. It proves equivalence between arbitrary two-terminal, one-symbol key relay and scalar linear acyclic network coding. Counterexamples for multiple terminals include a ternary linear relay on the four-terminal complete graph that resists three perfect-matching wiretap sets although no same-size linear causal network code succeeds, even with private randomness.
main_result: The work proves a two-terminal equivalence and explicit multi-terminal separations between key relay and linear secure network coding.
application_angle: These criteria can guide protocol selection and feasibility analysis when designing multi-user QKD and trusted-relay networks.

title: Enabling Mie Resonances for Optomagnetism in Epitaxially Grown Garnet Nanodisks via Photonic Crystals
abstract: An all-garnet photonic-crystal substrate compatible with epitaxial growth on gadolinium gallium garnet is proposed for controlling the optomagnetic response of a single bismuth iron garnet nanodisk. The photonic environment modifies the spectral positions and relative strengths of the electric- and magnetic-dipole contributions and redistributes the optical field inside the disk. Compared with a reference nanodisk on a homogeneous substrate evaluated near the broad maximum of its summed multipolar response, the peak axial optical contribution to the inverse Faraday effect in the examined cross-sections is enhanced by factors of approximately 7.3 and 6.3 in the magnetic- and electric-dipole-dominated regimes, respectively. The enhancement reaches approximately 7.9 at the maximum of the summed multipolar scattering contributions. These results demonstrate spectral control of the magnitude and spatial distribution of the local optomagnetic response through the photonic environment, without changing the nanodisk geometry.
one_liner: An all-garnet photonic crystal boosts the inverse-Faraday response of an epitaxial garnet nanodisk by up to about 7.9×.
why_it_matters: Photonic-environment engineering offers strong, spectrally tunable optomagnetism without altering the magnetic nanostructure's geometry.
detailed_summary: The proposed all-garnet photonic-crystal substrate remains compatible with epitaxial growth of a bismuth iron garnet nanodisk on gadolinium gallium garnet. It shifts and reweights electric- and magnetic-dipole Mie contributions while redistributing the internal optical field. Relative to a homogeneous substrate, the peak axial inverse-Faraday contribution rises by about 7.3× and 6.3× in magnetic- and electric-dipole-dominated regimes, reaching about 7.9× at the summed scattering maximum.
platform_or_system: Epitaxial bismuth iron garnet nanodisk on all-garnet photonic crystal
main_result: Photonic-crystal coupling provides up to about 7.9-fold enhancement and spectral control of the nanodisk's local optomagnetic response.
application_angle: The design could improve nanoscale all-optical magnetic control, magneto-optic sensing, and integrated spin-photonic devices.

title: Non-Convex Optimization via Quantum Tunneling Search on a Photonic Chip
abstract: Non-convex optimization plays an important role in modern machine learning since plenty of real-world problems have objective functions or constraints with non-convex properties. The non-convex nature of landscapes gives rise to numerous local minima and saddle points, dramatically hindering the ability of gradient descent-based methods to explore the landscape and obtain global optima. Here we present quantum tunneling search (QTS), an algorithm based on quantum tunneling walk and local annealing, which effectively explores the non-convex landscape by leveraging the quantum tunneling effect. In experiments, we map an objective function to the potential term of the waveguide Hamiltonian by controlling the refractive index with the femtosecond direct laser writing technique. With a proper input state, the average probability distributions on 10-micrometer-spaced 29 x 1 and 21 x 9 waveguide arrays highlight the local minima of various 1D and 2D non-convex landscapes, respectively. By further introducing the varying Hamiltonian approach, more efficient search and even the identification of the global minimum are achieved. Our work experimentally verifies that QTS is a successful and efficient non-convex optimization solver, demonstrating quantum speedups over classical stochastic gradient descent (SGD), which serves as a practical application of near-term analog quantum simulators in the field of machine learning.
one_liner: A laser-written photonic chip uses quantum tunneling walks and local annealing to search one- and two-dimensional non-convex landscapes.
why_it_matters: The experiment positions analog photonic simulators as specialized hardware for escaping local minima in difficult optimization problems.
detailed_summary: The objective function is encoded as the potential term of a waveguide Hamiltonian through femtosecond direct laser writing. Measurements on 29 × 1 and 21 × 9 arrays with 10 µm waveguide spacing produce probability distributions concentrated near local minima of one- and two-dimensional landscapes. A varying-Hamiltonian protocol improves search efficiency and enables identification of the global minimum in tested cases.
main_result: The chip experimentally performs quantum-tunneling-based search over non-convex landscapes and reports advantages over stochastic gradient descent in the studied instances.
application_angle: It offers a near-term analog photonic accelerator concept for optimization workloads arising in machine learning and related fields.

title: Hong$-$Ou$-$Mandel-like interference between two independent narrowband thermal states
abstract: Narrowband photonic sources are promising candidates in quantum networks for a direct interface with atomic quantum memories. However, building a large-scale quantum network requires many indistinguishable sources, and matching the frequencies of independent narrowband sources is generally challenging. Here, we propose a method to measure the frequency difference between two narrowband light sources in the single-photon power regime by studying Hong$-$Ou$-$Mandel-like (HOM) interference between thermal states. Our results show that the absolute value of the frequency difference can be extracted from the temporal coincidence counts, and these results agree well with our theoretical model. We also demonstrate that the beat signal of the HOM-like interference between two thermal states has a similar oscillation profile to the HOM interference between two heralded single-photon sources, confirming that this method can be used to find the zero detuning of two heralded single-photon sources.
one_liner: HOM-like interference between independent thermal sources measures narrowband frequency mismatch at single-photon power levels.
why_it_matters: The method could simplify spectral alignment of independent photon sources before interfacing them with narrowband quantum memories.
detailed_summary: Two independent narrowband thermal states interfere, and their temporal coincidence signal contains an oscillatory beat set by the absolute frequency detuning. The measured frequency differences agree with the authors' theoretical model. The beat profile resembles that obtained from heralded single photons, supporting its use as a low-power proxy for locating zero detuning.
main_result: Temporal coincidence measurements recover the absolute source-frequency difference and identify the zero-detuning condition at single-photon-level powers.
application_angle: This provides a practical calibration tool for matching independent emitters in quantum-network nodes and memory interfaces.

title: Quantum Keynesian Beauty Contest with Continuous Variables
abstract: The development of quantum computing has opened up opportunities to re-explore conventional game models by the integration of quantum processes. Through the established framework of quantum game theory, we examine the problem of speculative pricing in the Keynesian Beauty Contest model -- the $p$-Beauty Contest ($p$-BC). In the $p$-BC, players are rewarded with the optimal payoff for successfully bidding at some fraction $p$ of the average of all of the players' bids. Consequently, \textit{rational} plays in the $p$-BC inexorably lead to boom or bust strategies for $p>1$ or $p<1$ respectively. We demonstrate a quantum continuous-variable implementation of $p$-BC where the boom-and-bust rational behavior is mitigated through a global transformation of the players' bids generated by increasing multimode squeezing. While we focus on a quantum mechanical implementation of the $p$-BC, we show that an entirely analogous game can be formulated via classical channels by a global mediator. Thus we identify global mediation as the underlying game-theoretic mechanism for quenching boom and bust phenomena in our model. We analyze the quantum $p$-BC for two, three, and many players in a mean-field type implementation. We derive an analytical form for the probability distribution of the payoff under single-value measurements of the quantum processing circuit, and explore how the rational behavior differs from the expected-value measurement setting.
one_liner: A continuous-variable quantum game uses multimode squeezing to suppress boom-or-bust equilibria in a p-beauty contest.
why_it_matters: The analysis clarifies how globally correlated continuous-variable processing changes strategic equilibria, while identifying global mediation as the operative mechanism.
detailed_summary: The authors formulate two-, three-, and many-player p-beauty contests using continuous-variable modes and a global transformation generated by multimode squeezing. Increasing squeezing mitigates the rational boom-or-bust behavior associated with p greater or less than one. Analytical payoff distributions are derived for single-shot measurements and compared with expected-value strategies, while a classical mediated analogue shows that the effect is not uniquely quantum.
main_result: Multimode squeezing suppresses extreme rational bidding behavior, but the same game-theoretic effect can be reproduced by a classical global mediator.
application_angle: The work informs implementations of correlated decision and game-theory protocols on continuous-variable photonic processors.

title: Chlorophyll-a Fluorescence-Based Optical Temperature Sensor Using Food-Grade Chlorella Extract
abstract: This letter reports the development of an optical temperature sensor based on the fluorescence of an extract obtained from \textit{Chlorella}, a unicellular microalga commercially available as food-grade biomass. Using a straightforward ethanolic extraction route, the sensing platform exploits the characteristic emission of chlorophyll-\textit{a} as the optical transducing parameter. The operating principle relies on thermal fluorescence quenching, which promotes a decrease in emission intensity with rising temperature. In the temperature range from $28.6$ to $43.0~^{\circ}\text{C}$, the sensor exhibited a linear response ($R^2 = 0.9963$) with a sensitivity of $(-8.9 \pm 0.2) \times 10^{-3}~^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}$. Dynamic testing over consecutive heating--cooling cycles confirmed the sensor operation under sub-degree thermal oscillations and enabled the characterization of the system's photobleaching drift ($3.65\%\cdot\text{h}^{-1}$). The results reported herein demonstrate the feasibility of exploiting sustainable, bio-derived microalgal pigments as functional photoactive materials for optical thermometry.
one_liner: Food-grade Chlorella extract enables fluorescence thermometry through temperature-dependent quenching of chlorophyll-a emission.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates a low-cost, bio-derived optical sensing material with quantified sensitivity, cycling behavior, and photobleaching drift.
detailed_summary: An ethanolic extract of food-grade Chlorella serves as the fluorescent transducer, with chlorophyll-a emission decreasing as temperature rises. From 28.6 to 43.0 °C, the normalized response is linear with R² = 0.9963 and sensitivity of −(8.9 ± 0.2) × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹. Heating–cooling tests resolve sub-degree oscillations and quantify photobleaching drift at 3.65% per hour.
main_result: The bio-derived sensor delivers a highly linear thermal response over 28.6–43.0 °C while tracking sub-degree temperature variations.
application_angle: The simple extraction and food-grade feedstock support inexpensive, sustainable optical thermometers for moderate-temperature monitoring.

title: Squeezed terahertz light from nonlinear diamagnetism in ultrastrongly coupled two-dimensional electrons
abstract: Two-dimensional electron gases in terahertz cavities are among the most mature platforms for ultrastrong light--matter coupling, yet their collective response is captured by the linear Hopfield model, which has an exact classical correspondence. We show that the intrinsic band nonparabolicity of the electrons, recently revealed through nonlinear diamagnetism, turns this system into a quantum Kerr oscillator that squeezes terahertz light. Using a non-rotating-wave theory with ultrastrong-coupling-consistent input--output, an ab initio cavity bath, and a self-consistent model of electron heating, we predict output squeezing of 1.8--2.4\,dB with present GaAs samples in weakly confined cavities with quality factors of order $10^2$, and up to $\approx9$\,dB with modest improvements in mobility or cavity frequency. Carrier heating sets limits through a material figure of merit, which yields a simple design rule that the optimal cavity quality factor scales inversely with the ultrastrong-coupling strength.
one_liner: Nonlinear diamagnetism turns ultrastrongly coupled two-dimensional electrons into a Kerr oscillator predicted to squeeze terahertz light.
why_it_matters: The proposal leverages a mature cavity platform and gives concrete material and resonator design rules for generating nonclassical terahertz radiation.
detailed_summary: Intrinsic electronic-band nonparabolicity introduces nonlinear diamagnetism beyond the linear Hopfield description, producing an effective quantum Kerr oscillator. A non-rotating-wave input–output model, ab initio cavity bath, and self-consistent carrier-heating treatment predict 1.8–2.4 dB output squeezing for present GaAs samples at cavity quality factors near 10². Modest mobility or cavity-frequency improvements could raise the predicted squeezing to about 9 dB.
platform_or_system: GaAs two-dimensional electrons in a terahertz cavity
main_result: The model predicts measurable terahertz output squeezing with existing samples and up to approximately 9 dB after modest platform improvements.
application_angle: The design could provide compact nonclassical terahertz sources for quantum sensing, spectroscopy, and continuous-variable processing.

title: Thulium- and Holmium-Doped Silica Fibres for 2 μm High-Power and Highly-Efficient Lasers
abstract: Silica optical fibres, originally developed as a low-loss transmission medium for telecommunications, have evolved into a versatile platform for compact and efficient high-power lasers. This review discusses recent progress in thulium- and holmium-doped active fibres emitting within the 2 μm spectral band, with an emphasis on material and waveguide approaches that address power scaling through thermal-load mitigation and enhanced laser efficiency. In particular, the temperature dependence of absorption and emission cross-sections are reviewed, and their implications for spectral gain, amplified spontaneous emission and high-power laser operation are discussed. Structured-core thulium fibres are then considered as a route to combining the high local Tm3+ concentration required for efficient two for- one cross-relaxation with a reduced average dopant concentration, lower longitudinal heat load, and a pedestal-free waveguide design. Finally, recent results on holmium-doped silica fibres prepared by nanoparticle-assisted modified chemical vapour deposition are summarised. Crucially, the Al/Ho ratio is identified as a key compositional parameter governing laser efficiency, while a high absolute alumina content supports a long fluorescence lifetime and enables high Ho3+ concentrations without excessive clustering. These advances have enabled core-pumped holmium fibre lasers with slope efficiencies reaching 84% and output powers approaching 100W. Collectively, these development illustrate how control of spectroscopy, composition, and transverse dopant distribution can extend the performance of silica fibre lasers across the 1.7-2.2 μm spectral region.
one_liner: This review maps material and waveguide advances that enable efficient, high-power thulium- and holmium-doped silica-fibre lasers near 2 µm.
why_it_matters: It connects dopant distribution, host composition, spectroscopy, and thermal management to practical scaling toward 100 W-class 2 µm fibre sources.
detailed_summary: The review examines temperature-dependent Tm and Ho absorption and emission cross-sections and their effects on gain, amplified spontaneous emission, efficiency, and heat load. Structured-core thulium fibres combine locally high Tm³⁺ concentration for two-for-one cross-relaxation with lower average doping and reduced longitudinal heating. For nanoparticle-assisted Ho fibres, the Al/Ho ratio and absolute alumina content govern efficiency, lifetime, and clustering, supporting reported slope efficiencies up to 84% and output powers near 100 W.
platform_or_system: Tm- and Ho-doped silica fibre lasers
main_result: Recent holmium-fibre designs reach 84% slope efficiency and approach 100 W output through controlled composition and dopant distribution.
application_angle: High-efficiency 2 µm fibre sources are relevant to lidar, spectroscopy, sensing, materials processing, and longer-wavelength laser systems.

title: Higher-Group Statistics on Lattices
abstract: Crossing a domain wall can permute anyons, and intersecting strings can create a particle. These couplings between defects of various dimensions are specified by higher groups. We develop a lattice framework defining higher-group statistics as Berry phases of closed sequences of hopping operators, invariant under local modifications of the operators. Our central example is a closed Majorana chain, a 1-dimensional topological superconductor, embedded in 3 dimensions. We construct a loop-flip process with phase $+i$, refining the usual $\pm 1$ loop-flip invariant through intermediate transfer of fermion parity between the chain and physical fermions. In two dimensions, charge-wall statistics distinguish two $\mathbb Z_4$ toric codes enriched by $\mathbb Z_2$ charge-conjugation symmetry, with identical anyon statistics but distinct gauged theories: the quantum doubles of the dihedral group $D_4$ and the quaternion group $Q_8$. We provide two complementary constructions of statistical processes. The first extends the Smith normal form algorithm in [Phys. Rev. X $\textbf{16}$, 011010 (2026), arXiv:2412.01886] to higher groups, generating processes from lattice geometry and prescribed local moves. For a finite higher group $\mathbb G$, we prove that statistical processes on a $d$-sphere are classified by $H_{d+2}(B\mathbb G,\mathbb Z)$. The second constructs processes directly from homology classes without examining exponentially many defect configurations, enabling us to study statistics for complex higher-group structures where the previous method is computationally prohibitive. These processes detect boundary anomalies of higher-group symmetry-protected topological phases. For example, we distinguish 2-group anomalies in 1, 2, and 3 dimensions. Higher-group statistics provide new invariants for characterizing coupled defects in quantum many-body systems.
one_liner: A lattice framework extracts Berry-phase invariants for coupled defects governed by higher-group symmetries.
why_it_matters: The framework supplies computable invariants for diagnosing coupled topological defects, boundary anomalies, and candidate topological quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The authors define higher-group statistics as Berry phases generated by closed sequences of lattice hopping operations and prove invariance under local operator modifications. A three-dimensional embedded Majorana chain exhibits a loop-flip phase of +i through intermediate fermion-parity transfer. They classify processes on a d-sphere by H_{d+2}(B𝔾,ℤ) and develop a homology-based construction that avoids enumerating exponentially many defect configurations.
platform_or_system: Lattice topological phases with Majorana chains
main_result: Higher-group statistical processes are classified homologically and resolve defect phases and anomalies missed by conventional anyon statistics.
application_angle: The invariants could support verification and classification of defect-based topological states considered for fault-tolerant quantum devices.

title: UV and deep-UV ultrafast harmonic generation enhanced by resonant gold nano-pillar metasurface
abstract: We report experimental observations and full-vector numerical simulations of second and third-harmonic generation from a two-dimensional periodic gold nano-pillar metasurface, for efficient ultrafast light conversion from near-infrared to the UV and deep-UV spectral ranges. The metasurface is designed to support an angle-tunable plasmonic resonance in the near-infrared spectral range, with its resonance wavelength shifting as a function of the pump angle of incidence. Under resonant conditions, strong electromagnetic-field confinement near the nano-pillar corners enhances the nonlinear light-matter interactions. Compared with a flat gold mirror, the nanostructured metal exhibits enhanced nonlinear frequency conversion, with conversion efficiencies of second and third-harmonic generation increased by two and three orders of magnitude, respectively. Full-wave theoretical modeling of linear and nonlinear light-matter interaction in nanoscale structures validates the experimental results. We demonstrate that periodically arranged square gold pillars can be engineered to achieve enhanced second and third-harmonic generation at wavelengths that can be tailored through the structural design, without requiring complex geometries or hybrid structures that pose fabrication challenges. The close agreement between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements further advances our understanding of surface-mediated nonlinear optical processes in metals and highlights the potential of metallic nanostructures as ultrafast light sources in the UV and deep-UV.
one_liner: Resonant gold nanopillars enhance ultrafast second- and third-harmonic generation into UV and deep-UV bands.
why_it_matters: The simple metasurface geometry offers a fabrication-friendly route to compact, wavelength-tailorable ultrafast UV sources.
detailed_summary: A periodic array of square gold nanopillars is engineered with an angle-tunable near-infrared plasmonic resonance that concentrates fields near pillar corners. Experiments show second-harmonic enhancement by two orders of magnitude and third-harmonic enhancement by three orders relative to a flat gold mirror. Full-vector nonlinear simulations reproduce the measured behavior and connect the enhancement to resonant surface fields.
main_result: The resonant metasurface boosts second- and third-harmonic conversion by approximately 100× and 1000×, respectively, over flat gold.
application_angle: Its tunable output and uncomplicated geometry are attractive for integrated ultrafast UV spectroscopy, imaging, and photochemical excitation.

title: Noise robust super-Heisenberg scaling in time-dependent quantum sensing by subspace-twirled dynamical decoupling
abstract: In quantum parameter estimation, time-dependent Hamiltonians can enable ultraprecise estimates of a physical parameter beyond the standard Heisenberg limit, also called the super-Heisenberg limit. However, achieving optimal scaling of the measurement precision typically requires an adaptive quantum control scheme which is resource-intensive and hard to implement in general. Furthermore, this advantage is often severely eroded by environmental noise. We propose the use of a dynamical decoupling scheme based on subspace twirling -- the averaging of random unitaries over a subspace rather than the entire Hilbert space -- to overcome these two limitations. We first prove necessary and sufficient conditions for subspace twirling to preserve the encoding signal while simultaneously removing environmental noise. We then establish conditions and provide performance guarantees for when time dependent Hamiltonians undergoing subspace twirling can achieve super-Heisenberg scaling without adaptive controls. Finally, we illustrate our results using an explicit example where a qubit sensor undergoing a subspace twirl simultaneously suppresses noise and achieves super-Heisenberg scaling. These results offer guidance for the design of ultraprecise quantum sensors under time-dependent and noisy conditions.
one_liner: Subspace-twirled dynamical decoupling preserves time-dependent signals while suppressing noise and enabling super-Heisenberg scaling.
why_it_matters: It offers a nonadaptive control strategy for retaining nonlinear precision scaling in noisy quantum sensors.
detailed_summary: The work derives necessary and sufficient conditions under which random-unitary averaging over a selected subspace removes environmental noise without erasing parameter encoding. It then establishes conditions and performance guarantees for super-Heisenberg scaling under time-dependent Hamiltonians without adaptive control. A qubit-sensor example demonstrates simultaneous noise suppression and enhanced scaling theoretically.
main_result: Subspace twirling can suppress environmental noise while preserving the signal structure required for nonadaptive super-Heisenberg precision scaling.
application_angle: The scheme provides design rules for robust ultraprecise sensors where adaptive feedback is too costly or difficult to implement.

title: Asymmetric Frequency Conversion and Violation of Kirchhoff's Law of Thermal Radiation in Phased Floquet Metasurfaces
abstract: We study a system of three closely spaced conducting sheets, whose thermal emission largely violates Kirchhoff's law through nonreciprocal frequency conversion enabled by Floquet phenomena. We leverage surface mode transitions controlled by temporal modulation of one of the metasurfaces, resulting in largely asymmetric frequency conversion. Our findings broaden the capabilities of Floquet metasurfaces for wave conversion and energy manipulation, paving the way towards magnet-free nonreciprocal photonic devices with opportunities for thermal management and efficient photonic refrigeration.
one_liner: Phased temporal modulation produces asymmetric frequency conversion and strongly non-Kirchhoff thermal emission in a three-sheet metasurface.
why_it_matters: Magnet-free control of nonreciprocal thermal radiation could enable compact thermal-management and photonic-refrigeration components.
detailed_summary: The proposed structure uses three closely spaced conducting sheets, with temporal modulation driving transitions between surface modes. Phased modulation makes frequency conversion strongly directional, causing thermal absorptivity and emissivity to depart substantially from the reciprocal Kirchhoff relation. The study presents a theoretical route to nonreciprocal thermal photonics without magnetic bias.
main_result: Floquet-driven surface-mode transitions yield strongly asymmetric frequency conversion and a large violation of conventional Kirchhoff thermal-radiation balance.
application_angle: The architecture may support magnet-free thermal emitters, directional energy routing, and photonic refrigeration.

title: Lattice response theory for subsystem symmetry-protected topological phases
abstract: We develop a framework to study subsystem symmetry-protected topological (SSPT) phases using lattice response theory. We begin with a systematic construction of spacetime lattice gauge fields from general microscopic $X$-type symmetry actions on qudit systems, including global symmetries, subsystem symmetries, and more general modulated symmetries. Given a gauge-invariant response action, we then construct a corresponding entangler and explicitly show that it implements stacking with the SSPT phase described by the response action. We show that a broad class of SSPT phases can be described by intersection pairings and realized by cluster entanglers. We also study SSPT phases beyond intersection pairings, including those described by subsystem analogues of type-II group cocycles involving the Bockstein homomorphism. We construct a new 3+1d SSPT phase protected by two 2-foliated planar subsystem symmetries and a global 0-form symmetry, whose response action is a subsystem analogue of a type-III cocycle. On its boundary, the 0-form symmetry acts by stacking with a 2+1d linear SSPT phase, signaling a mixed 't Hooft anomaly.
one_liner: A lattice response framework constructs and classifies subsystem-symmetry-protected phases and their anomalous boundaries.
why_it_matters: Explicit entanglers and response actions provide tools for engineering and diagnosing structured many-body resource states.
detailed_summary: The authors construct spacetime lattice gauge fields directly from microscopic qudit symmetry actions, covering global, subsystem, and modulated symmetries. Gauge-invariant response actions are mapped to explicit entanglers that stack a system with the corresponding SSPT phase, including broad families generated by cluster entanglers. A new 3+1-dimensional phase exhibits a mixed boundary anomaly involving planar subsystem and global symmetries.
main_result: The framework converts SSPT response actions into explicit lattice entanglers and reveals phases beyond intersection-pairing constructions.
application_angle: These constructions may guide preparation and validation of symmetry-protected entangled states for quantum simulation and fault-tolerant architectures.

title: Implementation of a 1D Gaussian-modulated CV-QKD under finite-size parameter estimation
abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) is a promising technology for quantum-secure communications, offering high secret-key rates and straightforward integration with coherent optical communication systems. Conventional Gaussian-modulated CV-QKD encodes information in both optical-field quadratures, increasing requirements for state preparation, modulation, and calibration, while potentially introducing additional preparation imperfections. Unidimensional (1D) Gaussian modulation offers a simpler alternative by encoding information in only one quadrature, while the conjugate quadrature constrains the protocol's security. However, an integrated experimental 1D implementation combining independent-laser coherent reception with practical reconciliation, finite-size parameter estimation, and privacy amplification remains challenging. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a 1D Gaussian-modulated CV-QKD system over 12~km of standard single-mode fiber using a local local oscillator (LLO) architecture with independent lasers and an integrated offline classical post-processing chain. The implementation includes coherent detection, digital signal processing, information reconciliation, parameter estimation, physicality-constrained security analysis, and privacy amplification. The 1D system achieves a privacy-amplified rate of $1.421$~Mbit/s under the asymptotic security treatment and $0.364$~Mbit/s under the finite-size scenario. These results establish an experimental baseline for the performance--complexity trade-off associated with unidimensional Gaussian modulation and provide an experimental basis for developing lower-complexity CV-QKD transmitters.
one_liner: A 12 km one-quadrature CV-QKD link with independent lasers achieves 0.364 Mbit/s after finite-size security analysis.
why_it_matters: The experiment combines simplified optical modulation with a complete processing chain and quantitatively secure finite-data operation.
detailed_summary: The experiment implements unidimensional Gaussian modulation over 12 km of standard single-mode fiber using independent transmitter and receiver lasers in a local-local-oscillator architecture. Its offline chain includes coherent detection, DSP, reconciliation, parameter estimation, physicality-constrained security analysis, and privacy amplification. The privacy-amplified rate reaches 1.421 Mbit/s asymptotically and 0.364 Mbit/s with finite-size parameter estimation.
main_result: The integrated system delivers a finite-size privacy-amplified key rate of 0.364 Mbit/s across 12 km of standard fiber.
application_angle: Single-quadrature encoding can reduce transmitter, calibration, and modulation complexity while retaining practical metropolitan secure-key throughput.

title: A deployed four-city entanglement-based QKD network with real-time key delivery, benchmarked against finite-key security bounds
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) generates shared secret keys whose security rests on the laws of physics rather than on computational assumptions. We report the entanglement-based segment of the Slovak national quantum communication infrastructure, connecting four cities in western Slovakia over deployed telecommunication fiber. Polarization-entangled photons generated at a central node are passively routed by wavelength to form a trusted-node-free, fully meshed sub-network of three cities, with the fourth connected through the central node and all links operated simultaneously. We also introduce a matrix formalism for passive wavelength routing that enables the algorithmic construction of uniquely and fully connected topologies. Unlike most previous demonstrations, which estimate key rates from raw coincidences, all rates reported here are obtained after the complete post-processing chain, with keys delivered in real time via ETSI GS QKD 014. With partial non-local chromatic dispersion compensation, we obtain 13.5 bit/s over 109 km, and 4.3 bit/s over 32.1 dB of accumulated loss between two cities without a direct fiber link. Benchmarking against finite-key security bounds shows that the implemented heuristic privacy amplification can exceed the finite-key bound, and that replacing detect-and-discard with error correction would increase the finite-key rate by a factor of 4.1-6.6, and yield a positive finite-key rate on the 142.9 km link where the implemented scheme yields none.
one_liner: A four-city entanglement-based QKD network delivers real-time keys over deployed fiber while exposing gaps between heuristic and finite-key rates.
why_it_matters: It combines field deployment, simultaneous multi-link operation, standardized key delivery, and a security-aware diagnosis of post-processing losses.
detailed_summary: A central source distributes polarization-entangled photons by passive wavelength routing across a four-city Slovak telecom-fiber network. Complete post-processing delivers keys in real time through ETSI GS QKD 014, reaching 13.5 bit/s over 109 km and 4.3 bit/s across 32.1 dB loss. Finite-key benchmarking reveals that the deployed heuristic privacy amplification can exceed the security bound and identifies error correction as a route to 4.1–6.6-fold higher finite-key rates.
main_result: The network simultaneously operated all links and delivered real-time keys, including 13.5 bit/s over 109 km and 4.3 bit/s across 32.1 dB loss.
application_angle: The work provides a deployment-oriented architecture and concrete post-processing upgrades for secure metropolitan and national quantum networks.

title: Observation of Genuine Multi-Time Quantum Memory
abstract: Memory effects in open quantum systems do not by themselves imply quantum memory, since non-Markovian dynamics can often be reproduced by classical-memory models. Known criteria certify the presence of quantum memory in the environment by comparing the evolution of the system at two different times. We show that quantum memory can remain hidden from all such pairwise tests and become detectable only when three or more times are considered jointly. We derive an analytical three-time witness and use it to certify quantum memory in a minimal qubit example in which every pair of times has a classical-memory explanation, thus establishing a strict hierarchy of quantum memory effects. Genuine multi-time quantum memory does not rely on fine-tuned time-dependent Hamiltonians or gate-based evolution. We experimentally demonstrate the hierarchy of quantum memory in a time-continuous realization on a superconducting-qubit platform with time-independent couplings.
one_liner: A superconducting-qubit experiment reveals quantum environmental memory that is invisible to every pairwise-time test but detectable across three times.
why_it_matters: It establishes an experimentally observed hierarchy of temporal quantum memory relevant to diagnosing and controlling non-Markovian quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The authors derive an analytical three-time witness that distinguishes genuine quantum memory from dynamics reproducible by classical-memory models. They construct a minimal qubit case in which every two-time marginal admits a classical explanation, while the joint three-time process does not. The hierarchy is demonstrated in a continuous-time superconducting-qubit system using time-independent couplings.
main_result: The experiment certifies genuine three-time quantum memory despite all pairwise-time observations being compatible with classical memory.
application_angle: Multi-time witnesses can improve characterization of temporally correlated noise and memory effects in superconducting processors and quantum communication devices.

title: Stiffness in Confined Quantum Walks
abstract: We investigate boundary-induced stiffness in discrete-time quantum walks confined to a finite lattice by unitary reflecting boundaries implemented through coin-flip operations. We define a dimensionless spreading stiffness from the instantaneous variation of the spatial width relative to the asymptotic spreading rate of the corresponding unconfined Hadamard walk and compare localized, Gaussian, and truncated-uniform initial states. The long-time response retains a strong dependence on the initial spatial profile: the localized and truncated-uniform states show an overall increase in stiffness with increasing confinement size, whereas the Gaussian state exhibits a nonmonotonic dependence with a broad maximum at intermediate sizes. The first and second stiffness moments satisfy the expected asymptotic consistency relation in the high-stiffness regime. The normalized Kullback--Leibler divergence reveals a slower spatial reorganization and qualitatively different finite-size trends, showing that dynamical stiffness and spatial homogenization are distinct properties. These results indicate that unitary confinement produces an intrinsically nonstationary regime whose long-time properties emerge from the interplay between boundary reflections, system size, and the spatial structure of the initial state.
one_liner: Reflecting boundaries create nonstationary stiffness in confined quantum walks, with long-time behavior strongly controlled by the initial wavepacket profile.
why_it_matters: The results clarify how finite geometry and state preparation shape transport in quantum-walk simulators and photonic lattice architectures.
detailed_summary: The study defines a dimensionless spreading stiffness from variations in spatial width relative to an unconfined Hadamard walk. Localized and truncated-uniform states become generally stiffer with increasing confinement size, whereas Gaussian states show a broad intermediate-size maximum. Kullback–Leibler analysis shows that dynamical stiffness and spatial homogenization capture distinct aspects of the confined evolution.
main_result: Boundary-induced stiffness exhibits state-dependent finite-size scaling and remains distinct from the rate of spatial homogenization.
application_angle: The framework can guide boundary and input-state engineering in photonic quantum walks used for transport simulation and quantum information processing.

title: Traces of Vacuum Squeezing: A Superconducting Transmission-Line Analogue of Cosmological Particle Creation
abstract: Particle creation in time-dependent quantum fields is a central phenomenon in early-universe cosmology, yet it remains experimentally inaccessible in its original context. We show theoretically that superconducting circuits based on a waveguide-like transmission line loaded with dc-SQUIDs can provide a direct analogue of a scalar field in a radiation-dominated Friedmann--Robertson--Walker universe in conformal time. The mode equation of the circuit reduces to the Weber equation, the same equation governing cosmological particle creation in a radiation-dominated background, admitting an exact solution in terms of parabolic cylinder functions and an exponentially suppressed particle spectrum. We analyse the conditions under which the analogy holds, which require a compromise between the duration of the pulse, the uniformity of the modulation and the symmetry of the SQUIDs, and show that dissipation does not erase the cosmological signal. We use the anomalous moment of each mode as a witness of the Bogoliubov mixing: it vanishes for any thermal state and survives dissipation, and, together with the photon number, it certifies squeezing, and with the purity of the state, it identifies whether the pairs created from the vacuum dominate.
one_liner: A dc-SQUID-loaded superconducting transmission line is proposed as an analogue simulator of cosmological particle creation and vacuum squeezing.
why_it_matters: It provides an exact circuit-to-cosmology mapping and experimentally accessible correlation witnesses that remain informative under dissipation.
detailed_summary: The proposed transmission line maps onto a scalar field in a radiation-dominated Friedmann–Robertson–Walker universe, with both systems governed by the Weber equation. Exact parabolic-cylinder-function solutions predict an exponentially suppressed photon spectrum. The anomalous mode moment, photon number, and state purity jointly diagnose Bogoliubov mixing, squeezing, and whether vacuum-created pairs dominate, while modeled dissipation does not erase the signature.
main_result: The theory identifies feasible modulation conditions and a dissipation-robust correlation witness for analogue cosmological photon-pair creation.
application_angle: The design offers a microwave-circuit route to experimentally study quantum-field dynamics, vacuum amplification, and squeezing under controlled conditions.

title: Statistics of Fock-space correlation lengths in the many-body localised phase
abstract: The presence of long-ranged, many-body resonances in the many-body localised phase of disordered quantum systems is manifest in strong inhomogeneities of eigenstate amplitudes on the Fock space. We develop a quantitative, microscopic theory for this, centred on two-point Fock-space correlation functions. Exact diagonalisation of the disordered tilted-field Ising chain uncovers a stark contrast: typical correlations decay perfectly exponentially, whereas average correlations exhibit subexponential decay with systematic system-size dependence driven by rare resonant nodes. We show that this behaviour stems from an underlying distribution of Fock-space correlation lengths with a variance that scales inversely with system size. Crucially, the interplay of this distribution with the high-dimensional geometry of the hypercubic Fock-space graph, leads to the qualitative difference between the typical and average behaviours. The theory also allows us to derive the singularity spectrum of the many-body localised eigenstates, and to establish theoretically the anomalous symmetry violation of quantum multifractality as an inherent consequence of the Fock-space geometry.
one_liner: Exact diagonalization links rare many-body resonances to a broad distribution of Fock-space correlation lengths in the localized phase.
why_it_matters: It supplies microscopic diagnostics for distinguishing typical localization from rare-resonance-dominated averages in finite quantum many-body systems.
detailed_summary: Exact diagonalization of a disordered tilted-field Ising chain finds purely exponential decay for typical Fock-space correlations but subexponential decay for their average. The contrast arises from rare resonant nodes and a correlation-length distribution whose variance scales inversely with system size. Combining this distribution with hypercubic Fock-space geometry also yields the eigenstate singularity spectrum and explains anomalous multifractal-symmetry violation.
main_result: The work explains the split between typical exponential and average subexponential Fock-space correlations through rare resonances and finite-size correlation-length statistics.
application_angle: These diagnostics can help benchmark localization, resonant errors, and ergodicity breaking in programmable spin arrays and quantum simulators.

title: Quantum Metrology and Quantum Battery in a Hyperfine-Coupled Spin System
abstract: We investigate multiparameter quantum metrology and the energetic properties of an effective electron--proton spin system inspired by the hyperfine structure of the hydrogen atom. Considering the external magnetic field $\mathcal B$ and the hyperfine coupling strength $Λ$ as unknown parameters, we derive the quantum Fisher information matrix and establish the corresponding quantum Cramér--Rao bounds for their simultaneous estimation. We analyze the estimation precision and the correlations between the two parameters, showing that the weak-commutativity condition is satisfied despite the noncommutativity of the associated symmetric logarithmic derivatives. Independently, we explore the energetic properties of the system under a unitary charging protocol, characterizing its ergotropy, anti-ergotropy, storage capacity, and energy-basis coherence. We investigate the dependence of these quantities on the magnetic field, hyperfine coupling, temperature, and charging time. Our results provide a comprehensive characterization of the metrological properties and energetic performance of a hyperfine spin-based quantum system, highlighting its potential as a platform for quantum sensing and energy storage.
one_liner: A hyperfine-coupled electron–proton spin model is analyzed for simultaneous field and coupling estimation alongside unitary quantum-battery charging.
why_it_matters: It unifies multiparameter sensing limits and energy-storage metrics in a minimal spin system, identifying dependencies on field, coupling, temperature, and time.
detailed_summary: The authors derive the quantum Fisher information matrix and Cramér–Rao bounds for jointly estimating magnetic field and hyperfine coupling. Although the symmetric logarithmic derivatives do not commute, the weak-commutativity condition required for compatible estimation is satisfied. A separate unitary-charging analysis quantifies ergotropy, anti-ergotropy, storage capacity, and energy-basis coherence across field, coupling, temperature, and charging time.
main_result: The model supports compatible simultaneous estimation of magnetic field and hyperfine coupling while exhibiting tunable quantum-battery performance.
application_angle: The analysis provides design guidance for hyperfine-spin sensors and small quantum energy-storage devices, though experimental validation remains outstanding.

title: QuantumInputOutput.jl: A Julia framework for input-output theory with quantum pulses and the SLH formalism
abstract: The interaction of traveling photonic pulses with quantum systems is a fundamental process for many quantum technologies such as quantum communication, control, and measurement protocols. The so-called SLH formalism, named for the triple of operators that parametrize the dynamics, in combination with virtual emission and absorption cavities provides a general toolbox to describe such processes. However, modeling open quantum systems driven by propagating quantum pulses becomes cumbersome once several components, channels, and temporal modes are involved. Here we present QuantumInputOutput.jl, an open-source framework that automates this derivation process: first, symbolic expressions for the Hamiltonian and Lindblad operators are derived using predefined SLH rules and symbolic quantum algebra. Next, the obtained operators are converted to (time-dependent) numerical matrices or are used to obtain higher-order mean-field equations. The numerical expressions are presented in a form immediately suitable for solving the time evolution of the master equation and analyzing the output modes via correlation functions. Besides its usefulness for numerical simulations, the framework also provides a convenient tool to derive symbolic expressions for one-dimensional quantum systems such as multilevel emitters in cavities or waveguides.
one_liner: QuantumInputOutput.jl automates symbolic and numerical modeling of propagating quantum pulses interacting with open quantum networks.
why_it_matters: It reduces the effort needed to model multicomponent photonic systems for quantum communication, control, and measurement.
detailed_summary: The open-source Julia framework applies SLH composition rules and symbolic quantum algebra to derive Hamiltonians and Lindblad operators for networks driven by traveling quantum pulses. It converts these expressions into time-dependent numerical matrices or higher-order mean-field equations suitable for master-equation evolution and output-mode correlation analysis. Virtual emission and absorption cavities support arbitrary pulse-mode descriptions in systems such as multilevel cavity or waveguide emitters.
main_result: The framework automates the path from an SLH network specification to simulation-ready open-system dynamics and output correlation functions.
application_angle: It enables faster design and testing of pulse-mediated quantum links, photonic interfaces, and distributed measurement protocols.

title: Resilient Transmission of Highly Structured Light via Active Convolved Illumination
abstract: Wave propagation through lossy and noisy systems as well as spatiotemporally dynamic random media often limits the complex information that can be reliably transmitted or retrieved. Progress in adaptive optics, wavefront shaping, machine learning, and wave propagation theories has significantly advanced physical and computational correction techniques. However, many approaches remain constrained by restrictive operating conditions, limiting their ability to meet growing application-specific demands, such as higher spatial resolution in imaging and greater data capacity in communications, particularly in highly dynamic environments. Recently, active convolved illumination (ACI) was proposed as a novel framework for preserving the spatial structure of optical modes during propagation through strongly distorting environments, such as atmospheric turbulence. ACI aims to bypass the prohibitive complexity of global distortion tracking by combining spectrally localized characterization with compensation using a correlated auxiliary source. Here, we provide a comprehensive review of ACI, detailing the formulation of correlation-injecting and auxiliary sources and the role of segmented reciprocal-space characterization and distortion compensation. We explore extensions in free-space optical communication and potential high-precision phase measurement, and numerically evaluate interferometric strategies for experimental implementation. This work highlights ACI as a potentially versatile framework for distortion-resilient light transmission, with broad interdisciplinary utility ranging from atmospheric physics and remote sensing to telecommunications, target tracking, and biomedical diagnosis, offering flexible deployment either as a standalone paradigm or hybridized with existing optical systems.
one_liner: Active convolved illumination preserves structured optical modes by locally characterizing distortions and compensating them with a correlated source.
why_it_matters: The approach could improve spatial-mode communication and precision imaging through rapidly changing turbulence without full global distortion tracking.
detailed_summary: This review formulates active convolved illumination using correlation-injecting and auxiliary sources, segmented reciprocal-space characterization, and distortion compensation. The method targets strongly distorting, dynamic channels while avoiding the complexity of tracking the full global transfer function. Numerical studies examine interferometric implementation strategies and extensions to free-space communications and phase measurements.
main_result: ACI is presented as a flexible framework for preserving complex optical-mode structure through strongly distorting propagation channels.
application_angle: Potential uses include turbulence-resilient optical communications, remote sensing, target tracking, precision phase measurement, and biomedical imaging.

title: Probing Spatiotemporal Quantum Correlations with Two-Qubit Relaxometry
abstract: Quantum impurities and spin qubits are powerful local probes of magnetic fluctuations, but conventional relaxometry reduces their information to a local relaxation rate at a single frequency. Building on advances in two-qubit sensing of spatial correlations, we show how two complementary protocols probe finite-time correlations in interacting quantum matter. Phase-cycled Bell-state relaxometry isolates the signed contribution of correlated relaxation to the joint ground-state population. To second order in the probe-environment coupling, the resulting population contrast measures a finite-time integral of the energy-ordered cross-correlator. In the longitudinal regime, XY8 covariance probes the complementary symmetrized cross-correlator within a tunable frequency window. For a gapless quantum spin chain, the signals reveal interaction-dependent algebraic scaling and ballistic propagation. Luttinger-liquid theory links sign changes as the qubit frequency is swept to the propagation time between the probes. It also predicts distinct spatial power laws for the Bell signal before the correlation front and at late times, when the sensing window resolves the qubit frequency. Matrix-product-state calculations for the spin chain test the pre-front scaling at zero and finite magnetization and extract the propagation velocity from Bell oscillations at zero magnetization. The probe coupling geometry determines which spin and momentum sectors contribute to the measured signals.
one_liner: Two-qubit Bell-state relaxometry and XY8 covariance reveal finite-time, spatially separated correlations in interacting quantum matter.
why_it_matters: The protocols extend qubit sensors beyond local noise spectra to resolve correlation signs, propagation fronts, velocities, and momentum sectors.
detailed_summary: Phase-cycled Bell-state relaxometry isolates correlated relaxation through a joint-ground-state population contrast that measures a finite-time energy-ordered cross-correlator. In the longitudinal regime, XY8 covariance accesses the complementary symmetrized cross-correlator within a tunable spectral window. Luttinger-liquid theory and matrix-product-state calculations predict and test algebraic scaling, correlation-front behavior, sign changes, and ballistic propagation in a gapless spin chain.
platform_or_system: Two spin qubits coupled to a quantum spin chain
main_result: The complementary protocols recover distinct spatiotemporal cross-correlators and extract interaction-dependent scaling and propagation velocity.
application_angle: The scheme could turn pairs of solid-state spin qubits into local probes of transport, collective excitations, and nonlocal dynamics in quantum materials.

title: Note on quantum optimal measurements of CMB spectral distortions
abstract: As quantum sensing techniques continue to push the frontier of detection of ultra-weak signals, one may wonder if a sophisticated quantum strategy could be used to enable measurement of spectral distortions in the cosmic microwave background. Using quantum Fisher information techniques, we prove that the optimal strategy is simple frequency-binned intensity measurement. This proof strategy also enables us to provide numerical estimates for the information-theoretic minimum observation time required to observe the $μ$- and $y$-distortions expected from $Λ$CDM cosmology. As case studies, we compare these results to the PIXIE and SPECTER mission concepts, and show that they are within a few orders of magnitude of this fundamental limit.
one_liner: Quantum Fisher information shows that frequency-binned intensity detection is optimal for measuring CMB μ- and y-type spectral distortions.
why_it_matters: It rules out an advantage from more elaborate quantum measurements and establishes fundamental observation-time benchmarks for future CMB missions.
detailed_summary: The authors use quantum Fisher information to determine the optimal measurement for ultraweak cosmic microwave background spectral distortions. They prove that simple frequency-binned intensity measurements attain the quantum limit for the considered signals. Numerical bounds on the minimum observation time for ΛCDM μ- and y-distortions are then compared with the PIXIE and SPECTER mission concepts.
main_result: Frequency-binned intensity measurement is quantum optimal, and proposed missions lie within a few orders of magnitude of the fundamental sensitivity limit.
application_angle: The bounds clarify where detector, optical, and mission-level improvements can matter when designing future CMB spectrometers.

title: 1.56 THz Full-Field Rydberg-Atom Imaging with 0.3 mm-scale Spatial Response
abstract: THz imaging via Rydberg-atom up-conversion offers a powerful full-field modality with high sensitivity and rapid acquisition. However sub-millimeter imaging above 1 THz is still constrained by source power and beam-delivery loss. In this paper, we demonstrate a \(50~\mathrm{mm} \times 50~\mathrm{mm}\) full-field imaging at 1.56~THz by implementing the \(11P_{3/2} \rightarrow 10D_{5/2}\) transition of a cesium Rydberg-atom vapor. The measured spatial response FWHMs are \(0.314~\mathrm{mm}\) in horizontal and \(0.354~\mathrm{mm}\) in vertical for a \(0.5~\mathrm{mm}\) pinhole, alongside a sensitivity of \(31.7~\mathrm{fW}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}/(6.5 \times 6.5)~μ\mathrm{m}^{2}\), and a frame rate up to \(300~\mathrm{fps}\). Under matched illumination, relay, and image-processing conditions, mask imaging at 1.56 THz reproduces finer features and edges with substantially higher edge contrast, deeper intensity-trough separation in line profiles, and recovered detail that remains blurred or unresolved at 0.55 THz. Furthermore, preliminary imaging of a \(200~μ\mathrm{m}\) tissue slice suggests morphological correspondence with H\&E histology histology, offered as a proof-of-concept for label-free tissue characterization. By validating the wavelength-dependent resolution scaling in Rydberg THz imaging, this work establishes frequency scaling as a general design principle for sub-millimeter Rydberg-THz imaging.
one_liner: Cesium Rydberg-atom up-conversion enables 1.56 THz full-field imaging over 50 mm with roughly 0.3 mm spatial response.
why_it_matters: The system combines sub-millimeter response, femtowatt-scale sensitivity, and 300 fps acquisition for fast THz inspection and imaging.
detailed_summary: The imager uses the cesium 11P3/2-to-10D5/2 Rydberg transition to up-convert a 1.56 THz field across a 50 mm by 50 mm field of view. Measured response widths are 0.314 mm horizontally and 0.354 mm vertically for a 0.5 mm pinhole, with 31.7 fW s^-1/2 sensitivity per 6.5 μm pixel and frame rates up to 300 fps. Matched comparisons show sharper features than at 0.55 THz, while a 200 μm tissue slice provides an initial label-free imaging demonstration.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates 1.56 THz full-field imaging with approximately 0.3 mm response, high frame rate, and improved feature recovery over 0.55 THz.
application_angle: The platform is relevant to rapid nondestructive inspection, security screening, materials analysis, and label-free biomedical tissue characterization.

title: DRAG-Inspired Single Flux Quantum Control of Superconducting Qubits
abstract: Scalable control remains a major challenge for superconducting quantum processors due to the wiring, thermal load, and hardware complexity associated with conventional microwave-based architectures. A framework for qubit control based on Single Flux Quantum (SFQ) digital electronics is presented. For transmon qubits, optimized control sequences are constructed from regular pulse trains framed by arbitrary subsequences (ramps), enabling DRAG-inspired leakage suppression in the discrete SFQ regime through genetic-algorithm optimization. For representative $Y_{π/2}$ gates, the resulting sequences achieve simulated coherent-control infidelities below $10^{-4}$, including leakage from the computational subspace. The objective of the proposed approach is to demonstrate that coherent errors intrinsic to SFQ control can be reduced to a comparable level for a more scalable cryogenic control architecture. Memory requirements are reduced by storing only the optimized ramps, while a modular controller architecture supporting both regular and arbitrary pulse generation is proposed. The logical complexity of this architecture is estimated from the Josephson-junction counts of its constituent SFQ cells. The proposed approach therefore combines low coherent-control error with reduced memory overhead and provides a basis for scalable cryogenic SFQ control architectures.
one_liner: DRAG-inspired optimization suppresses leakage in digital SFQ pulse trains for simulated transmon gates below 10^-4 infidelity.
why_it_matters: It advances compact cryogenic qubit control that could reduce microwave wiring, thermal load, and waveform-memory requirements at scale.
detailed_summary: The proposed controller drives transmons with regular Single Flux Quantum pulse trains bracketed by optimized arbitrary ramp subsequences. A genetic algorithm adapts DRAG-like leakage suppression to discrete SFQ control, producing simulated Yπ/2 gates with coherent infidelity below 10^-4, including leakage. Only the ramps need stored waveforms, and the work outlines a modular controller with Josephson-junction-count estimates.
main_result: Optimized discrete SFQ sequences achieve simulated Yπ/2 gate infidelities below 10^-4 while reducing waveform-memory overhead.
application_angle: Cryogenic digital control could support denser superconducting processors with fewer room-temperature microwave channels and lower interconnect heat load.

title: Deep, label-free, volumetric lifetime microscopy via low-noise, single pulse sampling
abstract: Fluorescence lifetime imaging (FLIM) provides label-free metabolic contrast, but conventional time-correlated single-photon counting requires thousands of excitation pulses per pixel to avoid pile-up distortion, limiting imaging speed and increasing motion artifacts and photodamage. Here, we develop single-pulse analog sampling that combines sub-photoelectron read noise with a jitter-immune, frequency-domain estimator for accurate lifetime measurement at low photon counts. Single low-flux traces achieve a photon economy of $F < 1.5$ at 100--150 detected photons, enabling accurate lifetime estimation from a single excitation pulse in label-free, volumetric samples. In in vivo zebrafish eyes, single-shot acquisition recovered the lifetime content of 20-pulse averaging at one-twentieth the exposure, resolving endogenous lipofuscin heterogeneity. In intact mouse kidney, scattering and reduced photon throughput impaired lifetime contrast; this was mitigated by lightweight denoisers that enabled label-free lifetime imaging to 200 micron depth at one pulse per pixel. These results establish single-shot FLIM as a route to deeper, faster, motion-tolerant, low-photodamage lifetime imaging.
one_liner: Single-pulse analog FLIM achieves label-free volumetric lifetime imaging with low exposure and improved motion tolerance.
why_it_matters: It could substantially accelerate deep metabolic imaging while reducing pile-up, photodamage, and motion artifacts in living tissue.
detailed_summary: The authors combine sub-photoelectron analog read noise with a jitter-immune frequency-domain lifetime estimator. At 100–150 detected photons, a single low-flux trace reaches a photon economy below 1.5. Single-shot imaging reproduced 20-pulse lifetime content in zebrafish eyes at one-twentieth the exposure, while lightweight denoisers enabled one-pulse-per-pixel imaging to 200 µm in mouse kidney.
main_result: The system performs accurate single-pulse FLIM in vivo and reaches 200 µm depth in scattering kidney tissue with denoising.
application_angle: The approach supports faster, lower-photodamage metabolic microscopy of moving, intact biological samples.

title: Local gluing classification and bulk-locked clock rings for $\mathbb{Z}_N$ models on a Klein bottle
abstract: We classify local reflection gluings of the $\mathbb{Z}_N$ plaquette model on lattice Klein bottles and solve the obstructed literal seam. Within the monomial far-corner ansatz, all commuting gluings form a family labelled by a unit $u$ of $\mathbb{Z}_N$. They exist for every $N$ at even seam length and, at odd length, exactly when $-1$ is a square modulo $N$. We determine the anyon transport, including exchange seams with $P^2=C$ for charge conjugation $C$, and the relation phases that distinguish an unfrustrated code from a commuting but frustrated Hamiltonian. For the literal gluing, the $2L_x$ noncommuting plaquettes form self-dual clock rings whose sectors are locked by the bulk. This gives an exact reduction of the spectrum to clock-ring spectra, closed-form ring ground energies for $N=2,4$, and a closed-form ground-state degeneracy.
