We further determine twisted-coefficient homology on the stated surface domains and compare it with logical modules on registered lattice grids; composite dimensions need not give squares of cyclic groups. Dressed-isometry gates and monodromy are reported with their finite-grid scope. Finally, the qudit Gottesman--Knill theorem bounds the computational interpretation: Clifford deformations and Weyl measurements with stabilizer inputs and no external magic states cannot supply a non-stabilizer resource. Charge-conjugation measurements that do supply such states lie outside this operation model. The new results concern explicit seam classification, phase-sensitive consistency and bulk-locked spectra, not a new general no-go theorem or a universal computing architecture.
one_liner: A classification of local reflection seams reveals exact gluing conditions and bulk-locked clock-ring spectra in lattice Klein-bottle codes.
why_it_matters: The results clarify how non-orientable topology, seam frustration, and anyon transport constrain qudit stabilizer-code constructions.
detailed_summary: Within a monomial far-corner ansatz, commuting reflection gluings are classified by units of Z_N and exist at odd seam length only when −1 is a quadratic residue modulo N. The obstructed literal seam reduces exactly to self-dual clock rings whose sectors are locked by the bulk, yielding closed-form degeneracy and selected ground energies. The work also distinguishes commuting but frustrated seams and bounds the computational role of the resulting Clifford operations.
platform_or_system: Z_N lattice plaquette code on a Klein bottle
main_result: The paper classifies commuting seams, derives their anyon transport, and exactly reduces the obstructed seam spectrum to bulk-locked clock rings.
application_angle: It provides design rules and limitations for topological qudit codes incorporating reflection defects or non-orientable connectivity.

title: A Necessary and Sufficient Condition for Complete TE/TM Separability in Fully Anisotropic Waveguides
abstract: A necessary and sufficient condition is established for complete transverse-electric/transverse-magnetic (TE/TM) separability in waveguides homogeneously filled with a fully anisotropic and lossless medium. The permittivity and permeability tensors are Hermitian positive-definite and may contain nonzero transverse--longitudinal coupling terms. Complete TE/TM separation occurs if and only if the transverse permeability block is proportional to the transpose of the transverse permittivity block and the corresponding transverse--longitudinal coupling vectors satisfy the same proportionality relation after complex conjugation. The longitudinal constitutive entries remain independent apart from positive definiteness. The condition is derived directly from the source-free Maxwell equations, and independent analyses of the TE and TM modes lead to the same material relation. Since no boundary condition enters the derivation, the criterion is independent of the boundary type. Full-vector waveguide mode analyses using our in-house programs for perfect-electric-conductor and Bloch-periodic waveguides, with material tensors satisfying and violating the condition, agree with the theoretical results.
one_liner: A tensor-level criterion exactly determines when fully anisotropic, lossless waveguides admit complete TE/TM mode separation.
why_it_matters: The criterion can simplify mode solvers and guide anisotropic material design without depending on a waveguide's boundary type.
detailed_summary: Complete separation occurs exactly when the transverse permeability block is proportional to the transpose of the transverse permittivity block and their transverse–longitudinal couplings obey the corresponding conjugated relation. Longitudinal tensor entries remain otherwise independent subject to positive definiteness. Full-vector simulations of PEC and Bloch-periodic waveguides confirm separation for compliant tensors and its failure when the condition is violated.
main_result: The authors derive and numerically validate a boundary-independent necessary-and-sufficient condition for complete TE/TM separability.
application_angle: The result enables systematic material selection and reduced-complexity modeling for anisotropic photonic and electromagnetic waveguides.

title: Underlying orbital U(1) symmetry in quantum limit cycles
abstract: Quantum limit cycles exhibit harmonic Liouvillian spectra, yet their underlying orbital $U(1)$ structure is not generally explicit in the absence of physical rotational symmetry. Here, we construct a unitary representation of orbital phase translations through a similarity transformation that maps the harmonic nondecaying Liouvillian sector onto a Hermitian angular-momentum Hamiltonian. The resulting phase states possess homogeneous Fubini--Study geometry independently of the physical orbit's shape. For ideal quantum limit cycles, the corresponding density matrix also exhibit homogeneous Bures geometry. At finite size, we show how phase diffusion damps slow Liouvillian harmonics while preserving the effective orbital $U(1)$ symmetry. The resulting loss of phase-state distinguishability and contraction of the effective geometry are quantitatively predicted by the microscopic slow Liouvillian spectrum. Our results establish a connection between orbital phase symmetry, quantum geometry, and finite-size phase diffusion in open quantum systems.
one_liner: Quantum limit cycles possess an effective orbital U(1) phase symmetry even when their physical trajectories lack rotational symmetry.
why_it_matters: The framework links measurable Liouvillian spectra to phase geometry and diffusion in finite open quantum oscillators.
detailed_summary: A similarity transformation maps the harmonic nondecaying Liouvillian sector to a Hermitian angular-momentum Hamiltonian, defining unitary orbital phase translations. The resulting phase states have homogeneous Fubini–Study geometry, and ideal-cycle density matrices have homogeneous Bures geometry. At finite size, slow Liouvillian harmonics quantitatively predict phase diffusion, distinguishability loss, and geometric contraction.
platform_or_system: Open quantum oscillator exhibiting a limit cycle
main_result: The work constructs an effective orbital U(1) representation and derives finite-size phase diffusion directly from the slow Liouvillian spectrum.
application_angle: It offers a principled way to characterize phase stability and coherence in quantum oscillators used for synchronization, control, or sensing.

title: Benchmarking superconducting quantum processors with percolating entanglement quality
abstract: The capability to create large entanglement resources is a key performance attribute of quantum processors, and the size of the resource is often used as a benchmark of processor scale. Recent graph-state experiments have reported entanglement clusters spanning entire chips with hundreds of qubits. However, cluster size alone does not capture the entanglement quality of individual couplings or differences in coupling topology. Here, we introduce percolating entanglement quality (PEQ), a topology-normalized benchmark based on conditional two-qubit negativity and a topology-specific bond-percolation threshold. As an experimental demonstration, we prepare a native graph state on a 64-qubit square-lattice superconducting processor with defects, identify a 52-qubit entanglement cluster, and evaluate the PEQ of the processor. Applying PEQ to previously reported chip-wide graph-state measurements on heavy-hex-lattice processors, we show that PEQ differs substantially among processors whose entanglement clusters span the entire chip. PEQ provides a single chip-wide score without selecting a best-performing qubit subset or path. This score allows processors with different coupling topologies to be compared on a common scale and can inform the design of coupling topologies for scalable chips.
one_liner: A topology-normalized metric benchmarks chip-wide entanglement quality using conditional negativity and bond-percolation thresholds.
why_it_matters: PEQ distinguishes processors that form similarly large graph-state clusters but differ substantially in coupling quality and topology.
detailed_summary: Percolating entanglement quality combines conditional two-qubit negativity with the bond-percolation threshold of the processor topology. The authors prepare a native graph state on a defective 64-qubit square-lattice superconducting processor and identify a 52-qubit entangled cluster. Applying PEQ to prior heavy-hex results reveals quality differences that chip-spanning cluster size alone obscures.
main_result: PEQ provides a single topology-normalized chip-wide score and is demonstrated on a 52-qubit entanglement cluster.
application_angle: The benchmark supports fairer cross-topology processor comparisons and can guide coupling-layout design for scalable quantum chips.

title: Local Quantum Metrology: Precision Limits for Observers in QFT
abstract: How precisely can an observer estimate a parameter related to a quantum field? This question is answered for quantum-mechanical systems using the SLD--Bures--Fisher metric and the quantum Cramér--Rao bound. However, local algebras in relativistic quantum field theory are of type III: they carry no trace and normal states have no density matrices, so the SLD quantum Fisher information and the quantum Cramér--Rao bound cannot be defined in the usual way. We define the SLD (Bures) quantum Fisher information on arbitrary von Neumann algebras through Uhlmann's transition probability and prove a quantum Cramér--Rao bound for collective measurements. We also show that the bound is sharp, and equals the largest classical Fisher information obtainable by measurements in the region.
one_liner: Quantum Fisher information and a sharp quantum Cramér–Rao bound are extended to local type-III algebras in relativistic QFT.
why_it_matters: It establishes operational precision limits for local field measurements where density-matrix and trace-based metrology fail.
detailed_summary: The authors define SLD–Bures quantum Fisher information on arbitrary von Neumann algebras through Uhlmann transition probability, avoiding density matrices and traces. They prove a quantum Cramér–Rao bound for collective measurements and show that it is sharp. The bound equals the maximum classical Fisher information obtainable through measurements localized in the observer's region.
platform_or_system: Local von Neumann algebras in relativistic quantum field theory
main_result: A density-matrix-free quantum Fisher information is constructed, with a sharp local quantum Cramér–Rao bound valid for type-III algebras.
application_angle: The theory supplies rigorous sensitivity limits for localized probes of quantum fields, including relativistic and field-based sensing scenarios.

title: Spectral dependence of Berry phase and topological bound states in the continuum in Möbius resonators
abstract: The Möbius strip and the bulk Möbius resonator are of great interest to specialists in optics, acoustics, and quantum physics. Despite the apparent simplicity of the object and numerous publications, the Möbius resonator, like a magic box, still holds many surprises. Here, we demonstrate experimentally, theoretically and with a simple illustrative example that in a "thin" Möbius resonator with an odd number of twists, the longitudinal wavenumber is determined by the additional phase shift π (traditionally called the geometrical Berry phase) only if the total transverse index of the photonic mode is odd. For an even index, the Berry phase is zero. We also discovered "topological" quasi-bound states in the continuum in Möbius resonators with a square cross-section; they differ from "ordinary" ones by the exchange of azimuthal indices of the interfering modes in the anti-crossing region. Finally, we demonstrate an example of resonant topology by determining the dependence of the Berry phase on the Möbius resonator geometry based on the frequency difference between the eigenmodes of planar ring resonators and those of Möbius resonators. The discovered effects significantly expand our knowledge of the topology of single resonators and promise new practical applications.
one_liner: Experiments reveal parity-dependent Berry phases and topological quasi-bound states in the continuum in thin Möbius resonators.
why_it_matters: The results provide geometry- and mode-selective control of resonator topology, potentially enabling robust filtering, confinement, and photonic sensing.
detailed_summary: The work experimentally and theoretically shows that an odd-twist thin Möbius resonator acquires a π longitudinal phase shift only for modes with odd total transverse index; even-index modes have zero Berry phase. Square-cross-section resonators also host topological quasi-bound states in the continuum distinguished by an exchange of azimuthal indices near mode anticrossings. Frequency differences relative to planar ring resonators provide a direct probe of the geometry-dependent Berry phase.
main_result: Mode parity determines whether the Möbius resonator carries a π Berry phase, while square geometries support a distinct topological class of quasi-BICs.
application_angle: Mode-selective topology and high-Q quasi-BICs could support compact filters, sensors, and resonant photonic components with geometry-tunable responses.

title: Digital Coherent Twin-Field Quantum Key Distribution with Gaussian-Modulated Coherent States
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) enables information-theoretically secure key sharing between two distant parties. Recently, one promising QKD protocol which can distribute a secret key over long distances called twin-field QKD (TF-QKD) has been developed. However, it requires active compensation for experimental imperfections such as phase, polarization, and frequency fluctuations with expensive devices and this makes its experimental implementation challenging. Here, we propose a long-distance continuous-variable QKD (CV-QKD) protocol which is inspired by TF-QKD. Our protocol can remove these requirements by using Gaussian-modulated coherent states and digital signal processing which is widely used in recent digital coherent optical communication and experimental implementations of CV-QKD. For security analysis, we use a numerical optimization approach with a photon-number cutoff assumption. We propose a new set of constraints for numerical optimization which can efficiently constrain a highly non-Gaussian quantum state shared by two legitimate parties in our protocol. We show that the key rate of our protocol exceeds the key rate of a direct-transmission CV-QKD protocol at long distances and it can overcome the repeaterless bound.
one_liner: A twin-field-inspired CV-QKD protocol uses Gaussian modulation and digital coherent processing to remove demanding active optical compensation.
why_it_matters: It offers a potentially simpler route to long-distance QKD while numerically exceeding direct-transmission CV-QKD and the repeaterless bound.
detailed_summary: The proposed protocol combines Gaussian-modulated coherent states with digital coherent receiver techniques to estimate and correct phase, polarization, and frequency fluctuations in post-processing. Security is evaluated through numerical optimization under a photon-number cutoff, using new constraints designed for the highly non-Gaussian shared state. The calculated secret-key rate surpasses direct-transmission CV-QKD at long distance and can exceed the repeaterless bound.
main_result: Numerical security analysis predicts long-distance secret-key rates above direct-transmission CV-QKD and beyond the repeaterless bound without costly active compensation hardware.
application_angle: Compatibility with established coherent-communications DSP could reduce the optical stabilization burden of deployable long-haul quantum networks.

title: A Concise Introduction to Quantum Electromagnetics
abstract: This book introduces quantum electromagnetics to readers trained in classical electromagnetics, without assuming a systematic background in quantum mechanics. The central question is when classical descriptions suffice, and when the quantum states of matter or the field must be retained explicitly. Starting from familiar electromagnetic modes and material response, the discussion develops atomic dynamics, field quantization, and the interaction of quantized fields with quantum matter. Particular attention is given to how mode profiles, Green functions, and scattering matrices obtained from classical electromagnetic calculations enter quantum models. Atomic coherence, photon statistics, spontaneous emission, and cavity coupling are developed through derivations that identify the physical assumptions and limits of each description. Examples drawn from atomic clocks, Rydberg-atom receivers, and single-photon devices connect these concepts to excitation, propagation, and measurement in practical systems. Loss and noise are included in relating internal dynamics to measured signals and correlations. The final discussion examines how sensitivity and claims of quantum advantage depend on bandwidth, measurement resources, and the classical reference used for comparison. The aim is to help readers choose an appropriate model, carry out the calculation, and understand what its predictions mean for an electromagnetic measurement.
one_liner: This book connects classical electromagnetic solvers to quantum models of atoms, photons, cavities, receivers, and measurements.
why_it_matters: It gives hardware researchers a practical framework for deciding when quantum modeling is necessary and how classical field outputs enter device predictions.
detailed_summary: The text develops quantum electromagnetics from classical modes and material response through atomic dynamics, field quantization, and light–matter interaction. It explains how mode profiles, Green functions, and scattering matrices from classical solvers feed into quantum descriptions of spontaneous emission, cavity coupling, photon statistics, loss, and noise. Examples include atomic clocks, Rydberg receivers, and single-photon devices, with explicit attention to fair sensitivity and quantum-advantage comparisons.
main_result: The book provides a unified modeling workflow that links classical electromagnetic calculations to open quantum-system observables and measured correlations.
application_angle: The framework can guide model selection and performance assessment for quantum sensors, cavity devices, Rydberg receivers, and single-photon hardware.

title: Spin-adapted sample-based quantum diagonalization with randomized time evolution
abstract: Quantum algorithms based on the classical post-processing of measurement samples have emerged as effective and robust methods to approximate low-energy wavefunctions of many-body quantum systems on present-day and early-fault-tolerant quantum devices. This paper introduces a generic framework for enforcing spin symmetry within these approaches. We tailor this framework to SqDRIFT, a sample-based quantum diagonalization variant that uses the qDRIFT randomized compilation protocol to generate the quantum samples. We discuss how three key components of SqDRIFT (the initial-state preparation, the construction of the time-evolution circuits, and the classical post-processing) can be adapted to incorporate spin symmetry. We show that spin-pure circuits alone are not sufficient, since the sampled determinants generally span a subspace that is not closed under $\hat{S}^2$, and we restore this closure by completing the sampled electronic configurations. In classical simulations of 4-aminobenzonitrile and of an $[\text{Fe}(\text{NH}_{3})_{4}]^{2+}$ model complex, and in experiments on an IBM quantum processor for the oxo-Mn(Salen) complex, this spin-adapted post-processing yields roots that are exact spin eigenfunctions at every subspace size. On hardware, it does so with diagonalized subspaces two to three orders of magnitude smaller than those of the conventional constructions for the same circuit depth.
one_liner: Spin-adapted SqDRIFT produces exact spin eigenstates using dramatically smaller diagonalization spaces on IBM quantum hardware.
why_it_matters: Symmetry-aware sampling can reduce classical post-processing and measurement burdens for quantum chemistry on near-term and early fault-tolerant devices.
detailed_summary: The authors adapt initial-state preparation, randomized qDRIFT time evolution, and classical post-processing so sample-based quantum diagonalization respects total-spin symmetry. Because spin-pure circuits do not guarantee a sampled determinant space closed under S², the method completes sampled electronic configurations before diagonalization. Simulations and IBM hardware experiments yield exact spin eigenfunctions at every subspace size, with hardware subspaces two to three orders of magnitude smaller than conventional constructions at equal circuit depth.
main_result: Spin-adapted post-processing recovered exact-spin roots while reducing required hardware-derived diagonalization subspaces by 100–1000× at fixed circuit depth.
application_angle: The reduction could make spin-resolved electronic-structure calculations more practical under limited quantum sampling and classical-memory budgets.

title: Quantum phase estimation on a Rydberg quantum simulator
abstract: Determining the energy spectrum of a many-body quantum system is a central goal of quantum physics. Ground-state energies underpin materials science and quantum chemistry, whereas excited states govern dynamical phenomena such as quantum thermalization. Quantum simulators have greatly shaped our understanding of many-body systems, for example, by enabling access to microscopic mechanisms and nonlocal order parameters. However, experiments still struggle to access the full range of many-body spectral features and are typically limited to measuring energy gaps and excitations by spectroscopic means. Here, we address this challenge by demonstrating quantum phase estimation on an analog Rydberg quantum simulator. We reconstruct the complex-valued return amplitude, or Loschmidt echo, of an initial probe state. From its Fourier transform, we measure absolute ground-state energies and energy gaps in systems of up to 19 atoms in one and two spatial dimensions. Varying the initial probe state, we select distinct spectral windows within which we compute the longitudinal and transverse magnetization, and observe their competition across the many-body spectrum. Our results thereby demonstrate phase-sensitive many-body spectroscopy on an analog quantum simulator without auxiliary qubits or controlled evolution.
one_liner: Quantum phase estimation on an analog Rydberg array measures absolute energies and spin observables across spectra of up to 19 atoms.
why_it_matters: It extends analog simulators from gap spectroscopy to phase-sensitive reconstruction of many-body spectral windows without ancillas or controlled evolution.
detailed_summary: The experiment reconstructs the complex Loschmidt return amplitude of a probe state on one- and two-dimensional Rydberg arrays and Fourier-transforms it to recover spectral information. It measures absolute ground-state energies and gaps for systems containing up to 19 atoms. By changing the probe state, the authors select spectral windows and extract competing longitudinal and transverse magnetization across the many-body spectrum.
main_result: Phase-sensitive spectroscopy recovered absolute energies, gaps, and state-selective magnetization across many-body spectra without auxiliary qubits or controlled evolution.
application_angle: The method broadens the spectral diagnostics available for analog quantum simulation of materials, thermalization, and strongly correlated many-body physics.

title: Entropic quantum error correction for independent and correlated amplitude damping errors
abstract: The idea of using quantum entropy for quantum error correction (QEC) has existed for a long time. However, its computational complexity has limited its practical use: even a $[[4,1]]$ code for standard independent amplitude damping errors involves a $256\times 256$ Hermitian matrix, so the approach scales poorly as the codeword length increases. For correlated errors, the situation is even worse. In this paper, we show that, by using the insights developed in our previous paper and exploiting certain structures of quantum conditional mutual information, we can solve these problems exactly by hand, using only $2\times 2$ unitary matrices. By examining the entropy, we identify the leakage channels and the amount of leakage exactly, then define the recovery map accordingly. The rules defining our recovery map are simple, intuitive, and computationally inexpensive: for independent errors, it is based on 16 explicitly given orthonormal vectors and 6 instructions; for correlated errors, it is based on 6 explicitly given orthonormal vectors and 6 instructions. Our method sacrifices little in terms of performance: for the widely used entanglement fidelity, our simple QEC recovery map achieves a sharp result; for the worst-case fidelity, the best result is about $9\%$ better than ours; for correlated errors, there are no comparable results for short codewords. Among the known techniques, our recovery map is the first non-global one. The calculations use elementary linear algebra and calculus, and is presented in great detail.
one_liner: An entropy-guided recovery construction reduces amplitude-damping QEC design to explicit 2×2 operations for independent and correlated noise.
why_it_matters: The approach replaces costly global optimization with a simple non-global recovery map while retaining near-optimal fidelity for short quantum codes.
detailed_summary: The paper exploits conditional-mutual-information structure to identify leakage channels and construct exact recovery rules using only 2×2 unitary matrices. For independent amplitude damping, the map is specified by 16 orthonormal vectors and six instructions; the correlated-error version uses six vectors and six instructions. It attains a sharp entanglement-fidelity result, while the reported optimum worst-case fidelity is only about 9% higher, and provides the first non-global recovery map among the compared methods.
main_result: A computationally inexpensive, explicitly constructed recovery map handles both independent and correlated amplitude damping with near-optimal fidelity.
application_angle: Simple local recovery rules may ease implementation of noise-tailored QEC in hardware dominated by energy relaxation and temporally correlated damping.

title: Spin Interferometry Generated by Cavity Memory
abstract: We report the control and observation of coherent spin interferometry generated by cavity memory using an ensemble of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers coupled to a microwave cavity. The abrupt switch-on and switch-off of a detuned drive produce transient fields at the cavity frequency that supply the two spin rotations for Ramsey interferometry, observed using both microwave and fluorescence readout. Spectrally scanning the spin profile across the cavity and drive frequencies distinguishes cavity-generated Ramsey interference from conventional Rabi dynamics. Temporal weighting of the reflected microwave signal enables spectrally selective population readout at a single probe frequency. By programming the phase and amplitude of the drive envelope, we extend the same mechanism to more quantum control sequences, including spin-echo and Rabi control.
one_liner: Detuned-drive transients in a microwave cavity generate Ramsey, spin-echo, and Rabi control of an NV-center ensemble.
why_it_matters: The cavity acts as both a memory and a programmable control resource, offering compact pulse generation and selective readout for ensemble spin sensing.
detailed_summary: An ensemble of nitrogen-vacancy centers is coupled to a microwave cavity and driven off resonance. Abrupt drive switching creates cavity-frequency transients that implement the two rotations required for Ramsey interferometry, observed through microwave reflection and fluorescence. Envelope phase and amplitude programming extends the mechanism to spin-echo and Rabi sequences, while temporal weighting enables spectrally selective population readout at one probe frequency.
platform_or_system: NV-center ensemble in a microwave cavity
main_result: Cavity-memory transients were experimentally used for coherent Ramsey interferometry, spin echo, Rabi control, and selective spin-population readout.
application_angle: The approach could simplify programmable control and frequency-selective readout in cavity-enhanced NV magnetometers and ensemble quantum memories.

title: Chip-Based Discrete-Modulated Continuous-Variable Quantum Key Distribution with Uncertainty-Principle-Based Composable Security
abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution offers a promising platform for scalable quantum networks through its compatibility with standard telecommunications technology and photonic integration. High-order discrete modulation facilitates practical implementation while approaching the key-rate performance of ideal Gaussian modulation, but its finite-size composable security analysis entails substantial computational overhead. Here, we develop an uncertainty-principle-based security framework that enables finite-size composable key-rate evaluation against collective attacks for constellations up to 256-QAM. By introducing a heterodyne-measured ancillary mode into the entanglement-based source description, we incorporate additional source correlations into the security analysis that allow the Heisenberg uncertainty principle alone to provide a tight bound for the unknown correlations in a covariance matrix characterizing the whole system. Matrix symmetrization further reduces the key-rate optimization to a one-dimensional search, while subsequent mode reduction yields an analytical lower bound requiring no numerical search. Experimental demonstrations using 256-QAM on discrete-component and silicon-photonic-receiver platforms achieve finite-size composable secret key rates of 17.436 and 0.519 Mbps, respectively, over a 50 km fiber link. This approach facilitates the practical deployment of high-speed, real-time and compact quantum key distribution systems. Beyond quantum key distribution, the principle of tightening uncertainty-constrained bounds via source-mode expansion offers a paradigm for exploring the information-theoretic properties of complex non-Gaussian systems.
one_liner: A chip-compatible 256-QAM CV-QKD system delivers finite-size composable secret keys over 50 km fiber at up to 17.436 Mbps.
why_it_matters: The security analysis reduces costly optimization while supporting dense modulation, high key rates, telecom fiber, and silicon-photonic receivers.
detailed_summary: The work develops an uncertainty-principle-based finite-size security framework for discrete-modulated CV-QKD with constellations up to 256-QAM against collective attacks. An ancillary heterodyne-measured source mode tightens covariance bounds, while symmetrization reduces optimization to one dimension and mode reduction provides an analytical lower bound. Experiments over 50 km fiber achieve 17.436 Mbps with discrete components and 0.519 Mbps with a silicon-photonic receiver.
main_result: Finite-size composable secret key rates of 17.436 Mbps and 0.519 Mbps were achieved over 50 km using discrete and silicon-photonic receiver platforms.
application_angle: The method supports compact, high-speed, real-time QKD implementations compatible with telecom infrastructure and photonic integration.

title: Efficient Parameter Estimation through Quantum Extreme Learning
abstract: Quantum sensing protocols rely on the efficient processing of measurement outcomes to infer unknown physical parameters. Conventional optimal estimators, such as Bayesian inference and maximum likelihood estimation, require to construct a likelihood function whose efficient classical construction requires full knowledge of the dynamics, which may practically be infeasible. Model-free experimental construction of the likelihood is also very resource intensive. Here, we propose a quantum extreme learning-based framework for quantum parameter estimation which avoids the explicit construction of the likelihood function. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach using the transverse-field Ising model for estimating the external transverse field. Our results show that high estimation accuracy can be achieved using measurements at only a small number of training points. We further develop an interrogation-time optimization strategy that minimizes the estimation inaccuracy while keeping sampling fluctuations below a prescribed threshold. We further extend the framework to a two-time measurement protocol, in which measurement outcomes obtained at two distinct times are combined to enrich the feature space, thereby significantly enhancing the estimation accuracy. Our analysis shows that the estimation precision improves monotonically with the number of training points, while increasing the system size generally enhances the sensing performance, albeit non-monotonically. Finally, the protocol is shown to be robust against dephasing, making it suitable for near-term quantum devices.
one_liner: Quantum extreme learning estimates fields in an Ising sensor without explicitly constructing a likelihood model.
why_it_matters: Model-free inference with sparse training, optimized interrogation times, and dephasing robustness could reduce calibration and processing costs in quantum sensors.
detailed_summary: The proposed estimator maps measurement outcomes to an unknown transverse field without constructing a likelihood function or requiring full knowledge of the sensor dynamics. Simulations on the transverse-field Ising model show accurate estimates from a small set of training points. Optimized interrogation times control sampling fluctuations, and combining measurements at two times expands the feature space and improves accuracy under dephasing.
main_result: The framework achieves accurate, likelihood-free field estimation with sparse training and improves precision through optimized two-time measurements.
application_angle: It offers a practical inference route for near-term sensors whose dynamics are difficult to model or calibrate exhaustively.

title: Tunable Hybridization of Whispering Gallery Modes in High-Index Photonic Molecules
abstract: Photonic molecules formed by coupled dielectric microresonators provide a platform for controlling collective optical modes, yet the interplay between molecular topology, resonator detuning, and dielectric environment in determining their spectral response remains insufficiently quantified. Here, we systematically quantify the evolution of Whispering Gallery Mode (WGM) hybridization in high-index TiO$_2$ and perovskite coated TiO$_2$ microresonators with molecular topology, and establish the corresponding effective inter-cavity coupling using a combined numerical and analytical analysis. We further show that perovskite-shell incorporation provides a diameter and thickness-dependent modification of the effective coupling, producing a non-monotonic response rather than a uniform suppression of coupling. Despite the resulting closely spaced hybridized resonances in the high-index perovskite environment, the supermodes remain spectrally resolvable, with $Q$-factor of order \(10^3\) for representative modes. The observed spectral splitting is quantitatively related to the effective inter-cavity coupling strengths, revealing a non-monotonic coupling response to perovskite-shell incorporation that depends on resonator size and shell thickness. These results establish molecular topology and dielectric environment as distinct parameters for controlling WGM hybridization, inter-cavity coupling, and spectral response, providing a basis for the design of coupled resonator systems for applications in optical sensing, filtering, switching, and other resonant photonic devices.
one_liner: Topology and perovskite-shell geometry provide independent, non-monotonic control of WGM coupling in high-index photonic molecules.
why_it_matters: Quantified control of resolvable coupled-cavity supermodes enables tunable resonant components for sensing, filtering, and optical switching.
detailed_summary: Numerical and analytical modeling quantifies WGM hybridization and effective inter-cavity coupling in coupled TiO2 and perovskite-coated TiO2 microresonators. The coupling depends separately on molecular topology, resonator diameter, shell thickness, and dielectric environment. Perovskite shells produce a non-monotonic coupling response, while representative hybridized modes remain spectrally resolvable with quality factors near 10^3.
main_result: The study establishes geometry-dependent, non-monotonic tuning of inter-cavity coupling while retaining resolvable WGM supermodes with Q factors around 10^3.
application_angle: The design rules can guide compact coupled-resonator sensors, wavelength filters, switches, and other tunable photonic devices.

title: Transfer-Matrix Calculus for Infinite Matrix Product States
abstract: Long-range interactions, from the Coulomb repulsion between electrons to the power-law interactions of trapped ions and Rydberg atoms, are widespread in quantum many-body physics. For infinite systems, however, MPS algorithms, the standard classical reference in one dimension, conventionally rely on a computational compromise: replacing these interactions by fitted sums of exponentials. We develop transfer-matrix calculus (TMC), a unified framework for deriving infinite-MPS algorithms. In TMC, an interaction is written as a function of the transfer matrix, and one set of contraction rules then yields the effective Hamiltonians of DMRG and VUMPS, the tangent-space excitation action, and the energy variance, without an MPO. Long-range interactions thus enter with their prescribed distance dependence. For the half-filled lattice Coulomb chain with a $1/d$ interaction of strength $V$, theory predicts CDW order for all $V>0$, but at weak coupling this order is too weak for earlier numerics to resolve. Using TMC, we obtain infinite-MPS ground states at $V=2$ directly in the thermodynamic limit, with an energy variance per site of $2\times10^{-10}$. Our data, extrapolated to zero energy variance, indicate a small nonzero CDW amplitude, $m_0=0.002213(14)$, consistent with this prediction. The complete $V=2$ optimization workflow across the full series of bond dimensions takes less than a day on a single AMD MI250X GPU die. For an exactly solvable long-range hopping model, TMC reproduces the nonanalytic $|k|$ cusp of the one-particle dispersion that any fixed finite sum of decaying exponentials rounds off. We also use TMC to optimize first-quantized MPS directly in the thermodynamic limit. For half-filled free fermions, our entanglement entropy data show scaling consistent with central charge $c=1$ over the studied bond dimensions, as for second-quantized MPS.
one_liner: Transfer-matrix calculus treats prescribed long-range interactions in infinite MPS algorithms without exponential fitting or MPO construction.
why_it_matters: Accurate thermodynamic-limit simulations can benchmark long-range quantum hardware models, including trapped-ion and Rydberg-atom systems.
detailed_summary: Transfer-matrix calculus expresses long-range interactions directly as functions of the MPS transfer matrix and supplies common contraction rules for DMRG, VUMPS, excitations, and energy variance. It avoids matrix-product operators and fitted exponential approximations. On a Coulomb chain at V=2, the method reaches an energy variance per site of 2×10^-10 and resolves a CDW amplitude of 0.002213(14), with the bond-dimension series completed in under a day on one AMD MI250X GPU die.
main_result: The method accurately preserves prescribed long-range behavior and resolves weak CDW order directly in the thermodynamic limit with very low energy variance.
application_angle: It provides a high-accuracy classical benchmark for validating analog quantum simulators and processors with power-law or Coulomb-like interactions.

title: Tessa: Encoding Classical Data Across an Entire Quantum Processor
abstract: We present Tessa, a hardware-aware, device-wide scheme to encode classical data on quantum computers. We use it to experimentally encode and decode up to $1568$ real values using IBM's Phoenix and Fez quantum computers on a variety of data. Tessa's construction is an extension of QPIXL and QCrank. However, it checkerboards address and data qubits across a coupling graph with neighbouring data qubits sharing only a subset of address qubits. When using the device's coupling graph no SWAP gates or routing is required, but the construction works for any bipartite coupling graph. The shots required for readout are determined by the local coupling degree. As examples, we have used cat states (pixel art of cats), various pixel art, audio, MIDI, DNA sequences and protein amino acid sequences.
one_liner: Tessa encodes and decodes as many as 1,568 real values across IBM quantum processors without SWAP-based routing.
why_it_matters: Coupling-aware data placement uses an entire processor efficiently and exposes a practical route to large-scale quantum data-loading experiments.
detailed_summary: Tessa extends QPIXL and QCrank by checkerboarding address and data qubits across a bipartite hardware coupling graph. Neighboring data qubits share only subsets of address qubits, eliminating SWAP gates when the native graph is used and tying shot cost to local coupling degree. Experiments on IBM Phoenix and Fez processors encode and decode up to 1,568 real values drawn from images, audio, MIDI, DNA, and protein sequences.
platform_or_system: IBM Phoenix and Fez quantum processors
main_result: Device-wide experiments encoded and decoded up to 1,568 real values using native connectivity with no SWAP or routing gates.
application_angle: The scheme enables hardware-efficient loading of large classical datasets for quantum image, signal, and biological-sequence workflows.

title: Beyond Blossom: Accelerating MWPM Decoding for Surface Codes With Local Predecoding and Architecture-Aware Optimizations
abstract: Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) is widely used to decode surface codes, but its computational cost increases with code distance. We present Beyond Blossom, a state-of-the-art CPU-based MWPM decoder for surface codes. It combines algorithmic optimization through local predecoding, architecture-aware optimization, and pipeline-wide parallelism to reduce matching workload and execution overhead while preserving MWPM optimality. Across rotated surface codes with distances 9-33 and circuit-level physical error rates of 0.05%-0.3%, on a single CPU core, Beyond Blossom achieves a 4.23$\times$ geometric-mean speedup and up to 5.58$\times$ speedup over Sparse Blossom in PyMatching. At distance 33 and a physical error rate of 0.1%, with 8 CPU cores, decoding a block of 33 measurement rounds takes 21.40 $μ$s on average, equivalent to 0.65 $μ$s per round.
one_liner: A CPU-based surface-code decoder preserves MWPM optimality while reducing latency through local predecoding and architecture-aware parallelism.
why_it_matters: Fast classical decoding is essential for real-time fault-tolerant quantum control, especially as surface-code distance and syndrome volume increase.
detailed_summary: Beyond Blossom accelerates minimum-weight perfect-matching decoding using local predecoding, architecture-aware optimizations, and pipeline-wide parallelism without sacrificing MWPM optimality. Across rotated surface codes of distance 9–33, it delivers a 4.23× geometric-mean single-core speedup over Sparse Blossom and reaches 5.58× in the best case. At distance 33 and 0.1% physical error, eight CPU cores decode 33 measurement rounds in 21.40 μs, or 0.65 μs per round.
platform_or_system: CPU decoder for rotated surface codes
main_result: The decoder achieves up to 5.58× speedup and 0.65 μs latency per syndrome round while retaining exact MWPM decoding.
application_angle: The optimized CPU implementation can reduce the classical-control bottleneck in scalable, real-time surface-code quantum processors.

title: Dissipation as a Resource for Entanglement via High-Spin Mediator Purification
abstract: We study entanglement generation between two spin qubits mediated by a single, thermally mixed, high-spin ($S=5/2$) magnetic impurity, using the Lindblad master equation to compare coherent and dissipative control of the mediator. We show that no coherent drive, however strong or resonant, can purify the mediator beyond its thermal value --- a direct consequence of unitary evolution exactly preserving state purity --- while a dissipative channel purifies it up to the limit set by the optical pumping cycle itself, $\mathrm{Tr}[ρ_M^2]\approx0.8$. Modeling this channel with rates fixed by the measured optical pumping of a single Mn spin, we find that the entanglement it enables is not monotonic in the pump strength: it peaks at a finite rate and then decreases, since the same channel leaks decoherence to the qubits through the coupling that mediates their entanglement. At the experimental pumping rate, a single $80$ns pulse purifies the mediator, the resulting polarization persists for a timescale three orders of magnitude longer than the entangling dynamics, and the first-recurrence negativity rises from $0.18$ to $0.64$ at $12$K, remaining above $0.6$ up to $30$K. These results establish dissipation, not as noise to be suppressed, but as the very resource that makes robust entanglement generation possible.
one_liner: Optical pumping of a single high-spin mediator turns engineered dissipation into a resource for robust two-qubit entanglement.
why_it_matters: The work identifies a realistic route to strong spin-qubit entanglement at elevated temperatures using measured single-Mn optical-pumping rates.
detailed_summary: A Lindblad model compares coherent and dissipative control of two spin qubits coupled through a thermally mixed S=5/2 magnetic impurity. Coherent driving cannot increase mediator purity, whereas optical-pumping dissipation raises it to about 0.8, with entanglement optimized at a finite pumping rate. Using experimentally measured Mn pumping rates, an 80 ns pulse increases first-recurrence negativity from 0.18 to 0.64 at 12 K and keeps it above 0.6 up to 30 K.
platform_or_system: Spin qubits coupled by a single Mn impurity
main_result: Measured-rate optical pumping purifies the mediator and raises qubit negativity to 0.64 at 12 K, with values above 0.6 through 30 K.
application_angle: Engineered dissipation could enable thermally robust entangling operations in impurity-mediated solid-state spin-qubit hardware.

title: Complex fluid flow dynamics by bright scattershot boson sampling
abstract: Boson sampling machines have become a fruitful tool for establishing new concepts, which connect fundamental physics with computer science applications. Here, we exploit the intrinsically high-dimensional correlations generated by the measurement outcomes of a multiphoton boson sampling machine and demonstrate how a reconfigurable architecture can be programmed to autonomously model the time evolution of nonlinear dynamical systems that describe complex fluid flows. By extending on the original scattershot boson sampling (SBS) scheme to include higher photon number components -- a scheme which we label bright scattershot boson sampling (BSBS) --- this scheme overcomes scaling issues inherent to SBS-based schemes by utilizing all randomly generated input photon number distributions. We illustrate the capability of this scheme for two complex fluid-flow models: an eight-dimensional Lorenz-type model of two-dimensional thermally driven convection and a 16-dimensional model of global atmospheric circulation. Using a digital twin of the BSBS architecture based on multiphoton statistics, we show that the photonic approach accurately reproduces the temporal dynamics of both systems while being resilient to photon losses of up to 50 per cent. We also verified that the BSBS case outperforms a comparable run with coherent light. Moreover, its prediction horizon exceeds that of a classical reservoir-computing model with the same query complexity. These results highlight the potential of near-term photonic quantum computing for addressing relevant real-world tasks on noisy intermediate-scale devices.
one_liner: Bright scattershot boson sampling models nonlinear fluid dynamics using multiphoton correlations and remains resilient to 50% photon loss.
why_it_matters: It connects near-term photonic quantum processors to practical dynamical-system prediction beyond conventional sampling benchmarks.
detailed_summary: Bright scattershot boson sampling uses higher photon-number components and all randomly generated input distributions to mitigate scaling limitations of conventional scattershot schemes. A multiphoton-statistics digital twin reproduces an eight-dimensional convection model and a 16-dimensional atmospheric-circulation model while tolerating up to 50% photon loss. It outperforms a coherent-light counterpart and exceeds the prediction horizon of a classical reservoir computer at equal query complexity.
main_result: The BSBS architecture accurately predicts two nonlinear flow systems despite 50% photon loss and outperforms coherent-light and matched-query classical baselines.
application_angle: The approach positions noisy photonic quantum hardware as a programmable engine for forecasting complex nonlinear dynamics such as fluid and atmospheric flows.

title: Proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture: An Exposition
abstract: We give an exposition of a recent proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, which states that every degree-$d$ polynomial $p : \{0,1\}^n \to [0,1]$ has a variable of influence at least $\mathrm{poly}(\mathrm{Var}(p)/d)$. This implies that quantum query algorithms for decision problems can be efficiently simulated classically on most inputs. It also yields a near-equivalence between the status of the $\mathsf{BPP}$ vs. $\mathsf{BQP}$ problem in the random oracle and unrelativized worlds. We organize the proof around four main steps and discuss how each connects to the literature on the analysis of boolean functions and probabilistic combinatorics. To bring out the key ideas, we do not optimize parameters, and our presentation yields weaker exponents than the original. $\textbf{Authors' note.}$ The proof was discovered by David Turturean using a research system developed at Physical Superintelligence (PSI), in combination with a non-public Anthropic model. The proof was then shared with the authors, who worked to understand it and prepare this exposition. Anthropic's public models were used in this process. The authors did not receive financial compensation from Anthropic or PSI. This article is not intended for publication at a conference or in a journal.
one_liner: An exposition organizes the Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture proof into four steps connecting Boolean analysis and probabilistic combinatorics.
why_it_matters: The result links classical simulation of quantum queries on most inputs to the BPP-versus-BQP question.

title: Pauli propagation in adaptive local frames
abstract: The cost of Pauli propagation depends on the local basis in which the evolving operator is expanded. We show that its Pauli complexity splits into an occupation part, invariant under local rotations and bounded from below by the operator mass and length distributions, and a flavour part that a suitable basis can remove. We introduce frame-adaptive Pauli propagation (FAPP), which rotates the basis of every qubit, gate by gate, to the principal axes of the operator's local polarisation, exactly and within the memory structure of Pauli propagation. This simple rule achieves most of what the best local frame can, and the polarisation predicts how much any local frame can gain. In the Ising chain in transverse and longitudinal fields, FAPP lowers the truncation error at fixed memory by up to an order of magnitude and the memory by a size-independent factor of three; on the infinite two-dimensional lattice it needs up to seven times fewer strings for a given certified accuracy, and in Clifford circuits doped with T gates two to eight times fewer.
one_liner: Frame-adaptive Pauli propagation rotates local bases gate by gate to reduce operator-expansion memory and truncation error.
why_it_matters: Adaptive frames can make certified many-body and circuit simulations substantially more resource-efficient.

title: Lieb-Robinson bound for one-dimensional continuum fermions
abstract: The central difficulty in quantum many-body physics is that the Hilbert space dimension grows exponentially with the total degrees of freedom. A key feature to circumvent this problem is locality, which manifests dynamically through an approximate causal structure in the form of a Lieb-Robinson bound (LRB). LRBs have been proved for quantum spin systems and certain lattice boson systems, but so far never for realistic continuum systems. We present the first LRB that applies to a standard system of one-dimensional continuum fermions. It applies to initial states with controlled moments of local particle number and energy and is thus thermodynamically stable. Our result breaks the main technical barrier that has existed for using the vast locality toolbox on continuum systems.
one_liner: The first Lieb–Robinson bound for standard one-dimensional continuum fermions establishes approximate causal locality under controlled states.
why_it_matters: It extends powerful locality-based many-body methods beyond lattice models to realistic continuum systems.

title: Integer electron-count cuts in variational second-order reduced-density-matrix theory. II. A convergent hierarchy of rigorous relaxations for real-space pair-density representability
abstract: Variational second-order reduced-density-matrix calculations can dissociate molecules into fractionally charged fragments; Part I largely removed this failure with integer electron-count conditions on fixed partitions. Building on the realizability theory of point processes, we place these conditions in a convergent hierarchy of rigorous relaxations, defined by finite occupation linear programs (LPs) on spatial partitions, for real-space pair densities at fixed one-particle density. Every level contains all representable pair densities, the levels tighten under nested refinement, and their intersection characterizes pair densities admitting a symmetric $N$-particle probability-measure extension. In a fixed orbital basis the levels give monotonically increasing lower bounds to the full configuration-interaction energy, which they need not reach, even for the Coulomb repulsion. The spin-summed real-space cuts of Part I are its two-cell members. The LP optimum is also a measure: at fixed one-particle density it equals the $L^1$ distance of the coarse-grained candidate from representability and increases under refinement to that of the candidate, with a vanishing coarse-graining error; its primal law constructs a representable approximation, and its dual a violated valid inequality, used as a cut in molecular calculations. The count conditions are not implied by the usual positivity conditions: moment data that satisfy all three-particle positivity conditions, including $T_1$ and $T_2$, give through Gaussian orbitals a smooth pair density that violates an integer count. For atoms at fractional electron number, ensemble relaxations with the integer-count condition lie closer to the exact piecewise-linear energy than the zero-variance fixed-$N$ form.
one_liner: A convergent hierarchy of occupation linear programs imposes rigorous real-space pair-density representability constraints.
why_it_matters: The hierarchy suppresses fractional-charge errors and yields improving lower bounds for molecular energies.

title: Wavelength-resolved polarization characterization of supercontinuum vector beams
abstract: The polarization state of a supercontinuum (SC) vector beam provides a reference for quantitative polarimetry. We characterize an azimuthally polarized SC vector beam generated with an S-waveplate and azimuthal polarizers by wavelength-resolved Stokes imaging. Representative maps show an approximately tangential azimuthal angle and a small ellipticity parameter over much of the beam, together with the degree of polarization. The {\pm} 90° azimuthal angle boundary shifts by about 21° between 450 and 766 nm. A linear fit gives 21° {\pm} 7°, where the uncertainty is derived from the slope confidence interval and does not include uncharacterized systematic errors. Jones-matrix calculations examine candidate imperfections under specified assumptions. Attributing the measured boundary shift to this mechanism requires an intensity extinction ratio of about 7 or less at 766 nm if the offset at 450 nm is negligible and the shift corresponds to a uniform azimuthal angle change. The origin remains unresolved. The results motivate wavelength-dependent characterization and calibration of this probe for quantitative polarimetry.
one_liner: Wavelength-resolved Stokes imaging reveals a roughly 21-degree polarization-boundary shift across an azimuthal supercontinuum beam.
why_it_matters: Quantitative broadband polarimetry requires wavelength-dependent probe characterization and calibration.

title: Model-family selection and recovery-gate design in generator-based noise tomography
abstract: Family selection in generator-model noise tomography, usually quoted as a hardware property, is a hypothesis test whose shot floor is closed form under a purely coherent noise model, $N^{*}=λ_{\mathrm{req}}/(r_{\mathrm{b}} S)^{2}$, controlled by the absolute bias $r_{\mathrm{b}} S$ rather than by the relative residual $r_{\mathrm{b}}$, hence computable for any device from a calibration, before a single shot. The same computation prices the recovery gates: the fingerprint that fixes a family's residual and the Fisher information that ranks designs come from the same map, so there is no design-independent verdict and no family-independent design optimum. Whether a design can move that price is structural: a bias confined to the block every design measures identically is design-blind, while one that reaches the code blocks can be repriced by a factor of sixty-eight; the two platforms are its extremes, at $98.1\%$ and $48.0\%$. At the reference point the floor is $1.1\times10^{7}$ and $6.7\times10^{6}$ shots per component, and that point is the easy corner: the median of its own direction over the sampled points is $8.9\times10^{8}$, $83$ times dearer. At the $10^{5}$ shots a run spends the test has power $0.053$ at a level of $0.05$. Rebuilding the fingerprint under each of the sixty-four designs moves the floor by $68$ on one platform and $1.7$ on the other, and the most precise design costs ten times more shots for the verdict than the cheapest to test. All sixty-four placements are full rank: at three gates the rms varies by factors of $2.7$ and $3.9$ with placement alone, while the optimum over counts is flat. At five qubits the same rule moves the floor by $21$ while the verdict costs $10^{9}$ shots; against a real three-qubit calibration the floor is a requirement on systematic control before it is a shot count, and where that control is missing no budget supplies it.
one_liner: A closed-form shot floor connects noise-model family selection with recovery-gate design in generator-based tomography.
why_it_matters: It shows that model verdicts and optimal gate designs depend strongly on bias structure and systematic control.

title: An optimal quantum strategy for the $2$-hat game
abstract: We study the two-player hat game as a two-input, three-output non-local game. We calculate the quantum commuting value and show that it coincides with the quantum one. In particular, we show that \[ω_{\rm q}(H_2)=ω_{\mathrm{qc}}(H_2)=\frac{15+\sqrt{33}}{36}\approx 0.576238.\] We achieve the optimal quantum advantage using a shared non-maximally entangled qutrit state. To establish optimality, we exploit the game's symmetry under the dihedral group $D_8$ and apply its representation theory to substantially reduce the complexity of the underlying matrix problem. We also determine the no-signalling value $ω_{\mathrm{ns}}(H_2)=2/3$.
one_liner: The optimal quantum value of the two-player 2-hat game is derived and attained with a nonmaximally entangled qutrit state.
why_it_matters: The result exactly separates quantum, commuting, and no-signalling performance in this nonlocal game.

title: Proof of the Rényi QNEC
abstract: We give a general proof of the Rényi QNEC formulated using the Araki-Masuda weighted $L_p$ norms for all $p > 2$. This generalizes the algebraic proof of the QNEC applicable at $p=2$. Our approach utilizes a weighted version of a conditional $L_p$ norm which extrapolates the quantum expansion/ant-quantity. We elucidate some properties of the corresponding weighted conditional entropy both for half-sided modular inclusions and for general von Neumann subalgebras with a common cyclic and separating vector. The $p=2$ limit computes a conditional dynamical entropy originally defined in the context of black hole dynamics.
one_liner: A general proof establishes the Rényi quantum null energy condition for Araki–Masuda weighted norms with p greater than 2.
why_it_matters: It broadens the algebraic QNEC framework and connects weighted conditional entropy with black-hole dynamics.

title: Super-resolution quantum imaging via multiphoton correlation
abstract: The resolution of conventional imaging is fundamentally constrained by the diffraction limit. Here we demonstrate that this limit can be overcome using classical thermal light, through the correlation of multiphoton subsystems. By resolving the photon numbers detected in the two arms of a Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometer, the correlation function exhibits a narrowed peak or dip whose width is tunable via the average photon number. Temporal and spatial super-resolution enhancements up to 11.8-fold and 5.1-fold, respectively, are experimentally achieved. As a proof-of-principle experiment, a double-pinhole that is completely unresolved by standard ghost imaging becomes clearly distinguishable via the correlation of two-photon versus zero-photon. The principle of this super-resolution imaging can be interpreted as a combination of classical super-resolution imaging and quantum super-resolution imaging. This work provides a versatile platform for super-resolution imaging and lithography, and opens a new avenue for exploring the boundary between classical and nonclassical phenomena.
one_liner: Multiphoton correlations of classical thermal light achieve up to 11.8-fold temporal and 5.1-fold spatial super-resolution.
why_it_matters: The approach offers a versatile route to sub-diffraction imaging and lithography without requiring nonclassical light.

title: Three-dimensional polarization of thermal fields at arbitrary distances from thin-film emitters
abstract: Recent advances have shown that thermal radiation can exhibit strong polarization in both the near and far fields. However, most existing studies focus on paraxial far-field emission, where polarization can be described using conventional two-dimensional (2D) Stokes parameters. Non-paraxial thermal radiation, with three nonzero vector components, requires a fully three-dimensional (3D) polarization description. This work develops a generalized theoretical method for analyzing thermal-radiation polarization at arbitrary distances from an emitter. Fluctuation-dissipation theory is employed to determine the $3\times3$ coherence matrix of the thermally emitted electromagnetic field, from which generalized 3D Stokes parameters are obtained. This method is applied to planar slabs composed of isotropic, anisotropic, and nonreciprocal materials. The results reveal distinct polarization behavior across the near- and far-field regimes. Near-field polarization is strongly influenced by evanescent waves and polariton dispersion, whereas far-field polarization is primarily governed by polarization-dependent radiative properties, including differences between transverse-electric (TE) and transverse-magnetic (TM) emission. Slab thickness further modifies polarization by controlling supported modes and interference effects. In addition, circular polarization, which vanishes in reciprocal slabs, is observed in n-type doped InAs under an external magnetic field that breaks reciprocity. This work provides a unified framework for characterizing the polarization of thermal electromagnetic fields from the extreme near field to the far field.
one_liner: A 3D coherence-matrix framework describes thermal-field polarization from the extreme near field to the far field.
why_it_matters: It enables polarization analysis of nonparaxial emission from reciprocal, anisotropic, and nonreciprocal thin films.

title: Wide Field 3D Color Topography for Steep-slope Structures
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) topography measurement is essential for industrial inspection and scientific research. However, existing techniques are limited by an inherent trade-off between resolution, speed, color imaging capability and the ability to measure large-angle surfaces. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel method that integrates ring light illumination based wide-field 3D imaging with an iterative shape-from-focus (SFF) algorithm. The system employs coaxial epi-illumination combined with ring light illumination to simultaneously acquire information from flat regions and steep slopes. The proposed iterative SFF algorithm achieves high-resolution 3D topography measurement. Full-color 3D reconstructions of electronic chips and PCBs demonstrate that the proposed method enables fast scanning and sub-micrometer resolution and significantly extending the measurable inclination range for large-angle structures. This method fills a critical gap in existing technology for fast, natural-color, 3D imaging and measurement of samples with steep topographies.
one_liner: Ring and coaxial illumination combined with iterative shape from focus reconstructs full-color topography of steep structures.
why_it_matters: The method targets fast, submicrometer 3D inspection across both flat areas and large-angle surfaces.

title: Origin of devil's staircases and anomalous Arnold tongues of breathing solitons in optical Kerr resonators
abstract: Synchronization phenomena are ubiquitous across natural and engineered systems, and optical resonators supporting breathing solitons offer a natural platform for their investigation. In driven Kerr cavities described by the Lugiato-Lefever equation (LLE), breathing-soliton dynamics constitute a minimal setting in which such behavior can be systematically analyzed. Despite recent observations of intricate self-synchronization structures in mode-locked lasers-such as subharmonic entrainment, devil's staircases, and holes within Arnold tongues, i.e., regions of unsynchronized dynamics embedded within synchronized domains-their physical origin has remained elusive due to the complexity of laser dynamics. Here, we demonstrate that these phenomena emerge in the universal framework of the LLE. By reducing the problem to this model, we uncover the mechanism responsible for both the devil's staircase and the formation of holes within Arnold tongues. This provides a unified physical picture of synchronization in nonlinear systems, extending beyond optics and providing insight into analogous predictions and observations in fluids and other oscillatory media. In addition, we identify the regimes of high-order synchronization, enabling the generation of ultradense frequency combs, opening new directions for precision photonic applications.
one_liner: The Lugiato–Lefever model explains devil's staircases and holes in Arnold tongues for breathing Kerr-cavity solitons.
why_it_matters: The mechanism unifies nonlinear synchronization behavior and identifies regimes for ultradense frequency combs.

title: More particles or the pair? An exact test of how to improve mode-coupling theory
abstract: How a dense liquid arrests into a glass remains a central problem in physics. Mode-coupling theory (MCT), the leading microscopic theory of the glass transition, fails to reproduce mean-field caging. Two routes are proposed to repair it: tracking more-particle correlations, or enforcing repulsion within each colliding pair. Testing both on an exact benchmark liquid, we show that MCT lets touching spheres pass through each other at all orders: adding particles dilutes memory and worsens the transition, whereas restoring pair impenetrability recovers mean-field arrest and the cage size.
one_liner: An exact benchmark shows that enforcing pair impenetrability, not adding higher-order correlations, repairs mode-coupling theory's glass-arrest prediction.
why_it_matters: It identifies the missing physical constraint needed to recover mean-field caging and cage size.

title: Lensless single-pixel imaging through dynamic coded-aperture illumination
abstract: We demonstrate a lensless single-pixel imaging (SPI) system combining dynamic coded-aperture illumination with single-pixel detection. Binary digital micromirror device (DMD) masks generate tailored grayscale intensity fields through coherent propagation, without relay projection optics or temporal grayscale synthesis. Six target-field configurations---uniform, Rayleigh speckle, squared-Rayleigh speckle, and sparse binary fields with $p=10\%$, $5\%$, and $1\%$---are evaluated using binary and grayscale objects. Intensity-correlation and nonnegative total-variation-regularized reconstructions reveal that the preferred illumination depends on the object, reconstruction method, and evaluation metric. By combining rapid binary modulation, programmable grayscale illumination, and single-pixel readout, this implementation provides a flexible architecture for lensless computational imaging and joint design of optical encoding and reconstruction.
one_liner: A lensless single-pixel imager uses binary DMD masks and coherent propagation to create programmable grayscale illumination without relay optics.
why_it_matters: It enables flexible joint optimization of optical encoding and reconstruction in compact computational imagers.

title: Rotational Encoding of Objective Functions for Quantum Optimization
abstract: In this paper, we introduce the Angular Rotational Counter (ARC), a novel approach to represent objective functions that can be decomposed as a weighted sum of Boolean functions. ARC encodes the objective as an accumulated sum of quantum rotations onto a single-qubit register instead of a multi-qubit register used in much of the previous literature. We mathematically establish and experimentally validate that these rotations sum to the objective value for all possible solutions and derive the relationship between the resulting measurement probabilities and the objective. This design was applied to construct a quantum oracle for the state assignment problem of finite automata and state machines using a weighted Hamming distance cost function, which is a special case of the quadratic assignment problem. We evaluate this oracle design on 26 benchmarks and compare it with corresponding Boolean-based oracles on four cost metrics. Across these benchmarks, the oracle with ARC produces a mean reduction in the qubit count of 20.8%, gate count of 89.3%, circuit depth of 92.4%, and quantum cost of 90.6%. These results demonstrate substantial reductions in circuit cost for the evaluated benchmarks and establish rotational encoding as a promising approach for representing objective functions in optimization based on quantum search algorithms.
one_liner: ARC encodes weighted Boolean objectives as accumulated rotations on one qubit, sharply reducing quantum-oracle circuit resources.
why_it_matters: Across 26 benchmarks, it cuts mean qubit count by 20.8% and gate count, depth, and quantum cost by about 89–92%.

title: Proof of the QNEC, without assumptions and under a weight
abstract: We complete a proof of the quantum null energy condition (QNEC) in the mathematical framework of Half-Sided Translations and Modular Inclusions (HST/HSMI) removing an assumption that applied to previous proofs. Here we establish a theorem, which when translated to a physical setting implies that the relative entropy comparing the state of fields outside a stationary black hole with a Hartle-Hawking (HH) state is always a convex function of the horizon cut. Previous proofs only applied when a purification with finite null energy was available. We also obtain a QNEC generalization in which the HH Hilbert space is replaced with one based on a weight which is plausibly of relevance to evaporating black holes in flat space.
one_liner: A proof of QNEC using modular inclusions removes the prior requirement for a purification with finite null energy.
why_it_matters: The result broadens QNEC applicability and introduces a weight-based generalization relevant to evaporating black holes.

title: AI-Driven Discovery of Entanglement Witness in Spin Hamiltonians
abstract: Entanglement is a crucial resource in quantum science and engineering, but detecting it in many-body states from experimentally accessible observables remains challenging. Here we introduce EntNet, an AI-driven framework to discover compact combinations of spin observables that accurately distinguish entangled from fully separable many-body mixed states in one-dimensional spin-$1/2$ chains governed by short-range Hamiltonians. We construct local-unitary-invariant representations of measurable Pauli correlators up to four-body order, sparsely select 16 candidate invariant feature channels, and learn their spatial structure using a Transformer architecture with rotary positional embeddings. Using only expectation values of these low-order observables, EntNet achieves $>98\%$ recall on certified entangled states with near-zero false-positive rates on separable states. Remarkably, it exhibits transferability across system sizes and distinct Hamiltonian families, including frustrated and disordered spin models, with minimal loss of accuracy. Beyond detection, EntNet provides physical insight into entanglement detection by revealing a selective spatial organization of pair correlations, while its finite-temperature decision boundary tracks the excitation gap of Jordan-Wigner quasiparticles. These results establish a transferable and physically interpretable framework for data-driven discovery of entanglement witnesses from local correlation functions.
one_liner: EntNet learns compact, interpretable entanglement witnesses from low-order Pauli correlators in diverse spin-1/2 chains.
why_it_matters: It exceeds 98% recall with near-zero separable-state false positives and transfers across sizes and Hamiltonian families.

title: Semiclassical Asymptotics of Entanglement in Torus-Link States
abstract: We investigate the entanglement entropy of topological quantum states associated with $T_{d,\,dn}$ torus links in (2+1)-dimensional SU(2) Chern--Simons theory at level $k$. These links consist of $d$ components with pairwise linking number $n$, and the corresponding link-complement states provide a natural setting to study multipartite entanglement in topological quantum field theories. We analyze the semiclassical limit $k\to\infty$ of the entanglement entropy by deriving the asymptotic behavior of the moments of the reduced density matrix. To achieve this, we decompose the integrable-representation space into left-edge, right-edge, and bulk regions and employ the stationary-phase method to evaluate their respective contributions. We find that the leading asymptotic behavior is governed entirely by the two edge regions, while the bulk contribution is asymptotically suppressed. The resulting expression for the limiting entanglement entropy is given in terms of Hurwitz zeta functions and exhibits a dependence on the residue class of $k$ modulo $n$. We further investigate the dependence of the limiting entanglement entropy on the winding parameter $n$ and the number of link components $d$. In the large-$d$ limit, the entropy reduces to a binary entropy determined by two normalized weights associated with the left and right edges. Finally, we show that the two iterated limits, $k\to\infty$ and $d\to\infty$, commute, reproducing the result obtained previously by taking the large-party limit first.
one_liner: The semiclassical entanglement entropy of SU(2) Chern–Simons torus-link states is governed by edge contributions and Hurwitz zeta functions.
why_it_matters: It reveals residue-class dependence, bulk suppression, and commuting large-level and large-party limits.

title: Parameterized equivalence checking of quantum circuit generators via weighted automata
abstract: A generator builds a quantum circuit from the number of qubits and a bit string. We check a generator against a reference for all parameter values under six equivalence relations. For ladder programs, we prove that above a computable threshold the circuit matrices form a uniform matrix product operator, a weighted automaton of dimension independent of the number of qubits. Equivalence reduces to the zeroness of a difference automaton, checked modulo primes. The answer is a counterexample or "equal", exact or with a computed error bound. Experimentally, the method found errors missed by fixed-size checks and produced no incorrect verdicts.
one_liner: Weighted automata enable parameterized equivalence checking of quantum circuit generators across all qubit counts and input bit strings.
why_it_matters: The method returns exact or bounded-error verdicts and finds generator bugs missed by fixed-size testing.

title: Universal Fold Caustics in Anharmonic Matter-wave Lenses
abstract: Caustics provide a universal connection between classical ray focusing and structured wave patterns. We theoretically investigate this connection in non-linear matter waves focused by a short-duration anharmonic lens acting on a Bose-Einstein condensate. A semi-classical description shows how the leading cubic aberration transforms the harmonic focal point into a fold caustic, whose local wave field is described by an Airy canonical integral. Three-dimensional Gross-Pitaevskii simulations show that mean-field interactions modify the near-focus density and longitudinal momentum distribution, producing a secondary momentum-space feature absent from the non-interacting evolution. We quantify the information about the effective interaction strength carried by the $1D$ distribution using classical Fisher information and maximum-likelihood estimation. We obtain a relative uncertainty of $2.7\times10^{-3}$ for a sample of $10^5$ detected points along $z$. These results establish a framework for studying interaction-driven departures from single-particle caustic universality and promote matter-wave lenses as a sensitive probe of mean-field interactions.
one_liner: Anharmonic focusing of a Bose–Einstein condensate produces universal Airy fold caustics modified by mean-field interactions.
