abstract: Operating within the framework of the collisionless Boltzmann equation, we identify universal spectral profiles inherent in stimulated and coherent light scattering from laser-driven dilute-gas density gratings and derive physically intuitive solutions for such spectral shapes, expressing them in a manifestly causal closed form that satisfies the Kramers - Kronig relations and fulfills the fluctuation - dissipation theorem. Benchmarking against gold-standard experiments on dilute-gas stimulated light scattering verifies a high descriptive and explanatory power of these solutions and demonstrates their ability to isolate universality motifs in nonlinear scattering spectra as the key to fully understanding the physics behind dilute-gas nonlinear light scattering. As one of important outcomes, such analysis reveals the physical content of the bandwidth of dilute-gas nonlinear scattering spectra as an expression and a quantifier of the phase-mixing time, i.e., the time required for free-streaming gas particles with a mean thermal velocity to traverse the distance equal to the spacing of the laser-driven density grating.
one_liner: A causal kinetic model derives universal spectral profiles for nonlinear light scattering from laser-driven dilute-gas density gratings.
why_it_matters: The spectral bandwidth directly quantifies particle phase-mixing time and clarifies nonlinear gas-scattering physics.

title: Computational Power of Clifford and Ising Quantum Computers
abstract: We extend the efficient classical simulation of Ising quantum computers from braidings to measurements. We investigate several different definitions of efficient Clifford quantum computation by varying the power of the circuit generator. In case the circuit generator can see the entire input, we give a detailed proof that efficient simulation of classical computation would imply the separation of complexity classes $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{PSPACE}$. If the circuit generator sees only the input length, we prove that Clifford quantum computers decide what we call affine languages.
one_liner: The work extends classical simulation of Ising quantum computers to measurements and characterizes restricted Clifford computation.
why_it_matters: It sharpens the complexity-theoretic limits of Clifford and Ising quantum computing.

title: Optically modulated field-dependent electrical response in a non-collinear antiferromagnet/ferromagnet heterostructure
abstract: The interplay among optical, electrical, and magnetic stimuli offers opportunities to control the functional response of spintronic heterostructures. Here, we investigate the field-dependent electrical response of MgO/IrMn$_3$/Py/Au under radio-frequency (RF) excitation, white-light illumination, and direct-current (DC) bias. Under a 20 MHz RF signal with a nominal power of 2 W, the measured voltage in the dark remains at several tens of nanovolts. Upon illumination with approximately 1 W of white light, a pronounced field-dependent feature emerges around 315--320 Oe, reaching 0.9--1.0 $μ$V. The illumination-associated differential voltage is approximately 0.95 $μ$V. A DC current of 1 mA produces a response of approximately 1 $μ$V, while the simultaneous application of RF, DC, and optical excitation increases the voltage to approximately 1.8 $μ$V. Magnetic characterization reveals exchange bias with a blocking temperature near 380 K, while electrical resistance measurements show a pronounced dependence on magnetic-field orientation, consistent with the anisotropic response of the heterostructure. These results demonstrate that the field-dependent electrical response can be modulated through combined optical and electrical excitation, involving magneto-optical interactions and spin-dependent transport phenomena, potentially including spin Hall-related contributions and the magnetic spin Hall effect. This work provides insights into coupled optical, electrical, and magnetic-field effects in heterostructures based on non-collinear antiferromagnets and ferromagnetic layers.
one_liner: White light and combined RF/DC excitation enhance the field-dependent voltage response of an IrMn3/Py spintronic heterostructure.
why_it_matters: The result supports multimodal control of electrical signals in antiferromagnet–ferromagnet devices.

title: PriorTilt: Decoding quantum LDPC codes with sparse perturbations of belief propagation priors
abstract: Although belief propagation (BP) is a widely adopted decoder for classical low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, its accuracy is limited in the quantum setting. We introduce \PriorTilt{}, a variant of BP obtained by selectively perturbing a small fraction of its prior log-likelihood ratios using offsets determined by recent posterior and outgoing-message statistics, while preserving the same message-passing rules. We compare \PriorTilt{} with Relay-BP and beam search decoders for circuit-level decoding of three benchmark codes. \PriorTilt{} achieves a lower logical error rate (LER) than both baselines at every tested data point. For the $[[144,12,12]]$ Gross code BB144 at noise rate $p=10^{-3}$, the LER reductions reach $4.3\times$ relative to Relay-BP and $3.1\times$ relative to the beam search decoder. At $p=10^{-3}$, \PriorTilt{} has lower mean decoding times than Relay-BP on all three codes and achieves mean decoding speedups of approximately $2.6\times$--$3.0\times$ over the beam search decoder. For BB144 at $p=10^{-3}$, \PriorTilt{} achieves an LER approximately $610\times$ lower than the standard min-sum BP decoder with the same iteration budget, while perturbing fewer than $0.5\%$ of its priors per round on average.
one_liner: PriorTilt improves quantum LDPC decoding by sparsely adjusting belief-propagation priors while retaining standard message updates.
why_it_matters: It lowers logical error rates and decoding time across three circuit-level code benchmarks.

title: Rotor-driven piecewise cross polarization of wide quadrupolar lines: bath-contact pumping of vector and tensor order in dynamically polarized solids
abstract: In a dynamically polarized solid with a common nuclear spin temperature, spin-1 $^{14}$N in ammonia sits at $P_N\simeq0.14$ when the protons are at $0.90$, and a deuteron in a proton-rich matrix at $P_D\simeq0.29$. Hartmann--Hahn cross polarization (CP) from the protons could raise either toward $P_H$, but the first-order quadrupole interaction spreads the $^{14}$N line over $5$~MHz at $5$~T, far beyond any single contact bandwidth. We develop the theory of CP into one transition of a quadrupolar spin-1, with slow sample rotation carrying each crystallite through a fixed-frequency contact window. A bath contact is an idempotent map on the populations of the contacted transition, so repeated or continuous contacts accumulate rather than cancel, and the hit-once and parity constraints that force stepped rotation for pulsed inversions do not arise. In the small-reservoir limit the population ratio across the contacted transition becomes $(1+P_H)/(1-P_H)$, giving $\Pzz=+0.88$ in one contact and $\Pzz\to-1.8$ in two from $P_H=0.9$, beyond the unitary bound $[-0.85,+0.65]$. Under continuous rotation, a window at the Pake horn reaches every bond for an axis perpendicular to the field, while a window in the clean pedestal region, needed for a definite sign of tensor order, reaches a fraction $\sin2θ_c=0.943$ at the magic angle $54.74\degree$. Steady-state order is set by the contact rate against rotation-driven cross-branch relaxation, negligible for $^{14}$N. In the cubic limit one contact places the spin-1 at the proton temperature ($\Pzz=+0.85$), but only a resolved quadrupole splitting permits negative tensor order. The limiting resource is the proton spin lock, which must far exceed the $\simeq28$~kHz local field for a contact short compared with $T_{1ρ}$, unmeasured at $1$~K. Protocols are given for $^{14}$N in NH$_3$ and deuterons in NH$_2$D.
one_liner: A theory of rotor-driven cross polarization shows how repeated bath contacts can pump vector and tensor order in quadrupolar spin-1 nuclei.
why_it_matters: It offers protocols for strongly polarizing broad 14N and deuteron lines in dynamically polarized solids.

title: Quantum-walk transport oracles and amplitude estimation of a scalar range statistic in proton therapy
abstract: Quantum amplitude estimation (QAE) promises a quadratic reduction in the sampling cost of Monte Carlo (MC) particle transport, but two obstacles have kept it from radiotherapy physics: the lack of an efficient unitary encoding of charged-particle transport, and the mismatch between QAE's single-scalar output and the per-voxel structure of dose calculation. We address both. We construct a discrete-time quantum-walk transport oracle for protons in which an energy register is driven by an energy-dependent coin encoding a continuous-slowing-down surrogate of the stopping power, so that stochastic energy loss and range straggling follow from the circuit dynamics. The oracle is unitary, with one fresh coin qubit per step, and its gate count grows linearly in the number of energy levels. On it we formulate a scalar range statistic, the probability that a proton penetrates beyond a distal depth threshold, as a directly marked amplitude, and estimate it by maximum-likelihood amplitude estimation (MLQAE) with Grover iterations and finite shots. The oracle reproduces a Bragg-shaped depth-deposit profile agreeing with a classical MC of identical rules to within 0.27%, and Grover amplification matches $\sin^2((2k+1)θ)$ to machine precision up to $k=32$. At matched budget the MLQAE error falls as $N^{-0.93}$ against $N^{-0.49}$ for sampling, 4.8 times smaller at the largest budget. A three-gate resource analysis (output structure, amortization, error-corrected wall-clock) finds full dose maps structurally unfavourable irrespective of hardware, and the scalar statistic short of a wall-clock crossover at clinical scale: the oracle's derived cost of $1.0 \times 10^6$ logical gates per call ($3.5 \times 10^7$ with rotation synthesis), dominated by the multiplexed coin, is 160 to 5400 times the permitted budget. We report the reduction that would be required and identify the term responsible for it.
one_liner: A quantum-walk proton-transport oracle enables amplitude estimation of distal-range probability but remains too costly for clinical advantage.
why_it_matters: It identifies both a viable scalar target for quantum speedup and the gate-cost bottleneck blocking deployment.

title: Hopfion Superlattices in 3D Twisted Moiré Light Fields
abstract: Moiré superlattices have recently been extended from electronic materials to photonic systems, enabling complex topological light fields such as skyrmion bags. However, these realizations remain confined to two dimensions. Here, we demonstrate 3D moiré superlattices formed by twisting multi-volume spatiotemporal optical lattices, giving rise to previously undiscovered 3D quasiparticle topologies, including hopfion bags, hopfion quasicrystals, and hopfion-hopfionium nested superlattices. By tailoring the interference polarization textures of the moiré spacetime lattices, we achieve controlled topological transitions among these states, and tailored topological numbers of hopfion bags. These spatiotemporal supertopologies offer a promising platform for high-capacity information encoding in higher dimensions.
one_liner: Twisted spatiotemporal optical lattices generate 3D moiré superlattices containing hopfion bags, quasicrystals, and nested topologies.
why_it_matters: Controllable 3D optical topology could support high-capacity information encoding in higher dimensions.

title: Fully GPU-accelerated semistochastic Epstein-Nesbet perturbation theory
abstract: Second-order Epstein-Nesbet perturbation theory (EN-PT2) is an important tool for improving selected configuration interaction (SCI) energies, but the large external determinant space creates substantial memory and communication costs on GPU clusters. We develop a fully GPU-accelerated implementation of distributed semistochastic EN-PT2, fusing excitation generation, screening, and PT2 weighting in a single kernel traversal. Fixed-size random-phase CountSketch arrays limit memory use and replace large external determinant exchange with bounded collective summation. The implementation on one A100 completes EN-PT2 calculations 8.21-37.53 times faster than Arrow on 64 CPU cores at the same requested statistical standard error, and fixed-workload strong-scaling tests achieve 93.5% parallel efficiency on 16 GPUs across two nodes. Applications to an iron-oxo complex in a (60e, 187o) active space, iron-porphyrin references containing 200 million determinants per state, and neural-network quantum states establish the method's efficiency for perturbative corrections to large reference wave functions in the GPU era.
one_liner: A fused GPU implementation of semistochastic EN-PT2 uses CountSketch compression to reduce memory and communication costs.
why_it_matters: It delivers major speedups and strong multi-GPU scaling for corrections to very large quantum wave functions.

title: Revisiting the dispersions and quality factors of nanoshell plasmons
abstract: The dispersions and quality factors of a metallic nanoshell's plasmons may be readily tuned by varying the thickness of the nanoshell. This is because 1. Thickness determines the hybridization between the two nanoshell boundaries and 2. Thickness affects the electronic surface scattering rate and, therefore, the non-radiative decay rates of the plasmonic resonances. We find that prior theoretical works, focused primarily on the thin-nanoshell and retarded regimes, obtained qualitatively incorrect results for both the plasmonic dispersions and the associated plasmonic quality factors. Some of these errors have been pointed out in subsequent works, though the corrected results have not been reported, to our knowledge. Beyond obtaining the correct results (correct dispersions and quality factors as a function of nanoshell thickness), we scrutinize the assumption (used by many prior works) that Matthiessen's rule may be used to combine the effects of bulk and surface-mediated plasmonic scattering processes. To do so, we extend prior work by Dingle to the nanoshell geometry. Although we find qualitative agreement with the Matthiessen's rule approach, we find that Dingle's theory systematically predicts higher quality factors across the range of nanoshell thicknesses we consider.
one_liner: Revised calculations correct nanoshell-plasmon dispersions and quality factors while testing surface-scattering models beyond Matthiessen’s rule.
why_it_matters: Accurate thickness-dependent predictions improve the design and interpretation of metallic nanoshell resonances.

title: An Efficient Quantum Algorithm for Preparing Uniform Superpositions over Arbitrary Integer Intervals
abstract: We consider exact preparation of the uniform quantum state supported on an arbitrary nonempty interval of integer labels in an $n$-qubit register. For every $0\leq a<a+M\leq2^n$, we give an ancilla-free circuit using only one-qubit gates and singly controlled one-qubit gates. In the logical gate model specified in the paper, the direct construction has exact worst-case gate count $5n-9$ for $n\geq3$; its exact maxima for $n=1$ and $n=2$ are $1$ and $3$, respectively. A worst-case lower bound of $Ω(n)$ establishes asymptotic optimality in the register width. In addition, the gate complexity admits an instance-dependent bound $O(\log_2 M+ε)$, where $ε$ is an offset-dependent parameter defined in terms of binary Hamming weights. We also derive a reflected construction and a classical procedure that selects the lower-count exact circuit. The direct construction admits an $O(n)$ logical-depth upper bound. We also treat bitwise-XOR images of intervals and arithmetic progressions with power-of-two spacing.
one_liner: An ancilla-free, asymptotically optimal circuit exactly prepares uniform superpositions over arbitrary integer intervals.
why_it_matters: The construction provides linear worst-case gate count and efficient instance-specific circuits for a common quantum primitive.

title: Overcoming Dynamic Range Limitations in Computational Hyperspectral Imaging
abstract: Computational hyperspectral imaging offers compact spectral sensing, yet imaging high-dynamic-range (HDR) scenes remains challenging. Accurate spectral reconstruction requires encoded measurements to remain within the calibrated linear-response range and above the noise floor. Due to unequal spectral responsivities across the encoding mask, individual channels reach their reliability limits at vastly different incident signal levels. Measurement reliability therefore depends on both exposure time and encoding channel, making it challenging for a single exposure to preserve spectral information in highlights and shadows simultaneously. Here, we demonstrate a physics-guided multi-exposure fusion framework that operates directly in the encoded measurement domain. An analytical reliability prior and learned spatially varying, channel-specific adjustments jointly determine adaptive fusion weights. Measurement-domain spectral-angle supervision further constrains relative channel responses for downstream spectral inversion. The set-wise formulation accommodates varying numbers and configurations of input exposures. We further implement the framework on a 9-channel broadband-encoded stochastic hyperspectral camera, incorporating full-field sensor-response characterization and channel-aware reliability gating. Simulated HDR benchmarks show lower reconstruction errors than representative fusion methods, while controlled spectral measurements and practical HDR scenes confirm improved spectral fidelity and extended usable dynamic range. Measurements using an optical-density target further establish a 16.0-dB increase in spectral reconstruction dynamic range relative to the best fixed single exposure.
one_liner: Physics-guided fusion of multiple encoded exposures improves hyperspectral reconstruction across high-dynamic-range scenes.
why_it_matters: A nine-channel prototype extends spectral reconstruction dynamic range by 16.0 dB over the best fixed exposure.

title: Structural Perturbations and Full Field Evolution in Tapered Spun Ring-Core Fiber Amplifiers
abstract: We theoretically investigate the complex full-vector modal field evolution in tapered spun ring-core fiber amplifiers subject to structural perturbations, utilizing a combined coupled-mode theory and rate-equation model. To provide a comprehensive characterization, we introduce a normalized complex modal-state fidelity factor that simultaneously incorporates intensity, phase and polarization into a single quantitative measure. We demonstrate that the twist pitch of the structure can be purposely tuned to either suppress or leverage the effect of specific geometrical perturbations. These findings provide insight into the physical conditions governing modal stability, establishing a robust mechanism for highly efficient in-fiber OAM mode conversion.
one_liner: A coupled-mode and rate-equation model shows how twist pitch controls perturbation-driven modal evolution in tapered spun ring-core fiber amplifiers.
why_it_matters: Twist engineering could stabilize modes or enable efficient in-fiber orbital-angular-momentum conversion.

title: Time-Varying Photonics: A Review of Theory, Phenomena, and Experimental Platforms
abstract: Time-varying photonics opens new avenues for controlling waves through engineering material properties in time. In this review, we introduce the basic concepts and theoretical tools for describing temporal interfaces, time-periodic systems, and space-time media, as well as review representative experimental approaches across different photonic and wave platforms. We further discuss characteristic phenomena enabled by temporal modulation, including coherent wave control, parametric amplification, nonreciprocity, and topological effects. This review provides a unified pathway for understanding time-varying photonics and outlines its current challenges and future opportunities in both fundamental physics and practical applications.
one_liner: This review unifies the theory, phenomena, and experimental platforms of photonic media whose properties vary in time or space-time.
why_it_matters: It provides a common framework for temporal wave control, amplification, nonreciprocity, and topological photonics.

title: Polynomial Quantum Recurrent Channels for Matrix Inverse Actions: Deferred-Reset Dynamics and Chebyshev Filtering
abstract: We develop completely positive, trace-preserving polynomial recurrent channels for quantum solution-state preparation and derive fixed-point and time-varying tracking bounds. Across 2,880 synthetic configurations, resident Chebyshev recurrence improves accuracy-passing snapshot counts in 608 cases, ties in 2,271, and loses in one. A separate 360-scenario cost study shows that fresh recurrence is cheaper in all 184 jointly feasible scenarios (median resident-to-fresh cost ratio: 3.12), while resident recurrence uniquely satisfies accuracy requirements in 74 cases. At a logical noise rate of $10^-4$, neither recurrent method qualifies. Based on exact reduced-density simulations and assumed cost models, our results demonstrate conditional tracking advantages but no general end-to-end speedup or total-cost benefit.
one_liner: Polynomial recurrent quantum channels with Chebyshev filtering offer conditional tracking gains but no general speedup or cost advantage.
why_it_matters: The results clarify when retained quantum recurrence helps and expose its sensitivity to cost assumptions and logical noise.

title: Assessing the expressive power of a gauge-invariant PEPS ansatz across a topological phase transition
abstract: We investigate the expressive power of the gauged Gaussian fermionic projected entangled pair state (GGFPEPS) ansatz, which is a manifestly gauge-invariant tensor network ansatz for $(2+1)$-dimensional lattice gauge theories. In the GGFPEPS ansatz, the gauge field on each link is represented by coupling its configuration to the fermion number of virtual fermions placed at both ends of the link. This ansatz has been studied by variational Monte Carlo (VMC) methods in previous work~\cite{Emonts:2022yom}. However, the statistical error of VMC makes a precise determination of the variational parameters difficult, so that the expressive power of the ansatz could not be examined accurately. In this work, we reformulate the computation as a Grassmann tensor network (TN), in which the whole network is contracted deterministically, and introduce the higher-order tensor renormalization group (HOTRG), which allows us to perform calculations in large volumes up to $L=34$. We also evaluate the infinite volume system using the corner transfer matrix renormalization group (CTMRG). We find that the ansatz with only eight complex variational parameters accurately describes the pure $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory including the region of the topological phase transition, not only in the energy but also in the topological entanglement entropy. The critical coupling obtained from the peaks of their susceptibilities agrees quantitatively with the one predicted by continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo simulations~\cite{wu2012phase}. Furthermore, near the transition point, we show that the ansatz represents a state outside the plaquette product family, which is a one-parameter family of states assumed in the construction of the ansatz as a simple interpolation between the strong and weak coupling limits.
one_liner: A gauge-invariant PEPS with eight complex parameters accurately captures energy and topological entropy across a Z2 gauge transition.
why_it_matters: It shows that a compact tensor-network ansatz can represent topological critical behavior beyond simple plaquette-product states.

title: Lattice Hamiltonians for Chiral Gauge Theories
abstract: We present a lattice Hamiltonian for chiral gauge theories on the boundary of a slab. The formulation is gauge-fixed, so the gauge variables are the physical modes of the boundary field, and Gauss's law holds exactly. The bulk gauge field is determined by the boundary field and an integer label, which is the topological charge that the boundary generates and the bulk stores as a localized instanton. The bulk enters as a dielectric, and both gauge anomaly conditions become the question of whether the boundary satisfies Gauss's law on its own. For background gauge fields, we show that sectors that differ by a unit of bulk charge are degenerate after Pauli-Villars subtraction and the mirror fermions decouple. The boundary theory has no vacuum angle. Every term in the Hamiltonian is defined in terms of the boundary gauge variables, the integer label and the fermion modes, a starting point for quantum circuit construction.
one_liner: A gauge-fixed boundary Hamiltonian for chiral gauge theories enforces Gauss's law while storing boundary topology as bulk instanton charge.
why_it_matters: The explicit Hamiltonian supplies a potential starting point for quantum-circuit constructions of chiral gauge theories.

title: Reservoir-induced Quantum Phase Transitions in spin ensembles
abstract: In this work, we present a comprehensive analysis of an open quantum system consisting of a collection of N two-level atoms in the thermodynamic limit coupled to bosonic reservoirs. Our results demonstrate that, when the system-bath interactions lacks a metastable minimum, as in the counterterm-free case, the system can undergo a quantum phase transition set by the reservoir structure rather than by coherent internal dynamics. Using exact quantum Langevin equations, valid even in the overdamped regime near criticality, where the loss rates can exceed the resonance frequency of the softening mode, we locate the critical point via the complex excitation spectrum and obtain closed-form reflection and transmission spectra that display the mode softening and an increasingly asymmetric lineshape near the transition.
one_liner: Bosonic reservoirs can drive a spin-ensemble quantum phase transition whose soft mode appears in exact reflection and transmission spectra.
why_it_matters: It identifies bath structure as a source of criticality even in strongly overdamped open quantum systems.

title: Phase transitions and sharp localisation in anomalous localised resonance
abstract: We study how detuning and absorption determine the strength and spatial extent of anomalous localised resonance in a two-dimensional quasistatic coated structure with shell permittivity $-1+c\ell^p+i\ell$, where $\ell>0$ is the loss and $c\ne0$, $p>0$ are fixed. Detuning can carry the material path through narrow resonances, producing intermittent rather than sustained power growth. For an explicit family of noncircular shells and a smooth exterior dipole source, both fixed, we classify the dissipated power under a quantitative smallness condition on the deformation. Depending on the detuning exponent and conformal source distance, the power diverges along the entire path, exhibits divergent peaks with vanishing gaps, or decays, including the threshold cases. We also identify the sharp conformal boundary beyond which the field, normalized by the square root of the dissipated power, converges locally to zero along every divergent-power sequence. For resonant sources, tangential reference crossings yield an explicit nonzero limit for the exterior gradient energy divided by the dissipated power at the critical radius.
one_liner: Detuning, loss, and source distance produce distinct divergence, intermittent-resonance, and decay regimes in anomalous localized resonance.
why_it_matters: The analysis establishes sharp spatial and parameter thresholds for resonance and field localization in coated structures.

title: Multiparameter quantum estimation of circulant networks
abstract: Networks provide a natural description of interaction patterns, transport media, and communication architectures. Accurately characterizing their coupling structure is a key challenge in quantum technologies. We investigate the multiparameter quantum estimation of coupling strengths in circulant networks probed by continuous-time quantum walks. We derive the quantum Fisher information matrix, identify the optimal probe states and determine the ultimate precision allowed by quantum measurements, together with its scaling with the number of unknown couplings. We further analyze the precision achievable through position measurements of the walker, comparing the corresponding classical Cramér-Rao bounds for optimal and localized probe states with the quantum limit. Finally, we consider finite-resolution detection modeled by coarse-grained position measurements. Although coarse graining generally reduces estimation precision, we find that lower-resolution measurements can, in some instances, outperform other measurements with finer spatial resolution. Our results provide a systematic characterization of the fundamental and practical limits of coupling estimation in quantum-walk-based network inference.
one_liner: Quantum Fisher analysis establishes optimal probes and precision limits for estimating multiple couplings in circulant quantum-walk networks.
why_it_matters: It quantifies practical network-inference limits and shows that coarse detection can sometimes beat finer measurements.

title: Pool-free, residual-triggered ansatz growth for variational imaginary-time evolution: when a fixed operator order beats adaptive screening
abstract: Adaptive variational algorithms such as ADAPT-VQE and AVQITE screen an operator pool at every growth step, and ADAPT-VQE also re-optimizes all parameters. We study a pool-free alternative for variational imaginary-time evolution (VITE). The layers are fixed in advance by nested commutators of the Hamiltonian, grouped by symmetry and particle number, and the next layer is appended when the relative McLachlan residual exceeds a threshold. On five non-integrable systems (the mixed-field Ising chain and tori, and stretched H$_4$), this dynamic VITE reaches a relative error of $10^{-4}$ with 1.6-5.4 times fewer circuits than the cheapest of six to eight adaptive variants, including single-Pauli-string and qubit-excitation pools and batched ADAPT-VQE. On the chain the advantage persists from 8 to 16 sites. Screening and re-optimization account for most of the adaptive methods' cost. On the spin models, a longitudinal-field scan shows that the advantage requires broken integrability, which makes adaptive screening expensive. The advantage is lost on transverse-field Ising models, at tight targets (relative error $10^{-6}$) and where the schedule front-loads weak layers.
one_liner: Residual-triggered VITE with fixed commutator layers uses 1.6–5.4 times fewer circuits than tested adaptive methods on selected systems.
why_it_matters: Avoiding repeated operator screening and re-optimization can substantially reduce variational simulation costs in suitable regimes.

title: Normalizing Flows for Classical Simulation of Quantum Circuits in Phase Space
abstract: We present a novel framework to learn a representation of quantum circuits based on the phase space formulation of many-body systems. Given that $N$-qubit states can be represented as probability distributions on a smooth $2N$-dimensional manifold, we show how unitary gates can be parameterized as normalizing flows between these distributions, opening a new avenue for quantum circuit simulation using generative models. We evaluate our method on three common families of quantum circuits, and show that its accuracy exceeds that of current state-of-the-art neural network methods for large system sizes.
one_liner: Normalizing flows learn phase-space probability transformations for unitary gates and improve large-circuit simulation accuracy.
why_it_matters: The framework offers a generative-model route to classical simulation of many-qubit quantum circuits.

title: PINNverse meets Jordan--Wigner: learning the Hamiltonian of long spin chains
abstract: Inverse physics-informed neural networks (PINNverse) learn the parameters of a quantum Hamiltonian from measured expectation values, but the network output grows as $4^N$ with the number of qubits $N$. We show that, for spin chains with nearest-neighbor exchange interactions, the Jordan-Wigner transformation removes this exponential cost: the dynamics closes on an $N\times N$ one-body density matrix, so the network needs only $N^2$ outputs and the data are local observables measured in five global settings. Parasitic $ZZ$ couplings (crosstalk) are included through a time-dependent Hartree--Fock closure. With synthetic data, the same network first solves the equation of motion and then recovers the Hamiltonian parameters of chains of up to $50$ qubits, with couplings learned to better than $0.1\%$. Errors in the local frequencies of long chains are removed by a direct least-squares fit started from the network estimate.
one_liner: Jordan–Wigner reduction lets inverse PINNs learn nearest-neighbor spin-chain Hamiltonians with N² outputs instead of exponential scaling.
why_it_matters: Synthetic tests recover couplings within 0.1% for chains up to 50 qubits using local data from five global settings.

title: An Alignment Microscope for Imaging Rotational Wavepacket Dynamics
abstract: We introduce a new method for encoding polarization-angle-dependent molecular alignment signals directly into the transverse spatial profile of a femtosecond laser beam. The approach employs a pump-probe setup in a common-path geometry. A radial-azimuthal polarization converter placed in the probe beam produces a doughnut-shaped beam whose local polarization varies continuously with azimuthal angle, thereby encoding the full range of linear polarization orientations from 0 to $2π$ within a single transverse beam profile. Consequently, the angular dependence of the molecular response can be recorded simultaneously rather than reconstructed through sequential measurements at different polarization angles. By varying only the pump-probe delay, this spatial encoding enables single-shot acquisition of the complete angular response at each delay and real-time visualization of the evolving molecular alignment pattern as the delay stage is scanned. This technique has enabled the experimental realization of an alignment microscope.
one_liner: A structured-polarization probe maps every linear polarization angle onto one beam profile for single-shot molecular-alignment imaging.
why_it_matters: The common-path method enables real-time visualization of rotational wavepacket dynamics without sequential angle scans.

title: Two atoms with strong light-induced dipolar interactions
abstract: We study how two atoms scatter light when they are closer than an optical wavelength and observe multiple new phenomena due to the strong interactions between laser-induced electric dipole moments. We identify a narrow range of densities where a fraction of the scattered light is coherent and shows a collective enhancement factor of two compared to independent atoms. The dynamics of the two-atom wavefunction can be observed through momentum distributions which reveal resonant ejection and depletion. Due to the tight confinement, the total fluorescence intensity strongly depends on the scattering length, since it originates from a narrow resonant (Franck-Condon) region. Furthermore, we measure how the probe laser intensity modifies the scattering length, which establishes a new way to shift Feshbach resonances. Our work provides microscopic insight into what occurs during photoassociation and parity projection in optical tweezers.
one_liner: Two tightly confined atoms exhibit enhanced coherent scattering, resonant ejection, and laser-controlled shifts of their scattering length.
why_it_matters: The results clarify microscopic photoassociation and parity-projection dynamics while suggesting optical control of Feshbach resonances.

title: Memory of Initial States in Long-Time Dynamics Revealed by Non-Gaussianity
abstract: In quantum dynamics of few-body observables in quadratic systems, information about the initial state is retained in long-time averages, as captured by the generalized Gibbs ensemble. Here, we show that this memory extends beyond the averages to temporal fluctuations around them. By generating a manifold of non-Gaussian initial states and quantifying their non-Gaussianity via the corresponding entropy, we find that the magnitude of temporal fluctuations is a smooth function of the initial-state non-Gaussianity. This relation explains the qualitatively different scaling of fluctuations observed after quantum quenches: exponentially small fluctuations for non-Gaussian initial states and polynomially small fluctuations for Gaussian initial states. Therefore, our results identify non-Gaussianity as a key to uncovering initial-state memory beyond long-time averages.
one_liner: Temporal fluctuations in quadratic quantum systems retain a smooth, measurable dependence on the initial state's non-Gaussianity.
why_it_matters: Non-Gaussianity explains distinct fluctuation scaling and reveals initial-state memory beyond generalized Gibbs ensemble averages.

title: SGAA: Independent active alignment of optical subgroups with uncompensated aberrations
abstract: Uncompensated subgroup aberrations complicate subgroup-level active alignment (AA), as local image-quality extrema do not directly indicate the target alignment state. We propose SGAA, an image-learning-based method for independent active alignment of optical subgroups. Multi-field point spread functions (PSFs) from a dedicated test configuration characterize misalignment, while golden-sample reference calibration and unified regression predict adjustments toward a common optical target across toleranced specimens. In simulations with tolerances, one step reduced the mean differential wavefront RMS from $0.0592λ$ to $0.0086λ$, an 85.4% reduction. In alignment experiments on 100 production subgroups, SGAA increased the mean full-lens weighted modulation transfer function (WMTF) at 30, 50, and 80 lp/mm by 0.073, 0.065, and 0.040, respectively, relative to industrial MTF-based scanning. The 8 MP acceptance yield increased by 29.2 percentage points, and mean alignment time decreased from 43 s to 3.1 s. SGAA thus translates independent subgroup reference-state restoration into gains in full-lens imaging, acceptance yield, and alignment speed.
one_liner: SGAA learns subgroup misalignment from multi-field PSFs, improving lens quality and yield while cutting alignment time from 43 to 3.1 seconds.
why_it_matters: It enables rapid, independent alignment of production optics even when uncompensated aberrations obscure conventional quality extrema.

title: Physics-informed Bayesian optimization of high-order harmonic generation in gases
abstract: Optimization of high-order harmonic generation in gases is essential for attosecond science. Improving conversion efficiency from the infrared driving laser to the extreme-ultraviolet high-order harmonic radiation requires balancing microscopic single-atom dipole responses with macroscopic phase matching. The resulting conversion-efficiency landscape exhibits complex structures, such as the hyperbolic ridge in the pressure-length space, which can be difficult to accurately reconstruct using conventional Bayesian optimization. Here, we introduce a physics-informed Bayesian optimization framework that incorporates known physical scaling relations through nonlinear transformations of the search space. We first demonstrate the approach in the two-dimensional pressure-length space, where a direct grid scan enables detailed validation of the reconstructed landscape, before extending it to four dimensions, where exhaustive scanning becomes computationally impractical. In four dimensions, incorporating the pulse-duration scaling and a square-root transformation of conversion efficiency further improves the accuracy of the reconstructed landscape, as validated against an independent reference dataset. We also employ a threshold-based acquisition strategy to identify extended high-efficiency operating regions rather than isolated optimal points. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating physical knowledge into Bayesian optimization improves the exploration and reconstruction of multidimensional high-order harmonic generation landscapes, extending its capabilities beyond locating individual optima.
one_liner: Physics-informed transformations improve Bayesian reconstruction of multidimensional high-order harmonic generation efficiency landscapes.
why_it_matters: The method locates broad efficient operating regions with fewer evaluations, supporting practical optimization of attosecond light sources.

title: Exponential Control of Adiabatic Time Reflection by Complex-Time Singularities
abstract: Nearly identical temporal switching profiles can produce very different reflections even when both have small local adiabatic measures. In a lossless dielectric, we obtain this difference by adding a weak feature that changes the complex-time singularities while preserving monotonicity, endpoints, and central slope. A perturbation bounded by $0.6\%$ of the total inverse-permittivity change raises the reflected mode amplitude from $8.02\times10^{-10}$ to $1.28\times10^{-3}$. The complex action and pole residue predict this amplitude to within $0.32\%$. Within this waveform family, deviation and monotonicity constraints select three design regimes. At fixed deviation bound, reoptimization keeps the central feature's time scale comparable to the inverse incident angular frequency. The optimal amplitude is then proportional to $1/T$ as the switching time $T$ tends to infinity. Stretching a fixed profile gives exponential suppression. Full-wave Maxwell simulations resolve the backward packet, and filtering calculations quantify its sensitivity to modulation bandwidth.
one_liner: Tiny waveform changes that alter complex-time singularities can increase adiabatic time-reflection amplitude by more than six orders of magnitude.
why_it_matters: Complex singularities provide a predictive design principle for controlling temporal reflections beyond local adiabatic measures.

title: Coherent-Dissipative Crossover of Quantum Synchronization
abstract: Quantum synchronization in open systems can arise from both coherent interactions and collective dissipation, yet their interplay remains poorly understood. Here we develop a general framework for two quantum oscillators coupled through a fast mediator. Adiabatic elimination reveals two distinct synchronization channels, coherent exchange and collective dissipation, and yields an analytical description connecting dissipation and coherence-dominated regimes. We show that synchronization is governed by the joint balance of coherent coupling, dissipation, and reservoir-induced fluctuations, rather than by coherent coupling alone. Continuous monitoring of the shared output further converts reservoir information into a resource, substantially enhancing conditional synchronization, with the strongest gain near the coherent-dissipative crossover. These results establish a general mechanism for coherent-dissipative quantum synchronization and its measurement-enabled control in open quantum systems.
one_liner: A fast mediator produces coherent and dissipative synchronization channels whose crossover is strongly enhanced by continuous monitoring.
why_it_matters: The framework shows how reservoir information can become a resource for controlling synchronization in open quantum systems.

title: Multiparticle entanglement in a time-dependent electron--ion--photon system
abstract: Photoionization provides a natural setting for entanglement transfer in the time domain: an outgoing electron can become entangled with the residual ion, while subsequent spontaneous emission may transfer these correlations to an emitted photon. We quantify the entanglement dynamics of the composite electron--ion--photon system using the von Neumann entropy of the one-versus-rest bipartitions, showing that the initially entangled electron--ion system evolves through a genuinely multiparticle-entangled state before approaching an entangled electron--photon state. Logarithmic negativity further resolves the pairwise entanglement, revealing in particular transient ion--photon entanglement. Further, its enhanced sensitivity to weakly populated Schmidt modes additionally exposes high-dimensional entanglement associated with the photon-energy continuum.
one_liner: Photoionization and emission transfer entanglement from an electron-ion pair through a tripartite state to an electron-photon pair.
why_it_matters: The analysis resolves transient ion-photon correlations and high-dimensional entanglement across the photon-energy continuum.

title: Quantum Advantage in Assisted Work Distillation from Complementary Correlations
abstract: We establish an operational bridge between microscale thermodynamic work extraction and the foundational characterization of nonclassical correlations in bipartite quantum systems. Within the resource theory of thermal operations, we analyze a generalized framework of assisted work distillation where the trusted receiver's system is divided into separate, independent particle storage pools. We demonstrate that concurrent information-theoretic correlations measured across sets of mutually unbiased bases act as an explicit, quantifiable energy resource for local work extraction. Based on this paradigm, we derive a novel class of work-based Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen steering inequalities whose violations certify a one-sided device-independent quantum thermodynamic enhancement. Furthermore, by restricting the dimension of the untrusted party under a one-sided semi-device-independent trust framework, we introduce dynamically scaling work inequalities capable of witnessing superunsteerability. This allows us to activate and certify the hidden thermodynamic utility of weakly correlated entangled states that are otherwise completely invisible in standard, unconstrained scenarios.
one_liner: Complementary correlations across mutually unbiased bases provide a quantifiable resource for assisted local work extraction.
why_it_matters: Work-based steering inequalities certify thermodynamic quantum advantage and expose hidden utility in weakly correlated states.

title: Quantum-Informed Graph Decomposition
abstract: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a near-term quantum algorithm for solving combinatorial optimization problems, but its accuracy and resource requirements may scale poorly with problem size or structure, reducing its utility in practice. Approaches such as the Graph Decomposition for Optimization Algorithm (GDOA) seek to address this by iteratively reducing an input problem until it reaches a size where it can be solved using QAOA while maintaining the same optimal solution. This algorithm, however, requires solving integer programs that have exponentially many variables, and can result in suboptimal solutions, as the integer programs may contain slack terms. In this work, we propose a heuristic called the Quantum Enhanced Graph Decomposition (QEGD) algorithm. Its novelty lies in its use of QAOA as a subroutine for sparsifying a graph through local vertex-merging. The algorithm, when used to sparsify MaxCut problems that are then solved using QAOA, achieves higher approximation ratios across all tested graphs than GDOA for random 5-regular and 6-regular graphs. We then compare the time-to-solution and approximation ratio of QEGD to other QAOA variants a collection of Erdös-Rényi graphs. QEGD has higher approximation ratios on average than QAOA$^2$ and ParaQAOA on all tested graphs. It also results in higher average approximation ratios than DC-QAOA on sparse Erdös-Rényi graphs and comparable average approximation ratio on denser Erdös-Rényi graphs. However, its average wall-clock time is between 0.4\% and 5\% of the average DC-QAOA wall-clock time.
one_liner: QEGD uses QAOA-guided local vertex merging to sparsify MaxCut graphs before solving the reduced optimization problem.
why_it_matters: Tests show competitive or higher approximation ratios than several QAOA variants with substantially lower time than DC-QAOA.

title: Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization for Bounded-Payoff Imperfect-Information Games
abstract: Imperfect-information games with a graded-reward structure present significant computational challenges for equilibrium computation, since the payoff expectations must be estimated across exponentially large strategy spaces. Counterfactual Regret Minimization over the years has proven effective for approximating Nash equilibria, but Monte Carlo variants create a large overhead of sampling costs when the counterfactual values are estimated from sampled game-tree trajectories. We propose a novel Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization, a framework that uses Quantum Amplitude Estimation to reduce the computational complexity of the regret updates in bounded-payoff imperfect-information games, while preserving the convergence of its classical counterpart. We give a theoretical analysis of the resulting exploitability bound, discuss NISQ-compatible amplitude-estimation variants, the structure of their resource requirements, and outline what is needed to validate the potential advantage empirically.
one_liner: Quantum amplitude estimation accelerates counterfactual-value estimation in regret minimization for bounded-payoff imperfect-information games.
why_it_matters: The framework offers a potential quantum reduction in sampling costs while retaining classical convergence guarantees.

title: Low-energy spectral-window truncation for compact U(1) lattice gauge theory
abstract: We prove a nonasymptotic electric-flux truncation bound for the entire vacuum-relative low-energy window of the original pure compact $U(1)$ lattice Hamiltonian. On a three-dimensional periodic cubic lattice with $N\geq3$ sites per direction at $θ=0$, in the gauge-invariant zero-global-flux sector, the factorial-squared tail-norm estimate holds for every normalized vector in the window, without physical eigenvalue-isolation, window-edge gap, or nondegeneracy assumptions and without a window-dimension factor. It controls finite-time hard-wall evolution from the normalized projection of the same initial state. An analytic finite-volume strong-coupling example in this model certifies a nonvacuum band and an order-one plaquette signal change preserved by a specified finite cutoff. The same estimate yields precision-dependent sufficient cutoffs, an alternative linear isometric encoding by polar decomposition for reference-entangled inputs, and local electric-square readout bounds. At fixed positive bare coupling, physical volume, window width, and duration, cutoffs scaling as $β\log N/\log\log N$ with $β>2$ make state and bounded-readout truncation errors vanish under lattice refinement.
one_liner: A nonasymptotic bound controls electric-flux truncation across an entire low-energy window of compact U(1) lattice gauge theory.
why_it_matters: It supplies rigorous cutoff and encoding guarantees for finite-dimensional quantum simulations without spectral-gap assumptions.

title: Disorder-Induced Logarithmic Spreading and Localization of Quantum Fluctuations
abstract: Disorder can localize quantum particles, even in the presence of interactions, but its influence on quantum fluctuations beyond mean--field dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the propagation of quantum fluctuations in weakly interacting disordered bosonic systems by comparing the Bose--Hubbard model with the Gross--Pitaevskii equation. We find that, in contrast to ballistic spreading in the disorder--free system, quantum fluctuations exhibit logarithmic spreading at intermediate times under both random and quasiperiodic disorder, before eventually saturating. The spreading rate decreases algebraically with increasing disorder strength, and this behavior persists across different particle numbers and extends to two dimensions. Using a time--dependent Bogoliubov--de Gennes framework, we identify the localized mean--field wavefunction as a time--dependent pairing background that generates quantum fluctuations. The exponential suppression of fluctuation--generation rates with distance provides a physical mechanism for the logarithmically advancing fluctuation front. Our results reveal a distinct regime of disorder--controlled quantum--fluctuation dynamics and establish disorder as a means of controlling their spreading.
one_liner: Disorder makes quantum fluctuations spread logarithmically before localization in weakly interacting bosonic systems.
why_it_matters: The identified pairing mechanism explains the slow fluctuation front and suggests disorder as a control knob for quantum dynamics.

title: Intracycle Interference in Strong-Field Photoemission from a Tungsten Needle Tip
abstract: Electrons photoemitted by strong laser fields can rescatter, generating attosecond high harmonics. Spectral peaks arise from inter- and intracycle interference of coherent electron wave packets. While intercycle interference is well known, intracycle interference of plateau electrons has not been observed. We present carrier-envelope phase-resolved photoemission spectra from a nanometric tungsten needle tip driven at 1570 nm revealing such interference, supported by quantum orbit and TDSE simulations that elucidate attosecond-scale electron dynamics.
one_liner: CEP-resolved photoemission from a tungsten nanotip reveals intracycle interference among strong-field plateau electrons.
why_it_matters: The observation provides attosecond-scale insight into coherent electron motion and rescattering at nanostructures.

title: Classical phase unwrapping enables large-time-step unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization
abstract: For computing molecular energies on early fault-tolerant hardware, unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization (UQKSD) avoids both the deep circuits of quantum phase estimation and the Pauli-term sampling of variational methods by extracting the energies from a projected real-time propagator. At a small time step $τ$, nearly linearly dependent Krylov vectors make the overlap matrix ill-conditioned. Our tests at fixed total evolution time show that additional Krylov vectors then add no accuracy, while the thresholded energy becomes increasingly sensitive to the choice of cutoff. A larger time step improves the conditioning and reduces the Krylov dimension $M$ needed for a target accuracy, but the energies are then known only modulo $2π/τ$. We present Classical Unwrapping for Resolving Eigenvalues (CURE-QKSD), a classical post-processing method that leaves the UQKSD circuits and generalized eigenvalue problem unchanged and recovers the missing multiples of $2π/τ$ from phase-consistency landscapes of one or, when needed, two UQKSD runs. In noiseless tests on six molecules with 12--20 qubits, all 28 targeted energies are recovered in their aliased regimes with final errors of at most $1.1\times10^{-7}$~Ha. Under Gaussian noise with $σ=10^{-4}$, the median error of the ground or first excited state reaches chemical accuracy at large aliased time steps with $M=20$--$65$, whereas uncorrected principal-branch energies are off by $0.7$--$115$~Ha. CURE-QKSD therefore makes aliased time steps usable for UQKSD calculations with smaller, better-conditioned Krylov bases.
one_liner: CURE-QKSD classically unwraps aliased eigenphases, enabling UQKSD with larger time steps and better-conditioned Krylov bases.
why_it_matters: It reduces Krylov dimensions while recovering molecular energies accurately without changing the quantum circuits.

title: Edge quantum weight of finite Chern flakes and its topological floor
abstract: The zero-point energy of an $LC$ circuit measures the polarization fluctuation of an insulator coupled to it. In a crystal this fluctuation is the bulk quantum weight $K_{\rm bulk}$, which the Chern number $C$ bounds below by $|C|$. We show that a finite Chern flake adds an edge term that survives as the flake grows. The low-frequency transitions of its chiral edge have squared dipole matrix elements that sum to an edge weight $K_{\rm edge}\ge |C|$ per unit area, a floor that follows from the positive absorption of both circular polarizations and the known cancellation of circular dichroism between edge and bulk. At weak coupling, which a growing flake eventually leaves, a circuit slower than the edge modes reads $K_{\rm bulk}+K_{\rm edge}$, averaged over two field directions, and a faster one approaches $K_{\rm bulk}$, so the reading depends on whether the flake is made large or the circuit slow first. In exact free-fermion calculations on lattice flakes with $|C|=1$ and 2 the summed circular dichroism of the edge sector extrapolates to $|C|$ in magnitude, so that the floor is $|C|$. Above the floor, each edge channel adds a number fixed by the boundary shape and its edge velocities, which square and rectangular lattice flakes with one channel follow to within 0.003, while the circular dichroism counts only the net chirality. The avoided crossing of the circuit with the edge mode gives the edge weight in units of the Hall conductance quantum, up to a geometric factor of the capacitor.
one_liner: Finite Chern flakes carry a persistent edge quantum weight with a topological lower bound of |C| per unit area.
why_it_matters: It shows how chiral edges alter circuit measurements of polarization fluctuations and expose topology.

title: Nonreciprocal Josephson Dynamics of a $\mathcal{PT}$-Symmetric Atomtronic SQUID
abstract: We investigate non-Hermitian Josephson dynamics in an atomtronic quantum interference device (AQUID), formed by a ring Bose Einstein condensate with balanced atomic gain and loss regions and two moving optical barriers. The balanced gain and loss profile establishes a parity time symmetric potential while breaking spatial inversion symmetry, providing the essential ingredients for nonreciprocal Josephson transport. The dynamics are monitored nondestructively through the phase quadrature spectrum of an optomechanical cavity driven by Laguerre Gaussian beams coupled to the condensate. We demonstrate that increasing the local gain and loss strength softens the parity time symmetric collective mode towards an exceptional point, as verified by Bogoliubov de Gennes analysis. The associated coherent population exchange produces an additional characteristic splitting in the cavity output spectrum. For linearly translating barriers, non-Hermiticity provides an additional control parameter for tuning the critical current. When the barriers undergo simultaneous translation and rotation, the rotation induced phase modifies the interference between counter propagating currents, offering further control over the nonreciprocal response. Under periodic barrier modulation, we find more pronounced Shapiro steps in the current voltage characteristics due to the intrinsic parity time symmetric collective mode. Finally, we propose an alternative Hermitian realization using a tilted optical lattice, providing an experimentally accessible route to engineering biased transport and population transfer. Our results establish parity time symmetric atomtronic SQUIDs as a versatile platform for controlling nonreciprocal Josephson transport and collective excitations in driven quantum fluids.
one_liner: A PT-symmetric atomtronic SQUID uses balanced gain and loss to tune nonreciprocal Josephson transport and collective modes.
why_it_matters: The scheme offers controllable biased transport, enhanced Shapiro steps, and nondestructive cavity-based readout.

title: Tidal potential measured with distant optical clocks
abstract: Fibre-linked optical clocks sense tidal changes of the gravitational potential, but separating overlapping tidal components and quantifying their precision remain challenging. Using strontium and ytterbium clocks 692 km apart, we measure over 353 days a response of 0.95 (0.11) to the combined solid-Earth and ocean-loading tide and 1.01 (0.13) for the lunar semidiurnal group, and separate the lunar and solar-frequency semidiurnal contributions. A signal-to-noise model based on the actual sampling accounts for the lunar precision and guides future clock-network observations.
one_liner: Strontium and ytterbium clocks linked across 692 km resolve solid-Earth, ocean-loading, lunar, and solar tidal signals.
why_it_matters: The 353-day measurement demonstrates long-baseline optical-clock networks as probes of tidal gravitational potential.

title: Reading long-range information from a separable quantum record requires entangled measurements
abstract: Qubit probes record the relative orientation of neighboring, initially uncorrelated Ising spins through local interactions. Each probe encodes one bond label in two states with overlap $1-p$. The resulting probe record is fully separable. A receiver gets one copy and guesses whether two distant spins point in the same or opposite directions. On the square lattice, the best readout with separable measurement effects approaches success probability $1/2$ as the spin separation grows, for $0<p\le p_0=1-1/\sqrt2$. This includes all local operations with classical communication. The same conclusion holds for every measurement whose effects remain positive under partial transposition across every cut of the probes. For $p_*=0.29181\le p\le1$, a joint readout of the same record maintains a success probability above $1/2$ by a positive amount independent of distance. The overlap $[p_*,p_0]$ gives a strict separation between the readouts. A record that is created locally and contains no entanglement can therefore hold long-range information that only measurements with entangled effects can read.
one_liner: A separable probe record can encode long-range spin information that remains accessible only to entangled measurements.
why_it_matters: It separates information stored without entanglement from the nonlocal measurement resources required to retrieve it.

title: Error Resilience and Unitary 2-Designs
abstract: Encoding-error-decoding circuits provide a setting for studying protection of quantum information against errors. In these circuits, an encoding unitary is followed by an error layer, decoding by the inverse unitary, and ancilla postselection. For encoders drawn from unitary 2-design ensembles, these circuits exhibit an error-protecting phase below a threshold error strength in which the fidelity between the input and recovered logical states approaches unity. Here, we show how departures from Haar second-moment statistics of the encoder can destabilize the error-protecting phase and derive a universal inequality linking recovery fidelity to the second unitary frame potential, which quantifies the ensemble's proximity to a unitary 2-design. This connection is exemplified by matchgate circuits doped with a tunable number of non-Gaussian gates. We analytically show that undoped circuits lack a stable error-protecting phase in the thermodynamic limit and that increasing the doping restores the error protection mechanism as the encoder ensemble approaches an approximate unitary 2-design. Further examples of Hamiltonian encoders, including an experimentally motivated all-to-all spin model, follow the same mechanism. Our results identify recovery fidelity as a diagnostic of departures from unitary 2-design behavior in quantum many-body systems.
one_liner: Recovery fidelity is bounded by the encoder's second frame potential, linking error resilience to approximate unitary 2-designs.
why_it_matters: It identifies ensemble randomness and non-Gaussian doping as key ingredients for stable quantum error protection.

title: A New Computational Model for the Spin-Free Sum-of-Squares Energy Bounds of Electronic Hamiltonian
abstract: Optimizing spin-free sum-of-squares (SOS) energy bounds for electronic Hamiltonians leads to semidefinite programs whose expanded size grows rapidly with the orbital dimension. We derive an exact reformulation of an established spin-free SOS model as a convex quadratic problem over a single symmetric matrix constrained between zero and the identity. Explicit recovery maps connect feasible quadratic-program iterates to certificates in the original SOS formulation, and identify the Frank--Wolfe gap with the separation between recovered primal and dual objectives. We implement the quadratic action through GPU-accelerated Coulomb contractions and solve the reformulated problem using a cached implementation of fully corrective Frank--Wolfe, referred to here as the dimension-reduced simplicial method (DRSM) that caches operator products and optimizes convex-combination weights in a small corrective quadratic program. Numerical experiments cover 65 FCIDUMP models, molecular geometries, and regular hydrogen rings, including original-coordinate recovery checks on nine instances and comparisons with FISTA and a boundary-point SDP solver. On eight H100 GPUs, a cold-start calculation for C$_{720}$ with 10,080 spatial orbitals reaches a freshly recomputed Frank--Wolfe gap of $8.82\times10^{-9}$ hartree in 5.02 hours. Full-space hydrogen-ring calculations reach 10,000 orbitals, with cyclic reduction providing further computational savings. These results show how exact reformulation, data structure exploitation and reuse of Coulomb actions make optimization of the selected large-scale SOS relaxation practical.
one_liner: An exact dimension-reduced quadratic reformulation makes large spin-free sum-of-squares energy bounds GPU-tractable.
why_it_matters: The method scales certified electronic-energy optimization to systems with roughly 10,000 spatial orbitals.

title: Invariance can prevent overfitting and shortcut learning in Quantum Neural Networks
abstract: Many image classification tasks have labels that are unchanged by rotations and reflections. Equivariant quantum neural networks incorporate such symmetries by design, but the specific benefit of symmetry is difficult to isolate. Equivariant quantum circuits are usually compared with architectures that also differ in gates, structure or size. Here, we investigate the role of invariance in a controlled setting, classifying images whose labels are invariant under the dihedral group $D_4$. We compare four eight-qubit models with identical encoding, circuit structure and number of trainable parameters, and equivalent dynamical Lie algebras, and benchmark invariant implementations against non-invariant ones in terms of generalization error, robustness to shortcut learning and resilience to a realistic noise model. On four binary tasks, including MNIST and two scientific data sets of galaxies and red blood cells, the invariant models trained on a few tens of images show better generalization than non-invariant ones. Invariance also makes the models immune to orientation shortcuts: when trained with a class-dependent corner watermark, the non-invariant models learn the watermark and often drop to chance level when it is moved. We show that the gain in accuracy of invariant models persists also under a realistic noise model.
one_liner: Symmetry-invariant quantum neural networks generalize better and resist orientation shortcuts across image-classification tasks.
why_it_matters: Controlled comparisons isolate invariance as a practical defense against overfitting, shortcut learning, and realistic noise.

title: Operational limits of reference renewal for retained quantum-service results
abstract: We implement reference renewal to reconsider retained physical quantum-service results under a prespecified protocol. Twelve transitions retained six results each; ten completed renewal, eight met the prespecified endpoint, and five succeeded using retained results alone. The exact one-sided p=0.0546875 does not establish the recovery hypothesis. Incomplete references, binding failures and sequential waits expose operational limits. Offline reconstruction recovers decisions from preserved counts. Retrospective binding-plus-oracle checking accepts all 60 usable-transition results without renewal. With the exact oracle also supplying calibration scores, the study does not demonstrate incremental numerical-correctness utility of renewal.
one_liner: A reference-renewal study exposes binding, completeness, and waiting limits when reassessing retained quantum-service results.
why_it_matters: Its inconclusive recovery test and successful offline reconstruction clarify where renewal adds little correctness value.

title: Simulating closed- and open-system dynamics of Tavis--Cummings lattices on fault-tolerant quantum computers
abstract: Tavis--Cummings lattices couple cavities containing several emitters and host polaritonic many-body dynamics whose real-time correlations are costly to compute classically in two dimensions, especially when unequal emitter relaxation or dephasing rates break permutation symmetry. We analyze logical resources for fault-tolerant closed- and open-system simulation of an atom-resolved lattice with $L$ cavities, $N$ emitters per cavity, and photon cutoff $n\_{\max}$, including target observable estimation. Building on ladder-operator block encoding, we construct circuits for photon hopping and local light--matter exchange and combine them to encode the lattice Hamiltonian. By updating source and destination photon occupations in place, the hopping circuit eliminates the auxiliary $L\lceil\log_2(n\_{\max}+1)\rceil$-qubit photon register used by two-register implementations. Across three uniform-coefficient examples with $16$ to $256$ cavities, the controlled walk uses $4.75$--$8.11%$ fewer Toffoli gates than the paired two-register implementation under matched shared preparation, precision, control, and workspace conventions. For closed systems, we implement real-time evolution with generalized quantum signal processing and bound the cost of estimating retarded cavity spectral functions. For open systems with photon loss, emitter relaxation, and dephasing, we use a sampled first-order dilation and bound the runs and timesteps needed to estimate transient photon statistics such as $g^{(2)}(0)$. With state-preparation and measurement costs explicit, these estimates provide a reference for assessing fault-tolerant light--matter lattice simulation costs.
one_liner: Fault-tolerant resource estimates cover closed and open dynamics of atom-resolved Tavis-Cummings lattices.
why_it_matters: An in-place photon-hopping circuit lowers Toffoli costs and supports realistic estimates for light-matter observables.

title: The energetic cost of loading classical data in quantum computers
abstract: Quantum algorithms for machine learning, chemistry, and cryptanalysis often assume coherent access to classical data at negligible physical cost. We instead treat data loading as a hardware process and quantify the dynamic energetic cost of a quantum random access memory (QRAM) query on a superconducting processor. Using the metric-noise-resource framework, we relate query fidelity and power to gate duration, relative two-qubit drive strength, and the distribution of attenuation across a multi-stage refrigerator, while accounting for thermal photons and gate errors. We analyze the linear-depth multiplexer and the noise-resilient bucket-brigade architectures, adapting the latter to a native superconducting gate set and refining its fidelity analysis using the fully decomposed gate schedule. For a representative bucket-brigade QRAM query with a $12$-qubit address register we obtain a query fidelity of $0.969$. The query consumes $3.51\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{J}$ of dynamic energy, corresponding to an average dynamic power of $4.38\,\mathrm{W}$ and a peak of $64.4\,\mathrm{W}$. Our optimization shows that, at fixed target fidelity, the operating point and attenuation profile can change the average power by a factor of two or more.
one_liner: A hardware-level analysis quantifies the fidelity, energy, and power required for superconducting QRAM data loading.
why_it_matters: It shows that refrigeration and control choices can change QRAM power by over twofold at fixed fidelity.

title: Angle-Resolved Reflectance Measurements in the Vacuum Ultraviolet for Metallic Samples
abstract: The light yield of noble-element scintillation detectors depends strongly on the reflective properties of detector materials in the vacuum ultraviolet (VUV), where optical measurements are scarce. For this reason, we built a custom rotary setup at IFIC, equipped with a monochromator and operated in a gaseous argon atmosphere, to perform angle-resolved reflectance measurements in the specular reflection plane. We describe the setup and its extensive characterization, together with the procedure used to measure the bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) of materials at various angles of incidence, for wavelengths from 128 to 500 nm, covering both the argon (128 nm) and xenon (175 nm) scintillation wavelengths. To illustrate the capabilities of the setup, we present results for rough aluminum and stainless-steel surfaces as reference materials. Fitting the measured angular profiles with the analytical GGX microfacet model allows us to extract the real and imaginary parts of the refractive index and the surface roughness parameter of each sample. These parameters are then used to extrapolate the in-plane measurements to the full hemisphere and from gaseous argon to liquid media, enabling the inference of the hemispherical reflectance in gaseous argon, liquid argon and liquid xenon.
one_liner: A custom rotary setup measures angle-resolved VUV reflectance and extracts optical and roughness parameters for metallic detector materials.
why_it_matters: The data can improve optical modeling and light-yield predictions for liquid-argon and liquid-xenon scintillation detectors.

title: Quantum Thermal Transistor via Nonlinear Environmental Coupling
abstract: Thermal amplification enables sensitive control of heat currents, providing a basis for heat management and thermal signal processing in quantum devices. For a harmonic oscillator coupled to emitter, collector, and base thermal reservoirs, we recover the absence of thermal amplification when system-reservoir interactions permit only single-quantum exchange. A controlled weak-nonlinearity expansion, supported by numerical stationary solutions, shows that two-quantum exchange at the emitter enables amplification and predicts its onset. When two-quantum exchange dominates at the emitter and collector, varying the base temperature redistributes populations between even and odd oscillator sectors. This changes the emitter and collector heat currents far more than the base current, enabling large thermal amplification. We propose a realization using a longitudinally coupled auxiliary two-level system and bath spectral filtering, specifying conditions for its elimination to yield the required oscillator dynamics. These results establish nonlinear system-reservoir coupling as a resource for controlling heat flow and enabling thermal amplification.
one_liner: Nonlinear two-quantum reservoir coupling enables a harmonic oscillator to amplify thermally controlled heat currents.
why_it_matters: It identifies nonlinear environmental coupling as a practical resource for quantum heat management and thermal signal processing.

title: Structure of correlations for the single-$j$ model using quantum information theory
abstract: We say that a system undergoes a quantum phase transition when the mean-field ground state of a given Hamiltonian spontaneously breaks its symmetries depending on the Hamiltonian parameters. It is a widely accepted view that this phenomenon enables the mean-field state to absorb the maximum amount of correlations without losing its mean-field structure. However, it is still uncertain how those correlations are incorporated within the mean-field state and how the correlation structure changes when we get closer to the exact ground state by restoring the symmetries. In this work, we answer these questions by studying the single-$j$ model, which is a realistic fermionic nuclear model with abelian and non-abelian broken symmetries. We find that both types of symmetries have very different effects for the correlations within the mean-field state. This makes unclear the concept of the symmetry breaking process as a mechanism to absorb the maximum amount of correlations. Moreover, the symmetry restoration redistributes existing `fake' correlations between paired orbitals to more complex subsystems.
one_liner: Quantum-information measures reveal distinct correlation effects from abelian and non-abelian symmetry breaking in the single-j nuclear model.
why_it_matters: The findings refine how symmetry breaking and restoration are understood to organize correlations in fermionic many-body states.

title: The memory cost of sequential quantum state preparation
abstract: How much memory does a quantum device need to prepare systems one at a time? We address this question through the lens of quantum resource theories, which formalize physical restrictions on how the memory may interact with the stream of systems it processes. By comparing sequential with collective preparation, we show that under general assumptions both have the same asymptotic memory cost per output. Still, sequential preparation can require an unboundedly larger memory than collective one, and we investigate how this gap depends on the physical restrictions on the allowed interactions. For energy-conserving unitaries, we determine both optimal memory dimensions needed for preparing pure states from an energy eigenstate, and find that the extra memory required sequentially either remains bounded or grows logarithmically with the number of outputs. Under noisy operations, we reveal transformations for which one auxiliary qubit suffices for preparing arbitrarily many independent outputs collectively, while no memory of fixed dimension can deliver them sequentially. Finally, for sequential protocols that repeat a fixed interaction, we show that a $d$-dimensional memory that succeeds for $d^2$ rounds will succeed forever, and that such a sequential preparation is equivalent to quantum catalysis.
one_liner: Sequential and collective quantum state preparation share asymptotic cost but can differ without bound in required memory dimension.
why_it_matters: The results clarify when streaming quantum devices face memory penalties and connect repeated sequential preparation to quantum catalysis.

title: AI-assisted search for self-compressing gigawatt subcycle field waveforms
abstract: We explore the physics behind pulse self-compression to high-power subcycle field waveforms and search for the optimal regimes of such compression over the parameter space as laid out by multimode nonlinear dynamics of ultrashort laser pulses in gas-filled hollow fibers. With the pertinent physical criteria for pulse contrast and no pulse breakup formalized as operational stopping rules, a radical speedup of such search is achieved by delegating its tedious preliminary stages to generative pretrained transformer models.
