These results indicate that the suppression is independent of emitter strength. We attribute the attenuation to THz absorption by free charge carriers and trions that are either present due to charge transfer from the metallic layer or photoexcited by the laser pulse, which can significantly diminish the detectable STE signal. This finding provides an explanation for the discrepancy between weak STE signals from FM/TMD heterostructures and magnetotransport reports of sizable spin-orbit torques in similar systems, and highlights the need to account for photoinduced THz attenuation when interpreting ultrafast spin-to-charge conversion measurements in 2D TMD heterostructures.
one_liner: A monolayer of MoSe2 attenuates spintronic terahertz emission from Py/Au and Py/Pt heterostructures by about fourfold.
why_it_matters: Accounting for carrier and trion absorption may reconcile weak THz emission with strong spin-orbit effects seen in transport.

title: Lorentz Boosts and Governing Equations of the Quantum Geometric Tensor in 4D Energy-Momentum Space
abstract: In solids, the quantum geometric tensor (QGT), $Q_{μν}=g_{μν}-\frac{i}{2} Ω_{μν}$, combines the quantum metric and Berry curvature. Its imaginary part governs anomalous velocity and quantized Hall transport, while its real part determines the quantum weight and geometric contributions to flat-band superfluid stiffness and dielectric response. Here, we extend the QGT to four-dimensional (4D) energy-momentum space ($ω/c,k$), treating frequency and momentum as independent coordinates. Invariance of the real-spacetime plane-wave phase fixes their Lorentz transformation in energy-momentum space. Lorentz boosts of static Dirac and Weyl systems then generate frequency metrics, quadrupolar frequency-momentum shear metrics, and electric-like Berry-Maxwell fields. We identify five Lorentz-invariant contractions and derive the governing field equations and flow conservation laws for both the quantum metric and Berry curvature from static Weyl geometry and Lorentz covariance. We further connect Gaussian spectral amplitudes of the QGT to localized Gaussian events in 4D spacetime. Finally, we discuss experimental realizations in spacetime crystals or time-varying media and clarify how this unified quantum geometry of a gravitational-like metric and electromagnetic-like gauge fields connects geometric self-consistency with physical event dynamics.
one_liner: The quantum geometric tensor is extended to 4D energy-momentum space with Lorentz-covariant fields and governing equations.
why_it_matters: It unifies metric-like and gauge-field geometry and suggests tests in spacetime crystals and time-varying media.

title: Improved Low-Cost Quantum Error Mitigation with Benchmarked-Noise Zero-Noise Extrapolation (bnZNE)
abstract: We theoretically extend and experimentally demonstrate benchmarked-noise zero-noise extrapolation (bnZNE), a simple and low-cost method for quantum error mitigation which aims to outperform the highly popular ZNE method for an equal total shot cost by improving the classical extrapolation step. We recently proposed bnZNE as a new error mitigation method (Harris et al., arXiv:2603.10224 (2026)) and showed that it can mitigate noise to the same order as standard ZNE under gate-wise depolarizing noise. Here, we introduce randomized bnZNE which addresses the case of running multiple random circuits per noise level, allowing for the incorporation of noise-tailoring techniques like Pauli twirling and readout error mitigation, and test the method on the IBM and IQM hardware for a plethora of large-scale applications, observing bnZNE to consistently produce more accurate results than standard ZNE. Our approach enhances the extrapolation process to the zero-noise limit by using classically-simulable and structure-mirroring benchmark circuits, generated from the standard application circuit, to sensitively measure the effective error rate at each scaled noise level beyond simple integer values. We give a new method for generating tailored benchmark circuits for the IQM superconducting devices and test them experimentally. Our results demonstrate that bnZNE presents a versatile alternative to ZNE which can enable more accurate results at utility scales with an equivalent cost.
one_liner: Benchmarked-noise ZNE uses matched simulable circuits to estimate effective noise and outperform standard ZNE at equal shot cost.
why_it_matters: IBM and IQM experiments indicate a practical route to more accurate utility-scale results without extra sampling cost.

title: Reflection Zeros Set the Scattering Invariant of Finite Majorana Wires
abstract: Majorana modes, zero-energy excitations of superconducting wires that are their own antiparticles, could store quantum information protected from local noise. In transport experiments, however, ordinary bound states mimic their signature, a conductance peak at zero voltage, and whether Majorana modes have been observed remains debated. A sign, $Q$, of the electron reflection at zero energy marks the topological phase of a long wire, but what $Q$ certifies in a finite device has been unclear. Here we show for the first time that $Q$ counts reflectionless states, waves that enter through one contact and leave entirely through the other: $Q=-1$ when an odd number of them lie in the lower half of the complex energy plane. In a finite wire this means that the two Majorana modes are split by less than their coupling to the contacts. With equal contacts, every sign change of $Q$, including the bulk topological transition, is an exceptional point at which two such states merge and transmission is maximally flat. At zero temperature, $Q=-1$ exactly when the zero-bias conductance measured at a contact exceeds $e^2/h$. These results show what transport can certify about a Majorana device and how to read the invariant from conductance.
one_liner: For finite Majorana wires, the zero-energy reflection sign counts reflectionless states and maps directly to conductance.
why_it_matters: It clarifies exactly what finite-device transport can certify about Majorana splitting and topology.

title: Entanglement detection from moments of the realigned state: application to continuous-variable quantum systems
abstract: Certifying entanglement is a central problem in quantum information sciences, especially for continuous-variable quantum systems where full state tomography is experimentally demanding. We introduce a family of separability criteria based on the singular moments and weak moments of the operator obtained by applying the realignment map to the density operator. In practice, we find that the criterion based on the second-order moments of the realigned operator is already sufficient to witness the entanglement of a wide range of quantum optical states. The realigned moments can be readily accessed using an optical scheme consisting of a linear interferometer that couples several identical copies of the state, similarly to the multicopy technique used to measure the partial-transpose moments of a state [Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033064 (2026)]. We illustrate the detection capability of the second-order realigned-moment method for both Gaussian and non-Gaussian states, including lossy NOON states.
one_liner: Moments of the realigned density operator provide experimentally accessible entanglement tests for continuous-variable states.
why_it_matters: Second-order moments can detect diverse Gaussian and non-Gaussian entanglement without full state tomography.

title: Ergodicity breaking for data classification in a dissipative Ising model with competing two- and four-body interactions
abstract: We explore the close relationship between the processing of data and the dynamics of interacting many-body systems. For example, certain classes of quantum neural networks can be mapped onto dissipative quantum Ising models whose evolution is described by a Lindblad master equation. In these architectures, emergent nonlinearities lead to non-ergodic dynamics under which initial states located in different basins of attraction evolve towards distinguishable stationary states. This mechanism underlies the classification of quantum data. Motivated by this connection, we consider an Ising model with competing two- and four-body interactions. Using a combination of mean-field calculations and exact small-scale numerics, we show that the stationary state manifold can be designed to enable multi-class classification. We also investigate the structure of the ensuing basins of attraction, thereby showing that these systems allow for the classification of quantum states with nonlinear decision boundaries.
one_liner: A dissipative Ising model with competing two- and four-body interactions forms attractors for nonlinear multiclass classification.
why_it_matters: It shows how engineered ergodicity breaking can classify quantum states using nonlinear decision boundaries.

title: Pseudovortex-assisted generation of first-order vector modes
abstract: A practical method of generating first-order vector modes like radially and azimuthally polarized modes is using the so-called vortex waveplates. Shining these plates with Gaussian beams produces parasitic higher-order modes besides the target vector beam. The reason is that there is a mismatch between the incident Gaussian mode and the doughnut-shaped profile required for the vector beam. This imposes a limit on the fidelity of the generated mode with respect to the target vector beam. In this work we demonstrate theoretically and experimentally that this limit can be overcome if the input Gaussian beam is replaced with a pseudovortex beam, which is a doughnut-shaped mode without topological charge. We use a spatial light modulator to generate this input mode and a geometric-phase-compensated triangular cavity for mode analysis. We demonstrate vector mode fidelity as high as $0.921 \pm 0.013$, which is considerably better than $0.815 \pm 0.003$ obtained with Gaussian input. We also investigate the fidelity as a function of the input beam waist, leading to a theoretical upper bound for the fidelity of $8π/27 \approx 0.931$, in close agreement with the experimental results. This approach presents a reliable method of generating high-fidelity vector modes.
one_liner: A pseudovortex input suppresses parasitic modes in vortex-waveplate generation, raising first-order vector-mode fidelity to 0.921 ± 0.013.
why_it_matters: The method offers a practical route to cleaner radial and azimuthal polarization modes.

title: Physical Observables and Superselection
abstract: It is well-known that a physical state may be represented by a unit vector in a Hilbert space, whilst a physical observable may be represented by a self-adjoint operator on that same space. However, the introduction of a superselection rule on a Hilbert space imposes constraints such that not all self-adjoint operators can represent observables, which has further consequences for the states themselves as well as the physical processes that transform them. In this article, we review the concept of superselection from the view of how such rules would affect what we consider to be physical. Arguments for the existence of a superselection rule due to charge or possibly energy conservation are given and the emergence of effective superselection rules due to decoherence or the lack of a shared reference frame are also discussed.
one_liner: This review examines how fundamental and effective superselection rules restrict observables, states, and physical transformations.
why_it_matters: It clarifies the physical roles of conservation laws, decoherence, and shared reference frames.

title: Gaussian ergotropy and spatial correlations: accelerated vacuum versus a thermal field
abstract: Can the spatial correlations of a quantum environment be revealed through work extraction? We address this question using two harmonic-oscillator detectors coupled to either an accelerated vacuum or a matched inertial thermal field. We establish a quantitative connection between the spatial correlations of the environment and the equilibrium Gaussian ergotropy, showing that the leading extractable work is governed by a response-weighted spatial correlation. Although the two environments have identical local spectra, their different spatial correlations give rise to distinct work responses. We further identify a finite-distance blind point at which a single measurement configuration fails to distinguish the two environments. By reversing the direct coupling between the detectors, we develop a two-setting scheme that removes this ambiguity and reconstructs the underlying spatial correlations from work measurements. This reconstruction remains effective beyond the weak-coupling regime. We also show that spatial correlations can provide additional global work even when the detector pair is separable, demonstrating that entanglement is not a necessary resource for this advantage. Finally, we investigate the transient evolution of Gaussian ergotropy and reveal its oscillatory decay and dependence on acceleration and detector parameters. Our results establish Gaussian ergotropy as an operational probe of spatial correlations in bosonic environments.
one_liner: Gaussian ergotropy distinguishes an accelerated vacuum from a matched thermal field through their different spatial correlations.
why_it_matters: Work extraction becomes an operational probe of environmental correlations, even without entanglement.

title: Multi-particle quantum walk search on a two-dimensional lattice
abstract: In the present paper we study the formulation of a search problem and the efficiency of multi-particle quantum walk search algorithms. The discrete-time evolution of each particle in space is treated according to Grover's quantum walk evolution operator. We focus on the local interactions models, where the particles' states are modified only when two or more of them appear on the same grid site. The main focus is given to the two-dimensional grid in space. We study the dependence of the search algorithm asymptotic success time and probability on the interaction strength and the generated maximal entanglement between particles. We show that the interacting and non-interacting two- and three-particle search algorithm attains a constant factor improvement over the single-particle counterpart. In addition, we provide a new generalized model of interactions for multi-particle quantum walks.
one_liner: Interacting and noninteracting two- and three-particle quantum walks yield constant-factor search gains on a 2D lattice.
why_it_matters: The results clarify how particle number, local interactions, and entanglement affect quantum-walk search.

title: Generalized ladder operators and construction of families of superintegrable systems with Painlevé VI
abstract: We study quantum Hamiltonians whose separated angular component is expressed through a generic Painlevé VI transcendent. We construct generalized ladder operators for one-dimensional Schrödinger operators with a quadratic spectral variable. For the Painlevé VI angular Hamiltonian these operators satisfy $[N,J_\pm]=\pm2kJ_\pm$, where $N=\sqrt M$, and close through an eighth-degree norm polynomial. Combining the angular shifts with the radial shift operators of the oscillator, Coulomb and free Bessel systems yields higher-order integrals and deformed Racah-type polynomial algebras for the two-dimensional superintegrable models. This construction provides new families of Tremblay-Turbiner-Winternitz (TTW)- and Post-Winternitz (PW)-like Hamiltonians with integrals of arbitrarily high order and Painlevé VI in the potential. This framework also recovers models from the classification of third- and fourth-order integrals as particular cases. For a representative oscillator extension we compute the Casimir explicitly and recover the finite-dimensional energy spectrum from a deformed-oscillator realization. We then analyze the special-solution sector using the explicit families collected by Gromak, Laine and Shimomura. The resulting potentials are organized into a small number of spectral classes, and the distinction between formal zeros of the ladder norm and physical self-adjoint representations is made explicit. The regular nonclassical rational examples are rational Darboux deformations of the trigonometric Pöschl--Teller system and lead to strictly isospectral exceptional-Jacobi sectors or to state-adding representations with an isolated angular level. A singular branch produces an interior inverse-square barrier and a split-domain problem. For one regular exceptional sector and two state-adding sectors we display the polynomial algebras.
one_liner: Generalized ladder operators generate Painlevé-VI superintegrable Hamiltonians with high-order integrals and deformed Racah algebras.
why_it_matters: The framework unifies known models and produces new exactly structured quantum systems.

title: Efficient computation of PEPS gradients for optimized quantum state preparation on 2D topologies
abstract: Quantum state preparation is a fundamental subroutine for quantum computation. For complex, entangled initial states it is, however, difficult to prepare shallow quantum circuits approximating the state with sufficient accuracy. Tensor networks provide a promising avenue of synthesis of such circuits, but most approaches employ 1D Matrix Products States, which struggle to accurately express entangled states in higher dimensions. Here we present a hardware topology-aware quantum state preparation method based on gradient optimization of 2D projected entangled pair states (PEPS). Our approach combines local disentanglement, with global fine tuning based on PEPS gradient optimization. Towards this end we describe an efficient procedure for PEPS gradient computation. We test the convergence and performance of our method in numerical simulations.
one_liner: A topology-aware state-preparation method combines local disentangling with efficient PEPS-gradient optimization on 2D layouts.
why_it_matters: It may enable shallower preparation of complex entangled states on two-dimensional quantum hardware.

title: Explicit Absolutely Maximally Entangled states in dimensions twice a prime power
abstract: Absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states are pure multipartite states with maximally mixed reductions on every set of at most half the parties. We construct explicit families in local dimension $2q$, twice an odd prime power $q$, using an established coupling of qubits and $q$-level systems. The $q$-level states remove interference between branches, so the qubit states need maximally mixed reductions only on average. This gives AME$(9,2q)$ and AME$(11,2q)$ for every odd prime power $q\geq5$, AME$(13,2q)$ for $q\geq17$, AME$(15,2q)$ for $q\geq9$, and AME$(17,2q)$ for $q\geq67$. For every odd $N\geq3$, the same coupling gives AME$(N,2q)$ under the sufficient condition $q\geq\max\{N,2^{N-2}\}$ on the odd prime power $q$. Within this coupling, the smallest such $q$ must grow exponentially with $N$. Combined with known inputs and products, these families complete the nine-party classification: for integer $d\geq2$, an AME$(9,d)$ state exists if and only if $d\geq3$. Choosing the branch pairing also gives AME$(15,2p)$ states with a cyclic shift of the parties compensated by local unitaries, for every prime $p\equiv1\pmod{15}$.
one_liner: Explicit AME-state families are constructed in local dimensions twice an odd prime power, completing the nine-party classification.
why_it_matters: The constructions expand known multipartite entanglement resources and settle AME(9,d) existence.

title: Quantum Boltzmann Equation for Static Correlation with Cumulant Kernel Closure
abstract: We present a Quantum Boltzmann Equation for static correlation by mapping the Bogoliubov-Born-Green-Kirkwood-Yvon hierarchy to discrete atomic-orbital matrix mechanics via the Wigner-Weyl isomorphism to evaluate scattering of the correlated two-body cumulant. This Quantum Boltzmann Equation converges to the active-space static correlation limit and preserves pure $N$-representability constraints during the kinetic relaxation. To resolve scaling bottlenecks of explicit two-body cumulant methods, we project the two-body cumulant onto its lowest unitary invariant and evaluate a susceptibility-windowed orbital scattering scale via a single Coulomb-exchange contraction. Relaxing onto a hyperbolic-tangent cumulant attractor through Markovian collisional relaxation yields a parameter-free Quantum Boltzmann Equation Cumulant-Kernel that regularizes derivative cusps without thermal smearing. Using the collinear $\mathrm{H}_3$ exchange reaction, the symmetric $D_{4h}$ square $\mathrm{H}_4$ dissociation, the non-adiabatic avoided crossing in $\mathrm{BeH}_2$, the symmetric bond cleavage of $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$, the triple-bond dissociation of $\mathrm{N}_2$, the 11-molecule MR-MGN-BE17 dissociation test set, and the singlet diradical isomers of benzyne as case studies, we show that this kinetic relaxation resolves strong static correlation at zero electronic temperature.
one_liner: A parameter-free cumulant-kernel Quantum Boltzmann Equation captures zero-temperature static correlation across molecular benchmarks.
why_it_matters: It offers a scalable kinetic treatment of strong correlation while preserving representability constraints.

title: Programming Quantum Circuit Parameters with Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated the ability to generate parameters for variational quantum circuits without conventional optimization. However, the conditions under which this approach is effective remain unclear. Here, we investigate a frozen, general-purpose LLM that generates complete circuit parameter vectors from symbolic circuit and Hamiltonian descriptions, with optional iterative energy feedback. We evaluate the approach on general random Hamiltonians, structured parent Hamiltonians, and molecular systems. For general Hamiltonians, LLM-generated parameters exhibit larger energy errors than conventional Adam optimization, while additional feedback generally provides limited improvement. In contrast, for structured Hamiltonians, the LLM can generate promising low-energy parameter configurations, suggesting that identifiable physical and mathematical structure facilitates parameter inference. We also show that direct LLM predictions of minimum energies can violate the Hamiltonian spectral lower bound, whereas generated circuit parameters allow independent evaluation of physically realizable energy expectation values. Finally, we investigate blind circuit interpretation and find that the LLM can predict measurement outcomes even when it fails to identify the underlying quantum algorithm. These findings highlight the role of problem structure, the limitations of iterative LLM optimization, and the importance of independently verifiable predictions in quantum parameter programming.
one_liner: A frozen LLM generates useful circuit parameters for structured Hamiltonians but underperforms Adam on general instances.
why_it_matters: The study identifies when LLM quantum parameter programming works and why outputs need physical verification.

title: Non-interferometric tests of gravitational decoherence models with mechanical oscillators
abstract: Phenomenological models of quantum-gravity-induced decoherence can leave observable effects even in experiments that do not rely on interferometric measurements. We study three such models, based respectively on deformed relativistic symmetries, stochastic metric fluctuations, and a stochastic generalized uncertainty principle, all of which induce decoherence in the momentum basis. For a free particle, the models preserve momentum distribution and mean energy but produce position diffusion and momentum-space decoherence with model-specific momentum dependences. For a harmonic oscillator, the noncommutativity of the collapse operators with the oscillator Hamiltonian results in anomalous heating, with the three models leading to qualitatively different energy dynamics. The first gives heating at a constant rate, the second at a rate proportional to the kinetic energy, which can lead to exponential growth, and the third at a rate growing cubically with excitation. We further derive the stationary position power spectral density and show that all three models produce the same leading-order excess lineshape in the weak-noise regime, distinct from that of force noise. Comparing with existing mechanical platforms, we find that displacement-noise measurements can already constrain the fluctuation time of the first model below the Planck time, while occupation measurements could improve the bounds on the second model by up to fourteen orders of magnitude over those from ground-state heating of levitated particles. Summing the heating over all phonon modes of a solid, the residual heat release of low-temperature experiments constrains the first model far below the Planck time and the second at the Planck time. Our results establish heating and continuous measurements as complementary non-interferometric probes of gravity-related decoherence.
one_liner: Mechanical heating and displacement spectra provide non-interferometric tests of three momentum-decoherence models linked to quantum gravity.
why_it_matters: Existing oscillator platforms could substantially strengthen bounds on gravity-related decoherence.

title: Scalable Pauli propagation through $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear partitioning
abstract: Pauli propagation simulates quantum circuits and many-body dynamics by evolving observables in the Heisenberg picture as sparse sums of Pauli strings. As Pauli-string operations reduce to bit manipulations, its performance is limited by memory bandwidth and capacity rather than computational throughput. Pooling the memory of many cores and nodes is hindered by the deduplication step after every gate, which can require global synchronization. We avoid this bottleneck by partitioning the strings with an $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear hash function, which guarantees that a $k$-qubit channel couples each partition to at most $4^k$ partitions fixed by the gate, decomposing gate application into independent tasks with bounded communication. Benchmarks of our open-source implementation demonstrate efficient parallel scaling within and across compute nodes, enabling simulations with over $10^{11}$ Pauli strings and extending the accessible timescales of quantum many-body dynamics.
one_liner: An F2-linear partitioning scheme removes global deduplication bottlenecks in distributed Pauli propagation.
why_it_matters: It enables scalable simulations exceeding 100 billion Pauli strings across multiple compute nodes.

title: Near-Optimal Multiparameter Pure-State Metrology with a Constant Number of Bases
abstract: Multiparameter pure-state metrology is limited by the incompatibility of measurements optimized for different parameters. We characterize uniform sensitivity by the Fisher floor, the smallest fraction of the quantum Fisher information (QFI) retained over all pure states and parameter directions. We prove that a constant number of fixed orthonormal bases suffices for a nearly optimal Fisher floor, independently of the Hilbert-space dimension $d$. With high probability, five independent Haar bases already achieve a positive, dimension-independent floor, and larger constant families achieve approximate universal Fisher symmetry: they retain nearly one half of the QFI in every direction, the largest uniform fraction permitted by measurement incompatibility. The required number of bases is optimal up to a logarithmic factor in inverse accuracy. In contrast, $d+1$ mutually unbiased bases, when they exist, can minimize mean Fisher anisotropy among families of $d+1$ bases yet have a Fisher floor of at most $1/(d+1)$, showing that optimal average balance does not ensure uniform sensitivity.
one_liner: A constant number of random measurement bases retains a near-optimal, dimension-independent fraction of QFI in pure-state metrology.
why_it_matters: Uniform multiparameter sensitivity can be achieved without measurement resources growing with dimension.

title: Sharp Uniform Fisher Information Bounds from Projective Designs
abstract: Fixed measurements for multiparameter pure-state metrology must remain informative without knowing the input state. We quantify this requirement by the Fisher floor, the smallest fraction of the quantum Fisher information that a measurement retains over all pure states and tangent directions. We determine the Fisher guarantees, namely lower bounds on Fisher floors, implied by projective design order alone in every dimension $d\ge 2$. These guarantees are sharp at order $t=2$ and every odd order $t\ge 3$, and finite weighted designs attain them; at even orders, our bounds are nearly tight. As the order increases, the guarantees approach one half, the single-copy quantum limit. Sampling and spectral completion of any 3-design yield, with probability $1-O(1/d)$, a measurement with linearly many outcomes and a dimension-independent Fisher floor. Such a measurement separates all pure states in Hellinger distance, so pure-state maximum-likelihood estimation from $N$ copies attains mean infidelity $O(d/N)$ uniformly over pure states, optimal up to a universal constant factor.
one_liner: Projective-design order yields sharp, state-uniform Fisher-information guarantees for fixed measurements in pure-state metrology.
why_it_matters: Low-outcome measurements can achieve uniformly near-optimal pure-state estimation without prior state knowledge.

title: Ensemble phase transitions in measurement-unitary hybrid quantum circuits
abstract: The universal properties of state ensembles generated by quantum dynamics provide a refined lens into Hilbert-space ergodicity and deep thermalisation, or lack thereof. We investigate deep-ergodicity breaking transitions of an ancillary qubit entangled with a system undergoing dynamics via hybrid quantum circuits, where unitary evolution is interspersed with projective measurements. Specifically, we analyse the statistical properties of two distinct state ensembles: the trajectory ensemble (TE) conditioned on the measurement outcomes of the hybrid circuit, and the projected ensemble (PE) generated by further projective measurements of the system at the final temporal boundary. We find that both ensembles undergo non-analytic changes -- ensemble phase transitions -- at the critical point of the measurement-induced purification transition, despite their first moments remaining completely maximally mixed and blind to the transition. For Haar-random circuits, the TE transitions from a trivial identity ensemble to the uniform Haar ensemble, while the PE transitions from the Haar ensemble to a trivial singleton pure state. In Clifford circuits, absence of non-stabiliserness limits the PE to a $1$-design, while the TE forms a $k$-design for $k \leq 3$. We demonstrate that these genuine ensemble transitions offer a clear physical mechanism for the measurement-induced entanglement or purification transitions, illustrating how the capacity to ergodically steer a quantum subsystem shifts from the temporal boundary measurements in the mixed phase to the bulk trajectory measurements in the pure phase.
one_liner: Hybrid quantum circuits exhibit ensemble phase transitions at the measurement-induced purification critical point.
why_it_matters: Ensemble statistics reveal ergodicity changes that remain invisible in average quantum states.

title: Discrete Time Crystals from Anti-Unitary Floquet Driving and Dynamical Freezing
abstract: We show anti-unitary periodic drive paves a direct path for stabilizing a Discrete Time-Crystal by Dynamical Freezing (DF). The magnetization appears as an emergent conserved operator, and an exact pairing of two-cycle quasi-energies pins the subharmonic response. DF keeps the effective Hamiltonian $\textit{quasi-local}$; infinite-chain simulations show no detectable decay for a generic state with any finite magnetization. We outline an experimental realization of the anti-unitary drive.
one_liner: Anti-unitary Floquet driving stabilizes discrete time-crystalline order through dynamical freezing and quasienergy pairing.
why_it_matters: The mechanism offers a direct route to persistent subharmonic responses with quasi-local dynamics.

title: Long-lived light-driven bimagnons at finite momentum in NiO
abstract: Light can manipulate magnetic order and its excitations on ultrafast timescales, including through resonantly driven phonons. In antiferromagnets, light can also create correlated magnon pairs, or bimagnons. Unlike single magnons, whose damping has been measured and modeled in detail, little is known about the lifetime, interactions and decay of such correlated pairs: prior two-magnon measurements show broad linewidths or coherences that dephase within 200 fs. Here we pump the phonon-assisted two-magnon absorption of NiO with mid-infrared pulses, far below its bandgap, and probe the resulting magnetic dynamics at finite momentum with time-resolved resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS). Upon photoexcitation, the one-magnon linewidth and energy are essentially unchanged, indicating that the long-range magnetic order is preserved without the photocarrier-induced demagnetization characteristic of above-bandgap excitation. A pump-induced two-magnon signal appears on the energy-gain (anti-Stokes) side of the spectrum. Its spectral weight peaks 4 ps after the pump, well beyond our 0.5 ps time resolution, indicative of a delayed growth likely due to momentum redistribution of the light-induced magnon pairs across the Brillouin zone. This two-magnon signal decays with a time constant of $28\pm11$ ps, exceeding the previously reported two-magnon dephasing time by more than two orders of magnitude. These results establish long-lived light-driven bimagnon correlations beyond the one-magnon state, akin to the higher-order correlations measured in ultracold gases.
one_liner: Mid-infrared excitation creates finite-momentum bimagnons in NiO that decay over 28±11 ps while preserving magnetic order.
why_it_matters: The unusually long lifetime enables controlled studies of correlated magnetic excitations beyond single magnons.

title: Analytic spread complexity in three-level systems and the spacing-ratio distribution
abstract: The spread complexity characterizes the spreading of a quantum state over the Krylov basis and has been proposed to capture the correlations between energy levels. How such correlations manifest in the dynamics has been studied mainly numerically for large matrices. Here we consider three-level systems, the smallest setting with spacing correlations, and derive exact results for the spread complexity, the Krylov variance, and the Krylov entropy. At infinite temperature, the Krylov basis depends on the spectrum only through the ratio of consecutive level spacings, and the spectral variance enters only as an overall time scale. For Gaussian ensembles, these variables are statistically independent, and the averaged spread complexity and variance reduce to one-dimensional integrals over the spacing-ratio distribution encoding the level statistics. We establish universal late-time values of the complexity and variance, and an algebraic relaxation with exponents set by the Dyson index. We also outline the extension to $d$ levels, with the ensemble-averaged spread complexity expressed as a $(d-2)$-dimensional integral over the joint distribution of consecutive spacing ratios.
one_liner: Exact three-level formulas connect spread complexity, Krylov observables, and spectral spacing-ratio statistics.
why_it_matters: The results analytically expose how level correlations govern quantum-state spreading and late-time relaxation.

title: Quantum violation of Causal Friendliness in the instrumental scenario
abstract: How far can quantum theory depart from a classical worldview? Bell inequality violations show that no theory can simultaneously uphold absoluteness of observed events, freedom of choice, relativistic causality, and classical causal explanations. While generalized notions of causality, capable of incorporating quantum resources, can account for Bell correlations, the Local Friendliness theorem showed that, in extended Wigner's friend scenarios, the conflict between quantum theory and causal explanations persists even after classical causality is abandoned. This revealed a new form of nonclassicality stronger than what was revealed by Bell's theorem. However, Local Friendliness has been confined to Bell causal structures so far, and it remains unknown whether a related form of nonclassicality persists in more general causal networks. Here we answer this question by considering a Wigner's friend version of the instrumental network, a paradigmatic causal structure in which communication between parties is allowed, and, unlike the Bell scenario, relativistic causality does not impose any restriction. We show, both theoretically and in a proof-of-principle photonic experiment, that quantum correlations are incompatible with Causal Friendliness, which is the conjunction of the absoluteness of observed events and the generalized nonclassical causal constraints imposed by the network. Such constraints extend relativistic causality from Bell scenarios to networks of arbitrary structure. These results establish a form of quantum nonclassicality stronger than previously observed in instrumental-network violations of classical causality, generalizing Local Friendliness beyond Bell-Wigner scenarios and uncovering a new class of correlations with potential applications in future quantum technologies.
one_liner: Theory and a photonic experiment show that quantum correlations violate Causal Friendliness in an instrumental network.
why_it_matters: This extends Wigner's-friend nonclassicality beyond Bell scenarios to causal networks allowing communication.

title: Fast mixing and thermal phases from strong decay of correlations
abstract: We show that a strong form of correlation decay in quantum Gibbs states has far-reaching dynamical consequences. For a smooth path of geometrically local commuting Hamiltonians whose Gibbs states satisfy strong decay of correlations, we construct $\mathrm{O}(1)$-time quasi-local Lindbladian evolutions exactly connecting these states in both directions, together with $\mathrm{O}(1)$-time quasi-local Hamiltonian evolutions exactly connecting their canonical purifications. These quasi-local connections strengthen previously known quantum-channel circuit constructions based on the decay of connected correlation functions [R. Ma, V. Khemani, and S. Sang, PRX Quantum 7, 033052 (2026)], which approximately connect states within the same phase but have depths that grow logarithmically with system size. Furthermore, if the Gibbs-state path contains a product state, we prove that the single-site Glauber dynamics has a $Ω(1)$ spectral gap independent of the system size throughout the path. This establishes Glauber-dynamics fast mixing for models that may violate the strong spatial mixing condition used in prior proofs, including (1) the $q$-state Potts model throughout the high-temperature phase for any $q$ and any finite dimension; (2) the Ising model with a longitudinal field at low temperature, with frustrating perturbations that destroy monotonicity of the dynamics; and (3) the three-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ lattice gauge theory at low temperatures comparing to a field perturbation, even though the model supports classical memories at intermediate temperatures. Intriguingly, we establish fast mixing of these classical Markov chains using tools from quantum physics like Lieb-Robinson bounds.
one_liner: Strong correlation decay enables constant-time quasi-local state connections and size-independent Glauber spectral gaps.
why_it_matters: Quantum tools establish fast classical mixing across thermal regimes beyond earlier spatial-mixing conditions.

title: Optically-induced electric Aharonov-Bohm effect
abstract: Although it was proposed almost 70 years ago, the electric version of the Aharonov-Bohm (AB) effect, where the interference pattern of quantum charged particles is affected by electric fields that do not interact locally with them, was never experimentally implemented. Here we propose a feasible way to experimentally verify such an important effect, for an electron double-slit interferometer with the slits carved in a nonlinear crystal. The AB phase is generated by a quasi-DC electric field induced in the crystal with the passage of a light pulse (the optical rectification effect) while the electron is superposed in the two slits. We show that this procedure can change the interference pattern of a ensemble of electrons even if they are subjected to negligible electric fields during their propagation, considering feasible parameters.
one_liner: Optical rectification in a nonlinear double-slit crystal could produce an observable electric Aharonov-Bohm phase.
why_it_matters: The proposal offers a feasible test of the long-unrealized electric Aharonov-Bohm effect.

title: Efficient quantum-circuit simulation of classical control of computational order
abstract: We show that quantum circuits with classical control of computational order admit an efficient simulation by fixed-order quantum circuits: any such transformation acting on $N$ independent quantum channels can be deterministically, exactly, and universally simulated using at most $N^2$ queries. We generalize these constructions to extended, bipartite quantum channels and quantum instruments, and demonstrate that they can be implemented catalytically, without consuming the additional $N^2-N$ queries required for the simulation. In the case of quantum circuits with quantum control of computational order, we prove a similar simulation result, but restricted to unitary input channels (hence non-universal). These results show the limitations of the computational power of these classes of transformations in the studied scenarios.
one_liner: Fixed-order quantum circuits can exactly simulate classical control of N channel orders using at most N² queries.
why_it_matters: The result bounds the computational advantage available from classically controlled channel ordering.

title: The radical pair mechanism can generate nuclear-spin entanglement
abstract: The radical pair mechanism is a quantum-mechanical process underlying weak magnetic field effects in chemical and biological systems. While nuclear polarization and electronic entanglement in this mechanism have been studied extensively, the possibility of creating entanglement between nuclear spins has, to the best of our knowledge, remained unexplored. Here, we show that nuclear-spin entanglement can develop from initially maximally mixed nuclear spin states and evolve over repeated radical pair cycles. Its generation and persistence depend on the initial electronic state, the available reaction channels, and the interplay between recombination rates, hyperfine interactions, and the magnetic field. We demonstrate this behaviour in both a minimal two-nucleus model and a five-nucleus model inspired by the photosynthetic radical pair P700--$A_1$. Radical pair mechanism generated nuclear-spin entanglement offers a potential new resource for quantum technologies and opens avenues for exploring its role in biological systems.
one_liner: Repeated radical-pair reactions can generate and preserve entanglement between initially mixed nuclear spins.
why_it_matters: Nuclear entanglement may provide a new resource linking spin chemistry, quantum biology, and quantum technology.

title: In-plane diffusion, spurious drift and a physics-structured gap predictor for a free colloidal pair
abstract: When the diffusivity of a Brownian particle depends on position, its mean displacement acquires a noise-induced (spurious) drift whose magnitude is set by the stochastic convention $α$. We ask how much of this physics can be extracted from a pair of 1.95 $μ$m polystyrene spheres released from blinking holographic optical tweezers at five bath temperatures between 2 and 40 $^\circ$C. The single-sphere diffusivity inside the pair stays between 0.093 and 0.098 $μ$m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, whereas the Stokes-Einstein value for water rises from 0.126 to 0.361 $μ$m$^2$ s$^{-1}$; an isolated sphere reproduces the deficit, which is therefore not a pair effect. From the measured gap-dependent diffusivities $D_\parallel(h)$ and $D_\perp(h)$ we build a Fokker-Planck predictor of the future gap and score it on held-out releases. It recovers the 90% width of the gap distribution up to 800 ms but cannot discriminate between $α= 0$, $1/2$ and $1$, because the $α$-dependent mean shift is an order of magnitude smaller than that width. The ensemble spurious drift is consistent with zero at both ends of the temperature range, and the regression for $α$ never exceeds $R^2 = 0.22$. We therefore present a planar methods baseline and identify the measurements required to resolve $α$.
one_liner: A physics-based predictor captures colloidal-pair gap distributions but cannot resolve the stochastic convention parameter α.
why_it_matters: The study establishes a planar diffusion baseline and specifies what measurements are needed to detect spurious drift.

title: Finite-time spectral enhancement of transient quantum thermometry
abstract: Transient quantum thermometry extracts temperature information before a probe reaches thermal equilibrium. We study how finite interaction times affect thermometric precision for a harmonic-oscillator probe prepared in a number state and weakly coupled to a thermal bosonic reservoir. A second-order time-convolutionless master equation retains the finite-time reservoir response, allowing modes away from the probe frequency to shape the populations and their temperature dependence. For the baseline parameters, this response raises the quantum Fisher information about fivefold above the Markovian prediction, in agreement with an exact solution of the model. When the probability of leaving the initial state is small, we derive an analytical condition for this enhancement. To assess its operational significance, we examine the temperature information acquired per unit time. Under the exact dynamics, this rate is largest within the reservoir memory time. With negligible preparation and readout overhead, the optimum is about five times the best Markovian rate and 30 times an upper bound on the equilibrium rate. The advantage survives smooth switching, although overhead and longer coupling ramps reduce it.
one_liner: Finite reservoir memory boosts transient oscillator thermometry beyond Markovian and equilibrium precision rates.
why_it_matters: Short-time spectral effects can yield substantially faster temperature estimation when operational overhead is low.

title: Recursive Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz
abstract: The recursive quantum approximate optimisation algorithm~(RQAOA) shrinks an unconstrained combinatorial optimisation problem by eliminating one variable at a time, guided by correlations measured in variational quantum states. We extend this recursion to constrained problems by building on the quantum alternating operator ansatz, which restricts the evolution to feasible solutions through a feasible initial state and feasibility-preserving mixers. However, every elimination alters the feasibility structure, so that such a mixer for the original problem generally fails to be one for the subproblems. Previous extensions to Maximum Independent Set and Minimum Vertex Cover sidestep this with tailored reduction rules that keep every subproblem within the original problem class. We resolve this by identifying, for a given constraint structure, a broader problem class that is closed under all eliminations, and by efficiently constructing feasible initial states and feasibility-preserving mixers for every class member. We do so for monotone constraints, such as for the knapsack problem, for linear equality constraints with polynomially bounded weights, including Hamming weight constraints, and for combinations of equality constraints with a single inequality constraint, such as the cardinality-constrained knapsack problem. Conversely, we show that these restrictions cannot be lifted in general without leaving the realm of efficient constructions. Exact simulations on knapsack and vertex-weighted max-bisection instances demonstrate that our recursive scheme can outperform both its non-recursive counterpart and penalty-based QAOA and RQAOA.
one_liner: A recursive alternating-operator ansatz preserves feasibility while eliminating variables in broad classes of constrained optimization problems.
why_it_matters: It extends recursive quantum optimization beyond problem-specific reductions and can outperform penalty-based QAOA variants.

title: Red-Blue Hamiltonian Tomography via the Operator Lightcone Wavemap
abstract: We introduce a model-free method for Hamiltonian tomography based on the operator spreading wavefront. Given two tensor network simulations of the same quantum lattice (one with the nominal Hamiltonian and one with one or more perturbed bonds), the signed cross-entropy of the non-identity Pauli weight field $\mathcal{L}(v,t) = -\ln(n_{\rm pert}/n_{\rm base})$ identifies each perturbed bond by its causal signature: a red-blue sign flip at the two endpoints, visible from the first wavefront crossing. Combining measurements from $p$ strategically placed observation centers via an ensemble log-likelihood sum, a single broken bond is identified with an 82-fold margin over the next candidate on a $7\times7$ lattice. Extending to realistic coupling degradation ($δJ = -0.20$) and up to 8 simultaneous faults, the integrated log-ratio $Λ(v) = \ln(\mathcal{B}(v)/\mathcal{N}(v))$ achieves a per-bond detection rate above 90\% in a single seismic pass using only 6 simulations. An iterative re-scan strategy progressively resolves multi-bond cases as the signal clears with each recalibration pass. The method requires no model assumptions and no knowledge of the perturbation type or magnitude; the detection is deliberately blind.
one_liner: Operator-spreading wavefronts reveal perturbed quantum-lattice bonds through endpoint red-blue signatures without assuming a fault model.
why_it_matters: The method offers blind, simulation-based localization of multiple degraded couplings with few observation passes.

title: Magic of Dicke states: density, cost and yield
abstract: Dicke states are an elementary family of many-body quantum states, consisting of equal superpositions of all configurations of $L$ qubits with $n$ excitations. We show that their magic, as measured by the stabilizer Rényi entropy (SRE), is extensive at every filling $f=n/L$ except half-filling, and we obtain the magic density analytically, together with the subleading terms. In the context of fault-tolerant quantum computation, we also investigate the yield of Dicke states, and find that they can produce on average an extensive number of CCZ states (or $T$ states with a catalyst) at any $0<f<1$. This yield is not self-averaging, but fluctuates from run to run by $O(L)$, as if it were set by a hidden phase shared by all qubits. At half-filling, the SRE grows only logarithmically, while the preparation cost, average yield and relative entropy of magic remain extensive, so that a small SRE does not necessarily signal a weak resource. These results can be understood by viewing the Dicke state as a fixed-magnetization projection of a product of tilted spins.
one_liner: Dicke-state magic is extensive away from half-filling, while half-filled states retain extensive cost and yield despite logarithmic SRE.
why_it_matters: It shows that stabilizer Rényi entropy alone can substantially understate a state's fault-tolerant computational value.

title: Linear monitoring-feedback Model for Linearized gravity
abstract: Whether gravity has quantum degrees of freedom is a question of fundamental importance. We formulate a linear monitoring-feedback framework for gravitational interactions that includes local classical-record models of semiclassical gravity and, when quantum resources are supplied in correlated ancilla inputs, can reproduce linearized quantum-gravity dynamics. Auxiliary systems monitor the positions of massive bodies, and their records are fed back through a chosen gravitational response kernel. At the level of linear input-output theory, this construction makes the deterministic response explicit while exposing the force noise and correlations associated with the auxiliary sector. We organize the allowed ancilla correlations into three regimes. In Regime-I, independent ancillas have unsqueezed, uncorrelated sensing and back-action quadratures. A single object then has a minimum classical-gravity noise (CGN), S_F^min = 2 hbar M Omega_SN^2, where Omega_SN is the Schrodinger-Newton frequency set by the microscopic mass distribution. In Regime-II, arbitrary local sensing--back-action correlations are allowed, but the ancillas associated with different objects remain independent. The single-object CGN is then unrestricted, while the joint force-noise matrix obeys a determinant bound that is equivalent to the local classical-channel/no-entanglement bound. In Regime-III, cross-object correlations and a common nonlocal mediator are allowed. The commuting force noises can then be jointly squeezed, entanglement between the masses can occur, and--with a suitable retarded response and input state--the monitoring-feedback system can reproduce the noise and commutators of linearized quantum gravity, including non-Markovian quantum fluctuations.
one_liner: A monitoring-feedback framework spans classical semiclassical gravity and linearized quantum gravity through controlled ancilla correlations.
why_it_matters: It clarifies which noise correlations distinguish local classical gravitational channels from entangling quantum dynamics.

title: Quantum Data Processing Unit for Neutral-Atom Quantum Computers
abstract: Quantum computers need real-time classical processing to convert measurement data into feedback within device-specific timing constraints. We introduce the quantum data processing unit (QDPU), an architecture between a quantum device and its controller. Its core is a machine-learned quantum data model (QDM), adapted to the measurement response and noise characteristics of the device. We implement an FPGA pipeline for neutral-atom array assembly that performs occupancy detection and rearrangement scheduling in FPGA logic. One calibrated matched-filter lane classifies a $50\times50$ array in 12.5 $μ$s. An atom-loss model using a software reference planner evaluates a $35\times35$ target with a 60 s trap lifetime and 0.1% loss per moved atom. Removing an assumed 150 ms host round trip raises the predicted assembly success from 8% to 85% and reduces the wall-clock time per successful assembly from 19 s to 0.16 s. A GPU-based outer loop is proposed for refitting model parameters between runs. Its NVQLink transport is measured on the board: over 10 GbE to an NVIDIA DGX Spark, the median FPGA-to-host-to-FPGA round trip is 2.74 $μ$s for 128-byte messages forwarded by a CPU core. A separate 12-bit learned qLDPC kernel is placed and routed for the same FPGA target, with a derived latency of 0.84 ms per round for a $[[1122,148]]$ lifted-product code under code-capacity noise. A quantised GraphMP ranking kernel for the same code runs on the board with a median host-to-FPGA-to-host latency of 50.5 $μ$s with one shot in flight, excluding host-side BP+OSD post-processing. Together, these implementations illustrate a shared architecture with workload-specific models and timing requirements.
one_liner: A QDPU architecture uses FPGA and learned device models for low-latency neutral-atom assembly and quantum-error-decoding workloads.
why_it_matters: Moving feedback near the hardware could sharply improve atom-array assembly success and support real-time quantum control.

title: An Inverse-Designed Multilayer Selective Emitter for High-Efficiency Thermophotovoltaics
abstract: High thermophotovoltaic (TPV) conversion efficiencies have typically relied on photovoltaic cells that reflect sub-bandgap radiation back toward the emitter. Here, we numerically investigate an alternative approach in which spectral selectivity is engineered primarily on the emitter side. We optimize an emitter consisting of 16-layer aperiodic MgO/Si coating on tungsten, for coupling to a GaSb cell with an antireflection coating and an Au mirror. A detailed-balance framework incorporates polarization- and angle-resolved emissivity, multiple reflections, and Auger nonradiative recombination. At an emitter temperature of 1500 K, the optimized structure suppresses 97.1% of the incident-blackbody-equivalent sub-bandgap power at the source; a further 1.9% is returned to the emitter by the cell, leaving 1.0% absorbed parasitically in the cell. The resulting modeled radiative-to-electrical conversion efficiency reaches 47.0%, compared with 30.8% for a SiC emitter paired with the same cell, while maintaining a comparable maximum electrical power density. These findings indicate that emitter-side spectral engineering could substantially relax cell-side photon-recycling requirements and provide significant improvement in TPV conversion.
one_liner: An inverse-designed 16-layer MgO/Si tungsten emitter yields a modeled 47% TPV efficiency with strong sub-bandgap suppression.
why_it_matters: Emitter-side selectivity could reduce dependence on demanding cell-side photon recycling while preserving useful power density.

title: Fast forward-and-backward creation of non-equilibrium Gibbs state in driven dissipative quantum systems
abstract: We present the fast-forward (FF) approach to adiabatic time evolution of an open dissipative quantum system within the framework of the Gorini-Kosaakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad (GKSL) equation. Taking a harmonic oscillator (HO) and a quantum spin as prototype systems under a rapid change of the driving field and in contact with the heat reservoir, we reveal the protocol which creates the non-equilibrium Gibbs state. After preparing the Gibbs state under the fixed external field in advance, we begin to change adiabatically the field. To keep a quasi-adiabatic version of the Gibbs state as the solution of GKSL equation, we solve the inverse problem to obtain the non-adiabatic corrections both to Hamiltonian and to the dissipator. Then we apply the fast forward-and-backward (abbreviated as FF for convenience) time-rescaling, obtaining the FF variants of both Hamiltonian and detailed balance condition (DBC) among dissipative coefficients. The present scheme generates the time-periodic Gibbs state as if a limit-cycle solution of the innovated GKSL equation under the time-periodic driving field. Thanks to the FF variant of DBC, we see the energy conservation of power and heat current of the system, and reversibility of whole system including a reservoir. The requirement of positivity of the FF dissipative coefficients imposes a constraint on the speed of the FF driving. At low temperature, the upper speed limit of the FF periodic driving is found to be proportional to $\tildeβ^{-1/2}\exp(a\tildeβ)$ with $\tildeβ$ the scaled inverse temperature and $a$ the positive constant of $O(1)$.
one_liner: Fast-forward corrections to Hamiltonian and dissipative terms generate rapidly driven nonequilibrium Gibbs states under GKSL dynamics.
why_it_matters: The protocol accelerates open-system adiabatic evolution while retaining detailed balance, energy accounting, and reversibility.

title: Multitime Equilibration and Multitime Mpemba Effects
abstract: Equilibration of a quantum state leaves open whether its response to later interventions has also equilibrated. We establish multitime equilibration for a continuous process on a fixed observation window, retaining the autonomous system--environment dynamics and all internal time differences. A finite-time mean-square bound controls the full continuous-process norm through the effective energy dimension and energy-gap correlations. A factorial temporal-order bound lifts fixed-sector convergence to the full process, while a process-visible spectral measure distinguishes mean-square from pointwise equilibration. This framework defines multitime Mpemba effects by comparing preparations relative to one stationary process. In a semicircle-spectrum model, a preparation filter changes the decay exponent from $3/2$ to $5/2$ in every fixed sector and in the summed norm, despite a larger initial distance. A fixed unitary control and terminal measurement exhibit the same exponent improvement in their output probabilities. Noncommuting baths and a many-body spin environment separate this all-sector mechanism from selective finite-time acceleration.
one_liner: A continuous-process framework proves multitime equilibration and identifies preparation-dependent multitime quantum Mpemba effects.
why_it_matters: It extends equilibration from single-time states to responses under later interventions and reveals faster all-sector relaxation.

title: Compiling Matrix Formulas to Quantum Block Encodings
abstract: Realizing the promise of quantum applications such as chemistry or fluid dynamics requires building quantum circuits that efficiently encode and manipulate exponentially large matrices. This process forces researchers to grapple with the reality that a matrix expressible as one equation on paper can map to thousands of bit-level quantum logic gates, historically written by hand. Even worse, it often ends with a discovery that the needed resources grow so quickly with matrix size that the quantum algorithm loses its asymptotic speedup. In this work, we present MARBLE, a language that automatically synthesizes an efficient circuit from the publication-style formula for the entries of a matrix. MARBLE algebraically rewrites programs into symbolic combinations of simpler matrices that have known circuit realizations. It analyzes costs of possible representations, notably the subnormalization term that dominates time complexity. It then emits an OpenQASM circuit and certifies whether its cost is poly-logarithmic in problem size, as required by quantum algorithms. When evaluated on quantum applications ranging from fluid dynamics to physical Hamiltonians, MARBLE matches or surpasses 37 of 39 published baselines. On the low end, it automatically matches many theoretically optimal circuits, and on the high end, it improves on a published construction in fluid dynamics by 10,487x in subnormalization. MARBLE produces exponentially smaller circuits than the leading tool FABLE, and it successfully compiles matrices whose dimensions exceed 2^100 within five seconds on a laptop.
one_liner: MARBLE compiles publication-style matrix formulas into cost-analyzed quantum block-encoding circuits and OpenQASM.
why_it_matters: It automates a major circuit-design bottleneck while matching or improving 37 of 39 published constructions.

title: Uncertainty evaluation of length measurement by spectral domain interferometry with super-Gaussian windowing
abstract: In this study, we evaluate the measurement uncertainty of spectral domain interferometry with super-Gaussian windowing, which has significant potential for interferometer-based dimensional calibration services owing to its simple configuration and nanometer-level precision. A super-luminescent diode (SLD) with a broadband spectrum was used as the light source for high-precision length measurement, and a frequency-calibrated spectrometer captured the spectral interference signal. The length measurement results were compared with a laser displacement interferometer. To evaluate the measurement uncertainty, numerical simulations were performed by considering the intensity-noise level of the CCD in the spectrometer and the frequency-axis uncertainty of the spectrometer. Through a comprehensive uncertainty analysis supported by numerical simulations, the combined standard uncertainty of the measured length was evaluated as sqrt((10 nm)^2 + (9.7x10^(-6)xL)^2). The resulting uncertainty budget provides a metrological basis for extending SLD-based SDI with super-Gaussian windowing toward interferometric dimensional calibration tasks over the millimeter-scale range.
one_liner: A full uncertainty budget quantifies super-Gaussian-windowed spectral interferometry for nanometer-precision length measurement.
why_it_matters: The result supports traceable millimeter-scale dimensional calibration using a compact broadband interferometric setup.

title: Tight Quantum Query Bounds for Collision Finding over Arbitrary Bounded Types
abstract: We determine the bounded-error quantum query complexity of finding one $r$-collision in an $N$-input function of prescribed type, which specifies all equality-class sizes. For every fixed maximum class size and collision order, we give a tight bound as the maximum of scales determined by the numbers of classes of size at least $2,\ldots,r$. The lower bound holds for a uniformly random function of that type, and a matching algorithm succeeds on every such function. No intermediate class size is required to occur, and every feasible output alphabet is allowed. The characterization connects the abundant-collision regime associated with set equality to the sparse-target regime of $k$-distinctness. In particular, finding the unique $(k+1)$-collision in type $(k^n,k+1)$ has complexity $Θ_k(N^{3/4-1/[4(2^{k+1}-1)]})$, where $N=kn+k+1$, resolving an open problem of Belovs. For the lower bound, we introduce a filtered compressed permutation oracle that projects onto a harmonic database subspace after each complete function query. Its $O(T/N)$ comparison error over $T$ queries overcomes the square-root limitation of the unfiltered process. Hidden capacity extensions and moment estimates retain the populations at each intermediate collision order. Matching upper bounds use sampled collision lists and colored adaptive learning graphs, with a coherent decision-to-search conversion that avoids logarithmic overhead. We also give an alternative nested quantum-walk algorithm for three-collision search, matching the bound up to polylogarithmic factors.
one_liner: Tight quantum query bounds characterize collision finding for arbitrary bounded function types and resolve a problem of Belovs.
why_it_matters: The result unifies sparse and abundant collision regimes with matching lower bounds and algorithms.

title: No universal LOCC entanglement purification
abstract: Entanglement purification aims to obtain high-fidelity entangled states from noisy entangled states. This task becomes particularly challenging when the available input states are finite in number, only partially characterized, and may not be identical. Whether there exists a universal purification protocol applicable to such inputs has therefore been a longstanding question. This motivates the study of universal $n$-to-$1$ entanglement purification. Although no such LOCC protocol exists for the full set of two-qubit entangled states, it has remained open whether this no-go result extends to higher-dimensional bipartite states and multipartite states. In this work, we resolve this question by proving that, for any fixed finite local dimensions, no $n$-to-$1$ LOCC protocol is universal for all bipartite entangled states or all multipartite entangled states. We further show that the bipartite and multipartite no-go results persist under several natural extensions and establish an analogous no-go theorem for coherence purification under strictly incoherent operations.
one_liner: No finite-copy LOCC protocol universally purifies all bipartite or multipartite entangled states in fixed local dimensions.
why_it_matters: The theorem closes a longstanding universality question and extends the obstruction to coherence purification.

title: Reference-Assisted Qutrit Control and Conditional One-Round Distillation in a Charge-4e Superconductor Model
abstract: We formulate a charge-$4e$ parafermionic-vortex route to qutrit processing as a conditional theory with explicit operational assumptions. Sector preservation and same-label charge-conjugation covariance imply closure for every adaptive visible record. For charge-conjugation-invariant inputs, record probabilities are independent of the supported reference state; for arbitrary inputs, discarding the reference gives a population-weighted mixture of conjugate sector maps. We give a finite-depth stability bound for complete labelled instruments, including postselection and initial zero-sector contamination. A self-contained calculation reproduces the known dense single-qutrit closure of the registered Clifford-plus-Flip gate set. We also specify an abstract ternary CSS $[[11,1,5]]_3$ syndrome/recovery decoder: 243 classical representatives per CSS component correct all 3,609 Pauli errors of support weight at most two, and an exact integer dynamic program yields the full independent-Pauli logical enumerator. Its all-syndrome acceptance is distinct from the known $1/1728$ ideal acceptance of one-round strange-state Golay distillation. An accepted-run target-infidelity budget and a synthetic parameter protocol expose the remaining noise assumptions. Native charge-$4e$ syndrome extraction, material feasibility, a device threshold, and unconditional fault tolerance are not established.
one_liner: Develops a conditional charge-4e parafermionic-vortex framework for qutrit control, stability analysis, and ternary-code distillation.
why_it_matters: It clarifies what qutrit processing can achieve under explicit assumptions while identifying major unresolved hardware and fault-tolerance gaps.

title: Four-Sector Propagation-Trapping Decomposition and Inverse Design of Initial States in Grover-Coined Quantum Walks on Multiedge Path Graphs
abstract: Controlling propagation and trapping through initial-state preparation requires an explicit relation between the initial amplitudes and the corresponding directional probabilities. We establish this relation for a discrete-time Grover-coined quantum walk on a multiedge path graph with even degree d = 2M, where M is at least 2, and two equal directional blocks. Each block of an arbitrary local state is expressed as its mean component plus a zero-sum deviation. The Grover coin performs a pure exchange of the two block means and reverses the sign of each zero-sum deviation. Together with the graph routing, this gives a unique orthogonal decomposition into four sectors: propagation in opposite directions and bounded trapping on either side of the launch vertex. We derive the four sector probabilities and solve the inverse problem, constructing initial states for any prescribed nonnegative probability quadruple that sums to unity. Explicit representatives are given for d = 4 and d = 6. Sector-resolved simulations reproduce the predicted motion, conservation of sector weights, and local probability additivity, including repeated spatial overlaps. We also derive the local Grover action for an arbitrary partition into blocks of possibly unequal sizes, explicitly describing how their means are redistributed while each zero-sum deviation remains within its block and changes sign. The framework provides direct control of propagation and trapping within one fixed graph and walk operator through the preparation of the initial state.
one_liner: Decomposes Grover-coined walks on multiedge paths into four propagation and trapping sectors controlled by the initial state.
why_it_matters: The inverse construction enables prescribed directional and trapped probability distributions without changing the graph or walk operator.

title: Hardware-aware sampling and QPU-informed Monte Carlo with quantum annealers
abstract: We study how the physical representation of a logical model affects sampling by quantum annealers and its use in corrected Monte Carlo. The square-lattice Ising model provides controlled classical references. Fixed embeddings with one physical qubit per logical spin reach $36\times36$ spins. Comparisons with uniform two-qubit chains and mixed chain lengths show that matching mean energy leaves differences in magnetization and correlations. Extended-range conditional predictors improve the description of mixed embeddings, distinguishing their residual correlations from those of the tested uniform embeddings. Independent calibration checks and fixed-scale annealing scans show that temperature shifts alone do not determine distributional agreement. Normalized autoregressive models learned from QPU samples provide proposals with exact Metropolis--Hastings and multiple-try corrections on larger periodic lattices. These preserve the target distribution, although block updates alone relax critical magnetization slowly. Complementary direct-QPU updates reveal how block size and fitted-temperature correction affect acceptance and spin motion. Together, the results support prioritizing one-qubit representations and short uniform chains, while separating hardware sampling fidelity from the convergence of corrected Monte Carlo.
one_liner: Studies how quantum-annealer embeddings shape Ising samples and QPU-informed proposals for exactly corrected Monte Carlo.
why_it_matters: It separates hardware sampling fidelity from Monte Carlo convergence and favors one-qubit mappings or short uniform chains.

title: Polarization Lifetime as a Design Axis for Task-Adaptive Photonic Reservoir Computing
abstract: Photonic time-delayed reservoir computing (TDRC) based on conventional Class B lasers is limited by fragile external cavity mode (ECM) locking dynamics. Here, we show that engineering the polarization lifetime (T$_2$) with the carrier lifetime ($T$) reshapes the topology and stability of TDRC. Comparing four laser classes (Class A, Class B, Class C$_A$, and Class C$_B$), a finite polarization lifetime acts as an intrinsic dynamic filter, dissolving discrete ECM chaos grids into continuous, phase-tolerant operational basins. Information processing capacity (IPC) decomposition further exposes distinct computational profiles: matched Class C$_A$ achieves the highest nonlinear capacity (16.28) and the highest total capacity (19.29), whereas Class A exhibits the highest linear capacity (4.70). A task-dependent reversal governs hardware design: Class A and Class C$_A$ achieve comparable, and the lowest, NRMSE on short-horizon Mackey--Glass prediction (0.0103 and 0.0105, within one standard deviation), while the time-scale-matched Class C$_A$ dominates the higher-dimensional Lorenz (0.0506) and the experimental Santa Fe (0.4251) tasks. Linear-IPC ranking matches Mackey-Glass accuracy; nonlinear-IPC ranking matches the Lorenz exactly and Santa Fe within the mask-to-mask uncertainty. Under realistic quantum noise, resilience is dictated mainly by $T$, not T$_2$: Class A retains the lowest NRMSE (0.47) even at spontaneous emission factor $β$ = $10^{-1}$, whereas the long-carrier Class B degrades (0.98). A residual T$_2$-mediated benefit of 20$\%$ persists in the slow-carrier Class C$_B$ (0.78 vs. 0.98). Time-scale engineering thus offers a nuanced design paradigm for optical computing, where optimal hardware is set by the task's time-scale hierarchy rather than a universal figure of merit.
one_liner: Shows that jointly engineering laser polarization and carrier lifetimes creates task-specific regimes for photonic reservoir computing.
why_it_matters: It links laser time scales to linear, nonlinear, and noise-sensitive performance, challenging universal hardware rankings.

title: Sign-switchable and tunable macroscopic curvature of liquid jets by microscopic laser-induced cavitation
abstract: Localized forcing of liquid jets can trigger Rayleigh-Plateau breakup at low perturbation amplitudes or explosive fragmentation at high amplitudes, while controlled bending in the intermediate regime has remained unexplored. We show that femtosecond-laser-induced cavitation, seeded at the interface of a 100 micrometre-diameter water jet, produces a selectable curvature in 0.4-1 mm long segments. Cavitation rupturing at the liquid-air interface drives fast outward jetting and induces a slower recoil on the opposite boundary, which evolves on the capillary-inertial timescale and results in curving of the liquid segment. The curvature is governed by three laser parameters. Off-axis laser illumination on the jet shifts the refractive caustics and redistributes energy deposition between the front and rear interfaces. The resulting recoil imbalance determines the curvature sign, with a straight configuration in the balanced case. Laser energy offers additional control over the recoil impulse via plasma defocusing and nonlinear absorption in the liquid jet, where the response is bounded by axisymmetric deformation at low energy and explosive vaporization at high energy. Repetition rate sets the spacing between successive cavitation events and hence the length of the bent segment. Curvature extends across the segment for lengths of 6-10 jet diameters; shorter segments undergo Rayleigh-Plateau breakup, whereas longer ones bend mainly near their retracting ends. Our results offer a platform for optofluidic control of switchable and tunable macroscopic curvature in flowing liquid jets.
one_liner: Uses femtosecond-laser-induced cavitation to switch and tune the macroscopic curvature of microscopic flowing water jets.
why_it_matters: The method offers controllable jet bending through laser position, energy, and repetition rate for future optofluidic systems.

title: Antihelical Edge States in Photonic Metacrystals
abstract: Antihelical edge states represent a gapless form of boundary transport in which modes with opposite spin counterpropagate along a given boundary, while modes sharing the same spin propagate in the same direction on opposite boundaries. Here we show that such states arise naturally within a modified Kane-Mele framework realized in an electromagnetic-dual photonic metacrystal with staggered bianisotropy. Reversing the spin-dependent next-nearest-neighbor coupling on one sublattice reorganizes the bulk spectrum into a spin-polarized Dirac semimetal characterized by spin-dependent energy shifts of the Dirac cones rather than a bulk gap. This bulk reorganization generates tilted edge-mode dispersions in zigzag ribbons and gives rise to antihelical edge transport coexisting with bulk states. Full-wave simulations confirm the corresponding bulk and edge behaviors. Extending the analysis to finite geometries, simulations further reveal discrete corner-localized modes. A realistic design based on split-ring metaatoms is proposed to realize the required staggered bianisotropy and spin-dependent energy shifts of the Dirac cones. Furthermore, we show that the tensorial freedom of the bianisotropic constitutive relations enables continuous manipulation of the electromagnetic pseudospin basis while preserving the antihelical boundary transport. These results provide a practical route for engineering unconventional gapless boundary transport in photonic Dirac systems.
one_liner: Realizes antihelical edge transport in a staggered-bianisotropy photonic metacrystal described by a modified Kane-Mele model.
why_it_matters: It provides a practical route to tunable, gapless boundary transport and corner-localized modes in photonic Dirac systems.
